cards.a: An ionic compound has a high melting point (NaCl 801 °C) because Coulombic attractions between ions must be overcome throughout the lattice, and it conducts only when molten or dissolved, when the ions become mobile. A molecular compound has a low melting point (sucrose decomposes near 186 °C; ice 0 °C) because only weak intermolecular forces are broken, and it does not conduct in any state, since it has no mobile ions or electrons.
cards.h: → two properties, each compared with a particulate reason
cards.n: 'Ionic compounds conduct' with no state named earns nothing: solid NaCl is an insulator. The melting-point contrast borrows intermolecular forces from Unit 3.

cards.q: State the electronegativity-difference ranges used to classify a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic.
cards.a: ΔEN below about 0.4: nonpolar covalent. ΔEN about 0.4 to 1.7: polar covalent. ΔEN above about 1.7: ionic. These are teaching conventions on a continuum (all polar bonds have some ionic character), so the periodic positions of the elements and the compound's properties decide borderline cases.
cards.h: → two cut-off numbers, then the caveat
cards.n: Treating 1.7 as a physical law fails on HF (ΔEN 1.78, a molecular gas); say the ranges are approximate and that properties decide.

cards.q: Predict the bond type between calcium and bromine, given electronegativities Ca = 1.00 and Br = 2.96.
cards.a: Ionic. ΔEN = 2.96 − 1.00 = 1.96, above the ~1.7 convention, and Ca is a group 2 metal while Br is a group 17 nonmetal, so each Ca atom transfers two valence electrons to two Br atoms, giving Ca²⁺ and Br⁻ ions in CaBr₂ held by Coulombic attraction.
cards.h: → ΔEN, positions, then the ions formed
cards.n: Stopping at 'ionic' earns the claim only; the justification point needs the ΔEN or the metal/nonmetal positions plus the electron transfer.

cards.q: Apply electronegativity difference to classify the N-H bond in ammonia, given N = 3.04 and H = 2.20.
cards.a: Polar covalent. ΔEN = 3.04 − 2.20 = 0.84, within the ~0.4 to 1.7 range, and both are nonmetals, so the pair is shared unequally: N carries δ− and each H carries δ+. The three N-H bond dipoles, with the lone pair, make NH₃ a polar molecule.
cards.h: → ΔEN = 0.84 → label + partial charges
cards.n: Assigning δ− to hydrogen reverses the dipole; the more electronegative atom (N) takes the partial negative charge.

cards.q: Contrast how electrons are shared in a nonpolar covalent bond with how they are shared in a polar covalent bond.
cards.a: In a nonpolar covalent bond (Cl-Cl, C-H) the bonding electrons are shared equally because the atoms have equal or nearly equal electronegativity, so neither atom carries a charge. In a polar covalent bond (H-Cl) the more electronegative atom attracts the shared pair more strongly, so the electron density is shifted toward it, giving it δ− and the other atom δ+; the larger the ΔEN in a single bond, the larger the bond dipole.
cards.h: → equal vs shifted density, with δ symbols
cards.n: Writing full charges (H⁺ Cl⁻) for a polar covalent bond earns nothing: no electron is transferred outright, so the charges are partial (δ+, δ−).

cards.q: Identify the atom that carries the partial negative charge (δ−) in each single bond, using electronegativity trends: H-Cl · C-O · N-H · O-H · C-Cl · S-O · P-H · B-F · Si-O · C-N · Br-Cl · S-H
cards.a:
H-Cl → Cl (3.16 vs 2.20)
C-O → O (3.44 vs 2.55)
N-H → N (3.04 vs 2.20)
O-H → O (3.44 vs 2.20)
C-Cl → Cl (3.16 vs 2.55)
S-O → O (3.44 vs 2.58)
P-H → essentially nonpolar; P 2.19 vs H 2.20, no meaningful δ−
B-F → F (3.98 vs 2.04)
Si-O → O (3.44 vs 1.90)
C-N → N (3.04 vs 2.55)
Br-Cl → Cl (3.16 vs 2.96)
S-H → S (2.58 vs 2.20)
Rule: δ− sits on the atom farther right or higher in the periodic table; the dipole arrow points toward it.
cards.h: → more electronegative atom takes δ−
cards.n: Putting δ− on hydrogen because 'it is smaller' earns nothing; the partial negative charge follows the higher electronegativity (right and up in the table).

cards.q: Rank the bond dipoles of H-F, H-Cl, H-Br and H-I from largest to smallest, given electronegativities F 3.98, Cl 3.16, Br 2.96, I 2.66 and H 2.20, and justify the order.
cards.a: H-F > H-Cl > H-Br > H-I. ΔEN values are 1.78, 0.96, 0.76 and 0.46: in single bonds a greater electronegativity difference shifts more electron density toward the halogen, giving a larger partial charge and a larger bond dipole. Electronegativity falls down group 17 because the valence shell is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so the dipole shrinks from HF to HI.
cards.h: → order, ΔEN values, trend reason
cards.n: Ranking by bond length or molar mass earns nothing; the bond dipole in single bonds tracks the electronegativity difference (2.1.A.3.ii).

cards.q: Classify each bond as ionic, polar covalent or nonpolar covalent from the periodic positions of the atoms and their electronegativity difference: Na-Cl · C-C · C-H · O-H · Mg-O · Cl-Cl · K-Br · S-O · N-N · Ca-F · C-F · P-Cl · Li-I · Si-Si · Cs-F · O-O
cards.a:
Na-Cl → ionic (metal + nonmetal, ΔEN 2.23)
C-C → nonpolar covalent (ΔEN 0)
C-H → nonpolar covalent, effectively (ΔEN 0.35)
O-H → polar covalent (ΔEN 1.24)
Mg-O → ionic (ΔEN 2.13)
Cl-Cl → nonpolar covalent (0)
K-Br → ionic (ΔEN 2.14)
S-O → polar covalent (ΔEN 0.86)
N-N → nonpolar covalent (0)
Ca-F → ionic (ΔEN 2.98)
C-F → polar covalent (ΔEN 1.43, two nonmetals)
P-Cl → polar covalent (ΔEN 0.97)
Li-I → ionic (metal + nonmetal, ΔEN 1.68, borderline by number; LiI is a crystalline salt)
Si-Si → nonpolar covalent (0)
Cs-F → ionic (ΔEN 3.19, the most ionic bond)
O-O → nonpolar covalent (0)
cards.h: → positions first, ΔEN as the check
cards.n: Li-I shows why ΔEN alone misleads (1.68 is below 1.7): the metal + nonmetal pairing and the salt-like properties decide, which is the CED's own point in 2.1.A.4.

cards.q: Determine whether the bonding in a binary compound is best described as ionic or covalent from these observations: it is a colorless gas at room temperature, it condenses at 20 °C to a liquid that does not conduct electricity, and the electronegativity difference between its two elements is 1.78.
cards.a: Covalent (polar covalent, in discrete molecules). A gas at room temperature and a nonconducting liquid mean the substance is made of neutral molecules with no mobile ions; an ionic compound would be a high-melting solid whose melt conducts. Although ΔEN = 1.78 sits above the usual 1.7 cut-off, the CED says ΔEN is not the only factor and that properties are the best test; the compound is HF, a very polar molecular substance.
cards.h: → properties → particles → verdict; ΔEN as caveat
cards.n: 'Ionic because 1.78 > 1.7' earns nothing against the property evidence; the cut-off is a convention and the boiling point and nonconducting liquid settle it.

cards.q: Determine the type of bonding in a white crystalline solid that melts at 801 °C, does not conduct electricity as a solid, and conducts well when molten or when dissolved in water.
cards.a: Ionic. A very high melting point shows strong Coulombic attractions throughout a lattice, and conduction only when molten or dissolved shows that the charge carriers are ions that are locked in place in the solid and freed on melting or dissolving. A molecular solid would melt far lower and never conduct; a metal would conduct as a solid. The data match NaCl.
cards.h: → each observation → what the particles must be
cards.n: Naming 'high melting point' alone is not enough; the conductivity pattern (insulating solid, conducting melt) is the evidence that mobile ions, not electrons, exist.

cards.q: Determine the bond type in aluminum chloride from ΔEN (Al 1.61, Cl 3.16) and from the periodic positions of the atoms, then explain what its behavior (it sublimes at about 180 °C and the vapor contains Al₂Cl₆ molecules) says about which description is better.
cards.a: ΔEN = 3.16 − 1.61 = 1.55 predicts polar covalent, while metal + nonmetal predicts ionic; the two rules disagree. The properties settle it: an ionic solid would melt near 800 °C and conduct when molten, but AlCl₃ passes into the gas phase at only 180 °C as discrete Al₂Cl₆ molecules, so its bonding has substantial covalent character. Bonding is a continuum and properties are the best characterization.
cards.h: → ΔEN, position rule, then properties decide
cards.n: Picking one rule and ignoring the other earns little; the scored idea is that when ΔEN and periodic position disagree, the observed properties characterize the bonding.

cards.q: Explain why bond polarity is better described as a continuum rather than three sharply divided categories.
cards.a: Electron sharing becomes gradually more unequal as ΔEN grows; nothing physical changes at 0.4 or 1.7. Every polar bond has some ionic character and every ionic bond some covalent character, so the labels mark regions of one continuous scale, and properties decide borderline cases.
cards.h: → ΔEN varies continuously → partial charge varies continuously → labels are conventions
cards.n: 'Because chemists disagree on the cut-offs' earns nothing; the point is that the underlying electron shift is continuous.
o: The partial charges on the atoms grow smoothly with ΔEN, so there is no gap in nature between 'polar' and 'ionic'.
Even Li-I (ΔEN 1.68) forms a salt while HF (ΔEN 1.78) is molecular, which shows the cut-off is a convenience, not a boundary.

w.a: Bond polarity is a continuum because electronegativity values are only estimates.
w.why: blames measurement error rather than the continuous electron shift

w.a: Bond polarity is a continuum because a bond can switch between ionic and covalent over time.
w.why: bonds do not flip type; the sharing is fixed and intermediate

w.a: Bond polarity is a continuum because all bonds are really covalent.
w.why: denies ionic character instead of describing the gradual change

cards.q: Explain, using Coulomb's law and the shell model, why a fluorine atom attracts shared bonding electrons more strongly than a carbon atom does.
cards.a: F has more protons (9 vs 6) but its valence electrons are in the same n = 2 shell, and same-shell electrons shield each other poorly, so bonding electrons feel a larger effective nuclear charge at a smaller distance. By Coulomb's law that is a stronger attraction, so F has the higher electronegativity.
cards.h: → more protons, same shell, poor shielding → larger effective nuclear charge → stronger pull on bonding electrons
cards.n: 'Fluorine is closer to a full octet and wants one more electron' is octet folklore, not Coulomb's law, and earns nothing.
o: Across period 2 the nuclear charge rises while the valence shell stays n = 2, so the attraction on a bonding electron increases from C to F.
Fluorine's smaller radius puts the bonding electrons closer to a larger effective nuclear charge, which by Coulomb's law means a stronger attraction.

w.a: Fluorine attracts electrons more strongly because it has more electrons than carbon.
w.why: electrons repel; it is the proton count and shielding that matter

w.a: Fluorine attracts electrons more strongly because it needs only one electron to fill its octet.
w.why: restates a bookkeeping rule; no force or charge argument

w.a: Fluorine attracts electrons more strongly because it is a gas and carbon is a solid.
w.why: state of matter is irrelevant to the attraction on a bonding electron

cards.q: Explain why iodine has a lower electronegativity than fluorine even though an iodine atom has many more protons.
cards.a: Iodine's valence shell is n = 5, far from the nucleus, and its 46 core electrons shield most of the extra protons, so a bonding electron feels a similar effective nuclear charge at a much larger distance. By Coulomb's law the attraction weakens with distance, so I pulls shared electrons less strongly than F.
cards.h: → more shells → larger distance and more shielding → weaker Coulombic pull on the bonding pair
cards.n: 'Iodine is bigger so it is less reactive' describes a consequence, not the cause; the point needs distance and shielding in Coulomb's law.
o: Going down group 17 each element adds a shell, so the bonding electrons sit farther from a nucleus whose extra protons are cancelled by extra core electrons.
The shielding by inner shells keeps the effective nuclear charge roughly constant down the group while the radius grows, so the attraction on shared electrons weakens.

w.a: Iodine is less electronegative because it has more electrons to share.
w.why: the number of electrons does not set the pull on a bonding pair

w.a: Iodine is less electronegative because its nucleus is weaker.
w.why: the nucleus has 53 protons; it is shielding and distance, not a weak nucleus

w.a: Iodine is less electronegative because it is a solid at room temperature.
w.why: physical state has nothing to do with attraction for bonding electrons

cards.q: Explain why the C-H bond is treated as effectively nonpolar even though carbon is more electronegative than hydrogen.
cards.a: The electronegativity difference is tiny (2.55 − 2.20 = 0.35), so the shared pair shifts only slightly toward carbon and the partial charges are negligible. The bond dipole in a single bond scales with ΔEN, so a difference this small gives no dipole of consequence; hydrocarbons behave as nonpolar.
cards.h: → small ΔEN → tiny electron shift → negligible partial charges → no effective dipole
cards.n: 'Because the C-H bonds cancel by symmetry' answers a different question (molecular polarity); the bond itself is nearly nonpolar.
o: With ΔEN of only 0.35, well under the ~0.4 convention, the sharing is nearly equal and the bond dipole is negligible.
Carbon and hydrogen are both nonmetals of similar electronegativity, so neither gains a meaningful partial charge.

w.a: The C-H bond is nonpolar because carbon and hydrogen have the same electronegativity.
w.why: false; C is 2.55 and H 2.20, the point is that the difference is small

w.a: The C-H bond is nonpolar because hydrogen has no electrons to pull.
w.why: hydrogen contributes one electron to the shared pair like any bonded atom

w.a: The C-H bond is nonpolar because methane is a symmetric molecule.
w.why: symmetry explains molecular polarity, not the polarity of one bond

cards.q: Explain why a bond between a metal and a nonmetal is generally ionic while a bond between two nonmetals is generally covalent.
cards.a: Metals have low electronegativity and nonmetals high, so ΔEN is large and the nonmetal takes the metal's valence electrons outright; the ions then attract Coulombically. Two nonmetals attract electrons strongly and about equally, so neither can remove the other's electrons and they share the pair.
cards.h: → metal low EN, nonmetal high EN → large ΔEN → transfer; two nonmetals similar high EN → share
cards.n: 'Metals want to lose electrons' is not a mechanism; the point needs the electronegativity contrast and what a large versus small difference does to the electrons.
o: Ionic character grows with ΔEN, and a metal/nonmetal pair sits at the high-ΔEN end of the continuum while two nonmetals sit at the low end.
A metal atom holds its valence electrons weakly, so beside a strongly attracting nonmetal the electrons leave; between two strong attractors they stay shared.

w.a: Metals and nonmetals form ionic bonds because opposite kinds of elements attract.
w.why: 'opposites attract' is not an electronegativity argument

w.a: Two nonmetals bond covalently because nonmetals cannot form ions.
w.why: false; Cl⁻ and O²⁻ are nonmetal ions, the point is the similar electronegativity

w.a: A metal and a nonmetal form an ionic bond because the metal is a solid and the nonmetal is a gas.
w.why: physical state is irrelevant; the difference in attraction for electrons is what matters

cards.q: Explain why hydrogen fluoride is a molecular compound even though its electronegativity difference (1.78) lies above the usual ionic cut-off.
cards.a: ΔEN is only one factor: H and F are both nonmetals, so the pair is shared (very unequally), not transferred, and HF's properties, a gas at room temperature whose liquid does not conduct, show neutral molecules with no mobile ions. Properties, not the 1.7 convention, make it polar covalent.
cards.h: → ΔEN is one factor → both nonmetals share → properties show molecules, not ions
cards.n: 'It is an exception' earns nothing; the point is that ΔEN cut-offs are conventions and the periodic positions and properties decide.
o: The nonconducting liquid and low boiling point are the evidence: an ionic compound would be a high-melting solid that conducts when molten.
All polar bonds have some ionic character and HF has a lot, but it is still a shared pair between two nonmetals, so it is a very polar covalent bond.

w.a: HF is molecular because hydrogen can only form covalent bonds.
w.why: false; H⁻ exists in ionic hydrides such as NaH, and this dodges the property evidence

w.a: HF is molecular because 1.78 is close enough to 1.7 to round down.
w.why: treats the convention as a law and the answer as arithmetic

w.a: HF is molecular because fluorine is too small to form an ion.
w.why: F⁻ is common (NaF, CaF₂); size is not the issue

cards.q: Explain why a metallic solid conducts electricity while a covalent molecular solid does not, in terms of what the valence electrons are doing.
cards.a: In a metal the valence electrons are delocalized over the whole lattice of cations, not tied to any atom, so they move freely under an applied voltage and carry charge. In a molecular solid every valence electron is localized in a bond or lone pair within a neutral molecule, so nothing can carry charge.
cards.h: → delocalized valence electrons → mobile carriers; localized bonding pairs → none
cards.n: 'Metals have free electrons' without saying why (delocalization over the cation lattice) or contrasting the localized bonds of a molecule earns half at most.
o: Conduction needs mobile charge; a metal's electron sea supplies it, while a molecular solid's electrons are held in bonds between specific atoms.
Metallic bonding is nondirectional sharing among all atoms, so electrons can drift through the solid; covalent bonds pin electrons between two nuclei.

w.a: Metals conduct because they contain more electrons than molecular solids.
w.why: total electron count is irrelevant; it is whether the valence electrons are free to move

w.a: Metals conduct because metal atoms turn into ions that carry the current.
w.why: the cations are fixed in the lattice; the electrons carry the current

w.a: Molecular solids do not conduct because they have no electrons in their bonds.
w.why: covalent bonds are made of electrons; they are localized, not absent

cards.q: Explain what the minimum of a potential energy versus internuclear distance curve represents.
cards.a: The minimum marks the equilibrium bond length: the separation at which the attraction of each nucleus for the shared electrons exactly balances the nucleus-nucleus and electron-electron repulsions, so the potential energy is lowest. Its depth below zero (the energy of the separated atoms) is the bond energy, the energy that must be supplied to pull the atoms apart to infinite separation.
cards.h: → x-value meaning + y-depth meaning
cards.n: Quoting the bond energy with the minimum's sign (−436 kJ/mol for H₂) earns nothing; the bond energy is the positive depth of the well.

cards.q: State how bond order, bond length, and bond strength are related.
cards.a: Higher bond order means a shorter bond and a larger bond energy. Between the same two atoms: C-C 154 pm and 347 kJ/mol, C=C 134 pm and 614 kJ/mol, C≡C 120 pm and 839 kJ/mol. More shared electron density between the nuclei pulls them closer and holds them more tightly.
cards.h: → two linked trends with one worked example
cards.n: Stating the length trend without the energy trend (or vice versa) earns half; the CED asks for both, and they always move together for bonds between the same pair of atoms.

cards.q: Predict which bond is shorter and stronger: the C-C bond in ethane or the C=C bond in ethene, using bond order.
cards.a: The C=C bond in ethene. Its bond order is 2 (two shared pairs) versus 1 for the C-C single bond in ethane; the extra shared electron density between the nuclei attracts both nuclei more strongly, pulling them closer (134 pm vs 154 pm) and deepening the potential well (614 vs 347 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → higher bond order → shorter, stronger, with numbers
cards.n: 'Ethene is smaller' or 'ethene has fewer hydrogens' earns nothing; the point is the bond order and what more shared electrons do to the attraction between the nuclei.

cards.q: Predict which bond requires more energy to break: the O-H bond in water (467 kJ/mol) or the H-H bond in $H_2$ (436 kJ/mol).
cards.a: The O-H bond. Bond energy is the energy required to separate the bonded atoms, and 467 kJ/mol > 436 kJ/mol, so breaking one mole of O-H bonds needs 31 kJ more than breaking one mole of H-H bonds. On a potential-energy curve the O-H well is deeper.
cards.h: → which bond, the two numbers, the well depth
cards.n: Arguing from bond length alone (O-H 96 pm is longer than H-H 74 pm, yet stronger) shows length does not rank bonds between different atom pairs; use the given energies.

cards.q: Define bond dissociation energy.
cards.a: The energy required to break one mole of a given bond in the gas phase into separated atoms or fragments, in kJ/mol; it is always positive because the bonded state lies lower in potential energy than the separated atoms. On a potential-energy curve it is the depth of the well from the minimum up to zero. Tabulated values are averages over many compounds.
cards.h: → per mole, gas phase, always positive, well depth
cards.n: Giving a negative bond energy earns nothing; energy is absorbed to break a bond. The negative number belongs to bond formation.

cards.q: Compute the energy required to break all the C-H bonds in 0.500 mol of methane, given a C-H bond energy of 413 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 826 kJ. Each CH₄ molecule has four C-H bonds, so 0.500 mol CH₄ × 4 = 2.00 mol of C-H bonds; energy = 2.00 mol × 413 kJ/mol = 826 kJ, absorbed (positive).
cards.h: → bonds per molecule × moles × kJ/mol
cards.n: Answering 207 kJ (0.500 × 413) misses that each molecule holds four C-H bonds; the bond count per molecule is the first factor.

cards.q: Predict which bond is longer: the C-O bond in $CO_2$ or the C-O bond in methanol, $CH_3OH$.
cards.a: The C-O bond in methanol. Its Lewis diagram gives a C-O single bond (order 1, about 143 pm), while each C-O bond in O=C=O is a double bond (order 2, about 116 pm); a higher bond order means more shared electron density pulling the nuclei closer, so the double bond is shorter.
cards.h: → which bond + order from the Lewis diagram
cards.n: Deciding from molecular size or polarity earns nothing; the ranking rests on the bond order read from the Lewis diagram.

cards.q: Contrast an intramolecular force with an intermolecular force in terms of typical magnitude.
cards.a: Intramolecular forces are the chemical bonds (covalent, ionic, metallic) that hold atoms together within a molecule or lattice; covalent bond energies run from about 150 to 1000 kJ/mol (H-H 436). Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules and are much weaker, typically a few to a few tens of kJ/mol (water's hydrogen bonds about 20 kJ/mol). That gap is why water boils at 100 °C without any O-H bond breaking.
cards.h: → within vs between, with an order-of-magnitude each
cards.n: Saying 'boiling breaks the bonds in water' earns nothing; boiling overcomes intermolecular forces (Unit 3), the bonds survive.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the potential energy versus internuclear distance curve for H₂, whose bond length is 74 pm and bond energy 436 kJ/mol.
cards.a: Axes: horizontal, internuclear distance r (pm); vertical, potential energy (kJ/mol) with zero marked for the separated atoms. From the right the curve approaches zero from below as r grows large, falls smoothly to a single minimum at r = 74 pm and E = −436 kJ/mol, then rises very steeply, crossing zero and heading toward +∞ as r shrinks below about 50 pm. Label the minimum 'bond length 74 pm' and the vertical distance from the minimum to zero 'bond energy 436 kJ/mol'.
cards.h: → axes, asymptote, minimum coordinates, steep wall
cards.n: A symmetric U or a curve that reaches zero at the minimum earns nothing; the well must sit below zero with a steep left wall and a slow approach to zero on the right.

cards.q: Identify the bond length and the bond energy of Cl₂ from this description of its potential-energy curve: the potential energy is 0 kJ/mol at very large separation, decreases to a minimum of −243 kJ/mol at 199 pm, and rises steeply above zero below about 150 pm.
cards.a: Bond length 199 pm; bond energy 243 kJ/mol. The equilibrium bond length is the distance at the minimum, and the bond energy is the energy needed to lift the atoms from the minimum to the zero of separated atoms: 0 − (−243) = +243 kJ/mol. The 150 pm value is only where repulsion dominates, not a bond property.
cards.h: → x of the minimum, positive depth of the well
cards.n: Reporting the bond energy as −243 kJ/mol or reading 150 pm as the bond length earns nothing.

cards.q: Determine which curve belongs to N₂ and which to O₂ when two potential-energy curves are drawn on the same axes: curve X has its minimum at 110 pm and −945 kJ/mol, curve Y at 121 pm and −498 kJ/mol. Justify using Lewis diagrams.
cards.a: Curve X is N₂ and curve Y is O₂. The Lewis diagram of N₂ is :N≡N: (bond order 3); O₂ is O=O with two lone pairs on each O (bond order 2). The higher bond order puts more shared electron density between the nuclei, so the N≡N bond is shorter (110 pm) and its well deeper (945 kJ/mol) than O=O (121 pm, 498 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → Lewis bond orders → shorter and deeper curve
cards.n: Assigning by atomic mass ('oxygen is heavier so its bond is stronger') earns nothing; bond order from the Lewis diagram is the evidence.

cards.q: Rank each set by bond length (longest first) and state how bond energy runs across the same set: (i) C-C, C=C, C≡C · (ii) H-F, H-Cl, H-Br, H-I · (iii) N-N, N=N, N≡N · (iv) C-F, C-Cl, C-Br, C-I · (v) O-O, O=O · (vi) C-O in CH₃OH, in CO₂, in CO · (vii) C-Cl, Si-Cl
cards.a:
(i) C-C (154 pm) > C=C (134) > C≡C (120); energy rises 347 → 614 → 839 kJ/mol (bond order)
(ii) H-I (161) > H-Br (141) > H-Cl (127) > H-F (92); energy rises 299 → 366 → 431 → 567 (smaller halogen core)
(iii) N-N (145) > N=N (125) > N≡N (110); energy 160 → 418 → 945 (bond order)
(iv) C-I (214) > C-Br (194) > C-Cl (177) > C-F (135); energy 240 → 276 → 328 → 485 (atomic radius)
(v) O-O (148) > O=O (121); energy 142 → 495 (bond order)
(vi) CH₃OH C-O single (143) > CO₂ C=O (116) > CO C≡O (113); energy 358 → 799 → 1072
(vii) Si-Cl (202) > C-Cl (177) because Si has the larger core; but energy does NOT fall here: Si-Cl (about 380) is stronger than C-Cl (about 330), so length predicts strength only within a family
cards.h: → bond order first, then core size; one set breaks rule
cards.n: Set (vii) is the trap: Si-Cl is longer yet stronger than C-Cl, so 'shorter means stronger' is safe only for the same pair of atoms or a simple family.

cards.q: Calculate the energy change when 2.00 mol of gaseous hydrogen atoms combine to form H₂ molecules, given the H-H bond energy of 436 kJ/mol, and state whether energy is absorbed or released.
cards.a: −436 kJ; energy is released. 2.00 mol H atoms form 1.00 mol of H-H bonds (2 H → H₂), and forming a bond lowers the potential energy by the bond energy: 1.00 mol × 436 kJ/mol = 436 kJ released, so ΔE = −436 kJ. The system falls into the potential-energy well.
cards.h: → moles of bonds formed × bond energy, negative sign
cards.n: Reporting +872 kJ (2.00 × 436, wrong sign) earns nothing: two atoms make one bond, and bond formation releases energy.

cards.q: State Coulomb's law for the potential energy of two ions and identify how each variable affects the strength of the interaction.
cards.a: E ∝ q₁q₂/r (E = k q₁q₂/r), where q₁ and q₂ are the ion charges and r the distance between the ion centers (the sum of the ionic radii). Larger charges make E more negative (stronger attraction), in proportion to the product of the charges; a smaller distance, i.e. smaller ions, also makes the attraction stronger. Charge usually dominates because it can double or triple while r changes by tens of percent.
cards.h: → equation, then one line per variable
cards.n: Writing E ∝ q₁q₂/r² earns nothing for the energy form (1/r² is the force); either way, name both the charge and the distance effects.

cards.q: Estimate how many times stronger the Coulombic attraction between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ is than between Na⁺ and Cl⁻, using E ∝ q₁q₂/r and the ionic radii Na⁺ 102 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm, Mg²⁺ 72 pm, O²⁻ 140 pm.
cards.a: About 5 times. r(NaCl) = 102 + 181 = 283 pm; r(MgO) = 72 + 140 = 212 pm. Ratio = [(2)(2)/212] ÷ [(1)(1)/283] = 4 × (283/212) = 4 × 1.34 = 5.3. Both factors favor MgO: the charge product is 4 times larger and the ions are closer. The measured lattice energies, 3795 vs 788 kJ/mol (ratio 4.8), agree with the estimate.
cards.h: → two distances, charge product ratio × distance ratio
cards.n: Using only the charges (answer 4) earns the charge point but not the distance point; and squaring r treats E like a force.

cards.q: Predict which ion pair has the stronger Coulombic interaction and name the deciding factor: (i) Na⁺/F⁻ vs K⁺/F⁻ · (ii) Ca²⁺/O²⁻ vs K⁺/Cl⁻ · (iii) Mg²⁺/O²⁻ vs Mg²⁺/S²⁻ · (iv) Li⁺/Cl⁻ vs Cs⁺/Cl⁻ · (v) Al³⁺/O²⁻ vs Mg²⁺/O²⁻ · (vi) Na⁺/Cl⁻ vs Mg²⁺/Cl⁻ · (vii) Ba²⁺/O²⁻ vs Mg²⁺/O²⁻
cards.a:
(i) Na⁺/F⁻ → Na⁺ (102 pm) is smaller than K⁺ (138 pm), shorter distance
(ii) Ca²⁺/O²⁻ → charge product 4 vs 1 dominates
(iii) Mg²⁺/O²⁻ → O²⁻ (140 pm) smaller than S²⁻ (184 pm), same charges
(iv) Li⁺/Cl⁻ → Li⁺ (76 pm) far smaller than Cs⁺ (167 pm)
(v) Al³⁺/O²⁻ → charge product 6 vs 4, and Al³⁺ is smaller
(vi) Mg²⁺/Cl⁻ → charge product 2 vs 1, and Mg²⁺ is smaller than Na⁺
(vii) Mg²⁺/O²⁻ → same charges, Mg²⁺ (72 pm) smaller than Ba²⁺ (135 pm)
Rule: compare charges first; when charges tie, the smaller ions (shorter r) win.
cards.h: → charges first, then radii
cards.n: Naming 'more electrons' or 'heavier ion' as the factor earns nothing; Coulomb's law has exactly two variables, charge and distance.

cards.q: Explain why breaking a chemical bond always requires energy input.
cards.a: The bonded atoms sit at the minimum of the potential-energy curve, below the separated atoms, because the shared electrons attract both nuclei. Separating them means climbing out of that well, so energy equal to the bond energy must be absorbed: bond breaking is endothermic, bond formation exothermic.
cards.h: → bonded state at the well minimum → separated atoms higher → energy must be added to climb out
cards.n: 'Breaking bonds releases energy' is the classic biology-class error and earns nothing; energy is released only when new bonds form.
o: Bond energy is defined as the positive energy needed to reach the zero of separated atoms from the negative well minimum.
Attraction between nuclei and shared electrons must be overcome to pull the atoms apart, and overcoming an attraction costs energy.

w.a: Breaking a bond requires energy because the atoms are held together by strong forces.
w.why: names a force but not the potential-energy well or the sign of the change

w.a: Breaking a bond requires energy because the products are more stable than the reactants.
w.why: backwards; separated atoms are less stable (higher energy) than the bonded pair

w.a: Breaking a bond requires energy only if the bond is polar.
w.why: every bond, polar or not, lies below the separated atoms in energy

cards.q: Explain why the H-F bond is shorter and stronger than the H-I bond.
cards.a: Fluorine's core is much smaller than iodine's (valence shell n = 2 versus n = 5), so the H nucleus can approach the F nucleus more closely: H-F is 92 pm, H-I 161 pm. With the shared electron density closer to both nuclei the Coulombic attraction is stronger, so the H-F well is deeper (567 vs 299 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → smaller core → shorter internuclear distance → shared electrons closer to both nuclei → stronger bond
cards.n: 'Fluorine is more electronegative' explains polarity, not length; the scored reason is the size of the atom's core setting the bond length.
o: Bond length grows with the size of the atomic core, and bond energy falls as the shared electrons sit farther from the nuclei.
Iodine's inner shells keep the nuclei far apart, so the attraction between each nucleus and the bonding pair is weaker by Coulomb's law.

w.a: The H-F bond is stronger because fluorine has a higher electronegativity than iodine.
w.why: electronegativity sets the dipole, not the bond length; the core size does

w.a: The H-F bond is stronger because HF is a smaller molecule and small molecules are stable.
w.why: molecular size is not a bonding argument

w.a: The H-I bond is longer because iodine has more protons that push hydrogen away.
w.why: the nucleus attracts the bonding electrons; the extra distance comes from iodine's inner shells

cards.q: Explain why the potential energy rises steeply when two bonded atoms are pushed closer together than the equilibrium bond length.
cards.a: At the equilibrium length attraction and repulsion balance. Pushed closer, the two nuclei and the two electron clouds repel each other, and those like-charge repulsions grow faster than the attraction as r shrinks, so the net potential energy climbs sharply toward positive values.
cards.h: → shorter r → nucleus-nucleus and electron-electron repulsion grow faster than attraction → energy climbs
cards.n: 'The bond breaks when squeezed' earns nothing; the steep wall is repulsion between like charges, and the atoms spring back to the minimum.
o: Like charges repel, and the nuclei get close enough that their mutual repulsion dominates the attraction for the shared electrons.
The minimum is the balance point; any distance shorter than it is repulsion-dominated, so the curve rises.

w.a: The energy rises because the atoms lose their bond when they get too close.
w.why: the bond is not lost; the repulsion between nuclei raises the energy

w.a: The energy rises because the electrons run out of room and leave the bond.
w.why: electrons do not leave; their clouds overlap and repel

w.a: The energy rises because attraction increases at short distance.
w.why: stronger attraction would lower the energy, not raise it

cards.q: Explain why the potential-energy curve for a C=C bond has its minimum at a shorter distance and lower energy than the curve for a C-C bond.
cards.a: A double bond shares four electrons between the nuclei instead of two, so more electron density attracts each nucleus. The stronger attraction pulls the nuclei to a shorter equilibrium separation (134 vs 154 pm) and deepens the well (614 vs 347 kJ/mol): higher bond order, shorter and stronger bond.
cards.h: → more shared electrons → stronger nucleus-electron attraction → nuclei pulled closer, deeper well
cards.n: 'Double bonds are stronger because there are two of them' earns nothing; the point is the extra shared electron density between the nuclei.
o: Bond order sets both properties: each extra shared pair adds attraction between the nuclei and the bonding electrons, lowering the minimum and shifting it left.
The curve for the higher-order bond is deeper because more energy is needed to separate atoms held by two shared pairs.

w.a: The C=C curve is lower because ethene is more reactive than ethane.
w.why: reactivity of the pi bond is a different property; the well depth is the total bond energy

w.a: The C=C curve minimum is shorter because the carbon atoms are smaller in ethene.
w.why: the atoms are the same; the shared electron density changed

w.a: The C=C curve is exactly twice as deep as the C-C curve.
w.why: 614 is not 2 × 347; the second (pi) bond is weaker than the first

cards.q: Explain why the interaction between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions is much stronger than the interaction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
cards.a: Coulomb's law: E ∝ q₁q₂/r. The charge product for Mg²⁺/O²⁻ is (2)(2) = 4 versus (1)(1) = 1 for Na⁺/Cl⁻, and both Mg²⁺ (72 pm) and O²⁻ (140 pm) are smaller than Na⁺ (102 pm) and Cl⁻ (181 pm), so the ion centers are closer. Larger charges and a shorter distance both strengthen the attraction.
cards.h: → larger charge product and smaller ions → stronger Coulombic attraction
cards.n: 'MgO has stronger bonds' restates the claim; the point needs both Coulomb variables, or at least the charge product.
o: The doubled charges alone quadruple the attraction, and the smaller radii shorten r on top of that.
Lattice energies confirm it: about 3795 kJ/mol for MgO versus 788 kJ/mol for NaCl.

w.a: The MgO interaction is stronger because magnesium and oxygen are more reactive elements.
w.why: reactivity is not a Coulombic variable

w.a: The MgO interaction is stronger because MgO has a covalent bond and NaCl an ionic one.
w.why: both are ionic; the answer misclassifies instead of using charge and distance

w.a: The MgO interaction is stronger because the Mg²⁺ ion has more electrons than Na⁺.
w.why: Mg²⁺ and Na⁺ both have 10 electrons; charge and radius are what differ

cards.q: Explain why a smaller cation produces a stronger attraction to a given anion than a larger cation of the same charge.
cards.a: Interaction strength increases as the distance between ion centers decreases (E ∝ q₁q₂/r). A smaller cation has a smaller radius, so with the same anion the sum of the radii, r, is smaller; with the charges unchanged, the Coulombic attraction is stronger.
cards.h: → smaller radius → shorter center-to-center distance → stronger attraction at the same charges
cards.n: 'Smaller ions pack more tightly' earns nothing without the distance term of Coulomb's law.
o: With q₁q₂ fixed, E depends only on 1/r, and r is the sum of the two ionic radii.
LiF's ions are closer than CsF's, which is why LiF has the larger lattice energy.

w.a: A smaller cation attracts more strongly because it has a higher charge density that pulls electrons away from the anion.
w.why: polarization is not what the EK tests; the point is the shorter distance in Coulomb's law

w.a: A smaller cation attracts more strongly because it has fewer electrons to shield its nucleus from the anion.
w.why: shielding is an intra-atomic idea; ion-ion attraction depends on net charges and distance

w.a: A smaller cation attracts more strongly because small ions have a larger charge.
w.why: the charge is the same by the question's own premise

cards.q: Define lattice energy and list the two factors that control its magnitude.
cards.a: Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions combine to form one mole of the ionic solid (equivalently, the energy needed to separate one mole of the solid into gaseous ions), e.g. about 788 kJ/mol for NaCl. By Coulomb's law its magnitude grows with the charges on the ions (larger charge product, stronger attraction) and with smaller ionic radii (shorter distance between ion centers).
cards.h: → definition with the process, then charge and distance
cards.n: Listing 'mass' or 'number of electrons' as a factor earns nothing; Coulomb's law has only charge and distance, and charge is the dominant one.

cards.q: Rank the lattice energies of NaCl, MgO, and KCl and justify the order.
cards.a: MgO > NaCl > KCl (about 3795, 788 and 701 kJ/mol). MgO has 2+ and 2− ions, a charge product four times that of the 1+/1− salts, which dominates by Coulomb's law. NaCl beats KCl because Na⁺ (102 pm) is smaller than K⁺ (138 pm), so the Na⁺–Cl⁻ centers are closer and the attraction is stronger.
cards.h: → order, charge argument, then size tiebreaker
cards.n: Ranking by formula mass or by 'reactivity of the metal' earns nothing; compare the charge product first and the ion radii second.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger lattice energy, MgO or MgS, and justify.
cards.a: MgO. Both solids have Mg²⁺ with a 2− anion, so the charge product is the same; the difference is size. O²⁻ (140 pm) is smaller than S²⁻ (184 pm), so the Mg²⁺–O²⁻ distance is shorter and, by Coulomb's law, the attraction in MgO is stronger and its lattice energy larger.
cards.h: → charges tie → compare anion radii
cards.n: 'Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur' explains bond polarity, not lattice energy; the point here is the shorter interionic distance.

cards.q: Rank NaF, NaCl, and NaBr by lattice energy from largest to smallest, and justify.
cards.a: NaF > NaCl > NaBr (about 910, 788 and 732 kJ/mol). All three contain Na⁺ with a 1− halide, so the charge product is the same, and the ranking follows the anion radius: F⁻ (133 pm) < Cl⁻ (181 pm) < Br⁻ (196 pm). The smaller the anion, the shorter the Na⁺–X⁻ distance and the stronger the Coulombic attraction.
cards.h: → charges tie → anion radius sets the order
cards.n: An answer based on halogen electronegativity or reactivity earns nothing; with equal charges only the distance term of Coulomb's law changes.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger lattice energy, NaCl or $MgCl_2$, and justify using ionic charge.
cards.a: MgCl₂ (about 2326 kJ/mol versus 788 for NaCl). Mg²⁺ carries twice the charge of Na⁺ while the anion is the same Cl⁻, so the charge product in each cation–anion attraction doubles; Coulomb's law makes the interaction strength proportional to that product. Mg²⁺ (72 pm) is also smaller than Na⁺ (102 pm), which shortens the distance and reinforces the result.
cards.h: → charge product doubles, size agrees
cards.n: Saying 'MgCl₂ has more chloride ions so more bonds' earns nothing; the scored reason is the higher cation charge in Coulomb's law.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger lattice energy, LiF or CsI, considering both ionic charge and size.
cards.a: LiF (about 1030 kJ/mol versus 600 for CsI). Both are 1+/1− salts, so charge does not decide; Li⁺ (76 pm) and F⁻ (133 pm) are far smaller than Cs⁺ (167 pm) and I⁻ (220 pm), so the center-to-center distance is 209 pm in LiF versus 387 pm in CsI. By Coulomb's law the shorter distance gives the stronger attraction.
cards.h: → charge tied → compare the two distances
cards.n: Stopping at 'LiF has smaller ions' without connecting size to distance in Coulomb's law earns the claim but not the justification.

cards.q: Represent a particulate model of solid sodium chloride, describing a two-dimensional slice precisely enough to draw.
cards.a: A regular grid of alternating circles: small circles labeled Na⁺ and larger circles labeled Cl⁻, arranged so that every Na⁺ touches only Cl⁻ neighbors (above, below, left, right) and every Cl⁻ touches only Na⁺; equal numbers of each; rows and columns repeat identically across the whole slice with no gaps, no pairs and no molecules. Cl⁻ is drawn larger because it has three occupied shells while Na⁺ has two.
cards.h: → alternating charges, 1:1 count, sizes, repeating array
cards.n: Na–Cl 'molecules', equal-size circles or like ions side by side earn nothing; the array must fit Coulomb's law and the ion sizes (Unit 1 radius reasoning).

cards.q: Determine whether this particulate diagram of solid KBr is consistent with Coulomb's law, and explain: circles labeled K⁺ and Br⁻ are arranged in horizontal rows, each row containing only K⁺ ions or only Br⁻ ions, with the like ions touching along the row.
cards.a: Not consistent. Placing like-charged ions in contact along each row maximizes cation–cation and anion–anion repulsion, which raises the potential energy. A stable lattice puts each K⁺ in contact only with Br⁻ ions and each Br⁻ only with K⁺, alternating in every direction, so that the attractive forces are maximized and the repulsive forces minimized. The rows should alternate K⁺, Br⁻, K⁺, Br⁻.
cards.h: → verdict, which force the drawing maximizes, the fix
cards.n: 'It is wrong because ions should be in a cube' leans on a specific crystal structure, which the CED excludes; argue from attraction and repulsion only.

cards.q: Identify the errors in a student's particulate drawing of solid calcium chloride that shows equal numbers of Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ circles, with the Ca²⁺ circles drawn larger than the Cl⁻ circles.
cards.a: Two errors. (1) The ion ratio must be 1 Ca²⁺ : 2 Cl⁻ so that the charges sum to zero; equal numbers would leave the solid with a net positive charge. (2) Ca²⁺ (about 100 pm) is smaller than Cl⁻ (about 181 pm): the cation has lost its outer shell and holds its remaining electrons more tightly, while the anion has gained an electron and its shell expands. The Cl⁻ circles should be the larger ones.
cards.h: → ratio from charge balance, sizes from ion formation
cards.n: Fixing the ratio but keeping Ca²⁺ larger 'because calcium is a bigger atom' earns half; the radius of the ion, not the atom, is what the drawing must show (Unit 1 reasoning).

cards.q: Rank each set of ionic solids by expected melting point, highest first, and name the Coulombic factor that decides: (i) NaF, NaCl, NaBr, NaI · (ii) MgO, CaO, SrO, BaO · (iii) NaCl, KCl, RbCl, CsCl · (iv) KCl, CaO · (v) KF, KCl, KBr · (vi) KBr, NaCl, MgO
cards.a:
(i) NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI (993, 801, 747, 661 °C); anion radius grows F⁻ → I⁻
(ii) MgO > CaO > SrO > BaO (2852, about 2600, 2531, 1923 °C); cation radius grows Mg²⁺ → Ba²⁺
(iii) NaCl > KCl > RbCl > CsCl (801, 770, 718, 645 °C); cation radius
(iv) CaO > KCl (about 2600 vs 770 °C); charge product 4 vs 1
(v) KF > KCl > KBr (858, 770, 734 °C); anion radius
(vi) MgO > NaCl > KBr (2852, 801, 734 °C); charge first (MgO), then Na⁺ smaller than K⁺ and Cl⁻ smaller than Br⁻
Stronger attraction between the ions in the lattice means more energy is needed to free them, so the melting point rises with lattice energy.
cards.h: → charges first, then radii; lattice energy tracks mp
cards.n: Melting point tracks Coulomb's law for these pairs; some salts (LiF, MgCl₂) deviate because structure also matters, so exam items stick to simple pairs.

cards.q: Determine from the data which substitution lowers the lattice energy more, replacing the cation Na⁺ with K⁺ or replacing the anion Cl⁻ with Br⁻, and explain using the ionic radii Na⁺ 102 pm, K⁺ 138 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm, Br⁻ 196 pm. Lattice energies (kJ/mol): NaCl · 788 · KCl · 701 · NaBr · 732 · KBr · 671
cards.a: The cation swap. Na⁺ → K⁺ lowers the lattice energy by 87 kJ/mol (788 → 701) and by 61 (732 → 671), while Cl⁻ → Br⁻ lowers it by only 56 (788 → 732) and 30 (701 → 671). Coulomb's law explains it: with the charges fixed, the attraction depends on the center-to-center distance, and the cation swap lengthens it by 36 pm whereas the anion swap adds only 15 pm; the bigger increase in r gives the bigger drop.
cards.h: → two differences from the table, then compare Δr
cards.n: 'The anion, because anions are bigger' earns nothing; what matters is how much each swap lengthens r, and the cation swap lengthens it more.

cards.q: Determine the charge on the metal ion and the empirical formula of an ionic solid whose particulate diagram shows 8 large circles labeled X⁻ and 4 small circles labeled M, each M circle surrounded on all sides by X⁻ circles.
cards.a: M is 2+ and the formula is MX₂. The solid is electrically neutral, and there are twice as many X⁻ as M, so each M must carry 2+ to balance two 1− charges: 4 × (+2) + 8 × (−1) = 0. The alternating placement (each M touching only X⁻) is what Coulomb's law requires, attraction maximized and repulsion minimized.
cards.h: → count ratio → charge balance → formula
cards.n: Reading the ratio backwards (M₂X) or assigning M a 1+ charge because it is 'the smaller circle' earns nothing; charge neutrality sets the answer.

cards.q: Use a Born-Haber cycle to compute the lattice energy of NaCl: $ΔH_f$ = -411, $ΔH_sub(Na)$ = +109, $IE_1(Na)$ = +496, $D(Cl_2)$ = +243, EA(Cl) = -349 (all kJ/mol).
cards.a: ΔH = −789 kJ/mol for Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s), so the lattice energy is about 789 kJ/mol. By Hess's law the steps sum to the enthalpy of formation: −411 = 109 + 496 + ½(243) + (−349) + ΔH(lattice) = 377.5 + ΔH(lattice), so ΔH(lattice) = −788.5 ≈ −789 kJ/mol. Only half the Cl₂ bond energy enters because one Cl atom is needed per NaCl.
cards.h: → Hess's law sum, solve for the one unknown step
cards.n: Using the full 243 kJ/mol (answer −910 kJ/mol) earns nothing. The cycle borrows Hess's law from Unit 6; the 2.3 EK does not name lattice energy or the cycle.

cards.q: Explain why ionic solids are hard but brittle.
cards.a: Each ion is held by strong Coulombic attractions to oppositely charged neighbors in all directions, so the lattice resists deformation (hard). If a layer slides by one ion spacing, cations meet cations and anions meet anions; the sudden like-charge repulsion splits the crystal (brittle).
cards.h: → strong attractions in all directions → hard; shifted layer → like charges meet → repulsion cleaves
cards.n: 'Ionic bonds are strong' explains hardness only; the brittleness point needs the shifted layer bringing like charges together.
o: The regular alternating array is what makes the solid strong, and the same array makes any displacement catastrophic because it destroys the alternation.
Unlike a metal, whose electron sea still binds a shifted layer, an ionic lattice has no way to keep attraction across a slipped plane.

w.a: Ionic solids are brittle because their bonds are weak and break easily.
w.why: the attractions are very strong; the cleavage comes from repulsion after a shift

w.a: Ionic solids are hard and brittle because they are made of crystals.
w.why: metals are crystalline too and are not brittle; no force argument

w.a: Ionic solids shatter because the ions are too big to move.
w.why: size is irrelevant; a layer that does move meets like charges

cards.q: Explain why an ionic compound conducts electricity when molten or dissolved but not as a solid.
cards.a: Electrical conduction needs mobile charged particles. In the solid every ion is locked in a fixed lattice position by the surrounding opposite charges, so no charge can move. Melting or dissolving frees the ions to move independently, and the mobile cations and anions then carry the current.
cards.h: → conduction needs mobile charge → solid ions fixed → melt or solution frees them
cards.n: 'The solid has no charges' earns nothing: the charges are there, the point is that they cannot move until the lattice is broken up.
o: The charge carriers are the ions themselves, so they must be able to migrate, which is possible only in the liquid or the solution.
Solid NaCl is an insulator because its ions can only vibrate about fixed sites; molten NaCl conducts because the ions flow.

w.a: Molten ionic compounds conduct because heating releases their electrons.
w.why: the carriers are ions, not electrons; the ions do not lose electrons on melting

w.a: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because they contain no ions until dissolved.
w.why: the solid is made of ions already; they are just immobile

w.a: Ionic compounds conduct in water because water is a good conductor.
w.why: pure water is a poor conductor; the dissolved ions carry the current

cards.q: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
cards.a: Melting frees ions from their lattice sites, which means overcoming the strong Coulombic attractions between each ion and its many oppositely charged neighbors throughout the 3-D array. These attractions far exceed the intermolecular forces in a molecular solid, so a high temperature is needed.
cards.h: → melting frees ions → must overcome Coulombic attraction throughout the lattice → large energy
cards.n: 'Ionic bonds are strong' with no mention of what melting has to overcome, or a comparison to covalent bond strength, earns nothing.
o: Each ion is attracted to several neighbors at once, so disrupting the array costs far more energy than separating neutral molecules.
The energy needed scales with the lattice energy, which is large because the ions carry full charges at short distances.

w.a: Ionic compounds have high melting points because they are solids at room temperature.
w.why: restates the observation; no reason given

w.a: Ionic compounds have high melting points because ionic bonds are stronger than covalent bonds.
w.why: a covalent bond can be stronger; the point is the lattice-wide attraction that melting must overcome

w.a: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the ions are heavy.
w.why: mass has no bearing on the attraction between ions

cards.q: Explain why CaO has a much higher melting point than NaCl, using the factors that determine lattice energy.
cards.a: CaO is made of Ca²⁺ and O²⁻, a charge product of 4 versus 1 for Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so by Coulomb's law the ion–ion attraction and the lattice energy (about 3414 vs 788 kJ/mol) are far larger. More thermal energy is needed to free the ions: CaO melts near 2600 °C, NaCl at 801 °C.
cards.h: → 2+/2− versus 1+/1− → four-fold charge product → larger lattice energy → higher mp
cards.n: 'Calcium is more reactive' or 'CaO has stronger covalent bonds' earns nothing; the point is the ion charges in Coulomb's law.
o: Doubling both charges quadruples the Coulombic attraction, and the ion radii are similar, so charge decides.
Melting point rises with lattice energy, and lattice energy is dominated by the charge product.

w.a: CaO melts higher because oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine.
w.why: electronegativity is about bond polarity, not lattice attraction

w.a: CaO melts higher because calcium atoms are larger than sodium atoms.
w.why: larger ions would weaken the attraction; and Ca²⁺ is about the size of Na⁺

w.a: CaO melts higher because it has fewer ions per formula unit.
w.why: ion count per formula unit is not a Coulombic variable

cards.q: Explain why lattice energy generally correlates with the boiling point of an ionic compound.
cards.a: Both depend on the same attraction. Lattice energy measures how strongly the ions attract one another; boiling separates the ions into the gas, which means overcoming essentially those same Coulombic attractions. A larger lattice energy therefore needs more thermal energy, so a higher boiling point.
cards.h: → same Coulombic attraction governs both → larger lattice energy → more energy to separate ions → higher bp
cards.n: 'Higher lattice energy means stronger bonds so higher boiling point' is circular unless it says the boiling process separates the ions that the lattice energy binds.
o: Melting and boiling both loosen or separate the ions, so both track the strength of the ion–ion attraction that lattice energy quantifies.
Compounds with larger charges or smaller ions have larger lattice energies and, in the same way, higher melting and boiling points.

w.a: Lattice energy and boiling point are related because both are measured in kJ.
w.why: boiling point is a temperature; units are not a mechanism

w.a: They correlate because a high lattice energy makes the compound heavier.
w.why: lattice energy does not change the mass

w.a: They correlate because lattice energy is released when the compound boils.
w.why: boiling absorbs energy; lattice energy is released when the solid forms

cards.q: Explain why the ions in an ionic crystal arrange themselves in a regular, alternating array rather than randomly.
cards.a: Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. A regular array in which every cation is surrounded by anions and every anion by cations keeps attracting pairs close and repelling pairs apart, which gives the lowest potential energy; a random arrangement would put like charges in contact and raise it.
cards.h: → opposite charges attract, like repel → alternating neighbors maximize attraction, minimize repulsion → lowest energy
cards.n: 'Because that is the crystal structure' or naming a cubic lattice earns nothing (specific structures are excluded); the point is the energy argument.
o: The systematic 3-D array is the arrangement that maximizes the attractive forces among cations and anions while minimizing the repulsive ones.
Any like-charge contact costs energy, so the ions settle into the pattern that avoids it everywhere.

w.a: The ions form a regular array because ionic compounds are always crystalline solids.
w.why: restates the observation

w.a: The ions form a regular array because each ion shares electrons with its neighbors.
w.why: ions do not share electrons; the array is held by electrostatic attraction

w.a: The ions arrange randomly but look regular under a microscope.
w.why: false; the periodic array is what X-ray patterns and cleavage planes reveal

cards.q: Explain why a correct particulate model of sodium chloride draws the chloride ion larger than the sodium ion, even though a sodium atom is larger than a chlorine atom.
cards.a: Forming Na⁺ removes sodium's only n = 3 electron, leaving two occupied shells held tightly by 11 protons, so the ion shrinks. Forming Cl⁻ adds an electron to chlorine's third shell, raising electron–electron repulsion, so the ion expands: Na⁺ is about 102 pm and Cl⁻ about 181 pm.
cards.h: → Na⁺ loses its outer shell → shrinks; Cl⁻ gains an electron → more repulsion → expands
cards.n: 'Chlorine is heavier' earns nothing; the point is the shell lost by the cation and the electron gained by the anion (Unit 1 radius reasoning).
o: Cations are smaller than their atoms and anions larger, so the anion usually dominates the volume of a simple salt.
Na⁺ has 10 electrons held by 11 protons; Cl⁻ has 18 electrons held by 17 protons, so its outer shell is held less tightly and extends farther.

w.a: Cl⁻ is drawn larger because chlorine has more protons than sodium.
w.why: more protons alone would make it smaller; the shell count and the extra electron matter

w.a: Cl⁻ is drawn larger because negative ions are always larger than positive ions.
w.why: a rule of thumb, not a reason, and false across periods (e.g. Cs⁺ is larger than F⁻)

w.a: Cl⁻ is drawn larger because the sodium ion gives its size to the chloride ion.
w.why: nonsense mechanism; size follows electron shells and effective attraction

cards.q: Explain metallic bonding using the sea-of-electrons model and use it to account for two metal properties.
cards.a: A metal is a lattice of cations with the valence electrons delocalized over the whole solid, belonging to no single atom; the attraction between the cations and this electron sea is the metallic bond. Conductivity: the mobile electrons carry charge (and thermal energy) through the solid. Malleability and ductility: the bonding is nondirectional, so layers of cations can slide while the sea keeps binding them, and the metal deforms instead of shattering.
cards.h: → the model, then one mechanism per property
cards.n: 'Metals conduct because they are metals' or 'because metallic bonds are strong' earns nothing; each property must be traced to the delocalized electrons.

cards.q: Contrast a substitutional alloy with an interstitial alloy.
cards.a: In a substitutional alloy the added atoms have a radius comparable to the host's and take the place of host atoms at lattice sites (brass: Zn replaces some Cu; Cu 128 pm, Zn 134 pm). In an interstitial alloy the added atoms are much smaller and sit in the holes (interstices) between the host atoms without displacing them (steel: C in the gaps of the Fe lattice; Fe 126 pm, C 77 pm). Both keep the delocalized electron sea and are metallic.
cards.h: → two mechanisms, each with radius rule and an example
cards.n: Swapping the examples (calling steel substitutional) or omitting the size comparison that decides which forms earns nothing.

cards.q: Define an alloy.
cards.a: An alloy is a solid mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (metal or nonmetal) that keeps metallic properties because the delocalized electron sea persists. It is classified by how the added atoms fit in the lattice: substitutional when they replace host atoms of similar radius (brass, Cu/Zn), interstitial when much smaller atoms fill the gaps between host atoms (steel, Fe/C).
cards.h: → mixture, metallic, then the two types with examples
cards.n: Calling an alloy a compound earns nothing: its composition can vary continuously, so it is a mixture (solid solution), not a fixed formula.

cards.q: Identify whether steel, in which carbon atoms occupy gaps in an iron lattice, is a substitutional or interstitial alloy.
cards.a: Interstitial. Carbon atoms (about 77 pm) are much smaller than iron atoms (about 126 pm), so they fit into the interstitial spaces between the Fe atoms rather than replacing them at lattice sites. The trapped carbon atoms hinder the Fe layers from sliding, which is why steel is harder and stronger than pure iron.
cards.h: → label + radius comparison + consequence
cards.n: Answering 'substitutional because carbon replaces iron' earns nothing; the question itself says carbon sits in the gaps, and the radii confirm it.

cards.q: Identify whether brass, made of copper and zinc, is a substitutional or interstitial alloy.
cards.a: Substitutional. Copper (about 128 pm) and zinc (about 134 pm) atoms are of comparable radius, so zinc atoms take the place of copper atoms at lattice sites instead of squeezing into the interstices, which are far too small for an atom of that size. The delocalized electrons of both metals form the shared sea.
cards.h: → label + radius comparison
cards.n: 'Interstitial because zinc is the minor component' earns nothing; the amount added does not decide, the relative radii do.

cards.q: Represent a particulate model of a piece of solid copper, describing the drawing precisely enough to reproduce.
cards.a: A regular, closely packed array of identical circles, each marked with a + sign to show a copper cation core, in straight repeating rows. Between and around the circles, many small dots or a light shading labeled e⁻, spread evenly through the whole array and not attached to any one circle, representing the delocalized valence electrons (the electron sea). No bonds drawn between circles and no molecules.
cards.h: → cation cores in an array + electrons everywhere
cards.n: Drawing each atom with its own electrons, or lines for bonds between atoms, earns nothing; the essential feature is that the valence electrons are delocalized over the whole array.

cards.q: Represent a particulate model of brass, a substitutional alloy of copper with zinc, describing how it differs from the drawing of pure copper.
cards.a: The same regular array of cation circles with delocalized electrons dotted throughout, but a fraction of the copper circles are replaced, at their own lattice positions, by circles of nearly the same size labeled Zn (shaded differently). The Zn circles are scattered through the array, not clustered or in gaps, and the rows stay aligned. The electron sea surrounds both kinds of cation.
cards.h: → same lattice, some sites swapped for similar-size Zn
cards.n: Putting the Zn circles in the spaces between Cu circles describes an interstitial alloy and earns nothing for brass; Zn is comparable in size to Cu and substitutes.

cards.q: Represent a particulate model of steel, an interstitial alloy of iron with carbon, describing how it differs from the drawing of pure iron.
cards.a: The regular array of large Fe cation circles with delocalized electrons dotted throughout is unchanged; in addition, a few much smaller circles labeled C sit in the gaps between the Fe circles (the interstices), not on Fe lattice sites and not displacing any Fe. The C circles are drawn clearly smaller than the Fe circles, and the electron sea still fills the array.
cards.h: → same host array + small C in the gaps
cards.n: Drawing carbon the same size as iron, or replacing Fe atoms with C, earns nothing; an interstitial alloy needs a large size difference and atoms in the holes.

cards.q: Predict whether each alloy is substitutional or interstitial from the atomic radii (pm) given: brass Cu 128 / Zn 134 · steel Fe 126 / C 77 · bronze Cu 128 / Sn 140 · sterling silver Ag 144 / Cu 128 · nitrided iron Fe 126 / N 71 · cupronickel Cu 128 / Ni 124 · palladium hydride Pd 137 / H 37 · 14-karat gold Au 144 / Ag 144 / Cu 128
cards.a:
brass → substitutional (Zn within about 5% of Cu)
steel → interstitial (C is about 60% of Fe; fits the gaps)
bronze → substitutional (Sn about 9% larger than Cu; takes lattice sites)
sterling silver → substitutional (Cu about 11% smaller than Ag)
nitrided iron → interstitial (N far smaller than Fe)
cupronickel → substitutional (Ni within 3% of Cu)
palladium hydride → interstitial (H is tiny; fills the interstices)
14-karat gold → substitutional (Ag and Cu comparable to Au)
Rule: comparable radii (roughly within 15%) substitute; a much smaller atom (nonmetals such as H, C, N) goes interstitial.
cards.h: → similar radii substitute; much smaller go interstitial
cards.n: Classifying by 'metal + metal is substitutional, metal + nonmetal is interstitial' happens to work here but is not the reason; the CED's criterion is the relative radius.

cards.q: Identify which of these four particulate diagrams shows a pure metal, a substitutional alloy, an interstitial alloy, and an ionic solid: (A) identical large circles in rows with small dots spread between them; (B) alternating large and small circles labeled + and −, no dots; (C) large circles in rows with a few much smaller circles in the gaps, dots spread throughout; (D) rows of large circles with some replaced by circles of similar size but a different shade, dots spread throughout.
cards.a: A pure metal; D substitutional alloy; C interstitial alloy; B ionic solid. The dots (delocalized electrons) mark the three metallic drawings; B has none and instead alternates charged particles, as Coulomb's law requires for an ionic lattice. In D the added atoms replace host atoms at lattice sites (comparable radius); in C the added atoms are much smaller and occupy the holes between host atoms.
cards.h: → dots = metal; charges = ionic; replaced vs in-gap
cards.n: Mixing up C and D is the common slip: look at whether the added circle sits on a lattice site (substitutional) or in a gap (interstitial), not at how many there are.
x: A metal, D substitutional, C interstitial, B ionic

cards.q: Explain whether a student's model of solid sodium is consistent with metallic bonding: each Na circle is drawn with its own single valence electron attached to it, and no electrons are drawn between the circles.
cards.a: Not consistent. In a metallic solid the valence electrons are delocalized: they are spread over the whole lattice and are not associated with any individual atom. A model with each electron pinned to its own atom describes isolated atoms and would predict no electrical conductivity and no malleability. The electrons should be drawn spread throughout the array of Na⁺ cores.
cards.h: → verdict, what the model gets wrong, the fix
cards.n: 'It is wrong because sodium has more electrons' misses the point; the error is localization of the valence electrons, which the metallic model forbids.

cards.q: Identify the charge carriers when a solid metal conducts electricity and when a molten ionic compound conducts electricity, and explain the difference at the particulate level.
cards.a: Metal: delocalized valence electrons. Molten ionic compound: the cations and anions themselves. In the metal the electrons are free to drift through the fixed lattice of cations, so the solid conducts. In the ionic compound the electrons are held on individual ions, so nothing moves until the lattice is melted and the whole ions can migrate.
cards.h: → electrons vs ions, then why each is mobile
cards.n: Saying 'both conduct because they contain ions' earns nothing; in a metal the cations stay put and the electrons move.

cards.q: Explain why alloys are generally harder and less malleable than the pure metal.
cards.a: Atoms of a different size disrupt the regular lattice: an interstitial atom wedges between host atoms and a substituted atom of different radius distorts the rows. Layers can then no longer slide smoothly past one another under stress, so the alloy is harder and less malleable.
cards.h: → foreign atoms disrupt the regular lattice → layers cannot slide as easily → harder, less malleable
cards.n: 'The added atoms make stronger bonds' earns nothing; the point is that a distorted lattice resists the sliding of layers.
o: In pure copper every row is identical, so rows slip easily; zinc atoms of a different size in brass pin the rows.
Carbon in the interstices of iron locks neighboring Fe layers together, which is why steel is harder than iron.

w.a: Alloys are harder because mixing two metals adds their strengths together.
w.why: strength is not additive; the point is lattice disruption

w.a: Alloys are harder because the added element forms ionic bonds with the host metal.
w.why: an alloy stays metallic; no ionic bonds form

w.a: Alloys are harder because they contain more atoms.
w.why: atom count is irrelevant; the size mismatch is what blocks slipping

cards.q: Explain why metals are malleable and ductile using the electron-sea model.
cards.a: Metallic bonding is nondirectional: each cation is attracted to the delocalized electron sea, not to specific neighbors. When the metal is hammered or drawn, layers of cations slide, but every cation is still surrounded by the same sea, so the attraction persists and the metal deforms without breaking.
cards.h: → nondirectional attraction to the electron sea → layers slide → attraction preserved → deform without fracture
cards.n: 'Metal atoms can move' earns nothing without saying why the bonding survives the move; contrast the ionic case where a shift brings like charges together.
o: A slipped layer in a metal meets the same electron sea it left, unlike a slipped layer in an ionic crystal, which meets like charges and cleaves.
Because no bond points in a fixed direction, rearranging the cations costs little energy.

w.a: Metals are malleable because metallic bonds are weak and easily broken.
w.why: the bonds are not broken; the attraction to the electron sea persists during slipping

w.a: Metals are malleable because their atoms are soft.
w.why: 'soft atoms' is not a mechanism

w.a: Metals are malleable because the electrons push the atoms apart when hit.
w.why: the electrons hold the cations together; they do not separate them

cards.q: Explain why metals are good conductors of both heat and electricity using the electron-sea model.
cards.a: The valence electrons are delocalized and free to move through the whole lattice of cations. Under a voltage they drift and carry the current; heated at one end, fast-moving electrons travel through the solid and pass kinetic energy to cations and electrons elsewhere, so heat spreads quickly.
cards.h: → delocalized electrons mobile → carry charge under a voltage and carry kinetic energy through the solid
cards.n: 'Metals have free electrons' earns the electrical point only if it says they move under the voltage; the thermal point needs the electrons carrying energy through the lattice.
o: One feature, mobile electrons, explains both: charge transport gives electrical conductivity, energy transport gives thermal conductivity.
In an ionic or molecular solid no particle is free to move, which is why those solids conduct neither.

w.a: Metals conduct because their cations move through the solid carrying charge.
w.why: the cations are fixed; the electrons move

w.a: Metals conduct heat because metal atoms vibrate more than other atoms.
w.why: all solids vibrate; the delocalized electrons are what transport energy fast

w.a: Metals conduct electricity because metallic bonds are strong.
w.why: bond strength is not the mechanism; mobility of the electrons is

cards.q: Explain why metals are lustrous (shiny) using the electron-sea model.
cards.a: The delocalized electrons are not confined to fixed energy levels of single atoms, so they can absorb light of essentially any visible wavelength and immediately re-emit it from the surface. Because all visible wavelengths are reflected this way, the surface appears bright and mirror-like.
cards.h: → delocalized electrons absorb visible light freely → re-emit at the surface → reflective appearance
cards.n: 'Metals are polished' earns nothing; the point is the mobile electron sea interacting with light. Luster is not named in the EK, so it is lower priority.
o: The same mobile electrons that carry current respond to the oscillating electric field of light and re-radiate it.
Molecular and ionic solids lack free electrons, so they transmit or absorb light instead of reflecting it.

w.a: Metals are shiny because they are smooth.
w.why: a rough metal surface is still lustrous where it is clean; no electron argument

w.a: Metals are shiny because their cations reflect light.
w.why: the cations are fixed cores; the electrons interact with the light

w.a: Metals are shiny because they emit their own light.
w.why: metals reflect incident light; they do not glow at room temperature

cards.q: Explain why an alloy such as brass still conducts electricity even though it is harder than pure copper.
cards.a: Alloying changes the arrangement of the cation cores, not the kind of bonding: Zn atoms take lattice sites and add their valence electrons to the delocalized sea, so mobile electrons still carry current. Hardness comes from the distorted lattice resisting slip, a separate effect from electron mobility.
cards.h: → electron sea persists (Zn adds electrons) → mobile carriers remain; hardness is a lattice-slip effect
cards.n: 'It conducts because copper conducts' earns nothing; the point is that the delocalized electrons survive alloying while the lattice regularity does not.
o: Conductivity needs delocalized electrons and both metals supply them; malleability needs a regular lattice, which the alloy disrupts.
The two properties depend on different features of the model, so one can change while the other remains.

w.a: Brass conducts because it contains ions that move.
w.why: the cation cores are fixed; the electrons carry the current

w.a: Brass conducts because zinc is a better conductor than copper.
w.why: false and irrelevant; the point is that the electron sea persists

w.a: Brass conducts less than copper because alloys have no electron sea.
w.why: an alloy is still metallic; the sea remains

cards.q: Explain why a substitutional alloy forms between atoms of comparable radius while an interstitial alloy requires a large difference in radius.
cards.a: An atom can take a host's lattice site without badly distorting the array only if its radius is comparable (Cu 128, Zn 134 pm). The holes between host atoms are much smaller than the atoms, so only a much smaller atom (C 77 pm in Fe 126 pm) fits an interstice without pushing the host atoms apart.
cards.h: → lattice sites fit similar sizes → substitution; interstices are small → only small atoms fit
cards.n: 'Metals substitute and nonmetals go in the gaps' is a correlation, not the reason; the size of the site versus the size of the atom is the point.
o: The gaps in a metal lattice are a fraction of the host radius, so H, C and N fit but Zn does not.
A large atom in an interstice or a tiny atom on a lattice site would distort the array so much that the arrangement is unstable.

w.a: Substitutional alloys form when both elements are metals and interstitial alloys when one is a nonmetal.
w.why: the CED's criterion is relative radius, not metal versus nonmetal

w.a: Interstitial alloys need small atoms because small atoms are more reactive.
w.why: reactivity is irrelevant; the atom must physically fit the hole

w.a: Substitutional alloys form because the two metals have the same electronegativity.
w.why: electronegativity is not the criterion; radius is

cards.q: State the procedure for drawing a Lewis structure.
cards.a: Five steps. (1) Total the valence electrons, adding one per negative charge and subtracting one per positive charge. (2) Place the least electronegative atom (never H) in the center and join each outer atom to it by a single bond. (3) Complete the octets of the outer atoms (H takes 2). (4) Put leftover electrons on the central atom as lone pairs. (5) If the central atom still lacks an octet, turn outer lone pairs into double or triple bonds.
cards.h: → five numbered steps, then a recount
cards.n: Skipping the final recount is the classic loss: the finished diagram must hold exactly the step-1 total, however reasonable it looks.

cards.q: Apply valence-electron counting to draw the Lewis structure of a polyatomic ion such as SO₄²⁻.
cards.a: 32 electrons: S 6 + four O × 6 = 30, plus 2 for the 2− charge. Drawing: S in the center joined to four O atoms by single bonds (8 electrons); each O carries three lone pairs (24) and S none, which uses all 32 and gives every atom an octet. Enclose the structure in square brackets with 2− at the upper right.
cards.h: → count with the charge, place 32 electrons, brackets
cards.n: Subtracting 2 for the 2− charge (28 electrons) is the classic slip: a negative charge means extra electrons. Subtract only for a cation (NH₄⁺: 5 + 4 − 1 = 8).

cards.q: Identify the common exceptions to the octet rule.
cards.a: Three kinds. Incomplete octets: H holds only 2 electrons, Be 4 (BeCl₂) and B 6 (BF₃). Expanded octets: a central atom from period 3 or below (P, S, Cl, Br, I, Xe) can hold more than 8, as in PCl₅ (10), SF₆ (12) and XeF₄ (12), while C, N, O and F never exceed 8. Odd-electron species: NO (11 valence electrons) and NO₂ (17) cannot give every atom an octet.
cards.h: → three categories, each with examples
cards.n: Explaining expanded octets with d orbitals or sp³d hybrids goes past the CED, which excludes d-orbital hybridization; just note that period-3 and lower atoms can exceed 8.

cards.q: Identify why boron in $BF_3$ is an exception to the octet rule.
cards.a: Boron has an incomplete octet, only 6 electrons. BF₃ has 3 + 3(7) = 24 valence electrons: three B–F single bonds use 6 and three lone pairs on each F use 18, leaving none for boron. Moving an F lone pair into a B=F double bond would complete boron's octet but put a +1 formal charge on F, the most electronegative element, so the 6-electron structure is the accepted model.
cards.h: → count, place, then why no double bond
cards.n: Adding a lone pair to boron to 'complete the octet' needs 26 electrons, not 24: the total is fixed, the octet is not. The formal-charge point borrows Topic 2.6.

cards.q: Determine the total number of valence electrons to be shown in the Lewis diagram of each species: CH₄ · NH₃ · H₂O · CO₂ · HCN · N₂ · SO₂ · NO₃⁻ · NH₄⁺ · OH⁻ · CO₃²⁻ · PO₄³⁻ · ClO₄⁻ · H₃O⁺ · SF₄ · XeF₄ · CN⁻ · NO₂⁺
cards.a:
CH₄ → 4 + 4(1) = 8
NH₃ → 5 + 3(1) = 8
H₂O → 2(1) + 6 = 8
CO₂ → 4 + 2(6) = 16
HCN → 1 + 4 + 5 = 10
N₂ → 2(5) = 10
SO₂ → 6 + 2(6) = 18
NO₃⁻ → 5 + 3(6) + 1 = 24
NH₄⁺ → 5 + 4(1) − 1 = 8
OH⁻ → 6 + 1 + 1 = 8
CO₃²⁻ → 4 + 3(6) + 2 = 24
PO₄³⁻ → 5 + 4(6) + 3 = 32
ClO₄⁻ → 7 + 4(6) + 1 = 32
H₃O⁺ → 3(1) + 6 − 1 = 8
SF₄ → 6 + 4(7) = 34
XeF₄ → 8 + 4(7) = 36
CN⁻ → 4 + 5 + 1 = 10
NO₂⁺ → 5 + 2(6) − 1 = 16
Rule: a main-group atom brings the last digit of its group number (group 1 → 1, group 14 → 4, group 17 → 7); add one electron per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge.
cards.h: → group valence sums, then ± the charge
cards.n: Counting all electrons (CO₂ = 22) instead of valence electrons, or adding electrons for a positive charge, earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the central atom (or the chain of central atoms) in the Lewis diagram of each species: HCN · H₂CO · NO₃⁻ · SOCl₂ · POCl₃ · ClO₂⁻ · SCN⁻ · N₂O · SiH₄ · XeOF₄ · H₂O₂ · N₂H₄ · CH₃OH · HOCl
cards.a:
HCN → C (H–C≡N; H is always terminal)
H₂CO → C (bonded to 2 H and to O)
NO₃⁻ → N
SOCl₂ → S (less electronegative than O and Cl)
POCl₃ → P
ClO₂⁻ → Cl (O–Cl–O)
SCN⁻ → C (S–C–N; C is least electronegative)
