N₂O → N (N–N–O; the less electronegative element takes the center)
SiH₄ → Si
XeOF₄ → Xe
H₂O₂ → both O, chain H–O–O–H
N₂H₄ → both N, chain H₂N–NH₂
CH₃OH → C and O, chain H₃C–O–H
HOCl → O (H–O–Cl)
Rule: the least electronegative atom other than H goes in the center, usually the one that appears once; in oxyacids H bonds to O, which is why HOCl is H–O–Cl although Cl is less electronegative than O.
cards.h: → least electronegative, never H, symmetric skeleton
cards.n: Putting H in the center earns nothing, since H forms one bond. HOCl breaks the 'least electronegative' rule: in oxyacids the H is bonded to O.

cards.q: Represent the Lewis diagram of each species in words, giving every bond and the lone pairs on every atom: H₂O · NH₃ · CH₄ · HF · N₂ · HCN · CO₂ · H₂CO · C₂H₄ · C₂H₂ · CH₃OH · H₂O₂ · NH₄⁺ · OH⁻ · CN⁻
cards.a:
H₂O → O central, two O–H single bonds, 2 lone pairs on O
NH₃ → three N–H, 1 lone pair on N
CH₄ → four C–H, no lone pairs
HF → H–F, 3 lone pairs on F
N₂ → N≡N, 1 lone pair on each N
HCN → H–C≡N, 1 lone pair on N, none on C
CO₂ → O=C=O, 2 lone pairs on each O
H₂CO → C with two C–H and a C=O; 2 lone pairs on O
C₂H₄ → H₂C=CH₂, each C with two C–H; no lone pairs
C₂H₂ → H–C≡C–H; no lone pairs
CH₃OH → C with three C–H and one C–O; O with O–H and 2 lone pairs
H₂O₂ → H–O–O–H, 2 lone pairs on each O
NH₄⁺ → four N–H, no lone pair; brackets, + outside
OH⁻ → O–H, 3 lone pairs on O; brackets, − outside
CN⁻ → C≡N, 1 lone pair on C and 1 on N; brackets, − outside
Check: every C, N, O and F has 8 electrons, every H has 2.
cards.h: → skeleton, bonds, then lone pairs atom by atom
cards.n: A diagram with the right bonds but missing lone pairs on O, N or F earns nothing: every lone pair is drawn, and the electron total must match the count.

cards.q: Represent the Lewis diagram of each species whose central atom holds more than eight electrons, giving the total valence electrons, the bonds, and the lone pairs on the central atom (every F or Cl, and each terminal I, carries three lone pairs): PCl₅ · SF₆ · SF₄ · ClF₃ · XeF₂ · XeF₄ · BrF₅ · I₃⁻ · ICl₄⁻
cards.a:
PCl₅ → 40; five P–Cl single bonds, no lone pair on P (10 electrons around P)
SF₆ → 48; six S–F, no lone pair on S (12)
SF₄ → 34; four S–F, 1 lone pair on S (10)
ClF₃ → 28; three Cl–F, 2 lone pairs on Cl (10)
XeF₂ → 22; two Xe–F, 3 lone pairs on Xe (10)
XeF₄ → 36; four Xe–F, 2 lone pairs on Xe (12)
BrF₅ → 42; five Br–F, 1 lone pair on Br (12)
I₃⁻ → 22; I–I–I with two single bonds, 3 lone pairs on the central I (10); brackets, 1−
ICl₄⁻ → 36; four I–Cl, 2 lone pairs on I (12); brackets, 1−
Method: single-bond every outer atom, give each outer atom its octet, then put all leftover electrons on the central atom as lone pairs.
cards.h: → count, outer octets first, leftovers on the center
cards.n: Stopping at 8 electrons on S, Cl, Xe or I strands the leftovers, and the recount exposes it. Never expand the octet of C, N, O or F, which are period-2 atoms.

cards.q: Calculate the number of shared electrons and bonds in CO₂, HCN and N₂ by the needed-minus-available method (needed: 8 electrons for each C, N or O and 2 for each H; available: the valence electrons), and state which bonds must be multiple bonds.
cards.a: CO₂: needed 3 × 8 = 24, available 16, shared 8 electrons = 4 bonds; two O atoms share them, so O=C=O. HCN: needed 2 + 8 + 8 = 18, available 10, shared 8 = 4 bonds; H takes one, so C≡N is triple. N₂: needed 16, available 10, shared 6 = 3 bonds, N≡N. Lone-pair electrons = available − shared: 8 (two pairs on each O), 2 (one pair on N), 4 (one pair on each N).
cards.h: → needed − available = shared; ÷ 2 = bonds
cards.n: The shortcut fails for incomplete and expanded octets (BF₃, PCl₅): use it only when every atom obeys the octet (H the duet).

cards.q: Represent the Lewis diagram of acetic acid, CH₃COOH, describing every bond and every lone pair, and check the electron count.
cards.a: 24 valence electrons (2 C × 4 + 2 O × 6 + 4 H × 1). The CH₃ carbon has three C–H bonds and a single bond to the second carbon; the second carbon has a C=O double bond to one oxygen and a C–O single bond to the other, which is bonded to H. The C=O oxygen carries 2 lone pairs, the O–H oxygen 2 lone pairs, and neither carbon has any. Check: 6 single bonds (12) + 1 double bond (4) + 4 lone pairs (8) = 24.
cards.h: → skeleton, bonds, lone pairs, recount
cards.n: Giving both oxygens single bonds leaves the carboxyl carbon with 6 electrons; the C=O double bond is what completes its octet.

cards.q: Identify what is wrong with each student Lewis diagram and give the correct one: (i) CO₂ drawn as O–C–O with single bonds, three lone pairs on each O and one lone pair on C; (ii) HCN drawn as H–C=N with one lone pair on C and two on N; (iii) NH₃ drawn with three N–H bonds and no lone pair.
cards.a: (i) It shows 18 electrons for a 16-electron molecule and leaves C with only 6; correct: O=C=O with 2 lone pairs on each O. (ii) Every atom has an octet, but it shows 12 electrons for a 10-electron molecule; correct: H–C≡N with 1 lone pair on N. (iii) It shows 6 electrons for an 8-electron molecule and leaves N with 6; correct: add a lone pair on N.
cards.h: → recount, check each octet, give the fix
cards.n: Checking octets alone misses (ii): every atom has 8, yet the diagram holds 12 electrons for a 10-electron molecule. Always recount against the valence total.

cards.q: Identify the bonding pattern (number of bonds and lone pairs) each atom usually shows in a neutral molecule: H · C · N · O · F · Cl, Br or I as a terminal atom · B · Be · Si · P with an octet · S with an octet
cards.a:
H → 1 bond, 0 lone pairs (duet)
C → 4 bonds, 0 lone pairs (four single, two double, or one triple + one single)
N → 3 bonds, 1 lone pair
O → 2 bonds, 2 lone pairs
F → 1 bond, 3 lone pairs
Cl, Br, I (terminal) → 1 bond, 3 lone pairs
B → 3 bonds, 0 lone pairs (6 electrons, incomplete octet)
Be → 2 bonds, 0 lone pairs (4 electrons)
Si → 4 bonds, 0 lone pairs, like C
P (octet) → 3 bonds, 1 lone pair, like N
S (octet) → 2 bonds, 2 lone pairs, like O
Reason: bonds + lone pairs complete the octet, so for groups 14 to 17 the number of bonds is 8 minus the valence electrons. An atom that breaks its pattern carries a formal charge (Topic 2.6), as the O in H₃O⁺ (3 bonds, 1 lone pair) does.
cards.h: → bonds = 8 − valence electrons for groups 14–17
cards.n: The patterns are a check, not a law: CO (:C≡O:), H₃O⁺ and NH₄⁺ break them, and the atoms that break them carry formal charges.

cards.q: Explain why a hydrogen atom is never the central atom in a Lewis diagram.
cards.a: Hydrogen has one valence electron in the n = 1 shell, which holds only 2 electrons. One shared pair fills it, so hydrogen forms exactly one bond and has no room for a second. A central atom must bond to at least two others, so H always sits at the end of a chain.
cards.h: → one valence electron, n = 1 holds 2 → one bond fills it → cannot join two atoms
cards.n: 'Hydrogen is too small' names no electron reason; the scored idea is that a single bond fills hydrogen's duet.
o: After one bond hydrogen already has the 2 electrons of a full first shell, so it cannot share a second pair.
Every correct Lewis diagram shows H with exactly one bond, so it can only be terminal.

w.a: Hydrogen is never central because it is always written first in a formula.
w.why: formula order does not decide bonding; HCN starts with H yet C is central

w.a: Hydrogen is never central because it has no lone pairs to share.
w.why: central atoms share bonding electrons; the limit is hydrogen's one-bond capacity

w.a: Hydrogen is never central because it only forms ionic bonds.
w.why: H forms covalent bonds in H₂O, CH₄ and HCl

cards.q: Explain why the least electronegative atom other than hydrogen is usually placed at the center of a Lewis diagram.
cards.a: The central atom shares electrons with several neighbors. A less electronegative atom holds its electrons less tightly and, within a period, has fewer valence electrons, so it needs more bonds to reach an octet (C needs 4, F needs 1). Strongly electronegative atoms need only one or two bonds and sit at the edges.
cards.h: → center must form the most bonds → lower-EN atom has fewer valence electrons, needs more bonds → it goes in the middle
cards.n: 'Because it is written first' is a habit, not a reason; and HOCl shows the rule can fail, since H bonds to O in oxyacids.
o: The atom able to form the most bonds belongs in the center, and in a period that is the one with the fewest valence electrons, which is also the least electronegative.
Putting the most electronegative atoms on the outside lets them keep lone pairs, which matches their strong pull on electrons.

w.a: The least electronegative atom goes in the center because it is the largest atom.
w.why: size is not the criterion; the number of bonds needed is

w.a: The least electronegative atom goes in the center because it has the most lone pairs.
w.why: backwards; central atoms usually carry fewer lone pairs

w.a: The least electronegative atom goes in the center because electronegative atoms repel each other.
w.why: not an electron-sharing argument; outer atoms are placed by bond capacity

cards.q: Explain why sulfur can be surrounded by 12 electrons in SF₆ while oxygen never has more than 8 electrons around it.
cards.a: Sulfur is a period-3 atom: it is larger, so six F atoms fit around it, and its valence shell (n = 3) is not limited to the one s and three p orbitals that cap a period-2 atom at 8 electrons. Oxygen's valence shell is n = 2, whose 2s and 2p orbitals hold at most 8, and the small O atom has room for few neighbors.
cards.h: → S is period 3: larger atom, n = 3 shell not capped at 8; O is period 2: 2s + 2p hold only 8
cards.n: Invoking sp³d² hybrid orbitals goes past the CED, which excludes d-orbital hybridization; the size and period argument earns the point.
o: Expanded octets appear only on central atoms from period 3 down, such as P, S, Cl and Xe, because period-2 atoms have only four valence orbitals.
SF₆ exists but OF₆ does not, which is the size and period argument in one comparison.

w.a: Sulfur can have 12 electrons because it is less electronegative than oxygen.
w.why: electronegativity does not set how many electrons fit around an atom

w.a: Oxygen cannot exceed 8 because it already has 6 valence electrons.
w.why: sulfur also has 6 valence electrons; the period, not the group, differs

w.a: Sulfur has 12 electrons because each fluorine gives it two extra electrons.
w.why: each bond is one shared pair; the question is how much room sulfur has

cards.q: Explain why the Lewis diagram of N₂ must contain a triple bond.
cards.a: N₂ has only 10 valence electrons. With a single bond, octets on both N would need 14 electrons (one bond + six lone pairs); a double bond would still need 12. Only a triple bond with one lone pair on each N gives both atoms an octet with exactly 10 electrons, matching N₂'s short (110 pm), strong (945 kJ/mol) bond.
cards.h: → 10 electrons → a single or double bond needs 14 or 12 → only N≡N with one lone pair each fits
cards.n: 'Nitrogen likes three bonds' names a pattern, not the reason; the point is that only a triple bond fits two octets into 10 electrons.
o: By needed minus available, 16 − 10 = 6 shared electrons, which is three bonds between the only two atoms.
The measured bond length and bond energy match a bond order of 3, confirming the triple bond.

w.a: N₂ has a triple bond because 10 electrons divide evenly into bonds.
w.why: 10 electrons in bonds alone would be five bonds; the count must be checked against octets

w.a: N₂ has a triple bond because nitrogen is in group 15.
w.why: group number alone is not the electron-count argument

w.a: N₂ has a triple bond because triple bonds are the most stable kind of bond.
w.why: stability follows from the structure; it does not decide the electron count

cards.q: Explain why carbon forms four bonds and has no lone pairs in most of its neutral compounds.
cards.a: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 8 around it. Sharing each of its electrons in a bond gives four shared pairs, an octet, with none of its own electrons left for a lone pair. Fewer bonds would leave carbon short of an octet unless it carried a lone pair and a formal charge, as in CO or CN⁻.
cards.h: → 4 valence electrons → four shared pairs complete the octet → no electrons left for lone pairs
cards.n: 'Carbon always forms four bonds' is a pattern with exceptions (:C≡O:), not a reason; tie the bond count to the octet and the four valence electrons.
o: Bonds needed = 8 − valence electrons = 8 − 4 = 4, and all four of carbon's electrons are then in bonds.
In CH₄, C₂H₄ and CO₂ carbon shows four bonds in different combinations of single and multiple bonds, each giving an octet.

w.a: Carbon forms four bonds because it has four protons in its outer shell.
w.why: protons are in the nucleus; it is the four valence electrons

w.a: Carbon forms four bonds because it is in period 2.
w.why: N, O and F are in period 2 and form fewer bonds

w.a: Carbon forms four bonds because it has four lone pairs to share.
w.why: a neutral C atom has four single valence electrons, not four lone pairs

cards.q: State the formula for formal charge.
cards.a: Formal charge = (valence electrons of the free atom) − (nonbonding electrons on the atom) − ½(bonding electrons around it), which equals valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − number of bonds. Examples: O in H₂O, 6 − 4 − 2 = 0; N in NH₄⁺, 5 − 0 − 4 = +1; O in OH⁻, 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.
cards.h: → formula, then worked atoms
cards.n: Formal charge assumes perfectly equal sharing: it is bookkeeping, neither the real partial charge nor the oxidation number (O in H₂O: formal charge 0, oxidation number −2).

cards.q: Apply formal charge to decide which of several valid Lewis structures is preferred.
cards.a: First keep only structures that give C, N, O and F octets. Among those, prefer the one whose formal charges are closest to zero, with no like charges on adjacent atoms and any negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom; the charges must sum to the species' charge. Formal charge never rescues an octet violation: CO is :C≡O: (C −1, O +1), not C=O with zero charges and a 6-electron carbon.
cards.h: → octet filter first, then the formal-charge tests
cards.n: Using formal charge to justify an incomplete octet on C, N or O, or an expanded octet on a period-2 atom, earns nothing: the octet rule is the first criterion.

cards.q: Define resonance and explain what the true structure is.
cards.a: Resonance occurs when two or more valid Lewis diagrams differ only in where electrons (multiple bonds and lone pairs) are placed, with every atom in the same position. The true structure is a single resonance hybrid, the average of the contributors, in which those electrons are delocalized over the atoms involved; it does not switch between the drawings. Contributors are linked by a double-headed arrow (↔).
cards.h: → definition (electrons move, atoms do not), then the hybrid
cards.n: Saying the ion 'flips back and forth' earns nothing; the hybrid is one unchanging structure. Moving an atom gives a different compound (an isomer), not a resonance form.

cards.q: Predict the bond lengths in the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻.
cards.a: All three C–O bonds are equal, intermediate between a C–O single bond (about 143 pm) and a C=O double bond (about 120 pm); the measured value is about 128–129 pm. The three equivalent resonance structures each put the double bond on a different O, so every C–O bond in the hybrid has bond order (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 4/3.
cards.h: → equal lengths + why (average bond order)
cards.n: Predicting one short and two long bonds treats one resonance structure as real; the equal lengths are the experimental evidence for the hybrid.

cards.q: Decide which Lewis structure of $CO_2$ is preferred using formal charge: two C=O double bonds, or a C≡O triple bond paired with a C-O single bond.
cards.a: O=C=O. Both structures use 16 electrons and give every atom an octet, so formal charge decides. In O=C=O each O is 6 − 4 − 2 = 0 and C is 4 − 0 − 4 = 0. In O≡C–O the triple-bonded O is 6 − 2 − 3 = +1 and the single-bonded O is 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. All-zero formal charges make O=C=O the better model, and it predicts two equal C=O bonds, as measured.
cards.h: → both obey octets → compute formal charges → choose
cards.n: Minimizing formal charge is the tiebreaker only between structures that already satisfy the octet rule; it never licenses an octet violation.

cards.q: Compute the average N-O bond order in the nitrate ion, $NO_3^{-}$, from its resonance structures.
cards.a: 4/3 ≈ 1.33. Each of the three equivalent resonance structures has one N=O and two N–O bonds, and each bond is double in one structure and single in the other two, so its average order is (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 4/3. Equivalently, four shared pairs are spread over three N–O bonds.
cards.h: → sum of orders over the structures ÷ number of structures
cards.n: Answering 2 (one structure) or 1.5 (averaging one single and one double) misses that there are three equivalent contributors.

cards.q: Compute the formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion, $NH_4^{+}$.
cards.a: +1. N has 5 valence electrons, no lone-pair electrons and four bonds: 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1. Each H is 1 − 0 − 1 = 0, so the formal charges sum to +1, the charge of the ion.
cards.h: → V − lone-pair electrons − bonds
cards.n: Giving N a lone pair as in NH₃ (5 − 2 − 4 = −1) misdraws the ion: NH₄⁺ has 8 valence electrons, all in the four N–H bonds.

cards.q: Compute the formal charge on each oxygen atom in one Lewis resonance structure of ozone, $O_3$.
cards.a: Central O +1; double-bonded end O 0; single-bonded end O −1. In O=O–O (18 electrons) the central O has 1 lone pair and 3 bonds: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. The double-bonded O has 2 lone pairs: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. The single-bonded O has 3 lone pairs: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. The sum is 0, matching the neutral molecule.
cards.h: → one formula per oxygen, then the sum check
cards.n: Octets on all three O make the +1 and −1 unavoidable; the second resonance structure swaps the end charges, and the hybrid has two equal O–O bonds.

cards.q: Compute the formal charge on sulfur in $SO_4^{2-}$ using the Lewis structure with four S-O single bonds.
cards.a: +2. With four S–O single bonds and no lone pairs, S has 6 − 0 − ½(8) = +2; each O (three lone pairs, one bond) is 6 − 6 − 1 = −1, and +2 + 4(−1) = −2, the ion's charge. This structure keeps every atom at an octet; drawing two S=O double bonds lowers sulfur's formal charge to 0 but puts 12 electrons around S.
cards.h: → formula for S, then each O, then the sum
cards.n: Both sulfate structures appear in AP materials (octet vs minimum formal charge); a sum that is not −2, or a double bond giving O more than 8, earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the number of equivalent resonance structures needed to describe the bonding in $SO_3$.
cards.a: Three, for the octet structure. With 24 electrons, S has one S=O and two S–O bonds and no lone pair; the double bond can sit on any of the three O atoms, giving three equivalent contributors. The hybrid has three identical S–O bonds of order 4/3, consistent with the trigonal planar molecule's equal bond lengths.
cards.h: → count the positions the double bond can take
cards.n: The expanded-octet structure with three S=O bonds (all formal charges 0) needs no resonance; both give three equal bonds, but the answer 3 assumes octets.

cards.q: State the rule connecting the sum of formal charges in a Lewis structure to the overall charge of the species.
cards.a: The formal charges of all the atoms in a correct Lewis structure add up to the overall charge: 0 for a neutral molecule, +1 for NH₄⁺ (N +1, each H 0), −1 for NO₃⁻ (N +1, two single-bonded O −1 each, the double-bonded O 0). A structure whose formal charges do not sum to the charge has the wrong electron count.
cards.h: → rule + one ion checked
cards.n: Adding magnitudes (+1 and two −1 make 3) instead of signed values earns nothing; the signed sum must equal the net charge.

cards.q: Identify the number of equivalent resonance structures needed to describe the bonding in benzene, $C_6H_6$.
cards.a: Two. The six-carbon ring, each C also bonded to one H, can be drawn with alternating C=C and C–C bonds in two ways, the double bonds shifted by one position. The hybrid has six identical C–C bonds of order 1.5, about 140 pm, between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm), as measured.
cards.h: → count distinct placements of the alternating bonds
cards.n: Answering six (one per bond position) double-counts: only two distinct alternating patterns exist.

cards.q: Calculate the formal charge on each atom in each Lewis diagram: (i) H–C≡N: with a lone pair on N · (ii) :C≡O: with one lone pair on each atom · (iii) [:N≡O:]⁺ · (iv) H₃O⁺, O with three bonds and one lone pair · (v) OH⁻ · (vi) NH₂⁻, N with two bonds and two lone pairs · (vii) [:C≡N:]⁻ · (viii) BF₄⁻ · (ix) [S=C=N]⁻ with two lone pairs on S and on N · (x) O=N–O⁻ with one lone pair on N · (xi) N=N=O with two lone pairs on the end N and on O · (xii) ClO₄⁻ drawn with four Cl–O single bonds
cards.a:
(i) H 0, C 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, N 5 − 2 − 3 = 0
(ii) C 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, O 6 − 2 − 3 = +1
(iii) N 5 − 2 − 3 = 0, O 6 − 2 − 3 = +1 (sum +1)
(iv) O 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, each H 0
(v) O 6 − 6 − 1 = −1, H 0
(vi) N 5 − 4 − 2 = −1, each H 0
(vii) C 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, N 5 − 2 − 3 = 0
(viii) B 3 − 0 − 4 = −1, each F 7 − 6 − 1 = 0
(ix) S 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, C 0, N 5 − 4 − 2 = −1
(x) N 5 − 2 − 3 = 0, double-bonded O 0, single-bonded O 6 − 6 − 1 = −1
(xi) end N 5 − 4 − 2 = −1, central N 5 − 0 − 4 = +1, O 6 − 4 − 2 = 0
(xii) Cl 7 − 0 − 4 = +3, each O −1 (sum −1)
Formula: valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − bonds; the charges always sum to the species' charge.
cards.h: → V − lone-pair electrons − bonds, atom by atom
cards.n: Subtracting all the bonding electrons instead of the number of bonds doubles the penalty (C in HCN: 4 − 0 − 8) and earns nothing.

cards.q: Represent all the resonance structures of each species in words, then give the bond order of the bonds that resonance averages: NO₃⁻ · NO₂⁻ · O₃ · CO₃²⁻ · HCOO⁻ (formate) · SO₂ (octet structure) · C₆H₆
cards.a:
NO₃⁻ → 3 structures: N (no lone pair) with one N=O (that O has 2 lone pairs) and two N–O (each O 3 lone pairs); the double bond moves to each O in turn; N–O order 4/3
NO₂⁻ → 2: O=N–O with 1 lone pair on N; double bond on either O; order 1.5
O₃ → 2: O=O–O, central O with 1 lone pair, end O atoms with 2 and 3; double bond on either side; order 1.5
CO₃²⁻ → 3: C (no lone pair) with one C=O and two C–O; order 4/3
HCOO⁻ → 2: H–C with one C=O and one C–O; double bond on either O; C–O order 1.5 (C–H unchanged)
SO₂ → 2: O=S–O with 1 lone pair on S; order 1.5
C₆H₆ → 2: ring of alternating C=C and C–C, each C with one H; order 1.5
Each set is joined by double-headed arrows (↔), ions in brackets with the charge; only electrons move, never atoms.
cards.h: → move only the double bond; count positions; average
cards.n: Moving a hydrogen or an oxygen to another atom draws a different compound, not a resonance structure; only the placement of electrons changes.

cards.q: Determine which Lewis diagram of dinitrogen monoxide, N₂O (atoms connected N–N–O, 16 valence electrons, every atom with an octet), is the best model by calculating formal charges: (A) N=N=O · (B) N≡N–O · (C) N–N≡O.
cards.a: (B) is best. Formal charges (end N, central N, O): A −1, +1, 0; B 0, +1, −1; C −2, +1, +1. All three obey the octet rule, so formal charge decides: C has a −2 and puts + on oxygen, the worst case; A and B both have ±1 charges, but B places the −1 on O, the most electronegative atom. A still contributes to the hybrid; C does not.
cards.h: → formal charges for all three, then the tiebreakers
cards.n: Picking A because 'it has two double bonds, like CO₂' earns nothing; the tiebreaker is which atom carries the negative formal charge.

cards.q: Identify which of these species cannot be drawn with an octet on every atom (a duet on H), and state the reason: NO · CO · NO₂ · N₂O · ClO₂ · SO₂ · CH₃ (the methyl radical)
cards.a: NO, NO₂, ClO₂ and CH₃ cannot; CO, N₂O and SO₂ can. The first four have odd numbers of valence electrons (11, 17, 19 and 7). Lewis diagrams place electrons in pairs, so an odd total always leaves one unpaired electron and an atom with only 7 around it. CO (10), N₂O (16) and SO₂ (18) are even and have octet structures. Odd-electron species are a stated limitation of the Lewis model.
cards.h: → count each total; odd → no complete set of octets
cards.n: Calling NO₂ an expanded octet, or 'adding an electron' to reach 18, earns nothing; the odd count is a limitation of the model, not a drawing error.

cards.q: Explain why a molecule with resonance is more stable than any single contributing structure.
cards.a: In the hybrid, the electrons of the multiple bond are delocalized over several atoms instead of confined between two, so each is attracted by more nuclei and the electrons repel each other less. That lowers the potential energy, so the real species is more stable than any one contributor suggests.
cards.h: → electrons delocalized over more atoms → attracted by more nuclei, less repulsion → lower energy
cards.n: 'It switches between structures' earns nothing. Resonance stabilization goes a step past the 2.6 EK, whose scored idea is that the hybrid is the real structure.
o: Spreading the pi electrons over the whole ion lets the negative charge be shared by several atoms rather than concentrated on one, which lowers the energy.
The equal measured bond lengths show the electrons really are spread over all positions, an arrangement lower in energy than any single localized drawing.

w.a: A molecule with resonance is more stable because it switches rapidly between its structures.
w.why: the hybrid does not flip; it is one delocalized structure

w.a: A molecule with resonance is more stable because it has more bonds than one structure shows.
w.why: every contributor has the same number of bonds; the electrons are spread, not added

w.a: Resonance makes a molecule more stable because double bonds are stronger than single bonds.
w.why: each contributor has the same double bonds; delocalization is the point

cards.q: Explain why the two N-O bonds in the nitrite ion, $NO_2^{-}$, are equal in length even though each Lewis structure shows one single and one double bond.
cards.a: NO₂⁻ is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent structures, O=N–O⁻ and ⁻O–N=O, which differ only in where the double bond is. The real ion averages them: the pi electron pair is delocalized over both N–O bonds, so each has bond order 1.5 and the same length, between an N–O single and an N=O double bond.
cards.h: → two equivalent structures → electrons delocalized → both bonds order 1.5 → equal lengths
cards.n: 'The bonds take turns being double' earns nothing; neither drawing exists on its own, and only the hybrid predicts the equal measured lengths.
o: Neither Lewis structure alone is the ion; resonance is the refinement that makes the model predict equal bonds.
Each N–O bond is double in one contributor and single in the other, so on average each is one and a half bonds.

w.a: The bonds are equal because the ion switches rapidly between its two structures.
w.why: there is no switching; the hybrid is one structure

w.a: The bonds are equal because both oxygen atoms have the same electronegativity.
w.why: true but it does not explain why a single and a double bond would become equal

w.a: The bonds are equal because nitrogen forms two double bonds in the real ion.
w.why: that puts 10 electrons on nitrogen, a period-2 atom; the hybrid has bond order 1.5

cards.q: Explain the two criteria used to identify the most important resonance structure among several valid Lewis structures.
cards.a: First the octet rule: the best structures give C, N, O and F eight electrons, since a period-2 atom short of an octet is higher in energy. Second, formal charge: among those, the best has formal charges closest to zero and any negative charge on the most electronegative atom, which best holds extra electron density.
cards.h: → octet first → then formal charges near zero → negative charge on the most electronegative atom
cards.n: Naming formal charge alone, then choosing a structure that leaves carbon with six electrons because its charges are zero, is the classic loss.
o: CO shows the order of the criteria: :C≡O: has charges but complete octets, so it beats C=O with zero charges.
Separated charges cost energy, so a structure with fewer and smaller formal charges, placed on the atoms best able to carry them, is the better model.

w.a: The most important structure is the one with the most double bonds.
w.why: the number of double bonds is not a criterion

w.a: The most important structure is the one with every formal charge equal to zero, whatever the octets.
w.why: ignores the octet rule, which comes first

w.a: The most important structure is the one drawn first.
w.why: the order of drawing has no physical meaning

cards.q: Explain why the best Lewis diagram of carbon monoxide has a triple bond even though it gives carbon a formal charge of −1 and oxygen +1.
cards.a: The octet rule outranks formal charge. C=O with zero formal charges leaves carbon with only 6 electrons, while :C≡O: uses the same 10 electrons and gives both atoms an octet, so it is the better model despite the charges. The data agree: CO's bond (113 pm, 1072 kJ/mol) is shorter and stronger than a C=O double bond.
cards.h: → C=O leaves C with 6 electrons → octet rule comes first → C≡O wins despite ±1 → matches the short, strong bond
cards.n: 'C=O is best because every formal charge is zero' is the formal-charge argument that ignores the octet; it earns nothing.
o: Formal charge only chooses among structures that already satisfy the octet rule, and only the triple-bonded structure does.
The measured bond length and bond energy fit a bond order of 3, not 2, which confirms the triple bond.

w.a: C=O is the best structure because every atom has a formal charge of zero.
w.why: zero charges cannot rescue carbon's incomplete octet

w.a: CO has a triple bond because oxygen is more electronegative and wants the positive charge.
w.why: the +1 on O is the cost of the structure, not its reason

w.a: CO has a triple bond because carbon always forms four bonds.
w.why: carbon has three bonds and a lone pair here; the octet decides

cards.q: Explain why the C-O bonds in the carbonate ion are longer than the C-O bonds in CO₂ but shorter than the C-O bond in methanol, CH₃OH.
cards.a: Bond order sets the length. Methanol has a C–O single bond (order 1). Carbonate's three resonance structures spread one C=O double bond over three positions, so each C–O has order 4/3. CO₂ has two C=O double bonds (order 2). More shared density pulls the nuclei closer, so 1 < 4/3 < 2 gives long > medium > short.
cards.h: → single (1) vs resonance average (4/3) vs double (2) → higher order, shorter bond
cards.n: Answering from ion charge or molecular size earns nothing; the ranking needs each bond order, and carbonate's comes from resonance.
o: Each carbonate C–O bond is one and a third bonds, between methanol's single bond and CO₂'s double bonds, so its length falls between.
Resonance turns carbonate's one-double-two-single drawing into three identical, intermediate bonds.

w.a: Carbonate's bonds are longer than CO₂'s because the 2− charge pushes the atoms apart.
w.why: the charge is not the reason; the lower bond order is

w.a: Carbonate has one short double bond and two long single bonds, so on average its bonds are medium.
w.why: all three bonds are identical; there is no short and long pair

w.a: Carbonate's bonds are shorter than methanol's because carbonate has more oxygen atoms.
w.why: the number of O atoms does not set bond order

cards.q: Explain why no Lewis diagram of nitrogen dioxide, NO₂, can give every atom an octet.
cards.a: NO₂ has 5 + 2(6) = 17 valence electrons, an odd number. A Lewis diagram places electrons in bonding and lone pairs, so an odd total always leaves one unpaired electron, and the atom holding it (N in the usual diagram) has only 7 electrons around it. This is a stated limitation of the Lewis model.
cards.h: → 17 electrons (odd) → pairs cannot use them all → one atom holds 7 → a limitation of the model
cards.n: 'Nitrogen can only form three bonds' or 'NO₂ has an expanded octet' earns nothing; the point is the odd electron count.
o: Eight electrons on each of three atoms requires an even count, and 17 is odd.
The unpaired electron makes NO₂ a radical, which is why two NO₂ molecules join to form N₂O₄, pairing those electrons in an N–N bond.

w.a: NO₂ cannot have octets because oxygen is too electronegative to share electrons with nitrogen.
w.why: N–O bonds are shared pairs; the problem is the odd count

w.a: NO₂ has an expanded octet on nitrogen, so the octet rule does not apply.
w.why: nitrogen is a period-2 atom and cannot exceed 8

w.a: NO₂ lacks octets because it is a gas.
w.why: physical state has nothing to do with electron counting

cards.q: Explain why the cyanate ion, OCN⁻, is best drawn with the negative formal charge on oxygen, [O–C≡N]⁻, rather than on nitrogen, [O=C=N]⁻.
cards.a: Both structures use 16 electrons, give every atom an octet and carry a single −1 formal charge, so the tiebreaker is where that charge sits. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen (3.44 vs 3.04), so it better holds the extra electron density a negative formal charge represents; [O–C≡N]⁻ is the better model.
cards.h: → octets and charge counts tie → negative formal charge belongs on the more electronegative atom → O
cards.n: 'The triple bond makes it more stable' earns nothing: both structures have four shared pairs, and the tiebreaker is the electronegativity of the charged atom.
o: Negative formal charge is most favorable on the atom that attracts electrons most strongly, which in OCN⁻ is oxygen.
The third structure, [O≡C–N]⁻ with O +1 and N −2, is worst; comparing the other two leaves only the location of the −1 to decide.

w.a: [O–C≡N]⁻ is better because nitrogen likes triple bonds.
w.why: a preference for a bond type is not a formal-charge criterion

w.a: [O=C=N]⁻ is better because it is symmetric like CO₂.
w.why: the two end atoms differ, so symmetry is not an argument

w.a: The negative charge goes on oxygen because oxygen has more lone pairs.
w.why: the lone pairs follow from the charge; electronegativity is the reason

cards.q: State the central principle of VSEPR theory.
cards.a: Electron domains around a central atom (each bonded atom, whether joined by a single, double or triple bond, and each lone pair) repel one another by Coulombic repulsion and arrange themselves as far apart as possible, minimizing that repulsion. The domain arrangement sets the electron-domain geometry; the molecular shape is then named from the positions of the atoms only.
cards.h: → domains repel → maximum separation → geometry
cards.n: Counting a double or triple bond as two or three domains earns nothing: a multiple bond is one domain, which is why CO₂ and HCN are linear.

cards.q: Contrast electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry.
cards.a: Electron-domain geometry is the arrangement of all the domains around the central atom, bonding domains and lone pairs alike. Molecular geometry names the arrangement of the atoms only, so lone pairs shape it but do not appear in its name. The two match when the central atom has no lone pair (CH₄: both tetrahedral) and differ when it has one (NH₃: tetrahedral domains, trigonal pyramidal molecule; H₂O: tetrahedral, bent).
cards.h: → all domains vs atoms only, one example each way
cards.n: Naming the shape from the formula (AB₂, so 'linear' H₂O) instead of from the electron domains is the classic loss; count domains from the Lewis diagram first.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for a central atom with 2 electron domains and no lone pairs.
cards.a: Linear, 180°. Two domains get as far apart as possible on opposite sides of the central atom. Examples: CO₂, HCN, BeCl₂; the central atom is sp hybridized.
cards.h: → shape, angle, example
cards.n: A triple bond is still one domain, which is why HCN is linear even though its carbon forms four bonds' worth of shared pairs.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 3 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Trigonal planar, 120°. Three domains spread in one plane at equal angles. Examples: BF₃, SO₃, CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻; the central atom is sp² hybridized.
cards.h: → shape, angle, example
cards.n: With identical outer atoms the dipoles cancel, so BF₃ is nonpolar although every B–F bond is strongly polar.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 3 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Bent (angular), with the bond angle a little under 120° (SO₂ about 119°, NO₂⁻ about 115°). The electron-domain geometry is trigonal planar; the lone pair takes one position and pushes the two bonds slightly together. Examples: SO₂, O₃, NO₂⁻; the central atom is sp².
cards.h: → shape, angle below 120°, example
cards.n: SO₂ and H₂O are both 'bent', but SO₂ has 3 domains (about 119°) and H₂O 4 (104.5°); the angle, not the shape name, reveals the domain count.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 4 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Tetrahedral, 109.5°. Four domains point to the corners of a tetrahedron, the arrangement that keeps them farthest apart in three dimensions. Examples: CH₄, CCl₄, NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻; the central atom is sp³.
cards.h: → shape, angle, example
cards.n: Drawing it flat with 90° angles earns nothing; and 109.5° is exact only with identical outer atoms (CH₂Cl₂ is tetrahedral but slightly distorted).

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 4 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Trigonal pyramidal, with bond angles below 109.5° (NH₃ about 107°), compressed by the lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral: the lone pair occupies one corner, and the three atoms form the base of a pyramid with the central atom at its apex. Examples: NH₃, PCl₃, H₃O⁺; sp³.
cards.h: → shape, angle below 109.5°, example
cards.n: Calling NH₃ 'trigonal planar' because it has three atoms names the shape from the formula; the lone pair makes four domains and a pyramid.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 4 electron domains with 2 lone pairs.
cards.a: Bent, with a bond angle below 109.5° (H₂O about 104.5°). The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral; the two lone pairs take two corners and repel the bonds more strongly than bonds repel each other, squeezing the angle. Examples: H₂O, OF₂, SCl₂; sp³.
cards.h: → shape, angle, example
cards.n: 'Linear, because H₂O has two atoms bonded to O' is the formula trap; the two lone pairs make four domains and a bent shape.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angles for 5 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Trigonal bipyramidal: three equatorial positions 120° apart in a plane, and two axial positions above and below at 90° to that plane (180° to each other). Example: PCl₅. No hybridization label is assessed for five domains.
cards.h: → shape, the two angle sets, example
cards.n: Giving 72° or 108° (pentagon angles) earns nothing; the five positions are not equivalent: three equatorial at 120°, two axial at 90°.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 5 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Seesaw. The lone pair takes an equatorial position, where it has only two neighbors at 90° instead of three, and the four atoms form the seesaw; both angles close a little (SF₄: axial F–S–F about 173°, equatorial about 102°). Example: SF₄.
cards.h: → shape, where the lone pair sits, example
cards.n: Putting the lone pair axial gives a trigonal pyramid and earns nothing; an axial site has three 90° neighbors, an equatorial site only two.

cards.q: Predict the geometries for 5 electron domains with 2 and with 3 lone pairs.
cards.a: Two lone pairs: T-shaped (ClF₃, BrF₃), with angles slightly under 90°. Three lone pairs: linear (XeF₂, I₃⁻), 180°. In both, the lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, leaving the two axial atoms (plus one equatorial atom in the T).
cards.h: → two shapes, each with an example
cards.n: XeF₂ is linear and nonpolar despite three lone pairs, because they sit symmetrically in the equatorial plane and the two Xe–F dipoles cancel.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 6 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Octahedral, 90° between neighboring positions (180° between opposite ones). Example: SF₆. All six positions are equivalent, so there is no axial or equatorial choice; no hybridization label is assessed.
cards.h: → shape, angle, example
cards.n: Calling it 'hexagonal' (six atoms in a flat ring) earns nothing; the six atoms point along ±x, ±y and ±z.

cards.q: Predict the geometries for 6 electron domains with 1 and with 2 lone pairs.
cards.a: One lone pair: square pyramidal (BrF₅, IF₅), with angles slightly under 90°. Two lone pairs: square planar (XeF₄, ICl₄⁻), 90°, with the lone pairs opposite each other, 180° apart, which keeps them as far apart as possible.
cards.h: → two shapes, each with an example
cards.n: Square planar is nonpolar because the bond dipoles cancel, while square pyramidal keeps a net dipole along the axis through the lone pair.

cards.q: Identify the hybridization of a central atom from its number of electron domains.
cards.a: 2 domains → sp (ideal angle 180°); 3 domains → sp² (120°); 4 domains → sp³ (109.5°). Lone pairs count as domains, so CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O are all sp³, and a multiple bond counts once, so the C in CO₂ is sp.
cards.h: → three domain counts, each with label and angle
cards.n: Assigning sp³d or sp³d² to 5- or 6-domain atoms goes beyond the CED, which excludes d-orbital hybridization; name only the geometry there.

cards.q: Contrast sigma and pi bonds.
cards.a: A sigma bond forms by head-on (end-to-end) overlap along the internuclear axis; every single bond is one sigma bond and every multiple bond contains one. A pi bond forms by side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis; it is the second bond of a double bond and the second and third of a triple. Sigma overlap is greater, so a sigma bond is stronger, and a pi bond prevents rotation about the bond.
cards.h: → overlap type, where each occurs, strength, rotation
cards.n: Calling a pi bond stronger than a sigma bond earns nothing: it is weaker, which is why C=C (614 kJ/mol) is less than twice C–C (347 kJ/mol).

cards.q: Count the sigma and pi bonds in a molecule containing double and triple bonds.
cards.a: Every bond between two atoms contains exactly one sigma bond; a double bond adds one pi bond and a triple bond adds two. So σ = number of bonded atom pairs and π = (double bonds) + 2 × (triple bonds). HCN (H–C≡N): 2 σ, 2 π. Acrylonitrile, CH₂=CH–C≡N: 6 σ, 3 π.
cards.h: → one sigma per bonded pair, then add the pi bonds
cards.n: Counting a triple bond as three sigma bonds, or counting lone pairs as bonds, earns nothing; lone pairs are neither sigma nor pi.

cards.q: Predict whether a molecule is polar from its geometry and bond dipoles.
cards.a: Draw the Lewis diagram, find the molecular shape by VSEPR, then add the bond dipoles as vectors. If they cancel, the molecule is nonpolar: symmetric shapes (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral, square planar) with identical outer atoms. If they do not, because an asymmetric shape (bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal) or unlike outer atoms, it is polar.
cards.h: → Lewis → shape → vector sum of bond dipoles
cards.n: 'Polar' with no shape named rarely earns the point; the claim must cite the geometry and whether the bond dipoles cancel.

cards.q: Identify three molecules that contain polar bonds yet are nonpolar overall.
cards.a: CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar) and CCl₄ (tetrahedral); SO₃, PCl₅, SF₆, XeF₂ and XeF₄ also qualify. In each, identical outer atoms sit symmetrically around the central atom, so the equal bond dipoles cancel as vectors and the net dipole moment is zero.
cards.h: → three molecules, each with its shape
cards.n: 'Has polar bonds' is not 'is polar': the multiple-choice distractor counts polar bonds instead of adding the bond dipoles over the shape.

cards.q: Identify the number of lone pairs on the central atom of a T-shaped molecule such as $ClF_3$.
cards.a: Two. ClF₃ has 28 valence electrons; three Cl–F bonds and nine F lone pairs use 24, leaving 4 as two lone pairs on Cl. Five domains (3 bonding, 2 lone pairs) give a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; both lone pairs take equatorial positions, leaving a T-shaped molecule.
cards.h: → count electrons → domains → lone pairs
cards.n: 'Three atoms, so trigonal planar' names the shape from the formula; the two lone pairs make five domains and a T.

cards.q: Identify the electron-domain geometry and the molecular geometry of the central atom in $XeF_4$.
cards.a: Electron-domain geometry octahedral; molecular geometry square planar. XeF₄ has 36 valence electrons: four Xe–F bonds and twelve F lone pairs use 32, leaving two lone pairs on Xe, so Xe has six domains. The two lone pairs sit opposite each other (180° apart), leaving the four F atoms in a plane at 90°.
cards.h: → count → six domains → lone pairs opposite
cards.n: Answering 'tetrahedral' because Xe has four atoms is the formula trap; and give no hybridization for six domains, which the CED does not assess.

cards.q: Identify a molecule with a seesaw molecular geometry, and state its electron-domain count and lone pairs.
cards.a: SF₄ (34 valence electrons). S has four S–F bonds and one lone pair, five electron domains in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement; the lone pair is equatorial, leaving the seesaw. SeF₄ and IF₄⁺ are other examples.
cards.h: → example, then 5 domains = 4 bonds + 1 lone pair
cards.n: Calling SF₄ tetrahedral names the shape from the formula; its lone pair makes five domains. Give no hybridization for a 5-domain center.

cards.q: Contrast the F-S-F bond angles at the axial and equatorial positions of $SF_4$, caused by its single lone pair.
cards.a: Both shrink from the ideal. The axial F–S–F angle closes from 180° to about 173°, and the equatorial F–S–F angle closes from 120° to about 102°. The equatorial lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other, so both pairs of S–F bonds bend away from it.
cards.h: → two angles, ideal vs actual, one cause
cards.n: Saying only the equatorial angle changes misses half: the axial pair also bends off 180°, away from the lone pair.

cards.q: Determine, for the central atom of each species, the number of electron domains (lone pairs), the electron-domain geometry, the molecular shape, the ideal or approximate bond angle, and the hybridization: CO₂ · HCN · BF₃ · SO₂ · NO₃⁻ · CH₂O · CH₄ · NH₃ · H₂O · H₃O⁺ · PCl₅ · SF₄ · ClF₃ · XeF₂ · SF₆ · BrF₅ · XeF₄
cards.a:
CO₂ → 2 (0); linear; linear; 180°; sp
HCN → 2 (0); linear; linear; 180°; sp
BF₃ → 3 (0); trigonal planar; trigonal planar; 120°; sp²
SO₂ → 3 (1); trigonal planar; bent; about 119°; sp²
NO₃⁻ → 3 (0); trigonal planar; trigonal planar; 120°; sp²
CH₂O → 3 (0); trigonal planar; trigonal planar; about 120°; sp²
CH₄ → 4 (0); tetrahedral; tetrahedral; 109.5°; sp³
NH₃ → 4 (1); tetrahedral; trigonal pyramidal; about 107°; sp³
H₂O → 4 (2); tetrahedral; bent; about 104.5°; sp³
H₃O⁺ → 4 (1); tetrahedral; trigonal pyramidal; below 109.5°; sp³
PCl₅ → 5 (0); trigonal bipyramidal; same; 90° and 120°; —
SF₄ → 5 (1); trigonal bipyramidal; seesaw; below 90° and 120°; —
ClF₃ → 5 (2); trigonal bipyramidal; T-shaped; below 90°; —
XeF₂ → 5 (3); trigonal bipyramidal; linear; 180°; —
SF₆ → 6 (0); octahedral; octahedral; 90°; —
BrF₅ → 6 (1); octahedral; square pyramidal; below 90°; —
XeF₄ → 6 (2); octahedral; square planar; 90°; —
— : hybridization is not assessed for 5 or 6 domains.
cards.h: → domains → EDG → shape → angle → hybridization
cards.n: Naming the shape from the formula (AB₂ 'linear' for SO₂; AB₄ 'tetrahedral' for SF₄ and XeF₄) is the trap: count the domains from the Lewis diagram first.

cards.q: Predict whether each molecule is polar or nonpolar, naming the shape that decides: CO₂ · OCS · HCN · H₂O · SO₂ · BF₃ · SO₃ · NH₃ · CH₄ · CH₂Cl₂ · CHCl₃ · CCl₄ · PCl₅ · SF₄ · ClF₃ · XeF₂ · SF₆ · BrF₅ · XeF₄
cards.a:
CO₂ → nonpolar (linear; equal C=O dipoles cancel)
OCS → polar (linear, but the C=O and C=S dipoles differ)
HCN → polar (linear; the H–C and C≡N dipoles both point toward N)
H₂O → polar (bent)
SO₂ → polar (bent)
BF₃ → nonpolar (trigonal planar)
SO₃ → nonpolar (trigonal planar)
NH₃ → polar (trigonal pyramidal)
CH₄ → nonpolar (tetrahedral)
CH₂Cl₂ → polar (tetrahedral, but two kinds of outer atom)
CHCl₃ → polar (tetrahedral, unlike outer atoms)
CCl₄ → nonpolar (tetrahedral, identical outer atoms)
PCl₅ → nonpolar (trigonal bipyramidal)
SF₄ → polar (seesaw)
ClF₃ → polar (T-shaped)
XeF₂ → nonpolar (linear)
SF₆ → nonpolar (octahedral)
BrF₅ → polar (square pyramidal)
XeF₄ → nonpolar (square planar)
Rule: a symmetric shape with identical outer atoms cancels; an asymmetric shape or unlike outer atoms leaves a net dipole.
cards.h: → shape first, then: do the bond dipoles cancel?
cards.n: 'Polar because it has polar bonds' (CO₂, CCl₄) and 'nonpolar because its lone pairs cancel' (H₂O) both skip the vector sum over the actual shape.

cards.q: Identify, for each molecule, the hybridization and approximate bond angle around each carbon (and each other named atom), and the numbers of sigma and pi bonds: C₂H₆ · C₂H₄ · C₂H₂ · HCN · CH₂O · CO₂ · N₂ · CH₃CN (both C) · CH₂=CHCH₃ (all three C) · CH₃COOH (both C and the O of O–H) · CH₃OH (C and O)
cards.a:
C₂H₆ → each C sp³, 109.5°; 7 σ, 0 π
C₂H₄ → each C sp², 120°; 5 σ, 1 π
C₂H₂ → each C sp, 180°; 3 σ, 2 π
HCN → C sp, 180°; 2 σ, 2 π
CH₂O → C sp², 120°; 3 σ, 1 π
CO₂ → C sp, 180°; 2 σ, 2 π
N₂ → each N sp; 1 σ, 2 π
CH₃CN → CH₃ carbon sp³, 109.5°; CN carbon sp, 180°; 5 σ, 2 π
CH₂=CHCH₃ → CH₂ and CH carbons sp², 120°; CH₃ carbon sp³, 109.5°; 8 σ, 1 π
CH₃COOH → CH₃ carbon sp³, 109.5°; COOH carbon sp², 120°; O–H oxygen sp³, bent, below 109.5°; 7 σ, 1 π
CH₃OH → C sp³, 109.5°; O sp³, bent, below 109.5°; 5 σ, 0 π
Rule: count each atom's own domains (lone pairs included): 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³; each bonded pair is 1 σ, each extra bond of a multiple bond 1 π.
cards.h: → domains on each atom → label and angle → count σ, π
cards.n: Giving every carbon in a molecule the same label is the slip: hybridization is assigned atom by atom from that atom's own domain count.

cards.q: Rank the bond angle in each set from largest to smallest and give the deciding reason: (i) CH₄, NH₃, H₂O · (ii) CO₂, BF₃, CH₄ · (iii) BF₃, NF₃ · (iv) NO₂⁺, NO₂⁻ · (v) SO₃, SO₃²⁻ · (vi) CO₃²⁻, ClO₃⁻ · (vii) SO₂, H₂O
cards.a:
(i) CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ about 107° > H₂O about 104.5°; four domains each, and each added lone pair squeezes the bonds more
(ii) CO₂ 180° > BF₃ 120° > CH₄ 109.5°; 2, 3 and 4 domains, no lone pairs
(iii) BF₃ 120° > NF₃ about 102°; B has 3 domains, N has 4 (one lone pair)
(iv) NO₂⁺ 180° > NO₂⁻ about 115°; N has 2 domains versus 3 with a lone pair
(v) SO₃ 120° > SO₃²⁻ below 109.5°; S has 3 domains versus 4 with a lone pair
(vi) CO₃²⁻ 120° > ClO₃⁻ below 109.5°; C has 3 domains, Cl has 4 (one lone pair)
(vii) SO₂ about 119° > H₂O about 104.5°; both bent, but S has 3 domains and O has 4
Rule: fewer electron domains means a larger ideal angle; for the same count, each lone pair closes the angle.
cards.h: → domain count first, then lone pairs
cards.n: Ranking by the number of atoms, or giving SO₂ and H₂O the same angle because both are 'bent', skips the domain count that sets the ideal angle.

cards.q: Identify which of these compounds can exist as separate cis and trans isomers, and state the two structural requirements: ClHC=CHCl (1,2-dichloroethene) · Cl₂C=CH₂ (1,1-dichloroethene) · ClH₂C–CH₂Cl (1,2-dichloroethane) · CH₃CH=CHCH₃ (2-butene) · CH₂=CHCH₃ (propene)
cards.a: Only 1,2-dichloroethene and 2-butene. The requirements: (1) a C=C double bond, whose pi bond prevents rotation about the C–C axis, and (2) two different groups on each double-bonded carbon. 1,1-dichloroethene and propene each have two H atoms on one carbon, so swapping them gives the same molecule; 1,2-dichloroethane has only a sigma bond between the carbons, which rotates freely.
cards.h: → which two, then the two requirements
cards.n: Saying any molecule with a double bond has cis and trans forms earns nothing; each double-bonded carbon also needs two different groups.

cards.q: Explain why lone pairs compress bond angles below the ideal value.
cards.a: A lone pair is attracted by only one nucleus, so its electron density spreads out close to the central atom and takes more room than a bonding pair held between two nuclei. It repels the bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other, pushing the bonds together: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°.
cards.h: → lone pair held by one nucleus → broader cloud near the center → stronger repulsion → bonds squeezed
cards.n: 'Lone pairs are heavier' or 'hold more electrons' earns nothing: both kinds of domain hold two electrons; the difference is how spread out they are.
o: Repulsion ranks lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair, so each added lone pair closes the angle further.
A bonding pair is drawn out toward the outer atom, while a lone pair stays near the central atom, where it crowds the bonds.

w.a: Lone pairs compress bond angles because they attract the bonding pairs.
w.why: electron domains repel; they do not attract

w.a: Lone pairs compress bond angles because they contain more electrons than bonding pairs.
w.why: both hold two electrons

w.a: Lone pairs compress bond angles because the molecule has fewer atoms.
w.why: atom count does not create extra repulsion

cards.q: Explain why both lone pairs in $ClF_3$ occupy equatorial positions rather than one axial and one equatorial.
cards.a: Repulsion is strongest between domains 90° apart, and lone pair–lone pair repulsion is the largest kind. With both lone pairs equatorial they are 120° apart, so no lone pair–lone pair contact is at 90°; one axial and one equatorial would put them at 90°. The lower-energy arrangement leaves a T-shaped molecule.
cards.h: → 90° repulsions dominate → two equatorial lone pairs are 120° apart, never at 90° → lowest energy → T-shape
cards.n: 'Equatorial positions are bigger' is vague; the point needs the 90° contacts, especially the lone pair–lone pair one an axial placement would create.
o: An axial site has three neighbors at 90° and an equatorial site only two, so the bulkier lone pairs take the equatorial sites.
Placing the lone pairs to avoid the costliest (lone pair–lone pair at 90°) repulsion gives the lowest potential energy.

w.a: The lone pairs are equatorial because they are attracted to each other.
w.why: lone pairs repel each other

w.a: The lone pairs are equatorial because the fluorine atoms need the axial positions to form stronger bonds.
w.why: bond strength is not the argument; lone-pair repulsion at 90° is

w.a: The lone pairs go wherever there is room after the fluorines are placed.
w.why: placement follows repulsion minimization, not order of filling

cards.q: Predict whether $XeF_4$ is polar or nonpolar, and explain.
cards.a: Nonpolar. Xe has six electron domains (four bonds, two lone pairs); the lone pairs sit opposite each other, so the molecule is square planar. The four identical Xe–F bond dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel in opposite pairs, and the opposite lone pairs cancel too, giving no net dipole.
cards.h: → six domains → lone pairs opposite → square planar → bond dipoles cancel in pairs
cards.n: 'Polar, because Xe has lone pairs' earns nothing: lone pairs placed symmetrically cancel just as the bonds do.
o: Each Xe–F dipole has an equal one pointing the opposite way across the square, so the vector sum is zero.
The shape is square planar, not tetrahedral, because the two lone pairs take opposite octahedral positions; that symmetry cancels every dipole.

w.a: XeF₄ is polar because the Xe–F bonds are polar.
w.why: polar bonds cancel in a symmetric shape

w.a: XeF₄ is polar because xenon has two lone pairs.
w.why: the lone pairs are opposite each other and cancel

w.a: XeF₄ is nonpolar because xenon is a noble gas.
w.why: right claim, but noble-gas status is not a geometry argument

cards.q: Explain the hybridization of the central carbon in $CO_2$ and how its two pi bonds form.
cards.a: Carbon is sp: it has two electron domains (two C=O double bonds, no lone pair), so the molecule is linear, 180°. Each C=O is one sigma bond from head-on overlap plus one pi bond from side-by-side overlap of p orbitals; the two pi bonds lie in perpendicular planes, one with each oxygen.
cards.h: → two domains → sp, 180° → each C=O = σ + π → the two π bonds in perpendicular planes
cards.n: Deriving or sketching the hybrid orbitals is excluded from the exam; name sp from the domain count and describe the sigma and pi overlap, nothing more.
o: Two domains always mean sp and 180°; each double bond counts once as a domain and contributes one pi bond.
CO₂ has 2 sigma and 2 pi bonds, and the pi bonds use different p orbitals on carbon, so they are perpendicular.

w.a: Carbon in CO₂ is sp² because it forms double bonds.
w.why: hybridization follows the domain count (two), not the bond type

w.a: Carbon in CO₂ is sp³ because carbon always forms four bonds.
w.why: four bonds in two domains is sp; the domain count decides

w.a: The two pi bonds in CO₂ lie in the same plane, one above the other.
w.why: they use perpendicular p orbitals, one for each oxygen

cards.q: Predict whether $SF_4$ is polar or nonpolar, and explain.
cards.a: Polar. S has five electron domains (four bonds, one lone pair); the lone pair is equatorial, giving a seesaw. The two axial S–F dipoles nearly cancel, but the two equatorial ones, about 102° apart on the side away from the lone pair, add to a net dipole, so the molecule is polar.
cards.h: → five domains, one lone pair → seesaw → equatorial dipoles do not cancel → polar
cards.n: 'Nonpolar, because all four bonds are S–F' ignores the shape; identical outer atoms cancel only in a symmetric geometry.
o: A single lone pair makes the electron distribution lopsided, so the bond dipoles cannot cancel.
Compare XeF₄: its two lone pairs are opposite and cancel, while SF₄'s one lone pair has no partner.

w.a: SF₄ is nonpolar because it has four identical S–F bonds.
w.why: identical bonds cancel only in a symmetric shape

w.a: SF₄ is polar because sulfur has an expanded octet.
w.why: an expanded octet does not decide polarity; the seesaw shape does

w.a: SF₄ is tetrahedral, so it is nonpolar.
w.why: the lone pair makes five domains; the shape is a seesaw

cards.q: Explain why BF₃ is nonpolar but NH₃ is polar, although each has three polar bonds to its central atom.
cards.a: B in BF₃ has three electron domains and no lone pair, so the molecule is trigonal planar and the three equal B–F dipoles, 120° apart, cancel. N in NH₃ has four domains, one a lone pair, so the molecule is trigonal pyramidal; the three N–H dipoles all tilt toward the same side and add to a net dipole.
cards.h: → BF₃: 3 domains → planar → dipoles cancel; NH₃: 4 domains with a lone pair → pyramidal → dipoles add
cards.n: 'NH₃ is polar because nitrogen is more electronegative than boron' compares the wrong things; the shapes set by the domain counts decide.
o: Both are AB₃, so the formula cannot decide; the Lewis diagrams show the lone pair on N that BF₃ lacks.
Identical bonds in a symmetric arrangement always cancel; the lone pair breaks that symmetry in NH₃.

w.a: BF₃ and NH₃ are both AB₃ molecules, so both are trigonal planar and nonpolar.
w.why: names the shape from the formula; N has a lone pair

w.a: NH₃ is polar because it contains hydrogen atoms.
w.why: CH₄ contains hydrogen and is nonpolar; the shape decides

w.a: BF₃ is nonpolar because B–F bonds are nonpolar.
w.why: B–F bonds are very polar (ΔEN about 1.9); they cancel by symmetry

cards.q: Explain why a pi bond is weaker than a sigma bond, using the C=C bond energy (614 kJ/mol) and the C-C bond energy (347 kJ/mol) as evidence.
cards.a: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap on the internuclear axis, putting shared density directly between the nuclei. A pi bond forms by side-by-side p overlap above and below the axis, a smaller overlap, so it binds less. Evidence: the pi bond adds only 614 − 347 = 267 kJ/mol, less than the 347 kJ/mol sigma bond.
cards.h: → head-on overlap on the axis vs side-by-side off it → less overlap → weaker pi bond (267 < 347 kJ/mol)
cards.n: 'Pi bonds are weaker because they are the second bond' restates the fact; the scored reason is the smaller side-by-side overlap.
o: Greater orbital overlap puts more electron density between the nuclei and gives a stronger attraction, and head-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap.
A C=C bond is less than twice as strong as C–C because its second component is a pi bond with weaker overlap.

w.a: A pi bond is weaker because it contains fewer electrons than a sigma bond.
w.why: each holds one shared pair

w.a: A pi bond is weaker because it is longer than a sigma bond.
w.why: both join the same two nuclei; the kind of overlap differs

w.a: A pi bond is stronger than a sigma bond because double bonds are stronger than single bonds.
w.why: the double bond is stronger in total, but its pi part is the weaker component

cards.q: Explain why 1,2-dichloroethene exists as two different compounds, cis and trans, while 1,2-dichloroethane exists as only one.
cards.a: The C=C in dichloroethene is one sigma plus one pi bond. Twisting one carbon would break the pi bond's side-by-side p overlap, so rotation is blocked and Cl atoms on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans) are locked in as distinct compounds. Dichloroethane's C–C sigma bond rotates freely.
cards.h: → C=C has a pi bond → twisting breaks the side-by-side overlap → no rotation → cis and trans locked in
cards.n: 'Double bonds are rigid' earns little without the pi bond: rotation would destroy the pi overlap, while sigma overlap survives rotation.
o: Turning cis into trans would require breaking the pi bond, roughly 260 kJ/mol, so the isomers do not interconvert at room temperature.
A sigma bond's overlap is the same all the way around the bond axis, so rotating one CH₂Cl group leaves the bond intact and every arrangement is one compound.

w.a: Dichloroethene has isomers because its chlorine atoms are larger than hydrogen atoms.
w.why: size does not stop rotation; the pi bond does

w.a: Dichloroethane has no isomers because it has more hydrogen atoms.
w.why: the number of H atoms is not the reason; free rotation about the sigma bond is

w.a: Cis and trans dichloroethene are the same compound drawn two ways.
w.why: they are distinct compounds with different properties; rotation between them is blocked

cards.q: Explain why CO₂ is linear but SO₂ is bent, although both have the formula AB₂.
cards.a: The shape follows the electron domains, not the formula. In O=C=O carbon has two domains (two double bonds, no lone pair), so they sit 180° apart: linear. SO₂'s Lewis diagram (18 electrons) leaves a lone pair on S, so S has three domains, trigonal planar; with one position a lone pair, the molecule is bent, about 119°.
cards.h: → Lewis diagrams → C: 2 domains, no lone pair → linear; S: 3 domains incl. a lone pair → bent
cards.n: 'Both are AB₂, so both are linear' is the formula trap; count domains, including lone pairs, from each Lewis diagram.
o: Counting electrons shows the difference: CO₂ (16) has none left for carbon after the bonds and O lone pairs, while SO₂ (18) has one pair left, on sulfur.
The lone pair repels the S–O bonds and occupies one position of the trigonal planar arrangement, so the O atoms cannot be opposite each other.

w.a: SO₂ is bent because sulfur is larger than carbon.
w.why: atom size does not set the domain count

w.a: SO₂ is bent because its S–O bonds are single bonds.
w.why: bond order does not set the shape; the lone pair does

w.a: CO₂ and SO₂ are both linear because they have the same formula type.
w.why: names the shape from the formula

cards.q: Rank the intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest.
cards.a: Ion-dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > dipole-induced dipole > London dispersion, for species of similar size. The order holds only at similar size: dispersion grows with the number of electrons and polarizability, so a large nonpolar molecule (I₂, a solid) has stronger net attractions than a small polar one (HCl, a gas). Every intermolecular force is far weaker than a covalent, ionic or metallic bond.
cards.h: → ordered list + the size caveat
cards.n: Ranking by type alone earns nothing when sizes differ; 'heavier molecules have stronger forces' also earns nothing, the cause is more electrons and greater polarizability.

cards.q: Define London dispersion forces and state which substances have them.
cards.a: London dispersion forces are Coulombic attractions between temporary, fluctuating dipoles: at any instant the electron cloud of a particle is lopsided, giving it a momentary dipole that induces an opposite dipole in a neighbor. Every substance has them, atoms and ions included; they are the ONLY intermolecular force in nonpolar molecules and noble gases, and the strongest net force between large molecules.
cards.h: → origin (temporary dipoles) + scope
cards.n: 'Only nonpolar molecules have dispersion forces' earns nothing; polar molecules have them too, and in large molecules they usually dominate.

cards.q: Explain polarizability and how it controls London dispersion strength.
cards.a: Polarizability is how easily a particle's electron cloud is distorted into a temporary dipole. A larger cloud with more electrons, held farther from the nucleus, distorts more easily, so its instantaneous dipoles are bigger and dispersion forces are stronger. Shape matters too: a long, unbranched chain presents more surface for contact with its neighbors than a compact branched isomer of the same formula.
cards.h: → definition + electron count + shape
cards.n: 'Heavier molecules have stronger forces' earns nothing; mass is a proxy, the scored cause is more electrons and greater polarizability.

cards.q: State the requirement for hydrogen bonding.
cards.a: A hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O or F in one molecule must be attracted to a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a different molecule (or a different part of the same large molecule). Both partners are needed: the highly polarized H (large δ+) and the electronegative acceptor (δ−). It is an unusually strong intermolecular attraction, not a covalent bond.
cards.h: → which atoms + both partners
cards.n: Naming hydrogen bonding for any molecule that contains hydrogen (HCl, CH₄, H₂S) earns nothing; CH₃OCH₃ has O but no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.

cards.q: Explain the ion-dipole force and name a situation where it dominates.
cards.a: An ion-dipole force is the Coulombic attraction between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule. It dominates when an ionic solid dissolves in water: each Na⁺ is surrounded by water molecules with their δ− oxygen ends pointing inward, and each Cl⁻ by water molecules with δ+ hydrogen ends pointing inward. It is stronger than any force between neutral molecules because a full charge, not a partial one, is involved.
cards.h: → description + orientation + one context
cards.n: Drawing the hydrogen ends of water toward Na⁺ earns nothing; the sign of the partial charge facing the ion is the scored detail.

cards.q: Define ion-induced dipole and dipole-induced dipole forces.
cards.a: An ion (or a permanent dipole) distorts the electron cloud of a nearby nonpolar particle, inducing a temporary dipole that is then attracted to it. The strength tracks the polarizability of the nonpolar partner and the charge of the inducer. Dipole-induced dipole attraction between water and O₂ is why oxygen dissolves slightly in water.
cards.h: → what induces what + a consequence
cards.n: 'O₂ dissolves in water because it is polar' earns nothing; O₂ is nonpolar and only an induced dipole attracts it to water.

cards.q: Rank $CH_4$, $SiH_4$, and $GeH_4$ by boiling point, and justify using London dispersion forces.
cards.a: CH₄ < SiH₄ < GeH₄. All three are tetrahedral and nonpolar, so London dispersion is the only intermolecular force. GeH₄ has the most electrons and the largest, most polarizable electron cloud, so its temporary dipoles are largest and its dispersion forces strongest; more energy is needed to separate its molecules, giving the highest boiling point (CH₄ −161 °C, SiH₄ −112 °C, GeH₄ −88 °C).
cards.h: → ordered list + one cause
cards.n: Citing molar mass alone earns nothing; the point needs more electrons and greater polarizability. Polarity from Unit 2 (all tetrahedral, nonpolar).

cards.q: Rank HCl, HBr, and HI by strength of intermolecular forces, and explain why none of them hydrogen bond.
cards.a: HI > HBr > HCl. None has H bonded to N, O or F, so none hydrogen bonds; each is polar with dipole-dipole forces, but dispersion forces dominate and grow with the larger, more polarizable halogen. HCl has the largest dipole yet the weakest net force (boiling points: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C).
cards.h: → no H-bond; dispersion decides
cards.n: 'HCl has the strongest forces because it is most polar' earns nothing; dispersion growth with polarizability outweighs the shrinking dipole here.

cards.q: Identify the strongest type of intermolecular force (hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole, or dispersion only) in a pure sample of each substance: CH₄ · NH₃ · CO₂ · H₂O · HCl · CH₃OH · CH₃OCH₃ · Ne · SO₂ · CH₃COOH · HF · C₆H₁₄ · CH₂Cl₂ · BF₃ · H₂S · CH₃NH₂ · N₂ · CCl₄
cards.a:
CH₄ → London dispersion only (nonpolar)
NH₃ → hydrogen bonding (N–H)
CO₂ → dispersion only (linear, nonpolar)
H₂O → hydrogen bonding (O–H)
HCl → dipole-dipole (Cl is not N, O or F)
CH₃OH → hydrogen bonding (O–H)
CH₃OCH₃ → dipole-dipole (has O but no O–H)
Ne → dispersion only
SO₂ → dipole-dipole (bent, polar)
CH₃COOH → hydrogen bonding (O–H)
HF → hydrogen bonding
C₆H₁₄ → dispersion only
CH₂Cl₂ → dipole-dipole (tetrahedral but unsymmetrical)
BF₃ → dispersion only (trigonal planar, nonpolar)
H₂S → dipole-dipole (S not electronegative enough)
CH₃NH₂ → hydrogen bonding (N–H)
N₂ → dispersion only
CCl₄ → dispersion only (tetrahedral, nonpolar)
cards.h: → H on N/O/F? polar? else dispersion
cards.n: Naming hydrogen bonding for any H-containing molecule (HCl, H₂S, CH₄) earns nothing. All also have dispersion forces, often the larger share. Polarity is borrowed from Unit 2.

cards.q: Identify the strongest attraction between each pair of different species: I₂ and CCl₄ · Na⁺ and H₂O · HCl and H₂O · O₂ and H₂O · NH₃ and H₂O · CH₃OH and CH₃OCH₃ · Cl⁻ and H₂O · He and Ar · K⁺ and NH₃ · CO₂ and H₂O
cards.a:
I₂ and CCl₄ → London dispersion (both nonpolar)
Na⁺ and H₂O → ion-dipole (δ− O of water toward Na⁺)
HCl and H₂O → dipole-dipole (H of HCl is not on N, O or F)
O₂ and H₂O → dipole-induced dipole
NH₃ and H₂O → hydrogen bonding (N–H···O and O–H···N)
CH₃OH and CH₃OCH₃ → hydrogen bonding (methanol's O–H to the ether's O lone pair)
Cl⁻ and H₂O → ion-dipole (δ+ H of water toward Cl⁻)
He and Ar → London dispersion
K⁺ and NH₃ → ion-dipole (N lone pair toward K⁺)
CO₂ and H₂O → dipole-induced dipole
cards.h: → ion present? both polar? H on N/O/F facing a lone pair?
cards.n: 'CH₃OCH₃ cannot hydrogen bond' is true only with itself; its O lone pairs accept a hydrogen bond from methanol's O–H. Say which molecule donates the H.

cards.q: Describe the orientation of two HCl molecules that maximizes their dipole-dipole attraction, and identify the partial charges involved.
cards.a: Cl is more electronegative than H, so each HCl has a δ+ H end and a δ− Cl end. The attraction is strongest head to tail, with the δ+ H of one molecule pointing at the δ− Cl of its neighbor (H–Cl···H–Cl), or side by side antiparallel so that each δ+ lies beside a δ−. The force is Coulombic between the partial charges of DIFFERENT molecules and depends on orientation: two δ+ ends brought together repel.
cards.h: → δ+ toward δ−, head to tail or antiparallel
cards.n: Calling the H–Cl bond the intermolecular force, or drawing the two H ends together, earns nothing; the attraction is between opposite partial charges on separate molecules.

cards.q: Describe two noncovalent interactions that hold a protein in its folded shape, and identify the parts of the molecule involved.
cards.a: Hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups of the backbone (and between polar side chains with –OH, –NH₂ or –COOH); London dispersion between nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains clustered in the interior; ion-ion attractions (salt bridges) between –COO⁻ and –NH₃⁺ side chains; dipole-dipole between polar groups. All act between different regions of the same large molecule, and the shape they fix determines the protein's function.
cards.h: → two named interactions + the groups
cards.n: Naming the covalent peptide bonds as what holds the fold earns nothing; folding is set by noncovalent interactions between regions of the chain.

cards.q: Explain why H₂O, HF, and NH₃ boil far higher than the trend of their families predicts.
cards.a: Each has H bonded to a small, highly electronegative N, O or F, so its molecules hydrogen bond: the strongly δ+ H is attracted to a lone pair on a neighbor's N, O or F. These attractions are much stronger than the dipole-dipole and dispersion forces in H₂S, HCl or PH₃, so more energy is needed to separate molecules.
cards.h: → H on N/O/F → hydrogen bonds → much stronger attraction → more energy to separate → higher bp
cards.n: 'They are polar' earns nothing, since H₂S and HCl are polar too; the point needs hydrogen bonding named with the H on N, O or F.
o: Down each group dispersion grows with electron count, but the first member gains hydrogen bonding, an attraction strong enough to outweigh that trend.
Vaporization must overcome all intermolecular attractions; hydrogen bonds between the H on N, O or F and a neighbor's lone pair are the strongest such attraction, so these three need the most energy.

w.a: They boil higher because their bonds are stronger and harder to break.
w.why: boiling separates molecules; covalent bonds stay intact

w.a: They boil higher because they are the lightest members of their groups.
w.why: lighter molecules have weaker dispersion forces and should boil lower

w.a: They boil higher because they are polar molecules with dipole-dipole forces.
w.why: H₂S, HCl and PH₃ are polar too; only hydrogen bonding explains the jump

cards.q: Explain why a hydrogen bond is so much stronger than an ordinary dipole-dipole attraction.
cards.a: The H bonded to N, O or F is nearly stripped of electron density, so it carries a large δ+ on a very small atom, while the neighbor's N, O or F lone pair carries a large δ−. Large opposite partial charges that approach very closely give, by Coulomb's law, a much stronger attraction than ordinary dipoles.
cards.h: → large δ+ on a tiny H + lone pair δ− → very close approach → large Coulombic attraction
cards.n: 'It is a bond between hydrogen and oxygen' earns nothing; the hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between partial charges, not a covalent bond.
o: Coulomb's law: larger partial charges and a shorter distance between the H and the lone pair give a stronger attraction than ordinary dipoles achieve.
N, O and F are the most electronegative small atoms, so the bond to H is extremely polarized and the small H lets the two dipoles get unusually close.

w.a: Hydrogen bonds are stronger because they are covalent bonds between molecules.
w.why: a hydrogen bond is intermolecular and noncovalent; molecules stay intact

w.a: Hydrogen bonds are stronger because hydrogen is the lightest atom.
w.why: mass is irrelevant; the size of the partial charges and their separation matter

w.a: Hydrogen bonds are stronger because they occur in water, which has a high boiling point.
w.why: circular; the boiling point is the consequence, not the cause

cards.q: Explain why I₂ is a solid at room temperature although it is nonpolar, while HCl, a polar molecule, is a gas.
cards.a: I₂ has 106 electrons in a large, easily polarized cloud, so its temporary dipoles are large and its dispersion forces strong enough to hold the molecules in a solid. HCl has only 18 electrons; its weak dispersion forces plus its dipole-dipole attraction are much weaker in total, so it is a gas.
cards.h: → many electrons → high polarizability → strong dispersion in I₂ > weak dispersion + dipole-dipole in HCl
cards.n: 'I₂ is heavier' earns nothing; the point needs more electrons and greater polarizability giving stronger dispersion forces.
o: Dispersion forces are often the strongest net force between large molecules, and I₂ is large; HCl's small dipole cannot match them.
Net attraction = dispersion + dipole-dipole; for I₂ the first term is huge, for HCl both terms are small, so I₂ needs far more energy to separate its molecules.

w.a: I₂ is a solid because it has stronger covalent bonds than HCl.
w.why: the I–I bond is actually weaker than H–Cl, and bonds do not set the state of matter

w.a: I₂ is a solid because iodine molecules are heavier and sink.
w.why: mass is not a force; the scored cause is polarizability and dispersion strength

w.a: HCl is a gas because polar molecules repel each other.
w.why: polar molecules attract through dipole-dipole forces; they are just weaker here

cards.q: Explain why n-pentane boils at 36 °C while its isomer neopentane, 2,2-dimethylpropane, boils at 10 °C.
cards.a: Both are C₅H₁₂ with the same number of electrons and only dispersion forces. The long n-pentane chain lies alongside neighbors over a large contact area, so many temporary dipoles interact; compact, nearly spherical neopentane touches neighbors over a small area, so its dispersion forces are weaker and it boils lower.
cards.h: → same electrons → shape decides contact area → chain has more surface contact → stronger dispersion → higher bp
cards.n: 'n-Pentane has more dispersion forces because it is bigger' earns nothing; the two isomers have the same electrons, the difference is molecular shape and surface contact.
o: At equal electron count, dispersion strength depends on how much of two molecules' surfaces can approach; a chain offers far more than a sphere.
The spherical isomer packs with only point-like contacts, so fewer instantaneous dipoles interact and less energy is needed to separate the molecules.

w.a: n-Pentane boils higher because it has a higher molar mass.
w.why: isomers have identical molar mass

w.a: n-Pentane boils higher because it is polar and neopentane is not.
w.why: both are nonpolar hydrocarbons

w.a: Neopentane boils lower because its branches make it heavier and harder to vaporize.
w.why: contradictory and wrong; branching reduces contact area and lowers the boiling point

cards.q: Explain why nonpolar O₂ molecules are attracted to water molecules at all, even though O₂ has no permanent dipole.
cards.a: Water's permanent dipole distorts the electron cloud of a nearby O₂ molecule, inducing a temporary dipole in it; that induced dipole is then attracted to the water dipole, a dipole-induced dipole force. The attraction is weak, which is why O₂ is only slightly soluble in water.
cards.h: → water's dipole distorts O₂'s cloud → induced dipole → weak Coulombic attraction
cards.n: 'O₂ hydrogen bonds with water' earns nothing; O₂ has no H, and the only attraction is an induced dipole.
