cards.a: Written as separated ions: aqueous strong electrolytes, that is strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄), strong bases (Group 1 hydroxides, Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂) and soluble ionic salts labeled (aq). Kept as complete formulas: all solids (s), liquids (l) and gases (g), weak acids such as CH₃COOH and HF, weak bases such as NH₃, and molecular compounds such as H₂O and CO₂.
cards.h: → two lists
cards.n: Writing a weak acid such as CH₃COOH as H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ is the most common scoring error; only strong electrolytes exist as separated ions in solution.

cards.q: Write the net ionic equation for aqueous silver nitrate mixed with aqueous sodium chloride.
cards.a: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Molecular: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq). Complete ionic: Ag⁺ + NO₃⁻ + Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) + Na⁺ + NO₃⁻; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ appear unchanged on both sides, so they are spectators and cancel. Charge check: +1 + (−1) = 0 on the left, neutral solid on the right.
cards.h: → one equation + the spectators named
cards.n: AgCl written as ions, or Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ left in, earns nothing; the exam tells you AgCl is the precipitate, so the work is choosing what to keep.

cards.q: Identify the spectator ions when aqueous $Pb(NO_3)_2$ is mixed with aqueous NaCl.
cards.a: Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are the spectators. The precipitate is PbCl₂(s) (the exam would state that lead(II) chloride is insoluble), so the net ionic equation is Pb²⁺(aq) + 2 Cl⁻(aq) → PbCl₂(s). Sodium ions and nitrate ions remain dissolved and unchanged on both sides of the complete ionic equation, and by 4.7.A.5 all sodium and nitrate salts are soluble, so they can never precipitate.
cards.h: → two ions with charges + why
cards.n: Naming Pb²⁺ or Cl⁻ as spectators earns nothing; the ions that form the solid are the ones that change.

cards.q: Two solutions, aqueous iron(III) nitrate and aqueous sodium hydroxide, are combined. Compute the net ionic equation for the precipitation reaction that occurs.
cards.a: Fe³⁺(aq) + 3 OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s). Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators (sodium and nitrate salts are all soluble) and are omitted. The coefficient 3 on hydroxide balances both atoms and charge: left side +3 + 3(−1) = 0, matching the neutral solid.
cards.h: → one balanced net equation + charge check
cards.n: Fe³⁺ + OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃ leaves a net +2 unaccounted for and earns nothing; charge balance is checked, not assumed.

cards.q: Define the law of conservation of mass and state how it applies to physical and chemical changes.
cards.a: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a physical or chemical change; the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. It holds because atoms are only rearranged, never made or lost: in a phase change the same molecules persist, and in a reaction every atom in the reactants ends up in a product. A balanced equation expresses the law by showing equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides.
cards.h: → statement + atoms rearranged + balanced equation
cards.n: 'Mass is conserved because the equation is balanced' reverses the logic; the equation is balanced BECAUSE atoms are conserved.

cards.q:
Balance each equation with the smallest whole-number coefficients:
C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂
N₂ + H₂ → NH₃
KClO₃ → KCl + O₂
Ca(OH)₂ + H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + H₂O
C₄H₁₀ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
NH₃ + O₂ → NO + H₂O
Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
P₄ + Cl₂ → PCl₃
Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂
cards.a:
C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O
C₂H₅OH + 3 O₂ → 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O
4 Al + 3 O₂ → 2 Al₂O₃
Fe₂O₃ + 3 CO → 2 Fe + 3 CO₂
N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃
2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂
3 Ca(OH)₂ + 2 H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6 H₂O
2 C₄H₁₀ + 13 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 10 H₂O
4 NH₃ + 5 O₂ → 4 NO + 6 H₂O
Mg + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
P₄ + 6 Cl₂ → 4 PCl₃
2 Na + 2 H₂O → 2 NaOH + H₂
cards.h: → balance C, then H, then O last; check every element
cards.n: Changing a subscript (H₂O → H₂O₂) to make atoms match earns nothing; only coefficients may change, because a subscript changes the substance.

cards.q:
Write the net ionic equation for each mixing of aqueous solutions (the insoluble product is given where one forms):
HCl + NaOH
HNO₃ + KOH
CH₃COOH + NaOH
HCl + NH₃
BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ (BaSO₄ insoluble)
Pb(NO₃)₂ + KI (PbI₂ insoluble)
Na₂CO₃ + HCl
CuSO₄ + NaOH (Cu(OH)₂ insoluble)
Zn(s) + HCl
NaHCO₃ + HCl
H₂SO₄ + Ba(OH)₂ (BaSO₄ insoluble)
AgNO₃ + K₂CrO₄ (Ag₂CrO₄ insoluble)
HF + KOH
NaCl + KNO₃
CaCO₃(s) + HCl
HClO₄ + Sr(OH)₂
cards.a:
HCl + NaOH: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O(l)
HNO₃ + KOH: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O(l)
CH₃COOH + NaOH: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O(l)
HCl + NH₃: H⁺ + NH₃ → NH₄⁺
BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s)
Pb(NO₃)₂ + KI: Pb²⁺ + 2 I⁻ → PbI₂(s)
Na₂CO₃ + HCl: CO₃²⁻ + 2 H⁺ → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)
CuSO₄ + NaOH: Cu²⁺ + 2 OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂(s)
Zn(s) + HCl: Zn(s) + 2 H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂(g)
NaHCO₃ + HCl: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)
H₂SO₄ + Ba(OH)₂: 2 H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + Ba²⁺ + 2 OH⁻ → BaSO₄(s) + 2 H₂O(l); no spectators
AgNO₃ + K₂CrO₄: 2 Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻ → Ag₂CrO₄(s)
HF + KOH: HF + OH⁻ → F⁻ + H₂O(l)
NaCl + KNO₃: no reaction; every possible pairing is a soluble Na⁺, K⁺ or NO₃⁻ salt
CaCO₃(s) + HCl: CaCO₃(s) + 2 H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)
HClO₄ + Sr(OH)₂: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O(l)
cards.h: → split aqueous strong electrolytes only; cancel repeats
cards.n: A weak acid split into ions, a spectator left in, or a solid written as ions earns nothing; each line must also balance charge.

cards.q: Write balanced equations, with state symbols, for three physical changes: sodium chloride dissolving in water, ice melting, and solid carbon dioxide subliming.
cards.a: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); H₂O(s) → H₂O(l); CO₂(s) → CO₂(g). Each is balanced in atoms and charge, and each shows the same substance (or its constituent ions) on both sides: the formulas do not change, only the state symbols do. The CED says all physical and chemical processes can be represented by balanced equations.
cards.h: → three equations; formulas unchanged, states change
cards.n: NaCl(aq) as the product is fine in a molecular equation, but Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) shows what is actually present and is what particulate questions expect.

cards.q: Write the molecular, complete ionic, and net ionic equations for aqueous hydrochloric acid reacting with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: Molecular: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l). Complete ionic: H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) + Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). Net ionic: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), after cancelling the spectators Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Water stays as a molecule in every form because it is not a strong electrolyte. (H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2 H₂O is equivalent.)
cards.h: → three equations, spectators cancelled in the last
cards.n: NaCl written as a unit in the complete ionic equation, or H₂O split into ions, earns nothing; aqueous strong electrolytes are the only species separated.

cards.q: Determine whether the equation Al(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Al³⁺(aq) + Cu(s) is balanced, and correct it if it is not.
cards.a: It is not balanced: atoms match (1 Al, 1 Cu each side) but charge does not (+2 on the left, +3 on the right). Balanced: 2 Al(s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Cu(s), with +6 on each side and 2 Al and 3 Cu on each side. Charge must be conserved because the 6 electrons lost by two Al atoms are exactly the 6 gained by three Cu²⁺ ions.
cards.h: → check atoms, then charge; fix with coefficients
cards.n: Declaring it balanced because the atoms match earns nothing; an ionic equation must conserve charge as well as mass.

cards.q: Write the net ionic equation for aqueous acetic acid reacting with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and identify the spectator ion.
cards.a: CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). Na⁺ is the only spectator. Acetic acid is a weak acid, so it exists mainly as intact molecules in solution and is written as a whole formula; NaOH is a strong base and is written as Na⁺ and OH⁻; the acetate ion produced is a dissolved ion and is written separately. Charge: −1 on each side.
cards.h: → weak acid whole, OH⁻ separate, one spectator
cards.n: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O earns nothing here; it treats the weak acid as fully ionized. The weak acid must appear as CH₃COOH.

cards.q: Write a molecular equation, with state symbols, for a pair of aqueous reagents that would produce the net ionic equation Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).
cards.a: Any soluble barium salt with any soluble sulfate works, for example BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2 NaCl(aq), or Ba(NO₃)₂(aq) + K₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2 KNO₃(aq). The partner ions must be spectators, so choose ions whose salts are all soluble: sodium, potassium, ammonium or nitrate (4.7.A.5).
cards.h: → soluble Ba salt + soluble sulfate; spectators from 4.7.A.5
cards.n: Choosing BaSO₄ itself or an insoluble barium compound as a reagent earns nothing; both reagents must be dissolved so the ions are free to meet.

cards.q: Describe when a chemist would use the molecular equation, the complete ionic equation, and the net ionic equation to represent the same reaction in solution.
cards.a: Molecular equation: for stoichiometry with the compounds actually weighed or measured (grams of Na₂SO₄ needed), since it names whole substances. Complete ionic: to show every species in solution, spectators included, as when reasoning about conductivity or the ions left after mixing. Net ionic: to show the actual change and to recognize that different reagent pairs undergo the same reaction. The CED says the form depends on the context.
cards.h: → one use for each form
cards.n: 'The net ionic equation is always best' earns nothing; the point is choosing the form that carries the information the context needs.

cards.q: Verify that the equation 3 Cu(s) + 8 H⁺(aq) + 2 NO₃⁻(aq) → 3 Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 NO(g) + 4 H₂O(l) conserves both atoms and charge.
cards.a: Atoms: Cu 3 = 3; H 8 = 4 × 2 = 8; N 2 = 2; O 2 × 3 = 6 = 2 + 4 = 6. Charge: left 8(+1) + 2(−1) = +6; right 3(+2) = +6. Both are conserved, so the equation is balanced. Charge conservation here reflects the 6 electrons lost by 3 Cu atoms equalling the 6 gained by 2 nitrate ions (N +5 → +2).
cards.h: → element-by-element count, then total charge each side
cards.n: Checking only the atoms earns half; an ionic equation is not verified until the total charge on each side is shown to match.

cards.q: Explain what makes a solute a strong electrolyte and why that matters for ionic equations.
cards.a: A strong electrolyte dissociates or ionizes essentially completely in water: soluble ionic salts, strong acids, strong bases. Because it exists in solution as separate ions, it is written as separated ions in ionic equations; weak electrolytes and molecular solutes, mostly intact particles, are written whole.
cards.h: → complete dissociation → exists as ions → written as ions
cards.n: 'Strong electrolytes are strong acids' earns nothing; the definition is complete dissociation into ions, which is why soluble salts and strong bases qualify too.
o: An ionic equation shows what is really in the beaker; a solute that is essentially 100% ions must be drawn as ions, one that is mostly molecules must not.
Conductivity is the evidence: a strong electrolyte solution conducts well because it is full of mobile ions, and the equation is written to match.

w.a: A strong electrolyte is any compound that dissolves well in water.
w.why: solubility is not dissociation; sugar dissolves well and forms no ions

w.a: A strong electrolyte is a concentrated solution of an acid.
w.why: confuses concentration with degree of ionization

w.a: Strong electrolytes are written as ions because they are more reactive.
w.why: reactivity is irrelevant; they are written as ions because that is how they exist

cards.q: Explain why water, a product of a strong acid-strong base reaction, is not split into ions in the net ionic equation.
cards.a: Water is a very weak electrolyte: pure water holds only about 10⁻⁷ M each of H⁺ and OH⁻ among 55.5 M of H₂O, so it exists almost entirely as molecules. Ionic equations separate only species that exist as ions in solution, so water is written whole: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
cards.h: → water barely ionizes → exists as molecules → written whole
cards.n: Writing H⁺ + OH⁻ → H⁺ + OH⁻ (splitting the water) cancels everything and earns nothing; the product is the molecule.
o: Pure water barely conducts electricity, direct evidence that it is almost entirely molecules rather than ions.
The (l) state symbol marks water as a pure liquid, and pure liquids are never written as separated ions.

w.a: Water is not split because it is the product, and products are never written as ions.
w.why: false; dissolved ionic products such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are written as ions

w.a: Water is not split because it has covalent bonds and covalent compounds never form ions.
w.why: HCl is covalent yet ionizes completely; the criterion is degree of ionization

w.a: Water is not split because it is neutral.
w.why: NaCl is neutral too and is written as ions; neutrality is not the reason

cards.q: Explain why a net ionic equation must balance total charge as well as the number of atoms of each element.
cards.a: Charge is carried by electrons and protons, which a reaction rearranges but cannot create or destroy, so the total charge on each side must be equal. In Fe³⁺ + 3 OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃, +3 and 3(−1) sum to zero, matching the neutral solid; a coefficient of 1 on OH⁻ would invent two units of charge.
cards.h: → charge is carried by conserved particles → total charge unchanged → coefficients must make both sides equal
cards.n: 'Because the equation has to look balanced' earns nothing; the reason is conservation of charge, and the check is the arithmetic on each side.
o: In a redox equation, the electrons lost by one species are exactly the electrons gained by another, so no net charge appears or vanishes.
The complete ionic equation is charge-balanced, and removing identical spectator ions from both sides cannot change that balance, so the net equation must be too.

w.a: Charge must balance because every compound is neutral.
w.why: ionic equations contain charged species; neutrality of compounds is not the point

w.a: Charge must balance so that the atoms come out balanced too.
w.why: atoms can balance while charge does not, as in Al + Cu²⁺ → Al³⁺ + Cu

w.a: Charge balances automatically once the atoms are balanced.
w.why: false; charge must be checked separately

cards.q: Explain why hydrochloric acid is written as H⁺ and Cl⁻ in a net ionic equation while acetic acid is written as the intact molecule CH₃COOH.
cards.a: HCl is a strong acid: essentially every molecule gives its proton to water, so the solution holds H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and Cl⁻ and no HCl molecules. Acetic acid is weak: only a small fraction ionizes, so the solution is mainly CH₃COOH molecules. Ionic equations show species as they exist, so one is split and the other kept whole.
cards.h: → strong acid fully ionized → exists as ions; weak acid barely ionized → exists as molecules
cards.n: 'Acetic acid is organic so it stays whole' earns nothing; the reason is its small degree of ionization, and HF, an inorganic weak acid, is treated the same way.
o: A 0.1 M HCl solution conducts far better than 0.1 M acetic acid at the same concentration, evidence that one is essentially all ions and the other mostly molecules.
The reacting particle in the acetic acid case is the molecule itself, which donates its proton to OH⁻ directly, so the molecule belongs in the equation.

w.a: HCl is split because it is a gas dissolved in water and acetic acid is a liquid.
w.why: physical state of the pure substance has nothing to do with ionization in solution

w.a: Acetic acid stays whole because it is a larger molecule.
w.why: size is not the criterion; degree of ionization is

w.a: Both should be split, because both are acids and all acids produce H⁺.
w.why: weak acids produce only a little H⁺ and exist mainly as molecules

cards.q: Explain why the reaction of nitric acid with potassium hydroxide has the same net ionic equation as the reaction of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: Both acids and both bases are strong, so each mixture contains H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and OH⁻ as the only reacting ions; K⁺, NO₃⁻, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators that stay dissolved and unchanged. Cancelling them leaves H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) in both cases: the same proton transfer.
cards.h: → both strong → same reacting ions → different spectators cancel → same net change
cards.n: 'They are the same because both are neutralizations' earns nothing without identifying the identical reacting ions and the spectators that cancel.
o: The measured heat released per mole of water formed is the same for both, evidence that the same reaction, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, is occurring.
The identity of the counter-ions does not matter because each of them is a spectator that stays in solution unchanged.

w.a: They have the same net ionic equation because all acid-base reactions have the same net ionic equation.
w.why: false; a weak acid or weak base changes the net equation

w.a: They have the same net ionic equation because both produce a salt and water.
w.why: the salts differ; the point is that the salts' ions are spectators

w.a: They have the same net ionic equation because HNO₃ and HCl have the same molar mass.
w.why: irrelevant and false

cards.q: Define what a particulate (molecular-level) diagram represents, in contrast to a symbolic balanced chemical equation.
cards.a: A particulate diagram draws the individual atoms, molecules or ions as shapes (joined spheres for molecules, separate charged circles for ions), showing the actual number of each particle, its state (packed solid, loose liquid, dispersed gas or solute) and arrangement. A symbolic equation gives formulas with coefficients that state the ratio of particles, but no picture of count, state or arrangement. The diagram's counts must match the coefficient ratio.
cards.h: → shapes, counts and states vs formulas and ratios
cards.n: A diagram whose particle counts break the coefficient ratio of the equation is wrong however neat it looks; the ratio is the first thing a scorer checks.

cards.q: A diagram shows 6 molecules of $A_2$ and 8 of $B_2$ reacting as $A_2 + B_2 \to 2AB$. Compute the limiting reactant and the number of AB molecules formed.
cards.a: A₂ is limiting and 12 molecules of AB form. The equation needs A₂ and B₂ in a 1:1 ratio, so 6 A₂ consume only 6 of the 8 B₂; A₂ runs out first. Each A₂ that reacts yields 2 AB, so 6 × 2 = 12 AB. The after box must show 12 AB and the 2 unreacted B₂; atom check: 12 A and 16 B before, 12 A + (12 + 4) B after.
cards.h: → 1:1 ratio, smaller count runs out; product = 2 × limiting
cards.n: Answering '12 AB' with no leftover B₂ earns only part credit; the excess reactant stays in the after box because atoms are conserved.

cards.q: For $N_2+3H_2 \to 2NH_3$, a diagram shows 2 $N_2$ and 9 $H_2$ molecules. Apply particulate reasoning to find the limiting reactant and $NH_3$ molecules produced.
cards.a: N₂ is limiting and 4 NH₃ molecules form. Using all 2 N₂ requires 2 × 3 = 6 H₂, and 9 are available, so H₂ is in excess by 3 molecules. Each N₂ gives 2 NH₃, so 2 × 2 = 4 NH₃. The after box shows 4 NH₃ and 3 H₂; atom check: 4 N and 18 H before, 4 N + (12 + 6) H after.
cards.h: → H₂ needed vs H₂ available; product from the limiting one
cards.n: Choosing H₂ as limiting because 9 > 2 'seems like more is used' earns nothing; compare available amount to the amount the ratio requires.

cards.q: Contrast the information a particulate diagram can show with the information a symbolic chemical equation shows.
cards.a: A particulate diagram shows the actual number of each particle, which reactant is left over, the physical states (lattice, liquid, gas, hydrated ions) and how atoms are grouped into molecules or ions. A symbolic equation shows only identities, state symbols and the mole ratio through coefficients; it cannot show how many particles are present or that a reactant is in excess. The diagram is a snapshot of one sample; the equation is a ratio for any amount.
cards.h: → counts, leftovers, states vs identities and ratios
cards.n: 'The diagram shows the same thing as the equation but as pictures' earns nothing; name what only the diagram can show (actual counts, excess reactant, arrangement).

cards.q: Represent the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O with before-and-after particulate boxes, starting from 4 molecules of H₂ and 2 molecules of O₂. Describe exactly what each box contains.
cards.a: Before box: 4 molecules of H₂, each two small white spheres joined, and 2 molecules of O₂, each two large red spheres joined; 6 particles, 8 H atoms and 4 O atoms. After box: 4 molecules of H₂O, each one large red sphere bonded to two small white spheres in a bent shape; nothing else, because 4 H₂ : 2 O₂ is exactly the 2:1 ratio and neither reactant is left over. Atom check: 8 H and 4 O in both boxes.
cards.h: → two boxes, counts and shapes named, atom check
cards.n: Drawing single O atoms in the before box, or 2 H₂O because the coefficient is 2, earns nothing; oxygen is diatomic and the coefficients scale with the sample.

cards.q: Determine the balanced equation represented by this particulate diagram. Before box: 2 molecules each made of two dark blue spheres, and 6 molecules each made of two small white spheres. After box: 4 molecules each made of one dark blue sphere bonded to three white spheres, and nothing else.
cards.a: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ (or X₂ + 3 Y₂ → 2 XY₃). The blue pairs are diatomic molecules of one element (2 of them), the white pairs diatomic molecules of another (6 of them), and the products contain one blue and three white atoms each (4 of them). The ratio 2:6:4 reduces to 1:3:2, the smallest whole-number coefficients. Atom check: 4 blue and 12 white atoms in each box.
cards.h: → count each molecule type, reduce the ratio, check atoms
cards.n: Writing 2 N₂ + 6 H₂ → 4 NH₃ describes the picture but is not the balanced equation with lowest coefficients; reduce the ratio.

cards.q: Evaluate whether this particulate diagram is consistent with 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. Before box: 4 H₂ molecules and 2 O₂ molecules. After box: 4 H₂O molecules and 1 O₂ molecule.
cards.a: Not consistent: atoms are not conserved. Before: 8 H and 4 O. After: 4 H₂O contain 8 H and 4 O, and the extra O₂ adds 2 more O, giving 6 O. The diagram invents two oxygen atoms. Since 4 H₂ and 2 O₂ are in exactly the 2:1 ratio, both reactants are fully consumed and the correct after box holds only 4 H₂O. The diagram would be correct only if the before box had held 3 O₂.
cards.h: → count each element before and after; name the mismatch
cards.n: 'It is consistent because water is the product' earns nothing; consistency means the counts of every element agree between the boxes.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the before-and-after particulate boxes for mixing a solution containing 3 Ag⁺ and 3 NO₃⁻ ions with a solution containing 3 Na⁺ and 3 Cl⁻ ions (AgCl is insoluble).
cards.a: Before box (two solutions): 3 Ag⁺ and 3 NO₃⁻ drawn as separate labeled circles dispersed among water molecules on one side; 3 Na⁺ and 3 Cl⁻ likewise on the other. After box: a single cluster at the bottom of 3 Ag⁺ and 3 Cl⁻ alternating in a lattice, labeled AgCl(s), and still dispersed in the solution 3 Na⁺ and 3 NO₃⁻ as separate ions. No NaNO₃ units, no Ag⁺ or Cl⁻ left free (they were in a 1:1 ratio). Ion count is the same in both boxes.
cards.h: → free ions before; solid cluster + free spectators after
cards.n: Drawing NaNO₃ as paired units, or leaving Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ floating free, earns nothing; spectators stay dissolved and the precipitate is a neutral lattice.

cards.q: Represent the particulate view before and after 2 HCl(aq) reacts with 2 NaOH(aq), showing every ion and molecule present (ignore the water solvent).
cards.a: Before: 2 H⁺ (or H₃O⁺), 2 Cl⁻, 2 Na⁺ and 2 OH⁻, all as separate dispersed ions, because HCl and NaOH are strong electrolytes; no HCl or NaOH units. After: 2 H₂O molecules (bent, one O with two H), plus 2 Na⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ still separate and dispersed. No NaCl units and no H⁺ or OH⁻ remain, since the acid and base were present in equal number. Atom and charge counts match between the boxes.
cards.h: → four free ions before; water + spectators after
cards.n: Drawing NaCl as a bonded pair in the after box, or HCl molecules in the before box, earns nothing; strong electrolytes exist as separate ions.

cards.q: Determine the contents of the after box when a before box holding 2 CH₄ molecules and 5 O₂ molecules reacts completely according to CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O.
cards.a: After box: 2 CO₂, 4 H₂O and 1 O₂ left over. Two CH₄ need 2 × 2 = 4 O₂; 5 are present, so CH₄ is limiting and 1 O₂ survives. Products from 2 CH₄: 2 CO₂ (one C between two O, linear) and 4 H₂O (bent). Atom check: before 2 C, 8 H, 10 O; after 2 C, 8 H, and 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 O.
cards.h: → O₂ needed vs present; products; leftover drawn
cards.n: An after box with 2 CO₂ and 4 H₂O and no O₂ loses the point; the surviving O₂ is part of the representation.

cards.q: Identify the limiting reactant from this after-reaction particulate box for X₂ + 2 Y₂ → 2 XY₂: the box contains 4 XY₂ molecules and 3 unreacted X₂ molecules, and no Y₂.
cards.a: Y₂ was the limiting reactant. It has been completely consumed (none remains) while 3 X₂ are left over, so the reaction stopped when Y₂ ran out. Working back: 4 XY₂ required 4 Y₂ and 2 X₂, so the before box held 5 X₂ and 4 Y₂; the 2:1 Y₂:X₂ requirement made Y₂ run out first.
cards.h: → the reactant absent afterward is the limiting one
cards.n: Naming X₂ as limiting because 'more of it reacted' or because it has the smaller coefficient earns nothing; the limiting reactant is the one that is gone.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the particulate diagram of sodium chloride dissolved in water, showing how the water molecules are oriented around each ion.
cards.a: Separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, no NaCl pairs, each surrounded by several water molecules (draw each as an O with two H in a bent shape). Around Na⁺ the water molecules point their partially negative oxygen ends toward the ion; around the larger Cl⁻ they point a partially positive hydrogen end toward the ion. Equal numbers of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ appear, dispersed randomly through the box.
cards.h: → separate ions, water oriented by partial charges
cards.n: Water drawn randomly or with H toward Na⁺ earns nothing for the orientation point; the ion-dipole attraction (Unit 3) sets the orientation.

cards.q: Represent the particulate difference between a box of solid iodine and a box of iodine vapor after sublimation, and state what stays the same.
cards.a: Solid box: I₂ molecules (pairs of large purple spheres) packed in a regular, orderly, touching array. Vapor box: the same I₂ molecules, far apart and randomly placed, filling the box. What stays the same: every particle is still a diatomic I₂ molecule and the number of molecules is unchanged, because sublimation only overcomes the attractions between molecules; the I–I bonds are untouched. Drawing single I atoms in the vapor would show a chemical change.
cards.h: → same I₂ molecules: ordered, touching vs sparse, random
cards.n: Drawing the vapor as separate I atoms earns nothing; a physical change keeps the molecules intact.

cards.q: Represent the before-and-after particulate boxes for a zinc strip placed in a solution containing 2 Cu²⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻ ions, with enough zinc that 2 Zn atoms react.
cards.a: Before: a block of Zn atoms (identical grey spheres, packed) as the strip, and in the solution 2 Cu²⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻ drawn as separate labeled ions. After: the strip with 2 fewer Zn atoms and 2 Cu atoms deposited on its surface (different color), and in solution 2 Zn²⁺ and the same 2 SO₄²⁻, still separate. Charge check: +4 and −4 in solution both before and after. Each Zn atom gave 2 electrons to one Cu²⁺.
cards.h: → metal atoms swap places with ions; sulfate unchanged
cards.n: Drawing ZnSO₄ units, or leaving the Cu²⁺ in solution alongside new Zn²⁺, earns nothing; the ions that gained electrons are now metal atoms.

cards.q: Describe the checks a scorer applies to decide whether a student's particulate diagram is consistent with a given balanced equation.
cards.a: (1) Atoms: each element's count is identical before and after. (2) Ratio: the particles that reacted and formed match the coefficients (twice as many H₂ as O₂ react in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O). (3) Species: each particle is real and in the right state: diatomic elements as pairs, strong electrolytes as separate ions, molecular substances whole. (4) Excess reactant appears unchanged afterward. (5) Total charge is conserved.
cards.h: → atoms, ratio, correct species, leftovers, charge
cards.n: 'It has the right products' is only one check; a diagram fails if an element count or the coefficient ratio is off.

cards.q: Explain what a particulate diagram drawn after a precipitation reaction must show.
cards.a: It must show the precipitate as a neutral cluster of alternating cations and anions, the spectator ions still separate and dissolved in their original numbers, and any ions of the excess reactant left in solution. Every atom and every unit of charge in the before box must appear in the after box.
cards.h: → solid as a lattice cluster → spectators still separate → excess ions still free → counts conserved
cards.n: Omitting the excess reactant ions, or drawing the spectators as paired units such as NaNO₃, earns nothing; both misrepresent what is actually in the solution.
o: The diagram is a snapshot of the beaker: the solid that formed, the ions that never reacted, and the ions that were in excess are all still there.
Atoms and charge are conserved, so every ion in the before box appears in the after box, either inside the lattice or still dissolved.

w.a: The after box only needs to show the precipitate, since that is the product.
w.why: spectators and excess ions are still present and must be drawn

w.a: The after box should show the product salt and the spectator salt as neutral formula units.
w.why: dissolved spectators exist as separate ions, not units

w.a: The after box shows fewer ions than the before box because some became the solid.
w.why: the ions in the solid are still drawn; nothing disappears

cards.q: Explain why the number of each type of atom must be identical in the 'before' and 'after' boxes of a particulate reaction diagram.
cards.a: A chemical reaction only rearranges atoms into new combinations; it does not create or destroy them. So every atom of each element in the before box must reappear in the after box, bonded differently. This is conservation of mass at the particle level, the same law that balancing an equation enforces.
cards.h: → atoms rearranged, never made or lost → same count of each element → conservation of mass
cards.n: 'Because the equation is balanced' earns nothing on its own; the equation is balanced because atoms are conserved, and the diagram must obey the same law.
o: Mass is conserved in a reaction, and mass at the particulate level is atoms, so their numbers cannot change.
Bonds break and form during a reaction, but the nuclei are untouched, so each element's atoms are simply regrouped.

w.a: The atom counts match because the products weigh the same as the reactants only if you draw them that way.
w.why: circular; conservation is a law, not a drawing choice

w.a: The atom counts must match because molecules cannot be split in a reaction.
w.why: molecules are split; atoms are what persist

w.a: The atom counts match because every reaction has the same number of reactant and product molecules.
w.why: false; molecule counts change (N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃), atom counts do not

cards.q: Explain why a particulate diagram of hydrogen burning in oxygen must show the oxygen as O₂ molecules rather than as single O atoms.
cards.a: Oxygen gas exists as diatomic molecules, two O atoms bonded together. A diagram shows the species actually present, so the reactant must be drawn as O₂ pairs; lone O atoms would depict a different, highly reactive species that is not in the flask. The equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O likewise uses O₂.
cards.h: → elemental oxygen is diatomic → diagram shows real species → O₂ pairs, not O atoms
cards.n: Drawing lone O atoms 'because the water needs single O' earns nothing; the O–O bond is broken during the reaction, not before it.
o: The equation's coefficient ratio 2:1 counts O₂ molecules, so the diagram matches the equation only when oxygen is drawn in pairs.
The seven diatomic elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) are always drawn as pairs in their elemental state.

w.a: Oxygen must be drawn as O₂ because oxygen atoms are too small to draw alone.
w.why: nonsense; the reason is the actual molecular form of the element

w.a: Oxygen can be drawn either way as long as the total number of O atoms is right.
w.why: atom count is necessary but the species must also be real

w.a: Oxygen must be O₂ because water contains two hydrogens.
w.why: confuses the formula of the product with the form of the reactant

cards.q: Explain why the after box of a limiting-reactant particulate diagram must still contain the unreacted molecules of the excess reactant.
cards.a: The reaction stops when the limiting reactant is used up, so the surplus molecules of the other reactant have nothing left to react with and remain unchanged. Atoms are conserved, so those molecules cannot vanish; omitting them would leave the after box short of atoms of that element.
cards.h: → reaction stops at the limiting reactant → surplus has no partner → atoms conserved → must be drawn
cards.n: Drawing only the products 'because the reaction is complete' earns nothing; complete means the limiting reactant is gone, not that everything reacted.
o: The excess reactant is what a chemist would find if the mixture were analyzed afterward, so a truthful snapshot includes it.
The atom count of the excess element only balances between the boxes if the leftover molecules are included.

w.a: The leftover molecules are drawn to show that the reaction was incomplete.
w.why: the reaction was complete; the limiting reactant is fully consumed

w.a: The leftover molecules should be left out because they did not participate.
w.why: they are still present and atoms must be conserved

w.a: The leftover molecules should be drawn as products because they are in the after box.
w.why: they are unchanged reactant, not product

cards.q: Explain why a particulate representation of aqueous sodium chloride shows separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions rather than NaCl units.
cards.a: NaCl is a strong electrolyte: dissolving pulls the lattice apart into individual hydrated ions, so the solution holds free Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and essentially no NaCl pairs. A representation shows what is present, so the ions are drawn apart, each ringed by oriented water molecules, matching NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
cards.h: → strong electrolyte → lattice pulled apart into hydrated ions → no units exist to draw
cards.n: Drawing NaCl 'molecules' floating in water earns nothing; the solid has no molecules, and the solution has only separated ions.
o: The solution conducts electricity, which requires mobile charged particles, so the ions must be drawn free.
The (aq) state in Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) means each ion is individually surrounded by water, not paired with its partner.

w.a: The ions are drawn separately because NaCl is a covalent compound in water.
w.why: NaCl is ionic; the separation is dissociation, not a change of bonding type

w.a: NaCl should be drawn as units because it is a neutral compound.
w.why: neutral overall, but dissolved as separate ions

w.a: The ions are drawn separately only if the solution is dilute.
w.why: a strong electrolyte is dissociated at any ordinary concentration

cards.q: Contrast what happens to a substance's particles during a phase change with what happens during a chemical reaction.
cards.a: Phase change: the molecules or ions stay chemically identical; only the intermolecular attractions between them are overcome or re-formed, changing their spacing, order and motion (ice → liquid water: H₂O molecules leave the lattice, H-bonds between molecules loosen, O–H bonds untouched). Chemical reaction: bonds within the particles break and new bonds form, so the particles afterward are different substances (electrolysis: O–H bonds break, H–H and O=O bonds form).
cards.h: → IMFs change vs bonds break and form; one example each
cards.n: 'In a phase change the molecules move faster' describes motion, not what is broken; the point is intermolecular attractions versus chemical bonds.

cards.q: State the bond-based criterion the CED uses to classify a process as chemical or physical.
cards.a: A process that involves breaking and/or forming chemical bonds (covalent, ionic or metallic bonds within or between the particles of a substance) is typically classified as chemical. A process that involves only changes in intermolecular interactions, such as a phase change or the dissolving of a molecular solid, is typically classified as physical. The CED adds that some physical processes, such as dissolving a salt, do break bonds, so the classification can be argued.
cards.h: → bonds → chemical; IMFs only → physical; with the caveat
cards.n: 'Physical changes never break bonds' earns nothing against 4.4.A.2; say 'typically', and know the salt-dissolution exception.

cards.q: Classify each process by what is broken or formed, intermolecular interactions only (IMF) or chemical bonds (bond), and give the usual label, physical (P) or chemical (C): ice melting · liquid bromine evaporating · sugar dissolving in water · methane burning · dry ice subliming · water electrolyzed · steam condensing · iodine subliming · hydrogen peroxide decomposing · ethanol boiling · NaCl dissolving in water · HCl gas dissolving in water · NaCl melting · quartz (SiO₂) melting · rust forming on iron · wax solidifying
cards.a:
ice melting → IMF (H-bonds between molecules) · P
bromine evaporating → IMF (dispersion) · P
sugar dissolving → IMF (sugar–sugar H-bonds replaced by sugar–water) · P
methane burning → bonds (C–H, O=O broken; C=O, O–H formed) · C
dry ice subliming → IMF · P
water electrolyzed → bonds (O–H broken; H–H, O=O formed) · C
steam condensing → IMF formed · P
iodine subliming → IMF · P
H₂O₂ decomposing → bonds (O–O broken; O=O formed) · C
ethanol boiling → IMF · P
NaCl dissolving → ionic bonds broken, ion-dipole formed · usually P, arguable (4.4.A.2)
HCl(g) dissolving → H–Cl bond broken, H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ formed · C (ionization)
NaCl melting → ionic bonds loosened · P (no new substance)
quartz melting → covalent network bonds broken · P (no new substance)
rust forming → bonds (Fe–O formed) · C
wax solidifying → IMF formed · P
cards.h: → ask: which interactions break, and is anything new made?
cards.n: Labeling every bond-breaking process chemical earns nothing on the NaCl, molten-salt and quartz lines; a new substance, not bond breaking alone, is what the label tracks.

cards.q: Identify which interactions are overcome when liquid water boils and which are not, and use that to classify boiling.
cards.a: Boiling overcomes the hydrogen bonds (intermolecular attractions) between H₂O molecules so they can separate into the gas; the covalent O–H bonds within each molecule are not broken, so the vapor is still H₂O. Only intermolecular interactions change, so boiling is a physical process. The large heat of vaporization reflects the strength of water's hydrogen bonding, not bond breaking.
cards.h: → H-bonds broken, O–H bonds kept → physical
cards.n: 'Boiling breaks the bonds in water' earns nothing; that would produce hydrogen and oxygen, which boiling does not.
x: hydrogen bonds; O-H bonds intact; physical

cards.q: Identify the interactions broken and formed when sucrose dissolves in water, and classify the process.
cards.a: Broken: the hydrogen bonds and dispersion forces between sucrose molecules in the crystal, and some hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Formed: hydrogen bonds between the –OH groups of sucrose and water molecules. The C–C, C–O and O–H covalent bonds inside each sucrose molecule are untouched, so the molecules keep their identity and the process is physical.
cards.h: → IMFs swapped, covalent bonds intact → physical
cards.n: 'The sugar breaks down in water' earns nothing; the molecules are intact, only separated and surrounded by water.

cards.q: Describe the argument that dissolving sodium chloride in water is a chemical process and the argument that it is a physical process, as 4.4.A.2 allows.
cards.a: Chemical argument: the ionic bonds holding Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the lattice break and new ion-dipole attractions between the ions and water form; bonds broken and formed mark a chemical process, and the solution has a new property (it conducts). Physical argument: no substance of new composition forms; the ions are the same ions, a mixture results, and evaporation returns identical NaCl. Either earns credit if reasoned from the interactions.
cards.h: → bonds broken and formed vs same ions in a mixture
cards.n: Either label with no reference to which interactions break and form earns nothing; the credit is for the reasoning, not the label.

cards.q: Support the claim that a chemical change occurred with this data: a 2.50 g sample of a white solid was heated in an open crucible; a gas escaped, the residue had a mass of 1.58 g, and the residue melted at a much higher temperature than the original solid.
cards.a: The claim is supported. Mass fell from 2.50 g to 1.58 g while a gas escaped, so part of the original substance left as a different substance (atoms are conserved, so the lost mass is in the gas). The residue has a different melting point from the starting solid, and melting point is a property of a specific substance, so the residue is a new substance with a different composition. New substances mean bonds were broken and formed: a chemical change.
cards.h: → mass loss to a gas + new melting point → new substance
cards.n: 'A gas came off so it is chemical' alone earns nothing; the melting-point change is the evidence that the residue is a new substance, and the mass loss must be tied to the gas.

cards.q: Contrast boiling water with electrolyzing water using this evidence: boiling gives one gas that condenses back to water, while electrolysis gives two gases in a 2:1 volume ratio, one of which burns.
cards.a: Boiling is physical: the single gas is H₂O vapor, the same substance, which condenses back to liquid water, so only intermolecular attractions were overcome. Electrolysis is chemical: two different gases with their own properties (H₂ burns, O₂ supports burning) form in the 2:1 ratio that 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂ predicts, so O–H bonds were broken and H–H and O=O bonds formed; new substances exist that cannot be condensed back into water.
cards.h: → same substance back vs two new gases in a 2:1 ratio
cards.n: 'Electrolysis uses electricity so it must be chemical' earns nothing; the evidence is the two new gases and their fixed ratio.

cards.q: Identify what must be broken for quartz (SiO₂, a covalent network solid) to melt, and state how the CED would classify the melting.
cards.a: Covalent Si–O bonds must be broken, because every silicon atom is bonded to four oxygens throughout the crystal; there are no separate molecules held by intermolecular forces. Even so, melting is classified as a physical process: no new substance forms, the liquid is still SiO₂ and re-solidifies on cooling. This is the CED's point that some physical processes involve breaking chemical bonds (4.4.A.2), and it explains quartz's very high melting point (about 1700 °C).
cards.h: → covalent bonds broken, yet still SiO₂ → physical
cards.n: 'Melting only ever breaks intermolecular forces' earns nothing for a network solid; say which bonds break and why the label is still physical.

cards.q: Identify the interaction broken and the species formed when hydrogen chloride gas dissolves in water, and classify the process.
cards.a: The covalent H–Cl bond is broken as water accepts the proton: HCl(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). New species (hydronium and chloride ions) with a new composition form, and the solution conducts and is acidic, so this is a chemical change (ionization), not merely dissolving. Contrast HCl with sugar, which dissolves with its molecules intact.
cards.h: → H–Cl bond broken, ions formed → chemical
cards.n: 'HCl just dissolves, so it is physical' earns nothing; the bond is broken and the species in solution are ions, not HCl molecules.

cards.q: Evaluate a student's claim that the dissolution of sodium chloride must be chemical because the solution conducts electricity while the solid does not.
cards.a: The evidence is real but does not settle it. Conductivity shows the lattice was pulled apart into mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so ionic bonds broke and ion-dipole interactions formed, the chemical-side argument of 4.4.A.2. But the same ions existed in the solid, no substance of new composition formed, and molten NaCl conducts with no reaction at all. The data support 'bonds broken', not 'new substance'; either label is acceptable if argued this way.
cards.h: → free ions shown, not a new substance; weigh both sides
cards.n: 'Conductivity proves a chemical change' earns nothing without noting that the ions are unchanged; 'it is just physical' ignores the bonds broken.

cards.q: Identify whether heating blue copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, until it becomes a white powder is a physical or a chemical change, and justify from composition.
cards.a: Chemical change, by the composition criterion. The water bound to the copper ions in the crystal is driven off, so the composition changes from CuSO₄·5H₂O to CuSO₄ plus water, and the new solid has different properties (white, not blue). Adding water re-forms the blue hydrate, but reversibility does not make a change physical. Some texts call dehydration borderline, since the water leaves as a separate substance.
cards.h: → water lost from the formula → new composition → chemical
cards.n: 'It just dried out' earns nothing; the water is part of the compound's formula, and the color change marks a new substance.

cards.q: Explain why boiling water is classified as a physical process even though it requires a large input of energy.
cards.a: The energy overcomes the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, strong for intermolecular attractions, so molecules can escape into the gas. No covalent O–H bond breaks: the vapor is still H₂O. Only intermolecular interactions change and no new substance forms, so boiling is physical however much energy it takes.
cards.h: → energy breaks H-bonds between molecules → molecules intact → same substance → physical
cards.n: 'A lot of energy means bonds are breaking' earns nothing; the amount of energy does not decide the classification, the type of interaction broken does.
o: The vapor condenses back to identical water, showing that the molecules never changed identity.
Breaking O–H bonds would give H₂ and O₂, which boiling does not produce; the heat goes into separating molecules, not atoms.

w.a: Boiling is physical because it happens at a fixed temperature.
w.why: a fixed temperature does not distinguish physical from chemical

w.a: Boiling is physical because the water molecules break into hydrogen and oxygen and recombine.
w.why: false; O–H bonds are not broken

w.a: Boiling is physical because no energy is absorbed.
w.why: boiling absorbs a great deal of energy; the reason is what the energy does

cards.q: Explain why the dissolution of sodium chloride in water can plausibly be argued to be a chemical process.
cards.a: Dissolving breaks the ionic bonds holding Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the lattice and forms new interactions, ion-dipole attractions between each ion and water. Breaking and forming bonds is the CED's criterion for a chemical process, and the solution has new properties, such as conducting electricity, that the solid lacked.
cards.h: → ionic bonds broken → ion-dipole interactions formed → bonds changed → chemical by the 4.4 criterion
cards.n: 'It is chemical because the salt disappears' earns nothing; the argument must name the ionic bonds broken and the ion-dipole interactions formed.
o: The equation NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) shows the reactant and products as different species, which is the form of a chemical equation.
The process has a measurable enthalpy change arising from breaking lattice attractions and forming hydration interactions, like a reaction.

w.a: It is chemical because sodium and chlorine atoms are produced in the water.
w.why: false; the ions, not atoms, are present

w.a: It is chemical because salt water tastes different from water.
w.why: a property of the mixture, not evidence about bonds

w.a: It is chemical because you cannot get the salt back.
w.why: false; evaporation recovers it, and reversibility is not the criterion

cards.q: Explain why the products of a chemical change have properties different from those of the reactants.
cards.a: A chemical change rearranges atoms into new bonding patterns, so the products are new substances with different structures. Melting point, color, density and reactivity depend on particle structure and on the forces between particles; both changed with the bonds, so the macroscopic properties change too.
cards.h: → bonds rearranged → new particles with new structure → new IMFs and behavior → new properties
cards.n: 'Because they are different chemicals' restates the claim and earns nothing; connect the new bonding to the properties that depend on it.
o: Hydrogen and oxygen are gases that burn or support burning, while the water they form is a liquid that puts fires out; the H–H and O=O bonds became O–H bonds in a polar, hydrogen-bonding molecule.
Macroscopic properties emerge from particle structure, and a chemical change is precisely a change in particle structure.

w.a: Products have different properties because energy is released during the reaction.
w.why: energy release is a consequence, not the cause of new properties

w.a: Products have different properties because the atoms themselves are changed.
w.why: atoms are conserved; their bonding changes

w.a: Products have different properties because they are in a different phase.
w.why: phase can be the same; the change is in composition and structure

cards.q: Explain why melting sodium chloride is classified as a physical change even though ionic bonds are disrupted.
cards.a: Molten NaCl holds the same Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, now free to move instead of locked in the lattice; no substance of new composition forms, and cooling restores the same solid. Strong ionic attractions explain the high melting point (801 °C), but breaking them makes no new particles, so the change is physical.
cards.h: → lattice attractions overcome → same ions, mobile → no new substance → physical despite bond breaking
cards.n: 'Ionic bonds break, so it is chemical' earns nothing on its own; the CED says physical processes can involve bond breaking when no new substance results.
o: Molten and solid NaCl have the same composition and the same ions, so melting is a phase change, which the CED lists as physical.
The macroscopic evidence, a high melting point and a conducting liquid, reflects ionic attractions being overcome, not a reaction occurring.

w.a: Melting NaCl is physical because ionic compounds have no bonds, only attractions.
w.why: ionic attractions are the bonds; the argument is about no new substance

w.a: Melting NaCl is chemical because the liquid conducts electricity.
w.why: conductivity shows mobile ions, not a new substance

w.a: Melting NaCl is physical because it requires very little energy.
w.why: false; the melting point is about 800 °C

cards.q: State the relationship used to convert between mass and moles of a substance.
cards.a: n = m/M: moles = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol). Moles are the hub of every stoichiometry problem: mass → moles by dividing by M, moles of one species → moles of another by the coefficient ratio, then moles → mass by multiplying by the product's M. Example: 4.40 g C₃H₈ ÷ 44.1 g/mol = 0.0998 mol.
cards.h: → formula with units + where it sits in the road map
cards.n: Applying a coefficient ratio directly to grams earns nothing; the ratio connects moles only. (Molar mass is Unit 1 content.)

cards.q: Define the limiting reactant and state how to identify it.
cards.a: The limiting reactant is the reactant that is completely consumed first; it stops the reaction and fixes the maximum amount of product. To identify it, convert each reactant amount to moles, divide each by its coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smallest quotient marks the limiting reactant. Equivalently, compute how much product each reactant alone could make; the smaller amount is the theoretical yield and that reactant is limiting.
cards.h: → definition + moles ÷ coefficient test
cards.n: Picking the reactant with the smaller mass, or even the smaller number of moles, earns nothing; only moles divided by coefficient decides.

cards.q: State how to find the amount of excess reactant remaining after a reaction goes to completion.
cards.a: Remaining moles = initial moles of the excess reactant − moles consumed, where moles consumed = moles of limiting reactant × (coefficient of excess ÷ coefficient of limiting). Convert to grams with the molar mass only at the end if a mass is asked for. Example: 1.984 mol H₂ with 0.500 mol O₂ (2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O): H₂ consumed = 0.500 × 2 = 1.000 mol, H₂ left = 0.984 mol = 1.98 g.
cards.h: → initial − consumed, all in moles, then convert
cards.n: Subtracting grams from grams (16.0 g − 4.00 g) earns nothing; the subtraction must be done in moles of the same substance.

cards.q: Define theoretical yield, actual yield, and percent yield.
cards.a: Theoretical yield: the maximum amount of product predicted by stoichiometry from the limiting reactant, assuming the reaction goes to completion with no loss. Actual yield: the amount of product really obtained in the experiment. Percent yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100%. Both yields must be in the same units (both grams or both moles).
cards.h: → three definitions + formula
cards.n: A theoretical yield computed from the excess reactant is inflated and earns nothing; it must come from the limiting reactant.

cards.q: State the definition of molarity and its equation.
cards.a: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution: M = n(solute) ÷ V(solution in L), units mol/L. Rearranged, n = M × V gives the moles delivered by a measured volume, which is how solution stoichiometry starts: 25.0 mL of 0.200 M AgNO₃ contains 0.0250 L × 0.200 mol/L = 0.00500 mol.
cards.h: → formula with units + n = MV use
cards.n: Using milliliters in n = MV earns nothing; V must be in liters. Molarity itself is Unit 3 content (3.8).

cards.q: State the dilution relationship and the reason it works.
cards.a: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Adding solvent does not change the number of moles of solute (n = MV is the same before and after), so concentration falls in exact proportion to the increase in solution volume. It applies only to dilution; if the added solution reacts with the solute, moles change and stoichiometry, not this equation, is needed.
cards.h: → equation + moles conserved
cards.n: Using M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ for a titration or a precipitation earns nothing; those change the moles of solute. (Dilution is Unit 3 content.)

cards.q: Determine the concentration of sulfate ion in 0.10 M Al2(SO4)3.
cards.a: 0.30 M. Al₂(SO₄)₃ is a soluble strong electrolyte: Al₂(SO₄)₃(s) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 SO₄²⁻(aq), so each mole of formula units releases 3 mol of sulfate ions and [SO₄²⁻] = 3 × 0.10 M = 0.30 M. Likewise [Al³⁺] = 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 M. Charge check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0.
cards.h: → dissociation equation, then multiply by the subscript
cards.n: Answering 0.10 M ignores the subscript; the ion concentration follows the coefficients of the dissociation equation. (Ion concentrations are also Unit 3 content.)

cards.q: State the full sequence of steps for a mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem with a limiting reactant.
cards.a: (1) Write and balance the equation. (2) Convert each reactant mass to moles with n = m/M. (3) Divide each mole amount by its coefficient; the smallest quotient identifies the limiting reactant. (4) Use the coefficient ratio to convert moles of limiting reactant to moles of product. (5) Multiply by the product's molar mass for grams. (6) If asked, find leftover excess reactant by subtracting moles consumed from moles supplied.
cards.h: → six ordered steps
cards.n: Comparing raw masses or raw moles in step 3 earns nothing; the reactant with fewer moles is not automatically limiting.

cards.q: Compute the mass of $CO_2$ produced when 4.40 g of propane, $C_3H_8$, burns completely in excess oxygen.
cards.a: 13.2 g CO₂. C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O. n(C₃H₈) = 4.40 g ÷ 44.1 g/mol = 0.0998 mol. Mole ratio 3 CO₂ per C₃H₈: 0.0998 × 3 = 0.299 mol CO₂. Mass = 0.299 mol × 44.0 g/mol = 13.2 g. Oxygen is in excess, so propane sets the yield.
cards.h: → balance → mol fuel → ×3 → grams
cards.n: Multiplying 4.40 g by 3 earns nothing; the ratio applies to moles, and the molar masses of propane and CO₂ happen to be nearly equal, which hides the error.

cards.q: Compute which reactant is limiting when 2.00 mol Al reacts with 3.00 mol $Cl_2$ in $2Al + 3Cl_2 \to 2AlCl_3$.
cards.a: Neither is limiting; the amounts are exactly stoichiometric. Moles ÷ coefficient: Al 2.00 ÷ 2 = 1.00, Cl₂ 3.00 ÷ 3 = 1.00, equal quotients, so both reactants are consumed completely and 2.00 mol AlCl₃ (267 g) forms with nothing left over.
cards.h: → moles ÷ coefficient for each; compare
cards.n: Declaring Al limiting because 2.00 < 3.00 earns nothing; the comparison must be moles divided by coefficient.

cards.q: Compute the percent yield if 18.5 g of product is obtained from a reaction with a theoretical yield of 22.0 g.
cards.a: 84.1%. Percent yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100% = (18.5 g ÷ 22.0 g) × 100% = 84.1%. The 3.5 g shortfall is product lost to incomplete reaction, side reactions or transfer and filtration losses.
cards.h: → one ratio × 100
cards.n: Dividing theoretical by actual (119%) earns nothing; a yield above 100% signals wet or impure product, not a better reaction.

cards.q: $CaCO_3 \to CaO + CO_2$. Compute the mass of CaO produced from 50.0 g of $CaCO_3$ decomposing completely.
cards.a: 28.0 g CaO. n(CaCO₃) = 50.0 g ÷ 100.1 g/mol = 0.500 mol; the 1:1 ratio gives 0.500 mol CaO; mass = 0.500 mol × 56.1 g/mol = 28.0 g. The other 22.0 g leaves as CO₂ (0.500 mol × 44.0 g/mol), so mass is conserved.
cards.h: → mol CaCO₃ → 1:1 → grams CaO; check by difference
cards.n: Reporting 50.0 g because the ratio is 1:1 earns nothing; equal moles are not equal masses.

cards.q: Compute the theoretical yield of AgCl precipitate from 25.0 mL of 0.200 M $AgNO_3$ reacted with excess NaCl.
cards.a: 0.717 g AgCl. n(AgNO₃) = 0.0250 L × 0.200 mol/L = 0.00500 mol Ag⁺. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl is 1:1 and NaCl is in excess, so 0.00500 mol AgCl forms; mass = 0.00500 mol × 143.3 g/mol = 0.717 g (0.718 g with 143.5 g/mol).
cards.h: → n = MV → 1:1 → × molar mass
cards.n: Using 25.0 (mL) in n = MV, or the mass of AgNO₃ instead of AgCl, earns nothing; the limiting reagent's moles set the product's moles.

cards.q: Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas, at 1.00 atm and 298 K, produced when 2.43 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid (Mg + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K)).
cards.a: 2.45 L. n(Mg) = 2.43 g ÷ 24.31 g/mol = 0.100 mol; 1:1 ratio gives 0.100 mol H₂. V = nRT/P = (0.100 mol)(0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K))(298 K) ÷ 1.00 atm = 2.45 L. (At STP, 273 K and 1 atm, the same gas would occupy 0.100 × 22.4 = 2.24 L.)
cards.h: → mol Mg → mol H₂ → PV = nRT
cards.n: Using 22.4 L/mol at 298 K earns nothing; that value holds only at STP. Temperature must be in kelvin.

cards.q: Calculate the mass of water formed and the mass of the excess reactant left when 4.00 g of H₂ reacts with 16.0 g of O₂ (2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O).
cards.a: 18.0 g H₂O formed; 1.98 g H₂ left. n(H₂) = 4.00 ÷ 2.016 = 1.984 mol; n(O₂) = 16.0 ÷ 32.00 = 0.500 mol. Moles ÷ coefficient: H₂ 0.992, O₂ 0.500, so O₂ is limiting although its mass is four times larger. H₂O = 2 × 0.500 = 1.000 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 18.0 g. H₂ consumed = 1.000 mol; left = 1.984 − 1.000 = 0.984 mol × 2.016 g/mol = 1.98 g. Check: 20.0 g in, 18.0 + 1.98 = 20.0 g out.
cards.h: → mol each ÷ coefficient → product → leftover in moles
cards.n: Choosing H₂ as limiting because 4.00 g < 16.0 g earns nothing; the smaller mass is the excess reactant here.

cards.q: Calculate the mass of potassium chlorate that must decompose (2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂) to produce 0.480 g of oxygen gas.
cards.a: 1.23 g KClO₃. n(O₂) = 0.480 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 0.0150 mol. Ratio 2 KClO₃ per 3 O₂: 0.0150 × (2/3) = 0.0100 mol KClO₃. Mass = 0.0100 mol × 122.6 g/mol = 1.23 g. Working from a known product amount back to the reactant is the reverse road map the CED names in 4.5.A.1.
cards.h: → mol O₂ → × 2/3 → grams
cards.n: Inverting the ratio (× 3/2, giving 2.76 g) earns nothing; write the ratio as wanted ÷ given with the coefficients in that order.

cards.q: Calculate the mass of barium sulfate that precipitates and the concentration of chloride ion in the final mixture when 50.0 mL of 0.100 M BaCl₂ is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.100 M Na₂SO₄ (BaSO₄ is insoluble).
cards.a: 1.17 g BaSO₄; [Cl⁻] = 0.100 M. n(Ba²⁺) = 0.0500 L × 0.100 M = 0.00500 mol; n(SO₄²⁻) = 0.00500 mol; Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ is 1:1, so both are consumed and 0.00500 mol × 233.4 g/mol = 1.17 g forms. Chloride is a spectator: 0.00500 mol BaCl₂ gives 0.0100 mol Cl⁻, in a total volume of 0.100 L, so [Cl⁻] = 0.100 M (and [Na⁺] = 0.100 M).
cards.h: → n = MV each → 1:1 → mass; spectator moles ÷ total volume
cards.n: Dividing the chloride moles by 50.0 mL instead of the combined 100.0 mL earns nothing for the concentration point.

cards.q: Predict how the mass of CO₂ produced by burning propane changes (a) if the mass of propane is doubled while oxygen is in excess, and (b) if the mass of propane is doubled while oxygen is the limiting reactant.
cards.a: (a) The CO₂ doubles: with O₂ in excess, propane is limiting and the product is directly proportional to it through the 1:3 coefficient ratio. (b) No change: the amount of CO₂ is fixed by the limiting O₂ (5 O₂ per 3 CO₂), so extra propane simply remains unreacted. Product amount tracks the limiting reactant only.
cards.h: → tracks the limiting reactant, not the excess one
cards.n: 'More reactant always means more product' earns nothing; the relationship depends on which reactant is limiting.

cards.q:
Calculate each amount from the coefficient ratio:
2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O: mol H₂O from 3.0 mol O₂
N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃: mol H₂ to make 4.0 mol NH₃
4 NH₃ + 5 O₂ → 4 NO + 6 H₂O: mol O₂ for 2.0 mol NH₃
C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O: mol CO₂ from 0.40 mol C₃H₈
2 Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃: mol Cl₂ for 0.50 mol Al
2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂: mol O₂ from 0.20 mol KClO₃
Fe₂O₃ + 3 CO → 2 Fe + 3 CO₂: mol Fe from 1.5 mol CO
2 Na + 2 H₂O → 2 NaOH + H₂: mol H₂ from 0.60 mol Na
CaCO₃ + 2 HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂: mol HCl for 0.25 mol CaCO₃
2 C₄H₁₀ + 13 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 10 H₂O: mol O₂ for 1.0 mol C₄H₁₀
Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂: mol Zn for 0.80 mol HCl
2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂: mol O₂ from 0.50 mol H₂O₂
cards.a:
3.0 mol O₂ → 6.0 mol H₂O
4.0 mol NH₃ → 6.0 mol H₂
2.0 mol NH₃ → 2.5 mol O₂
0.40 mol C₃H₈ → 1.2 mol CO₂
0.50 mol Al → 0.75 mol Cl₂
0.20 mol KClO₃ → 0.30 mol O₂
1.5 mol CO → 1.0 mol Fe
0.60 mol Na → 0.30 mol H₂
0.25 mol CaCO₃ → 0.50 mol HCl
1.0 mol C₄H₁₀ → 6.5 mol O₂
0.80 mol HCl → 0.40 mol Zn
0.50 mol H₂O₂ → 0.25 mol O₂
cards.h: → given mol × (wanted coefficient ÷ given coefficient)
cards.n: Inverting the ratio is the classic slip; write the wanted substance's coefficient on top every time.

cards.q: Define gravimetric analysis.
cards.a: Gravimetric analysis determines the amount of an ion in a sample by precipitating it completely as an insoluble compound using an excess of a precipitating reagent, then filtering, washing, drying and weighing the precipitate; its mass is converted to moles, and stoichiometry gives the moles and mass of the target ion in the original sample. Example: Cl⁻ precipitated as AgCl with excess AgNO₃.
cards.h: → precipitate, isolate, weigh, convert by stoichiometry
cards.n: Omitting 'excess reagent' misses why the method works: the target ion must be the limiting reactant so that all of it ends up in the solid.

cards.q: Compute the mass percent of chloride in a sample if 0.250 g of sample yields 0.478 g of AgCl precipitate.
cards.a: 47.3% Cl⁻. n(AgCl) = 0.478 g ÷ 143.3 g/mol = 3.34 × 10⁻³ mol; the 1:1 formula means 3.34 × 10⁻³ mol Cl⁻. Mass of Cl⁻ = 3.34 × 10⁻³ mol × 35.45 g/mol = 0.118 g. Mass percent = (0.118 g ÷ 0.250 g) × 100% = 47.3%.
cards.h: → mol AgCl → mol Cl⁻ → g Cl⁻ → percent of sample
cards.n: Dividing 0.478 g by 0.250 g (191%) earns nothing; only the chloride share of the precipitate's mass counts.

cards.q: Compute the mass percent of sulfate in a sample if 0.500 g of sample yields 0.680 g of $BaSO_4$ precipitate $(M(BaSO_4)$ = 233.4 g/mol, $M(SO_4^{2-})$ = 96.07 g/mol).
cards.a: 56.0% SO₄²⁻. n(BaSO₄) = 0.680 g ÷ 233.4 g/mol = 2.91 × 10⁻³ mol = n(SO₄²⁻) (1:1 in the formula). Mass of sulfate = 2.91 × 10⁻³ mol × 96.07 g/mol = 0.280 g. Percent = (0.280 ÷ 0.500) × 100% = 56.0%.
cards.h: → mol BaSO₄ → mol SO₄²⁻ → grams → percent
cards.n: The mole equality holds only because BaSO₄ contains one sulfate per formula unit; for Ag₂CrO₄ the silver would be doubled.

cards.q: State the general sequence of steps in a gravimetric analysis procedure.
cards.a: Weigh and dissolve the sample; add an excess of the precipitating reagent so the target ion is completely converted to an insoluble solid; filter the precipitate; wash it with water to remove soluble spectator ions; dry it to constant mass; weigh it; then convert mass → moles of precipitate → moles of target ion → mass or percent in the sample.
cards.h: → dissolve, precipitate, filter, wash, dry, weigh, calculate
cards.n: Skipping 'excess reagent' or 'dry to constant mass' is where credit is lost; each omitted step corresponds to a named error.
x: dissolve → precipitate → filter → wash → dry → weigh

cards.q: Explain why the coefficients of a balanced equation give mole ratios rather than mass ratios.
cards.a: Coefficients count particles: 2 H₂ + O₂ means two H₂ molecules per O₂ molecule, and a mole is a fixed number of particles, so the ratio holds in moles. Equal numbers of different particles have different masses (2.016 vs 32.00 g/mol), so masses must be converted to moles before the ratio is applied.
cards.h: → coefficients count particles → moles count particles → masses differ per particle
cards.n: 'Because that is how equations work' earns nothing; the reason is that coefficients count particles and molar masses differ.
o: 4.0 g of H₂ is 2 mol but 4.0 g of O₂ is only 0.125 mol; the mass ratio 1:1 hides a 16:1 particle ratio, which is why the equation cannot be read in grams.
Gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure do follow the coefficients, because equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules (moles).

w.a: Coefficients give mass ratios because mass is conserved in a reaction.
w.why: conservation of total mass does not make individual masses proportional to coefficients

w.a: Coefficients give mole ratios because moles are easier to measure than grams.
w.why: grams are what is measured; moles are computed

w.a: Coefficients give mole ratios only for gases.
w.why: they give particle ratios for every substance

cards.q: Explain why an experimental percent yield is usually below 100%.
cards.a: The theoretical yield assumes all of the limiting reactant becomes the desired product and all of it is collected. In practice product is lost in transfer, filtration and washing, some stays dissolved, side reactions divert reactant, and the reaction may be incomplete, so the actual yield falls below it.
cards.h: → theoretical assumes complete conversion and collection → losses and side reactions → actual smaller
cards.n: 'Because of human error' earns nothing; name a specific mechanism of loss (incomplete reaction, side product, product left in solution or on the filter).
o: Atoms are conserved, so any reactant diverted into a by-product or left unreacted cannot appear as the intended product.
A precipitate is never perfectly insoluble, so a little product always remains in the filtrate.

w.a: Percent yield is below 100% because mass is lost during the reaction.
w.why: mass is conserved; product is lost or diverted, not mass destroyed

w.a: Percent yield is below 100% because the limiting reactant was not really limiting.
w.why: the limiting reactant sets the theoretical yield; this is not a loss mechanism

w.a: Percent yield is below 100% because the theoretical yield is always calculated wrongly.
w.why: the calculation is correct; the assumptions behind it are idealized

cards.q: Explain why a gravimetric precipitate must be washed and dried to constant mass.
cards.a: Washing removes dissolved spectator ions clinging to the crystals and drying removes water; both would otherwise be weighed as precipitate. The extra mass converts into extra moles of the target ion, so the result would be too high. Two successive weighings that agree show the water is gone.
cards.h: → spectators and water add mass → moles of analyte overstated → result too high
cards.n: 'To make it pure' earns nothing without the direction of the error; the point is that extra mass makes the result too high.
o: The calculation assumes every gram weighed is the precipitate compound; washing and drying make that assumption true.
Constant mass is the operational test that the drying error is gone, since a still-wet sample keeps losing mass.

w.a: The precipitate is dried so that it is easier to handle.
w.why: convenience, not the direction of the error

w.a: The precipitate is washed to remove excess product so the yield is not too high.
w.why: washing removes spectators and solvent, not product

w.a: Washing and drying are done because a wet precipitate would weigh too little.
w.why: wrong direction; water adds mass

cards.q: Explain why the precipitate used in a gravimetric analysis must be highly insoluble and easily filtered.
cards.a: The calculation assumes every target ion ends up in the weighed solid. An appreciably soluble precipitate leaves some of the ion in the filtrate, and a solid too fine to filter passes through or is lost; either way the measured mass, and so the calculated amount of analyte, is too low.
cards.h: → analyte must be 100% in the solid → solubility or filter loss → result too low
cards.n: 'So the experiment works' earns nothing; state which quantity would be lost and that the result comes out too low.
o: Using an excess of the precipitating ion pushes precipitation toward completion, but only a very insoluble compound makes the loss to solution negligible.
A coarse, crystalline precipitate is retained by the filter and washed cleanly; a colloidal one passes through or traps impurities.

w.a: The precipitate must be insoluble so that it forms quickly.
w.why: speed is not the issue; completeness of removal from solution is

w.a: The precipitate must be insoluble so it does not react with the wash water.
w.why: reaction is not the concern; dissolving is

w.a: An easily filtered precipitate is needed so the result is not too high.
w.why: wrong direction; loss of solid makes the result too low

cards.q: Explain the direction of error in a gravimetric percent result if some precipitate splatters out of the container and is lost during drying.
cards.a: The calculated percent is too low. The lost solid is never weighed, so the measured precipitate mass is smaller than the mass formed; it converts to too few moles of the target ion, while the sample mass in the denominator is unchanged, so the percent understates the true value.
cards.h: → precipitate mass measured too small → moles of analyte too few → percent too low
cards.n: Naming the loss without saying which measured quantity shrank, and in which direction the result moves, earns nothing.
o: The sample mass was recorded before the loss, so only the numerator of the percent calculation is affected, and it decreases.
Any loss of product after the reaction is complete lowers the actual mass recovered and hence every quantity computed from it.

w.a: The result is too high because some of the sample was lost.
w.why: wrong direction, and it was product, not sample, that was lost

w.a: The result is unaffected because the reaction had already finished.
w.why: the mass that is weighed is what matters, and it decreased

w.a: The result is too low because the precipitate was not dry.
w.why: wet precipitate would make the result too high; the loss is the issue here

cards.q: Explain why the reactant present in the smaller mass is not necessarily the limiting reactant.
cards.a: The coefficient ratio compares moles, not masses, and mass converts to moles through molar masses that differ widely. A small mass of a light substance can be more moles than a large mass of a heavy one: 4.00 g H₂ (1.98 mol) outlasts 16.0 g O₂ (0.500 mol) in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
cards.h: → coefficients compare moles → mass ÷ molar mass → light substance has many moles → small mass can be in excess
cards.n: 'Whichever there is less of runs out' earns nothing; the comparison must be moles divided by coefficient, never grams.
o: Even equal numbers of moles need not be stoichiometric; the coefficient ratio may demand two or three moles of one reactant per mole of the other.
Reactions happen particle by particle, and a balance measures mass, so the mass must be turned into a particle count before the ratio can be applied.

w.a: The reactant with the smaller mass is always limiting because it will be used up first.
w.why: false; moles per coefficient decide, not mass

w.a: The reactant with fewer moles is always limiting.
w.why: only after dividing by the coefficients

w.a: The limiting reactant is the one with the larger coefficient.
w.why: coefficients alone say nothing about the amounts present

cards.q: Explain why the theoretical yield of a reaction must be calculated from the limiting reactant rather than from the reactant in excess.
cards.a: The reaction stops when the limiting reactant is consumed, and atoms are conserved, so no more product can form than its atoms allow; the surplus of the other reactant stays unreacted. A yield computed from the excess reactant counts product that can never form, overstating the maximum.
cards.h: → reaction stops when the limiting reactant is gone → atoms conserved → product capped by it
cards.n: 'Because the limiting reactant is smaller' earns nothing; the reason is that product formation ends when it is consumed, whatever remains of the other reactant.
o: In a particulate diagram the excess molecules remain in the after box unreacted, showing they contribute nothing further to the product count.
Computing the product each reactant could make on its own and taking the smaller value is the same statement: the smaller is the real ceiling.

w.a: The theoretical yield comes from the limiting reactant because it is the most reactive substance.
w.why: reactivity is irrelevant; amount relative to the ratio is

w.a: The theoretical yield can come from either reactant since mass is conserved.
w.why: conservation limits, it does not equate, the two calculations

w.a: The theoretical yield comes from the limiting reactant because it has the smallest coefficient.
w.why: coefficients do not identify the limiting reactant

cards.q: Explain why doubling the amount of the excess reactant does not change the amount of product formed.
cards.a: Product is fixed by the limiting reactant through the coefficient ratio: product forms only while both reactants are available, and the limiting one is gone first. Extra excess reactant has no partner left, so it stays unreacted; product is proportional to the limiting reactant and independent of the excess one.
cards.h: → product tied to the limiting reactant → limiting is gone first → extra excess has no partner
cards.n: 'More reactant always gives more product' earns nothing; the relationship holds only for the reactant that limits.
o: In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O with 0.50 mol O₂ limiting, 1.98 or 3.96 mol H₂ both give 1.00 mol water; the leftover H₂ merely grows.
Atoms of the limiting element are conserved and all end up in product, so the product count cannot exceed what those atoms permit.

w.a: Doubling the excess reactant doubles the product because reactions are proportional.
w.why: proportional to the limiting reactant only

w.a: Doubling the excess reactant changes nothing because it does not take part in the reaction.
w.why: it does react, up to the amount the limiting reactant allows

w.a: Doubling the excess reactant lowers the product because it dilutes the mixture.
w.why: dilution can affect rate, not the stoichiometric amount

cards.q: Define a titration.
cards.a: A titration is a procedure in which a solution of accurately known concentration, the titrant, is added from a buret to a measured amount of the analyte until the analyte is exactly consumed by a specific, quantitative reaction (the equivalence point, signaled by the endpoint). The titrant volume gives its moles (n = MV), and the balanced equation converts them to moles of analyte.
cards.h: → known solution, measured volume, stoichiometric point
cards.n: 'Adding acid to base until it is neutral' earns nothing: titrations also use redox and precipitation reactions, and equivalence is set by stoichiometry, not by pH 7.

cards.q: Contrast the equivalence point with the endpoint of a titration.
cards.a: The equivalence point is where the titrant added has exactly consumed the analyte, the moles standing in the ratio of the balanced equation; it is set by stoichiometry and is not directly visible. The endpoint is the observable change, such as an indicator's color change or the first permanent pink of excess MnO₄⁻, that signals it. A well-chosen indicator puts the endpoint within a drop of the equivalence point.
cards.h: → stoichiometric point vs observed signal
cards.n: Using the terms interchangeably, or saying the indicator causes the equivalence point, earns nothing; the endpoint is the observable event that signals equivalence.

cards.q: State the general procedure for finding an unknown concentration from titration data.
cards.a: (1) Moles of titrant = molarity of titrant × volume delivered to the endpoint, in liters. (2) Moles of analyte = moles of titrant × (analyte coefficient ÷ titrant coefficient) from the balanced equation. (3) Concentration of analyte = moles of analyte ÷ volume of the analyte sample in liters (or mass = moles × molar mass for a solid sample).
cards.h: → n = MV → mole ratio → ÷ analyte volume
cards.n: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ holds only for a 1:1 ratio; used for H₂SO₄ + 2 NaOH it is off by a factor of 2. A titration answer without the mole-ratio step earns nothing.

cards.q: Define a primary standard and explain what standardizing a solution means.
cards.a: A primary standard is a solid of high purity and known formula that is stable in air and can be weighed accurately, such as potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP, KHC₈H₄O₄, 204.22 g/mol). Standardizing a solution means finding its exact concentration by titrating it against a weighed amount of a primary standard: moles of standard = mass ÷ molar mass, and the titrant volume then gives the molarity.
cards.h: → what makes a good standard + how it is used
