w.a: The products are drawn lower because there are fewer product molecules.
w.why: the number of molecules does not set the energy level

cards.q: Explain, using an energy diagram, why an exothermic reaction such as burning wood still needs a match to start.
cards.a: The energy diagram has a hump between the reactant and product levels, the activation energy. Although the products lie far below the reactants (ΔH < 0), the reactants must first gain enough energy to get over that barrier; the match supplies it, and the energy then released keeps the reaction going.
cards.h: → hump (Ea) between the levels → must be crossed first → match supplies Ea → released energy sustains burning
cards.n: Borrows Unit 5 activation energy. 'The reaction is endothermic at first' earns nothing: ΔH is the net change; the barrier is Ea, not ΔH.
o: ΔH compares only the starting and ending levels; the path between them rises first, and that rise (Ea) must be supplied before any energy is released.
Once some wood burns, the energy released lifts neighboring molecules over the barrier, so the match is needed only at the start.

w.a: Burning wood needs a match because the reaction is endothermic.
w.why: combustion has ΔH < 0; the barrier is Ea

w.a: The match is needed because it supplies the energy that the products release.
w.why: confuses the energy needed to start with ΔH

w.a: The match is needed because wood has no energy until it is heated.
w.why: the reactants have high chemical potential energy; they need Ea to react

cards.q: Explain why the energy diagram for condensing a gas to a liquid shows the liquid at a lower energy than the gas.
cards.a: As gas particles come together into a liquid, attractions form between them, and forming attractions releases energy. That energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the liquid has lower potential energy than the gas and the condensation arrow points down: ΔH_cond = −ΔH_vap.
cards.h: → attractions form → energy released to surroundings → liquid lower in PE → arrow down
cards.n: 'The liquid is lower because liquids are denser' earns nothing: the vertical axis is energy, and density plays no part in it.
o: Condensing is vaporizing in reverse; vaporizing absorbs ΔH_vap to overcome attractions, so condensing releases the same energy and ends lower.
The gas has more potential energy because its particles are separated against their attractions; letting them attract again releases that energy.

w.a: The liquid is lower because liquids are denser than gases.
w.why: density is not energy

w.a: The liquid is lower because condensation absorbs energy from the surroundings.
w.why: absorbing energy would put the liquid higher

cards.q: Explain why the energy diagram for 2 NO(g) → N₂(g) + O₂(g) is the mirror image of the diagram for N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO(g), ΔH = +180.6 kJ.
cards.a: Both diagrams connect the same two energy levels: N₂ + O₂ (lower) and 2 NO (180.6 kJ higher). Only the direction of travel changes. Going from 2 NO down to N₂ + O₂ releases exactly the 180.6 kJ absorbed going up, so ΔH = −180.6 kJ for the reverse process.
cards.h: → same two levels → opposite direction → same magnitude, opposite sign
cards.n: 'The reverse is also endothermic because NO is unstable' earns nothing; reversing the process reverses the ΔH arrow.
o: If going up and coming back down gave different amounts, a round trip would create or destroy energy, so the reverse ΔH must be −180.6 kJ.
The levels are properties of the substances, not of the direction, so only the arrow flips.

w.a: The reverse reaction has ΔH = +180.6 kJ because it involves the same substances.
w.why: same substances, opposite direction, opposite sign

w.a: The reverse reaction has a smaller ΔH because breaking NO is easier.
w.why: the magnitude is fixed by the same two levels

cards.q: Define heat and contrast it with temperature.
cards.a: Heat, q, is energy transferred between objects because of a temperature difference, measured in joules; it is a transfer, not something an object contains. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of an object's particles; it does not depend on how much material there is, and it decides the direction of heat flow, from hotter to colder.
cards.h: → two definitions + how they connect
cards.n: 'Heat is how hot something is' describes temperature; heat is the energy that moves because temperatures differ.

cards.q: Contrast heat and temperature at the particle level.
cards.a: Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy of the particles in one sample. Heat is the energy transferred between two bodies when faster-moving particles of the warmer body collide with slower particles of the cooler body at their contact. Temperature describes the state of one body's particles; heat is energy passing between bodies.
cards.h: → average KE vs energy passed on in collisions
cards.n: 'Heat is the kinetic energy of the particles' earns nothing: heat is only the energy transferred; temperature reflects the average KE.

cards.q: Define thermal equilibrium.
cards.a: Thermal equilibrium is the state reached when two bodies in thermal contact have the same temperature, so the average kinetic energy of their particles is the same and there is no net transfer of energy between them; collisions still pass energy both ways, but equally.
cards.h: → equal temperature, equal average KE, no net flow
cards.n: 'Both bodies have the same amount of energy' earns nothing: equal temperature means equal AVERAGE kinetic energy, not equal total energy.

cards.q: Predict the direction of net heat flow between two objects at different temperatures placed in contact, and state when net flow stops.
cards.a: Net heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one: particles of the hotter object have greater average kinetic energy and, on average, give energy away in collisions. The net flow stops when both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium), at a final temperature between the two starting temperatures.
cards.h: → direction + reason + stopping condition
cards.n: 'Cold flows into the warm object' earns nothing; energy is what moves, and only from higher to lower temperature.

cards.q: Explain why two objects at the same temperature can transfer different amounts of heat to identical surroundings.
cards.a: Temperature sets only the average kinetic energy per particle. How much energy an object gives up as it cools depends on how many particles it has and how much energy it releases per degree, i.e. its mass and specific heat (q = mcΔT). A more massive or higher-c object at the same temperature transfers more heat for the same temperature drop.
cards.h: → T = per-particle average; total energy depends on m, c
cards.n: 'Objects at the same temperature hold the same energy' earns nothing: a bathtub and a cup at 40 °C differ enormously in total energy.

cards.q: Contrast temperature as an intensive property with heat as an extensive quantity.
cards.a: Temperature is intensive: it is an average per particle, so a drop and a pot of boiling water are both at 100 °C. Heat is extensive: the energy transferred for a given temperature change scales with the amount of matter (q = mcΔT), so warming 2 kg of water by 10 °C takes twice the heat needed for 1 kg.
cards.h: → intensive vs extensive, one example each
cards.n: 'A bigger sample has a higher temperature' earns nothing: sample size changes how much heat is transferred, never the temperature itself.

cards.q: Represent, at the particle level, a hot copper block in contact with cold water just after they touch, showing how energy is transferred.
cards.a: Two regions sharing a boundary. Copper: atoms in an ordered lattice, each drawn with long vibration arrows (high average kinetic energy). Water: molecules drawn with short motion arrows (low average kinetic energy). At the boundary, a fast-vibrating copper atom collides with a slow water molecule; after the collision the copper atom's arrow is shorter and the water molecule's is longer. Label: net energy transfer from copper to water by collisions.
cards.h: → two regions, arrow lengths, a collision at the boundary
cards.n: Showing 'cold particles' moving from the water into the copper, or equal arrow lengths on both sides, earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify which sample has the greater average kinetic energy of its molecules and which has the greater total thermal energy: 100 g of water at 60 °C or 1.00 kg of water at 30 °C.
cards.a: Greater average kinetic energy: the 100 g at 60 °C, because it is at the higher temperature. Greater total thermal energy: the 1.00 kg at 30 °C, which has ten times as many molecules, each with only a slightly lower average kinetic energy. If the two touched, heat would still flow from the 60 °C sample to the 30 °C sample.
cards.h: → two answers, each with its reason
cards.n: Picking the 1.00 kg sample for greater average KE 'because it has more energy' confuses total energy with the per-particle average that temperature measures.

cards.q: Identify which quantities must be equal for two bodies at thermal equilibrium and which need not be: temperature · average kinetic energy of the particles · total thermal energy · mass · average speed of the particles.
cards.a: Must be equal: temperature and the average kinetic energy of the particles (the same statement in two forms). Need not be equal: total thermal energy (depends on the amount), mass, and average particle speed. If the bodies are different substances, the heavier particles move more slowly at the same average kinetic energy, and within each body the particles still have a wide range of speeds.
cards.h: → sort five quantities into equal / not necessarily
cards.n: Borrows Unit 3 kinetic molecular theory. 'Both bodies now hold the same energy' earns nothing: only the per-particle average KE equalizes.

cards.q: Estimate the final temperature when 100. g of water at 20.0 °C is mixed with 100. g of water at 60.0 °C in an insulated container.
cards.a: 40.0 °C. The two samples have equal mass and the same specific heat, so the heat lost by the warm water equals the heat gained by the cool water only when both change by the same number of degrees: 60.0 − 40.0 = 40.0 − 20.0 = 20.0 °C. Thermal equilibrium is reached at the average of the two temperatures.
cards.h: → value + why equal mc gives the midpoint
cards.n: Adding the temperatures (80.0 °C) earns nothing: the final temperature must lie between the two starting temperatures.

cards.q: Estimate whether the final temperature is closer to 20 °C or to 90 °C when a 10 g iron nail at 90 °C is dropped into 500 g of water at 20 °C (c: iron 0.45, water 4.18 J/(g·°C)), and justify.
cards.a: Very close to 20 °C (about 20.2 °C). The nail's mc is 10 g × 0.45 = 4.5 J/°C and the water's is 500 g × 4.18 = 2090 J/°C, about 460 times larger. Heat lost by the nail = heat gained by the water, so the water's temperature changes about 460 times less than the nail's: the nail cools almost all the way to 20 °C.
cards.h: → claim + compare the two mc values
cards.n: Averaging to 55 °C earns nothing: the midpoint applies only when both bodies have equal mc, and here the water's is about 460 times larger.

cards.q: Identify the direction of net heat flow in each case: an ice cube in a glass of lemonade · a hand holding a cold soda can · hot coffee left in a 20 °C room · a thermometer at 22 °C placed in boiling water · steam touching skin · a cold spoon placed in hot soup · a warm car engine after it is switched off in winter air · an ice pack on a sprained ankle · two blocks, both at 25 °C, touching
cards.a:
ice cube in lemonade → lemonade → ice
hand holding a cold can → hand → can
hot coffee in the room → coffee → room air
thermometer in boiling water → water → thermometer
steam touching skin → steam → skin
cold spoon in hot soup → soup → spoon
warm engine in winter air → engine → air
ice pack on an ankle → ankle → ice pack
two blocks both at 25 °C → no net flow (thermal equilibrium)
cards.h: → always hotter → colder; equal T → none
cards.n: 'Cold flows from the ice into the lemonade' earns nothing: only energy flows, always from the higher to the lower temperature.

cards.q: Explain what happens at the particle level when a hot object and a cold object are placed in contact until they reach the same temperature.
cards.a: Particles of the hot object have greater average kinetic energy. In collisions at the contact surface, energy passes on average from these faster particles to the slower particles of the cold object, so the hot object's average KE falls and the cold object's rises until the averages are equal: the same temperature.
cards.h: → hot particles faster → collisions at contact pass energy fast → slow → averages equalize → same temperature
cards.n: 'The cold particles absorb the heat particles' earns nothing: heat is not a substance; energy moves in collisions.
o: Collisions between the two sets of particles transfer kinetic energy, and the net transfer is out of the body with the higher average KE until both averages match.
Each collision tends to even out the energies of the colliding particles, so repeated collisions bring both bodies to the same average KE, which is thermal equilibrium.

w.a: The cold object's coldness moves into the hot object until they balance.
w.why: cold does not flow; energy moves from hot to cold

w.a: The particles of both objects end up moving at exactly the same speed.
w.why: only the average KE equalizes; speeds stay spread out

w.a: Heat flows until both objects contain the same amount of energy.
w.why: equal temperature, not equal total energy

cards.q: Explain why touching a metal object and a wooden object that are both at room temperature can feel different.
cards.a: Both objects are at room temperature, so their particles have the same average kinetic energy, lower than your skin's. Metal carries energy away from your skin much faster than wood, so more energy leaves your hand each second and your skin cools faster; you sense the rate of heat loss, not the object's temperature.
cards.h: → same temperature → same average KE → metal removes energy from skin faster → skin cools faster → feels colder
cards.n: 'The metal is colder than the wood' earns nothing: both are in thermal equilibrium with the room, so they are at the same temperature.
o: Your skin judges how fast it loses energy; the metal's particles pass energy on from the contact point much faster, so the skin's temperature drops faster.
Temperature is the same, but the rate of heat transfer out of the hand is greater for metal, and the sensation of cold tracks that rate.

w.a: The metal feels colder because metal is at a lower temperature than wood in the same room.
w.why: both are at room temperature

w.a: The metal feels colder because metal atoms have less kinetic energy than wood molecules.
w.why: same temperature means same average KE

w.a: The metal feels colder because it gives off cold faster.
w.why: cold is not given off; energy leaves the hand

cards.q: Explain why net heat transfer stops at thermal equilibrium even though the particles of the two bodies keep colliding.
cards.a: At thermal equilibrium the two bodies have the same average kinetic energy. Collisions still transfer energy in both directions, but on average as much energy passes from the first body to the second as from the second to the first, so the net transfer is zero and the temperatures stay equal.
cards.h: → equal average KE → energy passes both ways in collisions → equal amounts → net transfer zero
cards.n: 'The particles stop colliding once the temperatures match' earns nothing: collisions continue; only the NET transfer becomes zero.
o: With equal average KE, neither body's particles are faster on average, so collisions no longer favor one direction of energy transfer.
Energy exchange continues as a balanced two-way process, which is why the temperatures stay constant and equal.

w.a: Heat transfer stops because the particles stop moving at thermal equilibrium.
w.why: particles keep moving and colliding

w.a: Heat transfer stops because both bodies have run out of heat.
w.why: heat is not a stored substance that runs out

cards.q: Explain why heat flows from a small cup of tea at 80 °C into a large bathtub of water at 35 °C, even though the bathtub contains far more thermal energy.
cards.a: The direction of heat flow is set by temperature, the average kinetic energy per particle, not by total energy. The tea's particles have the greater average KE, so collisions at the contact pass energy, on average, from tea to bath until both reach the same temperature, barely above 35 °C.
cards.h: → direction set by temperature (average KE) → tea's particles faster on average → net transfer tea → bath
cards.n: 'Heat flows from the object with more energy' earns nothing: total energy does not set the direction; temperature does.
o: Heat flows from higher to lower temperature; 80 °C tea has faster-moving particles on average than 35 °C water, whatever the amounts.
The bath's large total energy is spread over vastly more particles, each with less average KE than a tea particle.

w.a: Heat should flow from the bathtub to the tea because the bathtub holds more energy.
w.why: total energy does not set the direction

w.a: No heat flows because the bathtub is too big to warm up.
w.why: size affects how much it warms, not whether heat flows

cards.q: Explain why a thermometer placed in a liquid eventually shows the liquid's temperature.
cards.a: The thermometer and the liquid exchange energy through collisions until they reach thermal equilibrium, where their particles have the same average kinetic energy. A thermometer reports its own temperature, and at equilibrium that equals the liquid's, so the reading stops changing only once equilibrium is reached.
cards.h: → collisions transfer energy liquid ↔ thermometer → thermal equilibrium → equal temperatures → reading = liquid's T
cards.n: 'The thermometer measures the heat in the liquid' earns nothing: it measures temperature, and only after reaching thermal equilibrium.
o: Energy flows between the thermometer and the liquid until their average kinetic energies match; the thermometer then reads the shared temperature.
A thermometer shows the right value only after net heat transfer has stopped, i.e. at thermal equilibrium with the liquid.

w.a: The thermometer reads the liquid's temperature instantly because it measures the liquid's heat.
w.why: it measures its own temperature after equilibrium

w.a: The thermometer shows the liquid's temperature because it absorbs all of the liquid's energy.
w.why: only enough energy to equalize temperatures is exchanged

cards.q: State the first law of thermodynamics in equation form.
cards.a: Energy is conserved: ΔE(system) + ΔE(surroundings) = 0, so ΔE(system) = −ΔE(surroundings). In a calorimeter this is used as q(system) = −q(surroundings), e.g. q_rxn = −q_soln or q_metal = −q_water. The textbook form ΔE = q + w says the system's energy changes by the heat added to it plus the work done on it.
cards.h: → conservation equation, then the calorimetry form
cards.n: The internal-energy vs enthalpy distinction is not assessed; what scores is energy conserved, so q lost by one body = −q gained by the other.

cards.q: Define specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, and heat capacity.
cards.a: Specific heat capacity, c: the energy needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C (1 K), in J/(g·°C). Molar heat capacity: the energy needed to raise 1 mol by 1 °C, in J/(mol·°C); it equals c × molar mass. Heat capacity, C: the energy needed to raise a whole object, such as a calorimeter, by 1 °C, in J/°C, used as q = CΔT.
cards.h: → three definitions, each with its units
cards.n: Mixing them up loses the units point: q = mcΔT needs grams, a molar heat capacity needs moles, and q = CΔT needs neither.

cards.q: State the equation relating heat transferred to temperature change.
cards.a: q = mcΔT: q is the heat in J, m the mass in g, c the specific heat capacity in J/(g·°C), and ΔT = T_final − T_initial. A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so ΔT is the same in either scale. A positive ΔT gives q > 0 (energy absorbed, the system's energy increases); a negative ΔT gives q < 0 (energy released).
cards.h: → equation, symbols with units, sign meaning
cards.n: Writing ΔT as initial − final flips every sign that follows; ΔT is always final minus initial.

cards.q: Determine the heat absorbed when 50.0 g of water is warmed from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C, given c = 4.18 J/(g·K).
cards.a: q = +2.09 × 10³ J (2.09 kJ) absorbed. q = mcΔT = (50.0 g)(4.18 J/(g·K))(30.0 °C − 20.0 °C) = (50.0)(4.18)(10.0) = 2090 J. ΔT is positive, so q is positive: the water gains energy.
cards.h: → one-line q = mcΔT with sign
cards.n: Converting to kelvin and multiplying by 303 K earns nothing: q = mcΔT needs the temperature DIFFERENCE, 10.0 in either scale.

cards.q: Define calorimetry.
cards.a: Calorimetry is the experimental measurement of heat transfer. A process is carried out inside an insulated container; the temperature change of a known mass of water (or of a calorimeter of known heat capacity) is measured, and q = mcΔT (or q = CΔT) gives the heat gained by these surroundings, which is equal in size and opposite in sign to the heat of the process.
cards.h: → what is measured, how q follows
cards.n: Calorimetry measures the SURROUNDINGS; reporting the water's q as the process's q without the sign change loses the point.

cards.q: Explain how a constant-pressure coffee-cup calorimeter measures the enthalpy change of a reaction.
cards.a: The reaction runs in water in an insulated foam cup open to the air, so pressure is constant and the heat of reaction is ΔH. Measure the solution's mass and its ΔT; compute q_soln = mcΔT; by conservation of energy q_rxn = −q_soln; then divide by the moles of the limiting reactant: ΔH = q_rxn/n, in kJ/mol with its sign.
cards.h: → setup, then three calculation steps
cards.n: Using only the solute's mass, or only the water added before mixing, earns nothing; m in mcΔT is the mass of the whole solution.

cards.q: Contrast a bomb calorimeter with a coffee-cup calorimeter.
cards.a: Coffee-cup calorimeter: an insulated cup open to the air, used for reactions or dissolving in solution; q = mcΔT with the solution's mass and specific heat. Bomb calorimeter: a sealed steel vessel inside a water bath, used for combustion; q = C_cal·ΔT with the calibrated heat capacity of the whole apparatus (J/°C). In both, q of the process = −q of the calorimeter.
cards.h: → setup, use and heat equation for each
cards.n: The constant-volume vs constant-pressure (internal energy vs enthalpy) distinction is excluded from the exam; the scored contrast is mcΔT versus C_cal·ΔT.

cards.q: State the relationship between the heat of the reaction and the heat gained by the solution.
cards.a: q_rxn = −q_soln. Energy is conserved, so the energy the reaction releases is exactly what the solution absorbs, and vice versa: equal magnitudes, opposite signs. A solution that warms (q_soln > 0) means q_rxn < 0, an exothermic reaction.
cards.h: → one equation + its reason
cards.n: Dropping the minus sign turns an exothermic result into an endothermic one and loses the sign point.

cards.q: Explain the simplifying assumptions made about the solution in coffee-cup calorimetry.
cards.a: The dilute solution is assumed to have the density of water (1.00 g/mL, so its volume in mL gives its mass in g) and the specific heat of water (4.18 J/(g·°C)). The cup, thermometer and air are assumed to absorb no heat, so all the energy exchanged goes into or out of the solution. Each assumption is a possible source of error in ΔT and so in ΔH.
cards.h: → density, specific heat, no heat lost
cards.n: 'Human error' earns nothing; name the specific assumption (heat absorbed by the cup, c of the solution not 4.18) and how it shifts the result.

cards.q: Compute the final temperature when 200. g of water at 25.0 °C absorbs 8.36 kJ of heat, given c = 4.18 J/(g·K).
cards.a: 35.0 °C. ΔT = q/(mc) = 8360 J ÷ (200. g × 4.18 J/(g·°C)) = 8360 ÷ 836 = +10.0 °C, positive because the water absorbed energy. T_final = 25.0 °C + 10.0 °C = 35.0 °C.
cards.h: → solve q = mcΔT for ΔT, then add
cards.n: Leaving q as 8.36 (kJ) gives ΔT = 0.0100 °C; convert kJ to J so the units match c in J/(g·°C).

cards.q: A 50.0 g metal sample cools from 100.0°C to 25.0°C while releasing 1250 J. Compute its specific heat.
cards.a: 0.333 J/(g·°C). The metal lost 1250 J, so q_metal = −1250 J, and ΔT = 25.0 − 100.0 = −75.0 °C. c = q/(mΔT) = (−1250 J) ÷ (50.0 g × −75.0 °C) = 0.333 J/(g·°C). The two negatives cancel, as they must: a specific heat is always positive.
cards.h: → c = q/(mΔT) with both signs
cards.n: A negative specific heat means one sign was dropped; for a cooling sample q and ΔT are both negative.

cards.q: Dissolving 5.00 g of NaOH in 100. g of water raises the temperature 8.60°C (c = 4.18 J/(g·K)). Compute the molar heat of solution.
cards.a: −30.2 kJ/mol. q_soln = mcΔT = (105 g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(8.60 °C) = 3.77 × 10³ J; the solution warmed, so q_dissolution = −3.77 kJ. n(NaOH) = 5.00 g ÷ 40.00 g/mol = 0.125 mol. ΔH_soln = −3.77 kJ ÷ 0.125 mol = −30.2 kJ/mol: exothermic.
cards.h: → q with total mass, flip sign, ÷ mol NaOH
cards.n: Using 100. g (water only) gives −28.8 kJ/mol; the dissolved NaOH is part of the solution that warms, so m = 105 g.

cards.q: Compute the heat capacity of a calorimeter if adding 500. J raises its temperature 4.00°C, with no other contents.
cards.a: 125 J/°C. With nothing else inside, all 500. J went into the calorimeter itself, so C_cal = q/ΔT = 500. J ÷ 4.00 °C = 125 J/°C: each 1 °C rise of the calorimeter absorbs 125 J.
cards.h: → C = q/ΔT with units
cards.n: Dividing by a mass or by 4.18 earns nothing: a heat capacity C belongs to the whole object and has units J/°C, not J/(g·°C).

cards.q: Calculate the final temperature when 50.0 g of copper (c = 0.385 J/(g·°C)) at 95.0 °C is placed in 100.0 g of water (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)) at 22.0 °C in an insulated cup.
cards.a: 25.2 °C. Heat lost by copper = heat gained by water: −(50.0)(0.385)(T_f − 95.0) = (100.0)(4.18)(T_f − 22.0). So 19.25(95.0 − T_f) = 418(T_f − 22.0); 1828.8 + 9196 = 437.25 T_f; T_f = 25.2 °C. It lies between 22.0 and 95.0 °C, close to the water's start because the water's mc is about 22 times the copper's.
cards.h: → −q_metal = q_water, solve for one T_f
cards.n: Setting q_metal = q_water without the minus sign gives 18.5 °C, outside the 22.0–95.0 °C range; that check catches the lost sign.

cards.q: Calculate the heat needed to raise the temperature of 2.50 mol of aluminum from 25.0 °C to 75.0 °C, given the molar heat capacity of aluminum is 24.2 J/(mol·°C) (molar mass 26.98 g/mol).
cards.a: 3.03 × 10³ J (3.03 kJ) absorbed. With a molar heat capacity use moles: q = n × C_m × ΔT = (2.50 mol)(24.2 J/(mol·°C))(50.0 °C) = 3025 J ≈ 3.03 kJ. The mass route agrees: 2.50 mol × 26.98 g/mol = 67.45 g, c = 24.2 ÷ 26.98 = 0.897 J/(g·°C), and 67.45 g × 0.897 × 50.0 °C = 3025 J.
cards.h: → q = n·C_m·ΔT, one line
cards.n: Multiplying the molar heat capacity by grams (67.45 × 24.2 × 50.0 = 81.6 kJ) is 27 times too large; match mol with J/(mol·°C).

cards.q: Identify, for each change, the process that changes the system's energy (heating/cooling, phase transition, or chemical reaction) and whether the system's energy increases or decreases: soup warming on a stove · ice melting in a drink · gasoline burning in an engine · steam condensing on a mirror · coffee cooling in a mug · baking soda decomposing in an oven · water freezing in a tray · iodine crystals subliming · a hot pan cooling on a counter · magnesium burning in air · a metal spoon warming in hot tea · liquid nitrogen boiling on a lab bench
cards.a:
soup warming → heating; energy increases
ice melting → phase transition; increases
gasoline burning → chemical reaction; decreases (exothermic)
steam condensing → phase transition; decreases
coffee cooling → cooling; decreases
baking soda decomposing → chemical reaction; increases (endothermic, driven by the oven)
water freezing → phase transition; decreases
iodine subliming → phase transition; increases
hot pan cooling → cooling; decreases
magnesium burning → chemical reaction; decreases
spoon warming → heating; increases
liquid nitrogen boiling → phase transition; increases
cards.h: → which of the three processes? energy in or out?
cards.n: Calling freezing 'cooling' earns nothing: at the freezing point the temperature is constant, and the energy leaves through a phase transition.

cards.q: Explain what a large specific heat capacity indicates about a substance.
cards.a: It takes a lot of energy to raise each gram by 1 °C, so for a given heat transfer the substance changes temperature only a little (ΔT = q/mc). It warms and cools slowly and can absorb or release much energy with a small temperature change, as water (4.18 J/(g·°C)) does.
cards.h: → large c → many J per g per °C → small ΔT for a given q → heats and cools slowly
cards.n: 'It holds more heat' earns nothing: heat is energy in transfer, not something a substance contains; say more energy is needed per gram per degree.
o: From q = mcΔT with q and m fixed, ΔT is inversely proportional to c, so a large c means a small temperature change.
A high-c substance absorbs a large amount of energy from its surroundings while its own temperature barely rises, which is why water is a good coolant.

w.a: A large specific heat means the substance gets hot very quickly.
w.why: reversed: large c means slow temperature change

w.a: A large specific heat means the substance is at a high temperature.
w.why: c is per gram per degree, unrelated to the current temperature

w.a: A large specific heat means the substance holds more heat inside it.
w.why: heat is transferred energy; no per-gram-per-degree comparison

cards.q: Predict which of two equal-mass samples absorbing equal heat undergoes the larger temperature change.
cards.a: The sample with the smaller specific heat capacity. From q = mcΔT, ΔT = q/(mc); with q and m the same for both samples, ΔT is inversely proportional to c, so the lower-c sample needs fewer joules per degree and its temperature changes more.
cards.h: → ΔT = q/(mc) → same q and m → ΔT ∝ 1/c → smaller c, larger ΔT
cards.n: Choosing the larger-c sample 'because it absorbs more heat' ignores that both absorb the same q; only c differs.
x: the one with smaller specific heat
o: Each gram of the lower-c sample needs fewer joules per degree, so the same number of joules buys more degrees.
Doubling c at fixed q and m halves ΔT, so the smaller c gives the bigger change.

w.a: The sample with the larger specific heat changes more because it absorbs more energy.
w.why: both absorb the same energy; the relation is inverse

w.a: Both samples change temperature equally because they have the same mass and absorb the same heat.
w.why: ignores that c differs between substances

cards.q: Predict which sample undergoes the smaller temperature change when both absorb the same heat: 50.0 g of water or 50.0 g of aluminum $(c_Al$ ≈ 0.90 J/(g·K)).
cards.a: The water. For equal masses and equal q, ΔT = q/(mc), so ΔT is inversely proportional to c. Water's c (4.18 J/(g·K)) is about 4.6 times aluminum's (0.90 J/(g·K)), so the water's temperature change is about 4.6 times smaller.
cards.h: → same q and m → ΔT ∝ 1/c → c(water) ≈ 4.6 × c(Al) → water's ΔT smaller
cards.n: 'Aluminum, because metals conduct heat' swaps conduction rate for heat capacity; q = mcΔT, not conductivity, decides ΔT.
o: Water needs 4.18 J per gram per degree versus 0.90 J for aluminum, so the same energy raises the water fewer degrees.

w.a: Aluminum changes temperature less because metals are good conductors of heat.
w.why: conductivity is irrelevant; the smaller c gives the larger ΔT

w.a: Both change by the same amount because they absorb the same heat and have the same mass.
w.why: ignores the different specific heats

cards.q: Explain how heat lost to the calorimeter and air affects a measured exothermic ΔH.
cards.a: The calculated ΔH is less negative than the true value. Some released energy warms the cup and air instead of the solution, so the measured ΔT and q_soln = mcΔT are too small; q_rxn = −q_soln is then too small in magnitude, and so is ΔH = q_rxn/n.
cards.h: → energy escapes → ΔT too small → q_soln too small → |ΔH| too small → ΔH less negative
cards.n: 'ΔH is more negative because heat was lost' confuses the loss with the release: the measurement captures LESS than the reaction released.
o: Only the energy that reaches the solution is counted, so every joule lost to the cup or air is missing from q and makes |ΔH| too small.
A smaller measured temperature rise means a smaller calculated heat released per mole, so the reported ΔH is closer to zero than the true value.

w.a: Heat lost to the air makes the measured ΔH more negative because more energy left the system.
w.why: the lost energy is not measured, so |ΔH| comes out smaller

w.a: Heat loss has no effect because the reaction releases the same energy either way.
w.why: the reaction does, but the measured ΔT does not

w.a: Heat loss makes ΔH positive because the solution cools.
w.why: the solution still warms, just less

cards.q: Explain why a decrease in the temperature of the water in a calorimeter shows that a dissolution process is endothermic.
cards.a: The water's temperature falls, so its particles lost average kinetic energy: q_water < 0. Energy is conserved, and the dissolving solute is the only thing exchanging energy with the water, so the dissolution absorbed that energy: q_dissolution = −q_water > 0, which is endothermic.
cards.h: → T falls → water loses energy → energy conserved → dissolution absorbed it → endothermic
cards.n: 'The dissolving released cold' earns nothing; the falling temperature is evidence that energy moved from the water into the dissolving system.
o: A cooling mixture means energy left the water; in an insulated calorimeter the only place it can go is into the dissolution process, so ΔH_soln > 0.
q_soln = mcΔT is negative for a falling temperature, and q_dissolution = −q_soln is therefore positive.

w.a: The temperature decreases because dissolving is exothermic and releases energy.
w.why: a release would warm the water

w.a: The temperature decreases because the solute was colder than the water.
w.why: the solute starts at room temperature; the change comes from dissolving

w.a: The temperature decreases because the solution now has more mass.
w.why: added mass does not lower the temperature

cards.q: Explain why, when a hot metal block is placed in cool water in an insulated cup, the heat lost by the metal is set equal to the heat gained by the water.
cards.a: Energy is conserved, and the insulated cup allows no transfer to the outside, so every joule leaving the metal enters the water: q_metal = −q_water. The transfer continues until both reach one final temperature, and that shared temperature is used in both mcΔT terms.
cards.h: → energy conserved + insulated → metal's loss = water's gain → one shared final temperature
cards.n: Writing q_metal = q_water with no minus sign puts the final temperature outside the range of the two starting temperatures.
o: The first law: the total energy of metal plus water is constant, so any decrease in the metal's energy is an equal increase in the water's.
With no heat escaping, the only place the metal's energy can go is the water, so the two heats are equal in size and opposite in sign.

w.a: The heats are equal because the metal and water have the same specific heat.
w.why: their specific heats differ; conservation, not c, is the reason

w.a: The heats are equal because both end at the same temperature change.
w.why: their ΔT values differ; they share a final temperature

cards.q: Define enthalpy of fusion and enthalpy of vaporization.
cards.a: ΔH_fus is the energy absorbed to melt one mole of a solid at its melting point (water: +6.01 kJ/mol). ΔH_vap is the energy absorbed to vaporize one mole of a liquid at its boiling point (water: +40.7 kJ/mol). Both are positive because melting and boiling are endothermic; freezing and condensing release the same amounts.
cards.h: → two per-mole definitions + sign
cards.n: Giving ΔH_fus as the energy released on melting reverses the sign; melting and boiling always absorb energy.

cards.q: State the equation for the heat involved in a phase change.
cards.a: q = n × ΔH of the phase change, with n in moles and the molar enthalpy in kJ/mol: q = nΔH_fus for melting and nΔH_vap for boiling, with −ΔH for freezing or condensing. There is no ΔT term, because the temperature is constant during a phase change, so q = mcΔT does not apply there.
cards.h: → q = nΔH + why no ΔT
cards.n: q = mcΔT with ΔT = 0 would give q = 0 for a plateau, contradicting the energy absorbed throughout it.

cards.q: Contrast a cooling curve with a heating curve.
cards.a: A cooling curve is the heating curve run backward: the temperature falls along the single-phase segments and holds constant at the condensation and freezing plateaus, at the same temperatures as boiling and melting. Every segment releases energy (q < 0), and each plateau releases exactly what the matching heating plateau absorbed: ΔH_cond = −ΔH_vap and ΔH_freeze = −ΔH_fus.
cards.h: → mirrored shape, same plateau temperatures, signs
cards.n: A plateau on a cooling curve does not mean nothing is happening: the sample releases energy at constant temperature while it freezes or condenses.

cards.q: State how to find the total energy needed to convert ice below 0 °C into steam above 100 °C.
cards.a: Add five terms in order: warm the ice, mcΔT with c_ice; melt it, nΔH_fus; warm the liquid from 0 to 100 °C, mcΔT with c_water; boil it, nΔH_vap; warm the steam, mcΔT with c_steam. Each sloped segment uses its own phase's c, the two plateaus have no ΔT, and all terms are converted to kJ before adding.
cards.h: → five terms in order
cards.n: Using 4.18 J/(g·°C) for the ice and steam segments, or dropping a plateau term, loses the point: each phase has its own c.

cards.q: Compute the heat required to vaporize 36.0 g of water at its boiling point, given $ΔH_vap$ = 40.7 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 81.3 kJ absorbed (q = +81.3 kJ; 81.4 kJ if M = 18.0 g/mol is used). n = 36.0 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 1.998 mol; q = nΔH_vap = 1.998 mol × 40.7 kJ/mol = 81.3 kJ. At the boiling point all of this energy goes into separating the molecules, so the temperature stays at 100 °C.
cards.h: → grams → moles → × ΔH_vap
cards.n: Adding an mcΔT term earns nothing here: at the boiling point ΔT = 0 and all the energy goes into the phase change.

cards.q: Compute the total heat needed to convert 10.0 g of ice at 0 °C into liquid water at 0 °C, given $ΔH_fus$ = 6.01 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 3.34 kJ absorbed. n = 10.0 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.555 mol; q = nΔH_fus = 0.555 mol × 6.01 kJ/mol = 3.34 kJ. Ice at 0 °C becomes water at 0 °C, so there is no temperature change and no mcΔT term.
cards.h: → grams → moles → × ΔH_fus
cards.n: Multiplying grams by ΔH_fus (10.0 × 6.01 = 60.1 kJ) earns nothing; ΔH_fus is per mole, so convert the mass first.

cards.q: Compute the total heat to convert 20.0 g of ice at −10.0°C to liquid water at 0.00°C ($c_{ice}$ = 2.09 J/(g·K), $ΔH_fus$ = 6.01 kJ/mol).
cards.a: 7.09 kJ (7.10 kJ if M = 18.0 g/mol is used). Warm the ice: q₁ = mc_iceΔT = (20.0 g)(2.09 J/(g·K))(10.0 K) = 418 J = 0.418 kJ. Melt it: q₂ = nΔH_fus = (20.0 ÷ 18.02 mol)(6.01 kJ/mol) = 6.67 kJ. Total = 0.418 + 6.67 = 7.09 kJ.
cards.h: → mcΔT for the ice, then nΔH_fus, then add
cards.n: Using water's c (4.18) for the ice, or skipping the warming step, gives the wrong total; the ice must reach 0 °C before any of it melts.

cards.q: Identify which segments of a heating curve require q = mcΔT and which require q = nΔH.
cards.a: The sloped segments, where one phase is warming (solid, liquid or gas), use q = mcΔT with that phase's c. The flat plateaus, where two phases coexist at constant temperature (melting, boiling), use q = nΔH_fus or q = nΔH_vap. On the slopes the energy raises the particles' average kinetic energy; on the plateaus it goes into overcoming attractions.
cards.h: → slopes vs plateaus, equation for each
cards.n: Applying q = mcΔT across a plateau earns nothing: ΔT there is zero although energy keeps flowing in.

cards.q: Compute the heat to melt 12.0 g of ice at 0°C and warm the water to 25.0°C $(ΔH_fus$ = 6.01 kJ/mol, $c_water$ = 4.18 J/(g·K)).
cards.a: 5.26 kJ. Melt: q₁ = nΔH_fus = (12.0 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol)(6.01 kJ/mol) = 4.002 kJ. Warm the meltwater: q₂ = mcΔT = (12.0 g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(25.0 °C) = 1254 J = 1.254 kJ. Total = 4.002 + 1.254 = 5.26 kJ, all absorbed.
cards.h: → nΔH_fus, then mcΔT, same units, add
cards.n: Adding 4.00 (kJ) to 1254 (J) as if the units matched gives nonsense; convert the mcΔT term to kJ first.

cards.q: Calculate the heat released when 10.0 g of steam condenses to liquid water at 100 °C, given ΔH_vap = +40.7 kJ/mol for water.
cards.a: q = −22.6 kJ (22.6 kJ released). n = 10.0 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.555 mol. Condensation is vaporization reversed, so ΔH_cond = −ΔH_vap = −40.7 kJ/mol, and q = 0.555 mol × (−40.7 kJ/mol) = −22.6 kJ. The temperature stays at 100 °C while this energy leaves.
cards.h: → moles, reverse the sign of ΔH_vap, multiply
cards.n: Reporting +22.6 kJ uses ΔH_vap unchanged; condensing releases the energy that vaporizing absorbs, so the sign flips.

cards.q: Calculate q, with its sign, for each phase change of water at constant temperature (18.02 g/mol, ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol, ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol): melting 36.0 g · freezing 54.0 g · vaporizing 45.0 g · condensing 18.0 g · condensing 0.750 mol · freezing 0.250 mol · melting 1.00 kg · vaporizing 1.00 kg
cards.a:
melting 36.0 g (1.998 mol) → +12.0 kJ
freezing 54.0 g (2.997 mol) → −18.0 kJ
vaporizing 45.0 g (2.497 mol) → +102 kJ
condensing 18.0 g (0.999 mol) → −40.7 kJ
condensing 0.750 mol → −30.5 kJ
freezing 0.250 mol → −1.50 kJ
melting 1.00 kg (55.5 mol) → +334 kJ
vaporizing 1.00 kg (55.5 mol) → +2.26 × 10³ kJ
cards.h: → grams → mol → × ΔH; + for melt/boil, − for freeze/condense
cards.n: One sign for every line earns nothing: freezing and condensing are the reverse processes, so their q is the negative of melting and vaporizing.

cards.q: Draw the heating curve for 1.00 mol of water heated at a constant rate from −20 °C to 120 °C, labeling the axes, the plateau temperatures, the phases on each segment, and the relative plateau lengths (ΔH_fus = 6.01, ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol; c: ice 2.09, liquid 4.18, steam 2.01 J/(g·°C)).
cards.a: Axes: temperature (°C, −20 to 120) vs time (or energy added). Rising line, ice, −20 → 0 °C. Flat plateau at 0 °C, ice + liquid. Rising line, liquid, 0 → 100 °C, about half as steep as the ice line (c twice as large). Flat plateau at 100 °C, liquid + gas, about 6.8 times longer than the melting plateau (40.7 ÷ 6.01). Rising line, steam, 100 → 120 °C, about as steep as the ice line.
cards.h: → five labeled segments, plateau ratio, slopes
cards.n: Two plateaus of equal length, or the liquid segment drawn steepest, earn nothing: water's large c makes the liquid line the shallowest.

cards.q: Calculate the molar enthalpy of vaporization of ethanol (M = 46.07 g/mol) from this run: a heater delivering a constant 100. J/s to 23.0 g of ethanol at its boiling point keeps the temperature at 78 °C for 193 s while all of the ethanol boils.
cards.a: +38.7 kJ/mol. Energy absorbed on the plateau: q = 100. J/s × 193 s = 1.93 × 10⁴ J = 19.3 kJ. n = 23.0 g ÷ 46.07 g/mol = 0.499 mol. ΔH_vap = q/n = 19.3 kJ ÷ 0.499 mol = 38.7 kJ/mol, positive because boiling absorbs energy.
cards.h: → power × time, then ÷ moles
cards.n: Trying to find q from a ΔT earns nothing: the plateau is at constant temperature, so the energy comes from power × time.

cards.q: Identify the melting point, the boiling point, and the phase(s) present in each interval of this heating curve for substance X, heated at a constant rate: the temperature rises from −40 °C to −10 °C between 0 and 2 min; stays at −10 °C from 2 to 5 min; rises from −10 °C to 60 °C between 5 and 9 min; stays at 60 °C from 9 to 20 min; then rises again.
cards.a: Melting point −10 °C; boiling point 60 °C. 0–2 min: solid only. 2–5 min: solid + liquid (melting). 5–9 min: liquid only. 9–20 min: liquid + gas (boiling). After 20 min: gas only. At a constant heating rate time is proportional to energy, so the 11-min boiling plateau shows ΔH_vap ≈ 11/3 ≈ 3.7 × ΔH_fus.
cards.h: → two temperatures, then phases per interval
cards.n: Reading the 60 °C plateau as 'gas only' earns nothing: liquid and gas coexist during the plateau; gas alone appears only after it ends.

cards.q: Calculate the total energy needed to convert 18.02 g of ice at −10.0 °C to steam at 110.0 °C (c_ice = 2.09, c_water = 4.18, c_steam = 2.01 J/(g·°C); ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol; ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → five terms, all in kJ, then add
cards.n: Adding the three mcΔT terms in joules to the plateau terms in kJ gives a meaningless total; convert first.

cards.q: Describe what happens to the average kinetic energy of the particles and to the attractions between them while a pure solid melts at its melting point.
cards.a: The average kinetic energy stays constant, because the temperature stays at the melting point. The energy absorbed goes into overcoming some of the attractions that hold the particles in fixed positions, so the particles' potential energy increases and they become free to slide past one another, though they remain in contact.
cards.h: → KE: constant; attractions: partly overcome, PE up
cards.n: 'The particles speed up as the solid melts' earns nothing: speeding up would raise the temperature, which stays constant on the plateau.

cards.q: Explain why a heating curve has flat plateaus.
cards.a: During a phase change the added energy goes into overcoming attractions between particles, raising their potential energy, not their average kinetic energy. Temperature reflects average kinetic energy, so it stays constant until the phase change is complete; only then does added energy speed the particles up again.
cards.h: → energy overcomes attractions → PE rises, average KE does not → temperature constant until the phase change ends
cards.n: 'No heat is being added during the plateau' earns nothing; energy flows in throughout, it just does not raise the temperature.
o: Temperature tracks average KE; on a plateau all the absorbed energy goes into separating particles against their attractions, so average KE and temperature are unchanged.
While two phases coexist, energy converts one phase to the other at a fixed temperature (q = nΔH), so there is no ΔT until one phase is gone.

w.a: The temperature stays constant because the heater stops adding energy during the phase change.
w.why: energy keeps flowing in the whole time

w.a: The plateau happens because the particles are breaking their covalent bonds.
w.why: phase changes overcome intermolecular attractions, not covalent bonds

w.a: The temperature stays the same because the particles move faster but spread farther apart.
w.why: faster particles would mean a higher temperature

cards.q: Explain why $ΔH_vap$ is much larger than $ΔH_fus$ for the same substance.
cards.a: Melting only loosens the particles: they stay in contact and most attractions remain. Vaporizing separates the particles completely, overcoming essentially all the remaining attractions. Far more attraction is overcome per mole in boiling, so ΔH_vap (40.7 kJ/mol for water) is much larger than ΔH_fus (6.01 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → melting: particles stay in contact, few attractions overcome → boiling: all overcome → more energy per mole
cards.n: Borrows Unit 3 attractions. 'Because boiling happens at a higher temperature' earns nothing: the plateau temperature does not set the energy per mole.
o: In a liquid, each particle still has nearly as many neighbors as in the solid; in a gas it has essentially none, so vaporizing breaks far more attractions.
Melting converts a fixed arrangement to a mobile one with little change in separation, while vaporizing increases the separation enormously against the attractions.

w.a: ΔH_vap is larger because boiling happens at a higher temperature than melting.
w.why: temperature does not set the energy per mole

w.a: ΔH_vap is larger because boiling breaks the covalent bonds inside the molecules.
w.why: no covalent bonds break in boiling

w.a: ΔH_vap is larger because gases have more mass than liquids.
w.why: mass is unchanged by a phase change

cards.q: Explain why a burn from 100 °C steam is more severe than a burn from the same mass of 100 °C liquid water.
cards.a: Steam first condenses on the skin, releasing ΔH_vap (40.7 kJ/mol, about 2.26 kJ per gram) at 100 °C, and then the condensed water cools just as the liquid would. The liquid delivers only the cooling energy (about 0.26 kJ/g down to body temperature), so steam transfers far more energy to the skin.
cards.h: → steam condenses on skin → releases ΔH_vap (exothermic) → then cools like the liquid → far more energy to skin
cards.n: 'Steam is hotter than boiling water' earns nothing: both are at 100 °C; the extra energy comes from condensation.
o: Condensation is vaporization reversed, so each gram of steam releases about 2.26 kJ on the skin before it even begins to cool.
Per gram, condensing releases roughly nine times as much energy as cooling liquid water from 100 °C to 37 °C (4.18 J/g per °C × 63 °C ≈ 0.26 kJ).

w.a: Steam burns more because steam is at a higher temperature than boiling water.
w.why: both are at 100 °C

w.a: Steam burns more because gas particles move faster and hit the skin harder.
w.why: same temperature, same average KE; ignores condensation

cards.q: Explain why the evaporation of sweat cools the skin.
cards.a: Evaporation is endothermic: water molecules escaping into the gas phase must absorb energy to overcome their attractions to neighboring molecules. That energy is taken from the skin by heat transfer, so the skin's energy decreases and its temperature falls.
cards.h: → evaporation is endothermic → energy absorbed to overcome attractions → drawn from the skin → skin cools
cards.n: 'Sweat is cold' or 'evaporation releases cold' earns nothing; the skin cools because it supplies the energy that vaporization absorbs.
o: Vaporizing water requires ΔH_vap per mole, and the skin in contact with the sweat is the source of that energy.
The skin is the surroundings of an endothermic phase change, so it loses the energy the evaporating water gains.

w.a: Sweat cools the skin because sweat is colder than the body.
w.why: sweat leaves the body warm; no energy transfer is named

w.a: Evaporation cools the skin because it releases energy into the air.
w.why: evaporation absorbs energy; it does not release it

cards.q: Explain why 50 g of ice at 0 °C cools a drink more than 50 g of liquid water at 0 °C.
cards.a: The ice must first melt, absorbing ΔH_fus (6.01 kJ/mol, about 334 J/g, so about 16.7 kJ for 50 g) from the drink while staying at 0 °C; only then does its meltwater warm like the added liquid would. The liquid water absorbs only the warming energy, so the ice removes more energy from the drink.
cards.h: → ice must melt first → absorbs ΔH_fus from the drink → then warms like the water → more energy removed
cards.n: 'Ice is colder than water' earns nothing: both are at 0 °C; the difference is the energy that melting absorbs.
o: Melting is endothermic, so the ice takes an extra 16.7 kJ from the drink at constant temperature before it starts to warm.
Both samples absorb the same energy warming from 0 °C, but the ice also absorbs nΔH_fus, so the drink loses more energy.

w.a: Ice cools more because it is at a lower temperature than the water.
w.why: both are at 0 °C

w.a: Ice cools more because solids have a higher specific heat than liquids.
w.why: ice's c is about half of water's; melting is the reason

cards.q: Define enthalpy and enthalpy of reaction.
cards.a: Enthalpy, H, is the quantity whose change equals the heat transferred at constant pressure. The enthalpy of reaction, ΔH_rxn, is the heat released (ΔH < 0, exothermic) or absorbed (ΔH > 0, endothermic) when the reaction occurs as written, per mole of reaction, at constant pressure: ΔH = q at constant pressure.
cards.h: → definition + sign meaning + constant pressure
cards.n: The enthalpy vs internal-energy distinction is excluded from the exam; what scores is ΔH = heat at constant pressure, negative when released.

cards.q: Explain what the unit kilojoules per mole of reaction means for an enthalpy value.
cards.a: It is the energy change for one 'mole of reaction': the reaction occurring once as written, with each coefficient read as moles. For 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ/mol means 571.6 kJ is released when 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ form 2 mol H₂O, which is 285.8 kJ per mole of H₂.
cards.h: → per mole of what + worked example
cards.n: Reading −571.6 kJ/mol as 'per mole of H₂' doubles every answer; divide by the species' coefficient to get a per-species value.

cards.q: State how to convert a measured $q_rxn$ into a molar enthalpy of reaction.
cards.a: ΔH = q_rxn ÷ n, with q_rxn = −q_soln converted to kJ and n the moles of the limiting reactant (divided by its coefficient if ΔH is to be per mole of reaction as written). Keep the sign: a solution that warmed gives q_rxn < 0 and so a negative ΔH, reported in kJ/mol.
cards.h: → one equation, which moles, which sign
cards.n: Dividing by the total moles mixed, or by the excess reactant, gives a magnitude that is too small; only the limiting reactant sets how much reaction occurred.

cards.q: Compute ΔH (kJ/mol) for a neutralization: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl + 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH mix and warm 6.67 °C (density 1.00 g/mL, c=4.18 J/(g·K)).
cards.a: −55.8 kJ/mol. q_soln = mcΔT = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(6.67 °C) = 2.79 × 10³ J, so q_rxn = −2.79 kJ. n(H₂O formed) = 0.0500 L × 1.00 M = 0.0500 mol (neither reactant is in excess). ΔH = −2.79 kJ ÷ 0.0500 mol = −55.8 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → q from calorimeter, flip sign, ÷ mol
cards.n: Using 50.0 g (one solution) in mcΔT halves q; the whole 100.0 g of mixed solution absorbs the energy.

cards.q: Calculate the heat released when 8.00 g of methane burns according to CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −890. kJ/mol.
cards.a: 444 kJ released (q = −444 kJ). n(CH₄) = 8.00 g ÷ 16.04 g/mol = 0.499 mol. The equation has 1 CH₄ per mole of reaction, so q = 0.499 mol × (−890. kJ/mol) = −444 kJ.
cards.h: → grams → mol → × ΔH
cards.n: Multiplying ΔH by grams (8.00 × 890) instead of moles earns nothing; ΔH is per mole of reaction.

cards.q: Calculate the mass of propane that must burn to release 1.00 × 10³ kJ, given C₃H₈(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 3 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(l), ΔH = −2220 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 19.9 g. Moles of reaction needed = 1.00 × 10³ kJ ÷ 2220 kJ/mol = 0.450 mol. There is 1 C₃H₈ per mole of reaction, so 0.450 mol C₃H₈ × 44.10 g/mol = 19.9 g.
cards.h: → kJ ÷ ΔH = mol, then × M
cards.n: Keeping one negative sign (−1000 ÷ 2220) gives a negative mass; divide magnitudes when solving for an amount.

cards.q: Calculate the heat released when 1.00 g of H₂ burns according to 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 142 kJ released (q = −142 kJ). n(H₂) = 1.00 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 0.496 mol. One mole of reaction consumes 2 mol H₂, so moles of reaction = 0.496 ÷ 2 = 0.248 mol, and q = 0.248 mol × (−571.6 kJ/mol) = −142 kJ.
cards.h: → mol H₂ ÷ coefficient × ΔH
cards.n: Ignoring the coefficient 2 gives −284 kJ, twice the true heat; ΔH is for 2 mol H₂ as written.

cards.q: Calculate the heat released when 2.00 mol of N₂ and 3.00 mol of H₂ react as completely as possible according to N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.2 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 92.2 kJ released (q = −92.2 kJ). H₂ is limiting: 3.00 mol H₂ reacts with only 1.00 mol N₂, which is exactly 1.00 mol of reaction as written. q = 1.00 mol × (−92.2 kJ/mol) = −92.2 kJ, and 1.00 mol N₂ is left over.
cards.h: → find the limiting reactant, then mol rxn × ΔH
cards.n: Basing q on the 2.00 mol N₂ (−184 kJ) counts reaction that cannot happen: the limiting reactant fixes the heat.

cards.q: Calculate the heat absorbed when 25.0 g of CaCO₃ decomposes by CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 44.5 kJ absorbed (q = +44.5 kJ). n = 25.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.250 mol; q = 0.250 mol × (+178 kJ/mol) = +44.5 kJ. The positive sign means the surroundings (the kiln or burner) must supply this energy to the reacting system.
cards.h: → grams → mol → × ΔH, with sign
cards.n: Reporting −44.5 kJ 'because the solid breaks apart' reverses the sign; a positive ΔH means energy is absorbed.

cards.q: Write the thermochemical equation for the combustion of one mole of liquid ethanol, C₂H₅OH (M = 46.07 g/mol), given that burning 1.00 g of it releases 29.7 kJ.
cards.a: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(l), ΔH = −1.37 × 10³ kJ/mol. Per mole: 29.7 kJ/g × 46.07 g/mol = 1368 kJ released, so ΔH is negative. The balanced equation has 1 mol ethanol per mole of reaction, so this ΔH belongs to the equation as written.
cards.h: → balanced equation with phases + ΔH per mol
cards.n: Writing ΔH = +1368 kJ, or attaching it to an unbalanced equation, loses the point: the sign is negative and ΔH belongs to the equation as written.

cards.q: Describe the energy transfers after an exothermic reaction in an open flask at 22 °C produces products at 60 °C.
cards.a: The reaction converted chemical potential energy into kinetic energy of the particles, so the products are hotter (60 °C) than the flask and air (22 °C). Their faster particles then collide with the cooler surroundings and transfer energy as heat until products and surroundings share one temperature (thermal equilibrium), essentially 22 °C in a large room. The total heat passed to the surroundings is −ΔH for the amount reacted.
cards.h: → PE → KE, then heat out until equal temperatures
cards.n: Saying the energy 'disappears' as the flask cools earns nothing: it is transferred to the surroundings, which is exactly what ΔH < 0 counts.

cards.q: Calculate q for each amount, given CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −890. kJ/mol: 1.00 mol CH₄ burned · 0.200 mol CH₄ burned · 4.00 mol O₂ consumed · 1.00 mol H₂O formed · 24.0 g CH₄ burned (16.04 g/mol) · 11.0 g CO₂ formed (44.01 g/mol) · 2.00 mol CH₄ mixed with 3.20 mol O₂
cards.a:
1.00 mol CH₄ → 1.00 mol rxn → −890. kJ
0.200 mol CH₄ → 0.200 mol rxn → −178 kJ
4.00 mol O₂ → 4.00 ÷ 2 = 2.00 mol rxn → −1.78 × 10³ kJ
1.00 mol H₂O → 1.00 ÷ 2 = 0.500 mol rxn → −445 kJ
24.0 g CH₄ → 1.496 mol rxn → −1.33 × 10³ kJ
11.0 g CO₂ → 0.250 mol rxn → −222 kJ
2.00 mol CH₄ + 3.20 mol O₂ → O₂ limiting, 1.60 mol rxn → −1.42 × 10³ kJ
cards.h: → amount ÷ coefficient = mol of reaction → × ΔH
cards.n: Multiplying ΔH by moles of O₂ or H₂O without dividing by their coefficient 2 doubles the heat; convert every amount to moles of reaction first.

cards.q: Predict the temperature change when 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 2.00 M NaOH, given that the same volumes at 1.00 M raise the temperature by 6.7 °C.
cards.a: About 13.4 °C, double. Twice the concentration in the same volumes means twice the moles of water formed (0.100 mol instead of 0.0500 mol), so twice the heat is released, while the mass of solution absorbing it (about 100 g) is unchanged; ΔT = q/(mc) therefore doubles.
cards.h: → value + what doubles and what does not
cards.n: Predicting the same ΔT because 'the same reaction occurs' ignores that q is proportional to the moles reacting while the mass stays 100 g.

cards.q: Calculate the temperature change when 0.100 mol of HCl is neutralized by excess NaOH in a solution of total mass 1.00 × 10³ g (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), given H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −55.8 kJ/mol.
cards.a: ΔT = +1.33 °C (the solution warms). Heat released = 0.100 mol × 55.8 kJ/mol = 5.58 kJ; the solution absorbs it, so q_soln = +5580 J. ΔT = q/(mc) = 5580 J ÷ (1.00 × 10³ g × 4.18 J/(g·°C)) = 1.33 °C.
cards.h: → q = nΔH, flip to the solution, ΔT = q/(mc)
cards.n: Leaving q in kJ (5.58) gives ΔT = 0.00133 °C; convert to joules to match c in J/(g·°C).

cards.q: Explain why ΔH is cut in half when every coefficient in a thermochemical equation is divided by 2.
cards.a: ΔH is the heat for the reaction exactly as written, so it is proportional to the amounts reacting. Halving every coefficient means half as many moles of each substance react, breaking and forming half as many bonds, so half as much heat is released or absorbed: ΔH is halved.
cards.h: → ΔH belongs to the equation as written → half the moles react → half the bonds → half the heat
cards.n: 'ΔH stays the same because it is a molar quantity' earns nothing: kJ/mol here means per mole of reaction as written, which halving changes.
o: The heat transferred is proportional to the moles that react; halved coefficients describe half the moles, so q and ΔH halve.
Doubling the halved equation must give back the original equation, so the halved ΔH must be exactly half the original.

w.a: ΔH stays the same because it is measured in kJ per mole.
w.why: per mole of reaction as written, which changes when the equation is halved

w.a: ΔH is halved because the temperature is halved.
w.why: temperature is not what scales; the moles reacting do

w.a: ΔH takes the square root when the coefficients are halved.
w.why: that is the rule for K, not for ΔH

cards.q: Explain how breaking and forming bonds in an exothermic reaction leads to a temperature increase of the reaction mixture.
cards.a: The products have lower chemical potential energy than the reactants: more energy is released forming their bonds than was absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds. Energy is conserved, so the released potential energy appears as greater kinetic energy of the particles, which shows up as a higher temperature.
cards.h: → products lower in PE → PE released → particles' KE increases → temperature rises
cards.n: 'Breaking bonds releases the energy that heats the mixture' earns nothing: breaking bonds absorbs energy; the release comes from forming stronger bonds.
o: The drop in chemical potential energy from reactants to products is converted to kinetic energy of the particles, and temperature measures average kinetic energy.
Net bond formation releases energy into the particles' motion, so they move faster and the mixture is hotter until it passes that energy to the surroundings.

w.a: The temperature rises because breaking the reactant bonds releases heat.
w.why: breaking bonds absorbs energy

w.a: The temperature rises because the products are hotter substances.
w.why: no mechanism: the PE-to-KE conversion is missing

w.a: The temperature rises because heat flows in from the surroundings.
w.why: that describes an endothermic process

cards.q: Explain why the temperature of a reaction mixture that warmed during an exothermic reaction falls back to room temperature after the reaction is over.
cards.a: The hot products have greater average kinetic energy than the particles of the container and air. Collisions transfer energy as heat from the warmer products to the cooler surroundings until both have the same average kinetic energy, the same temperature (thermal equilibrium); the energy ends up in the surroundings.
cards.h: → products hotter than surroundings → collisions carry energy outward → until equal average KE (thermal equilibrium)
cards.n: 'The reaction reverses and reabsorbs the heat' earns nothing; the energy is transferred to the surroundings, not taken back.
o: After the reaction, the products are simply a warm body in contact with cooler surroundings, so heat flows out until thermal equilibrium.
The energy released by the reaction first raises the mixture's temperature and is then passed on to the surroundings, which is why an exothermic reaction warms its surroundings.

w.a: The mixture cools because the products slowly absorb the heat back.
w.why: the energy leaves to the surroundings

w.a: The mixture cools because the reaction becomes endothermic once it stops.
w.why: no reaction is occurring; this is heat transfer

cards.q: Explain why mixing 100. mL of 1.00 M HCl with 100. mL of 1.00 M NaOH gives the same temperature change as mixing 50.0 mL of each.
cards.a: Doubling both volumes doubles the moles that react, so twice the heat is released, but it also doubles the mass of solution that absorbs that heat. Since ΔT = q/(mc), q and m both double and ΔT is unchanged.
cards.h: → twice the moles → twice q → but twice the mass → ΔT = q/(mc) unchanged
cards.n: 'Twice as much reacts, so ΔT doubles' earns nothing: it ignores that the heat is spread over twice as much solution.
o: The heat released per gram of solution is the same in both mixtures, so the temperature rise is the same.
Concentrations are unchanged, so each milliliter holds the same amount of reaction and the same heat; only the total amount doubles.

w.a: The temperature change doubles because twice as much acid and base react.
w.why: ignores that the mass of solution also doubles

w.a: The temperature change is halved because the heat is spread over a larger volume.
w.why: the heat doubles too

cards.q: Explain why ΔH is positive for an endothermic reaction in solution even though the solution's temperature decreases.
cards.a: ΔH describes the reacting system, not the solution. As reactants become higher-energy products, the system absorbs energy from the surrounding solution, so the solution's temperature falls (q_soln < 0) while the system gains energy: q_rxn = −q_soln > 0, so ΔH > 0.
cards.h: → ΔH is the system's change → system absorbs energy from solution → solution cools → q_rxn = −q_soln > 0
cards.n: Reading ΔH from the thermometer ('temperature fell, so ΔH is negative') takes the solution's point of view and earns nothing.
o: The solution is the surroundings; it loses the energy the reacting system gains, so the two signs are opposite.
The thermometer measures the surroundings, and a falling reading means energy went from the surroundings into the system.

w.a: ΔH is negative because the temperature decreased.
w.why: reads the sign from the surroundings

w.a: ΔH is positive because the reaction releases heat into the solution.
w.why: a release would warm the solution

cards.q: State how to calculate the enthalpy of a reaction from bond enthalpies.
cards.a: ΔH ≈ Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken in the reactants) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed in the products). Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it; if more is released than absorbed, ΔH < 0. Count only bonds that actually change, each multiplied by the number of times it occurs in the balanced equation.
cards.h: → broken minus formed, with why
cards.n: Writing formed − broken (the pattern of the ΔH°f formula, products − reactants) flips the sign of every answer.

cards.q: Using bond enthalpies H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 243, H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol, determine ΔH for H2 + Cl2 → 2 HCl.
cards.a: ΔH = −185 kJ (exothermic). Broken: 1 H−H + 1 Cl−Cl = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ absorbed. Formed: 2 H−Cl = 2 × 432 = 864 kJ released. ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ for the reaction as written.
cards.h: → broken sum, formed sum, subtract
cards.n: Counting one H−Cl bond (679 − 432 = +247 kJ) ignores the coefficient 2 and even flips the sign.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔH when the bonds formed in the products are stronger than the bonds broken in the reactants.
cards.a: ΔH is negative (exothermic). Forming the products' stronger bonds releases more energy than breaking the reactants' weaker bonds absorbs, so the system's potential energy decreases and the difference is released to the surroundings.
cards.h: → sign + released vs absorbed
cards.n: 'Stronger bonds need more energy, so ΔH is positive' confuses breaking with forming: here the stronger bonds are formed, which releases energy.

cards.q: Using bond enthalpies C-H = 413, O=O = 495, C=O = 799, O-H = 467 kJ/mol, compute ΔH for $CH_4 + 2O_2 \to CO_2 + 2H_2O$ (all gas).
cards.h: → count each bond type, broken − formed
cards.n: Counting 2 O−H (one per H₂O) instead of 4 gives +110 kJ; each of the 2 H₂O molecules has 2 O−H bonds.

cards.q: Using bond enthalpies N≡N = 941, H-H = 436, N-H = 391 kJ/mol, compute ΔH for $N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3$.
cards.a: −97 kJ/mol. Broken: 1 N≡N + 3 H−H = 941 + 3(436) = 2249 kJ. Formed: 2 NH₃ × 3 N−H = 6(391) = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2249 − 2346 = −97 kJ per mole of reaction, close to the value from enthalpies of formation, −92 kJ.
cards.h: → count each bond type, broken − formed
cards.n: Counting only 3 N−H bonds (one NH₃) gives +1076 kJ; two NH₃ molecules contain 6 N−H bonds.

cards.q: Using bond enthalpies C-H = 413, Cl-Cl = 243, C-Cl = 339, H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol, compute ΔH for $CH_4+Cl_2 \to CH_3Cl+HCl$.
cards.a: −115 kJ/mol. Only one C−H bond and the Cl−Cl bond break: 413 + 243 = 656 kJ. One C−Cl and one H−Cl bond form: 339 + 432 = 771 kJ. ΔH = 656 − 771 = −115 kJ/mol. The three C−H bonds that survive into CH₃Cl are left out (counting them on both sides cancels them).
cards.h: → only the bonds that change, broken − formed
cards.n: Breaking all 4 C−H bonds but re-forming none of them gives +1124 kJ; bonds that are unchanged must cancel.

cards.q: Explain why bond-enthalpy calculations of ΔH assume all reactants and products are in the gas phase.
cards.a: Tabulated bond enthalpies are average energies for breaking bonds in isolated gas-phase molecules, so a bond-enthalpy sum accounts only for covalent bonds. If a reactant or product is a liquid or solid, the energy of the intermolecular attractions (for example, condensing H₂O) is not included, so the estimate differs from the measured ΔH.
cards.h: → where the data come from + what is left out
cards.n: Borrows Unit 3 attractions. 'Liquids have stronger bonds' earns nothing: the missing term is intermolecular attraction, not covalent bond strength.

cards.q: Estimate ΔH for 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(g) using the bond enthalpies H−H = 436, O=O = 495 and O−H = 467 kJ/mol.
cards.a: ΔH ≈ −501 kJ (exothermic). Broken: 2 H−H + 1 O=O = 2(436) + 495 = 1367 kJ. Formed: 2 H₂O × 2 O−H = 4(467) = 1868 kJ. ΔH ≈ 1367 − 1868 = −501 kJ, close to the value from enthalpies of formation, 2(−241.8) = −483.6 kJ; bond enthalpies are averages.
cards.h: → count bonds from Lewis structures, broken − formed
cards.n: Counting only 2 O−H bonds formed (one per water) gives +433 kJ; each H₂O has two O−H bonds.

cards.q: Calculate the H−F bond enthalpy, given H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2 HF(g), ΔH = −540. kJ, and the bond enthalpies H−H = 436 and F−F = 158 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 567 kJ/mol. ΔH = broken − formed: −540. = (436 + 158) − 2(H−F). So 2(H−F) = 594 + 540 = 1134 kJ and H−F = 567 kJ/mol. The value is positive, as every bond enthalpy must be: it is the energy needed to break the bond.
cards.h: → set up broken − formed = ΔH, solve
cards.n: Forgetting that 2 H−F bonds form gives 1134 kJ/mol, twice the true value.

cards.q: Identify the bonds (type and number) that are counted for one molecule of each: CH₄ · C₂H₆ · C₂H₄ · C₂H₂ · H₂O · CO₂ · NH₃ · N₂ · O₂ · CH₃OH · HCN · H₂O₂ · C₃H₈ · CH₂O (formaldehyde)
cards.a:
CH₄ → 4 C−H
C₂H₆ → 1 C−C, 6 C−H
C₂H₄ → 1 C=C, 4 C−H
C₂H₂ → 1 C≡C, 2 C−H
H₂O → 2 O−H
CO₂ → 2 C=O
NH₃ → 3 N−H
N₂ → 1 N≡N
O₂ → 1 O=O
CH₃OH → 3 C−H, 1 C−O, 1 O−H
HCN → 1 C−H, 1 C≡N
H₂O₂ → 2 O−H, 1 O−O
C₃H₈ → 2 C−C, 8 C−H
CH₂O → 2 C−H, 1 C=O
cards.h: → draw the Lewis structure, count each bond type
cards.n: Borrows Unit 2 Lewis structures. Counting a double bond as two single bonds earns nothing: C=O (799) is not 2 × C−O (2 × 358).

cards.q: Estimate ΔH for 2 CH₃OH(g) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(g) using the bond enthalpies C−H = 413, C−O = 358, O−H = 467, O=O = 495 and C=O = 799 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → bonds per molecule × coefficient, broken − formed
cards.n: Reading C−O in methanol as C=O, or forming 4 O−H instead of 8, gives a wrong sum; list bonds per molecule, then multiply by coefficients.

cards.q: Identify the bonds broken and formed in C₂H₄(g) + Br₂(g) → C₂H₄Br₂(g), and use C=C = 614, Br−Br = 193, C−C = 348 and C−Br = 276 kJ/mol to estimate ΔH.
cards.a: Broken: 1 C=C and 1 Br−Br (614 + 193 = 807 kJ). Formed: 1 C−C and 2 C−Br (348 + 2 × 276 = 900 kJ). The four C−H bonds are unchanged and cancel. ΔH ≈ 807 − 900 = −93 kJ: exothermic.
cards.h: → list broken and formed, then broken − formed
cards.n: Breaking the C=C but forming no C−C, as if the carbons separated, gives +255 kJ; the double bond becomes a single bond, which must be counted as formed.

cards.q: Represent H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g) on an energy diagram that shows the bond-breaking and bond-forming steps separately (H−H = 436, Cl−Cl = 243, H−Cl = 432 kJ/mol).
cards.a: Vertical axis: potential energy (kJ). Left level: H₂ + Cl₂. An upward arrow of +679 kJ (436 + 243, bonds broken) to a high level labeled 2 H + 2 Cl (separated atoms). A downward arrow of −864 kJ (2 × 432, bonds formed) to a level labeled 2 HCl, which sits 185 kJ below the starting level; that net drop is labeled ΔH = −185 kJ.
cards.h: → up to atoms, down to products, net ΔH
cards.n: Drawing the atoms below the reactants, or the bond-forming arrow pointing up, shows bond breaking as releasing energy and earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain in terms of bond energies why a reaction is exothermic.
cards.a: Breaking the reactants' bonds absorbs energy and forming the products' bonds releases energy. A reaction is exothermic when the energy released forming the product bonds is greater than the energy absorbed breaking the reactant bonds, so the system's potential energy decreases and ΔH < 0.
cards.h: → breaking absorbs, forming releases → formed > broken → net PE decreases → ΔH < 0
cards.n: 'The reaction breaks bonds, which releases energy' earns nothing: breaking a bond always absorbs energy.
o: The products' bonds are, in total, stronger than the reactants' bonds, so the products sit lower in potential energy and the difference is released.
ΔH ≈ Σ broken − Σ formed is negative when the bonds formed have the larger total bond enthalpy.

w.a: The reaction is exothermic because breaking the reactant bonds releases energy.
w.why: bond breaking always absorbs energy

w.a: The reaction is exothermic because energy stored in the reactants' bonds is released when they break.
w.why: treats bonds as energy stores released on breaking

w.a: The reaction is exothermic because more bonds are formed than broken.
w.why: the number of bonds does not decide; their total strength does

cards.q: Explain why a bond-enthalpy calculation gives only an approximate ΔH.
cards.a: Tabulated bond enthalpies are averages over many different molecules, but the strength of a particular bond (a C−H bond, say) depends on the rest of its molecule. The method also treats every species as a gas and ignores intermolecular attractions, so the sum only estimates the true ΔH.
cards.h: → averages over many molecules → a given bond's strength differs → plus gas-phase assumption → estimate only
cards.n: 'Because the table values are rounded' earns nothing: the error comes from averaging over different molecular environments, not from rounding.
o: An average C−H value cannot match the actual C−H bond in every molecule, so each term in the sum carries a small error.
Enthalpies of formation are measured for the actual substances in their actual phases, which is why the ΔH°f route is more accurate.

w.a: Bond-enthalpy calculations are approximate because the numbers in the table are rounded.
w.why: the main error is averaging over molecules, not rounding

w.a: Bond-enthalpy calculations are approximate because they do not count every bond.
w.why: all changing bonds are counted; the values themselves are averages

w.a: Bond-enthalpy calculations are approximate because bonds break at different temperatures.
w.why: temperature is not the source of the approximation

cards.q: Explain why combustion reactions are strongly exothermic in terms of bonds.
cards.a: Combustion forms very strong bonds, C=O in CO₂ and O−H in H₂O, and breaks weaker C−H, C−C and O=O bonds. The energy released forming the products' bonds far exceeds the energy absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds, so ΔH is large and negative.
cards.h: → break weaker C−H, C−C, O=O → form very strong C=O, O−H → released ≫ absorbed → large negative ΔH
cards.n: 'Fuels store energy in their bonds, which is released when they break' earns nothing: breaking any bond absorbs energy.
o: For methane, forming 2 C=O and 4 O−H releases 3466 kJ while breaking 4 C−H and 2 O=O absorbs only 2642 kJ.
CO₂ and H₂O sit very low in potential energy because their bonds are strong, so reaching them from a fuel releases a large amount of energy.

w.a: Combustion is exothermic because the fuel's bonds release energy when they break.
w.why: breaking bonds absorbs energy

w.a: Combustion is exothermic because fire is hot.
w.why: describes the result, not the bond-energy cause

w.a: Combustion is exothermic because oxygen has a lot of energy stored in it.
w.why: no bond comparison; energy is not stored in a substance to be released

cards.q: Explain why breaking a chemical bond always requires an input of energy.
cards.a: In a bond, the shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, so the bonded atoms sit at the separation of lowest potential energy. Pulling the atoms apart works against that Coulombic attraction and raises the potential energy of the system, so energy must be supplied.
cards.h: → bonding electrons attracted to both nuclei → separating atoms opposes attraction → PE rises → energy absorbed
cards.n: Borrows the Unit 2 potential-energy curve. 'Bonds are stores of energy released when broken' is the classic wrong model and earns nothing.
o: A bonded pair of atoms is at the bottom of a potential-energy well; any separation moves the system uphill, which requires energy.
Separating opposite charges (nuclei and shared electrons) always takes energy, so bond breaking is always endothermic.

w.a: Breaking a bond releases the energy that was stored in it.
w.why: breaking absorbs energy; bonds are not energy stores

w.a: Breaking a bond needs energy only when the bond is a strong one.
w.why: every bond needs energy to break; strength sets how much

w.a: Breaking a bond needs energy because the atoms repel each other.
w.why: at the bond length the net force is attraction that must be overcome

cards.q: Explain why forming a bond releases the same amount of energy that breaking that bond requires.
cards.a: Forming a bond is the exact reverse of breaking it: the atoms move between the same two potential-energy levels in the opposite direction. Energy is conserved, so the energy released when the atoms come together equals the energy absorbed to pull them apart, 436 kJ/mol for H−H, for example.
cards.h: → forming is breaking reversed → same two PE levels → energy conserved → equal magnitude, opposite sign
cards.n: 'Forming a bond also takes energy because the atoms must collide' earns nothing: bond formation lowers potential energy and releases energy.
o: If forming released less than breaking absorbed, breaking and re-forming the bond would destroy energy, which conservation forbids.
A single tabulated bond enthalpy serves both processes: it is added for bonds broken and subtracted for bonds formed.

w.a: Forming a bond releases less energy than breaking it because some energy is lost as heat.
w.why: energy is conserved; the amounts are equal

w.a: Forming a bond also requires energy, just less than breaking it.
w.why: bond formation releases energy

cards.q: State the standard conditions implied by the degree symbol in ΔH°.
