cards.a: Every substance is in its standard state: gases at 1 bar (about 1 atm) partial pressure, solutes at 1 M, and pure solids and liquids in their most stable form at that pressure. Tabulated values are almost always given at 25 °C (298 K), but the degree sign itself does not fix a temperature.
cards.h: → gases, solutions, solids/liquids, and the 298 K convention
cards.n: Confusing standard conditions with STP (0 °C, 1 atm) earns nothing; tables of ΔH°f are at 25 °C.

cards.q: Define the standard enthalpy of formation.
cards.a: ΔH°f is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound forms from its elements, each in its standard state, under standard conditions; units kJ/mol. Example: H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH°f = −285.8 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → one mole, from elements, standard states
cards.n: Writing 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O as the formation equation makes 2 mol of product; the definition requires exactly one mole, even with fractional coefficients.

cards.q: State the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state.
cards.a: Zero, by definition: forming an element in its standard state from itself involves no change. Examples: O₂(g), N₂(g), H₂(g), Cl₂(g), Br₂(l), Hg(l), C(s, graphite), Fe(s) and Na(s) all have ΔH°f = 0.
cards.h: → the value + why + examples
cards.n: Only the standard-state form is zero: O₃(g), O(g), C(diamond), Br₂(g) and H(g) all have nonzero ΔH°f.

cards.q: State the equation for the standard enthalpy of reaction from enthalpies of formation.
cards.a: ΔH°rxn = ΣnΔH°f(products) − ΣnΔH°f(reactants), where each n is that species' coefficient in the balanced equation and elements in their standard states contribute zero. The result is in kJ per mole of reaction as written.
cards.h: → products minus reactants, each × coefficient
cards.n: Leaving out the coefficients, or subtracting products from reactants, loses the point; it is products minus reactants, each times n.

cards.q: Using ΔH°f values of -74.8 (CH4), -393.5 (CO2), and -285.8 kJ/mol (H2O liquid), determine ΔH° for CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l).
cards.a: ΔH° = −890.3 kJ/mol. ΔH° = [ΔH°f(CO₂) + 2ΔH°f(H₂O, l)] − [ΔH°f(CH₄) + 2ΔH°f(O₂)] = [−393.5 + 2(−285.8)] − [−74.8 + 0] = −965.1 + 74.8 = −890.3 kJ per mole of reaction: exothermic.
cards.h: → products − reactants, coefficients, O₂ = 0
cards.n: Writing −965.1 − 74.8 = −1039.9 kJ drops the double negative on the reactant side; subtract the whole reactant sum.

cards.q: Identify the standard states of bromine, mercury, carbon, and oxygen.
cards.a: Br₂(l), Hg(l), C(s, graphite) and O₂(g): the most stable form of each at 1 bar and 25 °C, so each has ΔH°f = 0. Bromine and mercury are the only elements that are liquids under these conditions.
cards.h: → four formulas with phases
cards.n: Writing Br(l), O(g) or C(diamond) earns nothing: bromine and oxygen are diatomic, and graphite, not diamond, is carbon's reference form.

cards.q: Using ΔH°f = 0 ($O_2$), -110.5 (CO), and -393.5 kJ/mol ($CO_2$), compute ΔH° for $2CO(g)+O_2(g) \to 2CO_2(g)$.
cards.a: ΔH° = −566.0 kJ. ΔH° = [2(−393.5)] − [2(−110.5) + 0] = −787.0 − (−221.0) = −566.0 kJ per mole of reaction as written, which is −283.0 kJ per mole of CO burned.
cards.h: → products − reactants with coefficients
cards.n: Forgetting the coefficient 2 on both CO and CO₂ gives −283.0 kJ, the value for only half the equation.

cards.q: Identify which is correctly written in its standard state: $O_2(g)$, O(g), or $O_3(g)$.
cards.a: O₂(g). Oxygen's standard state is the diatomic gas, its most stable form at 25 °C and 1 bar, so ΔH°f[O₂(g)] = 0. Atomic O(g) (+249 kJ/mol) and ozone O₃(g) (+143 kJ/mol) are higher-energy forms with positive ΔH°f.
cards.h: → one formula + why the other two are not
cards.n: Assigning zero to every form of an element (O₃ or O included) earns nothing; only the single most stable form is the reference.

cards.q: Using ΔH°f = -46.1 $(NH_3,$ g), -241.8 $(H_2O,$ g), and +90.3 kJ/mol (NO, g), compute ΔH° for $4NH_3(g) + 5O_2(g) \to 4NO(g) + 6H_2O(g)$.
cards.h: → products − reactants, coefficients, O₂ = 0
cards.n: Using ΔH°f of H₂O(l) (−285.8) instead of H₂O(g) gives −1169.2 kJ; the phase in the equation decides which value to use.

cards.q: Identify the standard states of nitrogen, sulfur, and sodium at 25°C.
cards.a: Nitrogen: N₂(g). Sulfur: S₈(s), rhombic sulfur. Sodium: Na(s). These are the most stable forms at 25 °C and 1 bar, so each has ΔH°f = 0.
cards.h: → three formulas with phases
cards.n: N(g), S(g) and Na(g) are not reference forms; they have large positive ΔH°f values because energy is needed to make them.

cards.q: Write the formation equation (one mole of product from its elements in their standard states) for each: H₂O(l) · CO₂(g) · NH₃(g) · CH₄(g) · C₂H₅OH(l) · NaCl(s) · CaCO₃(s) · NO(g) · HCl(g) · Fe₂O₃(s) · C₆H₁₂O₆(s) · KClO₃(s)
cards.a:
H₂O(l): H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l)
CO₂(g): C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
NH₃(g): ½ N₂(g) + 3/2 H₂(g) → NH₃(g)
CH₄(g): C(s, graphite) + 2 H₂(g) → CH₄(g)
C₂H₅OH(l): 2 C(s, graphite) + 3 H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l)
NaCl(s): Na(s) + ½ Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s)
CaCO₃(s): Ca(s) + C(s, graphite) + 3/2 O₂(g) → CaCO₃(s)
NO(g): ½ N₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → NO(g)
HCl(g): ½ H₂(g) + ½ Cl₂(g) → HCl(g)
Fe₂O₃(s): 2 Fe(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → Fe₂O₃(s)
C₆H₁₂O₆(s): 6 C(s, graphite) + 6 H₂(g) + 3 O₂(g) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s)
KClO₃(s): K(s) + ½ Cl₂(g) + 3/2 O₂(g) → KClO₃(s)
cards.h: → elements in standard states, 1 mol product, fractions OK
cards.n: Writing H, O or Cl atoms, or doubling to clear fractions, loses the point: diatomic elements appear as X₂ and the product must be exactly one mole.

cards.q: Identify whether each equation is a standard formation reaction, and give the reason for each that is not: C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) · 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l) · CO(g) + ½ O₂(g) → CO₂(g) · H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l) · Na(s) + ½ Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s) · Na(g) + ½ Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s) · C(s, diamond) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) · ½ N₂(g) + 3/2 H₂(g) → NH₃(g) · H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) · H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g) · Ca(s) + O(g) → CaO(s)
cards.a:
C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂ → formation reaction
2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O → not: makes 2 mol of product
CO + ½ O₂ → CO₂ → not: CO is a compound, not an element
H₂ + ½ O₂ → H₂O(l) → formation reaction
Na(s) + ½ Cl₂ → NaCl(s) → formation reaction
Na(g) + ½ Cl₂ → NaCl(s) → not: Na(g) is not sodium's standard state
C(diamond) + O₂ → CO₂ → not: diamond is not carbon's standard state
½ N₂ + 3/2 H₂ → NH₃ → formation reaction
H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) → not: a phase change, no elements
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl → not: makes 2 mol of product
Ca(s) + O(g) → CaO(s) → not: O(g) is not oxygen's standard state
cards.h: → 1 mol product? only elements? all in standard states?
cards.n: Accepting 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O because 'it is balanced' earns nothing: a formation equation must make exactly one mole of product.

cards.q: Calculate ΔH°f of C₂H₆(g), given 2 C₂H₆(g) + 7 O₂(g) → 4 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(l), ΔH° = −3119.4 kJ, ΔH°f(CO₂, g) = −393.5 kJ/mol and ΔH°f(H₂O, l) = −285.8 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → set up products − reactants = ΔH°, solve
cards.n: Forgetting to divide by the coefficient 2 gives −169.4 kJ/mol, twice the value for one mole of ethane.

cards.q: Calculate ΔH° for C₂H₅OH(l) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(l) using ΔH°f values of −277.7 kJ/mol for C₂H₅OH(l), −393.5 kJ/mol for CO₂(g) and −285.8 kJ/mol for H₂O(l).
cards.h: → products − reactants, coefficients, O₂ = 0
cards.n: Giving O₂(g) a nonzero value, or adding the reactant sum instead of subtracting it (−1922.1 kJ), loses the point.

cards.q: Calculate ΔH° for each physical process from the standard enthalpies of formation (kJ/mol): H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) [H₂O(l) −285.8; H₂O(g) −241.8] · Br₂(l) → Br₂(g) [Br₂(g) +30.9] · I₂(s) → I₂(g) [I₂(g) +62.4] · C(s, graphite) → C(s, diamond) [C(diamond) +1.9] · H₂O(g) → H₂O(l)
cards.a:
H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) → −241.8 − (−285.8) = +44.0 kJ/mol (vaporization at 25 °C)
Br₂(l) → Br₂(g) → +30.9 − 0 = +30.9 kJ/mol (vaporization)
I₂(s) → I₂(g) → +62.4 − 0 = +62.4 kJ/mol (sublimation)
C(graphite) → C(diamond) → +1.9 − 0 = +1.9 kJ/mol
H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) → −285.8 − (−241.8) = −44.0 kJ/mol (condensation)
cards.h: → products − reactants; standard-state element = 0
cards.n: The +44.0 kJ/mol is ΔH_vap at 25 °C; the 40.7 kJ/mol on heating curves is at 100 °C. Both are right for their temperatures.

cards.q: Explain why the standard enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) is zero while that of O₃(g) is not.
cards.a: ΔH°f is the enthalpy change to make a substance from its elements in their standard states. O₂(g) is oxygen's standard state, so 'forming' it from O₂(g) is no change: ΔH°f = 0. Making O₃ from O₂ is a real reaction that absorbs energy, so ΔH°f(O₃) = +143 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → ΔH°f measured from elements in standard states → O₂ is that state → no change → 0; O₃ needs a reaction → ≠ 0
cards.n: 'O₂ has no energy' earns nothing: zero is a reference point chosen by definition, not an absence of energy.
o: The formation equation for O₂(g) would be O₂(g) → O₂(g), which has no enthalpy change; for O₃ it is 3/2 O₂(g) → O₃(g), which absorbs energy.
Standard enthalpies of formation are measured relative to the most stable form of each element, and only O₂(g) is that form for oxygen.

w.a: ΔH°f of O₂ is zero because O₂ contains no energy.
w.why: zero is a reference, not an absence of energy

w.a: ΔH°f of O₃ is also zero because ozone is made only of oxygen.
w.why: only the standard-state form is the zero reference

w.a: ΔH°f of O₂ is zero because it is a gas.
w.why: many gases have nonzero ΔH°f; being the standard state is the reason

cards.q: Explain why ΔH°rxn can be calculated as the sum of the ΔH°f values of the products minus the sum of the ΔH°f values of the reactants.
cards.a: Picture a two-step path: decompose the reactants into their elements (the reverse of their formation reactions, contributing −ΣnΔH°f of the reactants), then form the products from those same elements (+ΣnΔH°f of the products). Energy is conserved, so ΔH for the overall reaction equals the sum of the two steps.
cards.h: → reactants → elements (−ΔH°f each) → products (+ΔH°f each) → energy conserved → sum of the steps
cards.n: Justifying with 'enthalpy is a state function' relies on a concept the CED excludes; argue from adding steps and conservation of energy.
o: The ΔH°f formula is Hess's law applied to the formation reactions: products are formed from elements, and reactants are 'unformed' into elements with the sign reversed.
Both reactants and products are measured against the same zero, the elements in their standard states, so their difference is the enthalpy change between them.

w.a: It works because the products always have more energy than the reactants.
w.why: false in general, and gives no reason for the formula

w.a: It works because ΔH°f values are measured by burning each substance.
w.why: how data are measured does not justify the subtraction

w.a: It works because elements have zero energy.
w.why: zero is a reference; the reason is the path through the elements

cards.q: Explain why ΔH°f of H₂O(l) (−285.8 kJ/mol) is more negative than ΔH°f of H₂O(g) (−241.8 kJ/mol).
cards.a: Forming liquid water can be viewed as forming water vapor and then condensing it. Condensation is exothermic, because attractions form between the molecules and release energy (44.0 kJ/mol at 25 °C), so the liquid ends 44.0 kJ/mol lower in energy: −241.8 − 44.0 = −285.8 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → liquid = gas + condensation → condensing releases 44.0 kJ/mol → liquid is 44.0 kJ/mol lower
cards.n: Borrows Unit 3 attractions. 'Liquid water has stronger O−H bonds' earns nothing: the difference is intermolecular, not covalent.
o: Both form the same covalent bonds; the liquid additionally has hydrogen bonds between molecules, whose formation releases extra energy.
The gap equals ΔH° for H₂O(g) → H₂O(l), −44.0 kJ/mol, the energy released when the vapor condenses.

w.a: Liquid water has a more negative ΔH°f because its O−H bonds are stronger.
w.why: the covalent bonds are the same; the difference is intermolecular

w.a: Liquid water has a more negative ΔH°f because it is colder than steam.
w.why: both values are at 25 °C; temperature is not the reason

w.a: Gaseous water has more energy because gases are always less stable.
w.why: no attraction or energy-release reasoning given

cards.q: Explain why the formation equation for NH₃(g) is written with fractional coefficients, ½ N₂(g) + 3/2 H₂(g) → NH₃(g).
cards.a: ΔH°f is defined per mole of compound formed, so the equation must produce exactly one mole of NH₃. One NH₃ needs one N atom and three H atoms, which is ½ mol of N₂ and 3/2 mol of H₂; the elements must stay in their diatomic standard states, so fractions are required.
cards.h: → ΔH°f is per 1 mol of product → 1 NH₃ needs 1 N and 3 H → from N₂ and H₂ → ½ and 3/2
cards.n: Clearing the fractions (N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃) describes 2 mol of NH₃, so its ΔH is −92.2 kJ, twice ΔH°f = −46.1 kJ/mol.
o: Coefficients in a thermochemical equation count moles, not molecules, so half a mole of N₂ is a perfectly real amount.
Doubling to whole numbers would double ΔH, and the result would no longer be the enthalpy of formation per mole.

w.a: The fractions are there because nitrogen atoms can be split in half.
w.why: coefficients are moles, not fractions of atoms

w.a: The fractions are needed because N₂ and H₂ are gases.
w.why: the phase has nothing to do with it

w.a: The equation could equally be written with whole numbers without changing ΔH°f.
w.why: doubling the equation doubles ΔH

cards.q: Explain how ΔH changes when a reaction is reversed or when its coefficients are multiplied.
cards.a: Reversing a reaction keeps the magnitude of ΔH and reverses its sign, so an exothermic step becomes endothermic by the same amount. Multiplying all coefficients by a factor c multiplies ΔH by c, because c times as many moles react and c times as much heat is transferred.
cards.h: → two rules, each with its reason
cards.n: Dividing ΔH by the factor, or flipping its sign when the equation is only multiplied, earns nothing; only reversal changes the sign.

cards.q: State Hess's law and justify it.
cards.a: Hess's law: when a process can be written as the sum of a series of steps, ΔH for the overall process equals the sum of the ΔH values of the steps. Justification: energy is conserved, so the net heat exchanged with the surroundings over the whole sequence must equal the sum of the heats exchanged in the individual steps.
cards.h: → statement + conservation-of-energy reason
cards.n: 'Enthalpy is a state function' is not the CED's reasoning (state functions are not assessed); justify with conservation of energy.

cards.q: State the rules for manipulating equations when applying Hess's law.
cards.a: (i) Reverse an equation: change the sign of its ΔH, keeping the magnitude. (ii) Multiply an equation by c: multiply its ΔH by c. (iii) Add the adjusted equations, cancelling species that appear on both sides in the same phase, and add their ΔH values to get ΔH for the target equation.
cards.h: → reverse, multiply, add
cards.n: Species cancel only if the formula and phase match; H₂O(l) on one side does not cancel H₂O(g) on the other.

cards.q: Using Hess's law with $C(s)+O_2(g)\to CO_2(g)$, ΔH=-393.5 kJ, and $CO(g)+\frac{1}{2}O_2(g)\to CO_2(g)$, ΔH=-283.0 kJ, find ΔH for $C(s)+\frac{1}{2}O_2(g)\to CO(g)$.
cards.a: ΔH = −110.5 kJ. Keep equation 1: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), −393.5 kJ. Reverse equation 2: CO₂(g) → CO(g) + ½ O₂(g), +283.0 kJ. Adding cancels CO₂ and ½ O₂, leaving C(s) + ½ O₂(g) → CO(g); ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ.
cards.h: → keep 1, reverse 2 (flip sign), add
cards.n: Reversing the equation but not the sign of its ΔH gives −676.5 kJ, the classic wrong answer.

cards.q: Given $2A \to B$, ΔH = +60. kJ and $B \to 2C$, ΔH = -90. kJ, compute ΔH for $2A \to 2C$.
cards.a: ΔH = −30. kJ. The equations already add to the target: 2A → B plus B → 2C gives 2A + B → B + 2C; B cancels, leaving 2A → 2C. ΔH = (+60.) + (−90.) = −30. kJ, so the overall process is exothermic.
cards.h: → add as given, cancel B, add ΔH
cards.n: Reversing a step that is already oriented correctly (giving ±150 kJ) earns nothing; check which side each target species is on before flipping.

cards.q: Given (1) graphite → diamond, ΔH = +1.9 kJ/mol, and (2) diamond + $O_2(g)$ → $CO_2(g)$, ΔH = -395.4 kJ/mol, compute ΔH for graphite + $O_2(g)$ → $CO_2(g)$.
cards.a: ΔH = −393.5 kJ/mol. Adding (1) and (2) as written gives graphite + diamond + O₂ → diamond + CO₂; diamond cancels, leaving graphite + O₂(g) → CO₂(g). ΔH = +1.9 + (−395.4) = −393.5 kJ/mol, which is ΔH°f of CO₂(g).
cards.h: → add as written, cancel diamond
cards.n: Reversing step 1 because diamond 'should' be a reactant gives −397.3 kJ; diamond is already a product of 1 and a reactant of 2.

cards.q: Given (1) $S(s) + O_2(g) \to SO_2(g)$, ΔH = -296.8 kJ, and (2) $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \to 2SO_3(g)$, ΔH = -197.8 kJ, compute ΔH for $S(s) + \frac{3}{2}O_2(g) \to SO_3(g)$.
cards.a: ΔH = −395.7 kJ. Keep (1): S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), −296.8 kJ. Halve (2): SO₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → SO₃(g), ½(−197.8) = −98.9 kJ. Adding cancels SO₂ and gives S(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → SO₃(g); ΔH = −296.8 + (−98.9) = −395.7 kJ.
cards.h: → keep 1, halve 2 and its ΔH, add
cards.n: Halving the equation but using the full −197.8 kJ gives −494.6 kJ; ΔH must be scaled by the same factor as the equation.

cards.q: Apply Hess's law bookkeeping to combine (1) $2A \to B$ and (2) $C \to 2A$ so their sum gives $C \to B$. Determine whether either equation must be reversed.
cards.a: Neither needs reversing. Adding (1) 2A → B and (2) C → 2A gives 2A + C → B + 2A; 2A appears on both sides and cancels, leaving C → B. So ΔH(C → B) = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂, with both values used as given.
cards.h: → decision + the sum shown
cards.n: Reversing (2) because A 'belongs' on the left earns nothing; decide by where each TARGET species (C and B) must end up.

cards.q: Predict whether heating 1 mol of water from 25°C to 100°C gives a different ΔH if done directly versus heated, cooled partway, then reheated to 100°C.
cards.a: No: ΔH is the same either way. Treat the indirect route as steps: heat 25 °C → x, cool x → y, reheat y → 100 °C. The cooling step is the reverse of part of the heating, so its ΔH has the same magnitude and opposite sign and cancels that part; the steps add up to the ΔH of heating 25 → 100 °C, about +5.65 kJ (18.02 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × 75 °C).
cards.h: → claim + the steps add up to the same total
cards.n: State functions are not assessed; the scored reasoning is Hess's-law addition of steps, with the cooling step cancelling part of the heating.

cards.q: State why ΔH must equal zero for a cyclic process that returns a system to its exact initial state.
cards.a: A cycle is a sequence of steps whose sum is no net change: every species ends where it started. By Hess's law the overall ΔH is the sum of the steps' ΔH values, and the return steps are the reverse of the outgoing ones (same magnitude, opposite sign), so the sum is 0. Anything else would create or destroy energy on each cycle.
cards.h: → steps sum to no change → reversed steps cancel → 0
cards.n: Answering only 'enthalpy is a state function' uses a concept the CED excludes; argue from adding reversed steps and conservation of energy.

cards.q: Calculate ΔH for 2 C(s) + H₂(g) → C₂H₂(g), given (1) C₂H₂(g) + 5/2 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + H₂O(l), ΔH = −1299.6 kJ; (2) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; (3) H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8 kJ.
cards.a: ΔH = +226.8 kJ. Double (2): 2 C + 2 O₂ → 2 CO₂, −787.0 kJ. Keep (3): H₂ + ½ O₂ → H₂O(l), −285.8 kJ. Reverse (1): 2 CO₂ + H₂O(l) → C₂H₂ + 5/2 O₂, +1299.6 kJ. Adding cancels 2 CO₂, H₂O(l) and 5/2 O₂: ΔH = −787.0 − 285.8 + 1299.6 = +226.8 kJ.
cards.h: → double 2, keep 3, reverse 1, add
cards.n: Reversing (1) but keeping −1299.6 kJ gives −2372.4 kJ; every reversed equation needs its sign flipped.

cards.q: Represent the dissolving of NaCl(s) in water as a sequence of two steps and determine ΔH_soln, given NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), ΔH = +787 kJ/mol, and Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), ΔH = −783 kJ/mol.
cards.a: Step 1, separate the ions of the lattice (endothermic): NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), +787 kJ/mol. Step 2, hydrate the gaseous ions (exothermic): Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), −783 kJ/mol. Adding cancels the gaseous ions: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), ΔH_soln = +787 − 783 = +4 kJ/mol, slightly endothermic.
cards.h: → two steps with signs, add, cancel the gas ions
cards.n: Borrows Unit 3 ion–dipole attractions. Treating step 1 as releasing energy ('the ionic bonds break and release energy') flips the sign of ΔH_soln.

cards.q: Determine ΔH for each equation, given A + B → C, ΔH = −100. kJ, and C → D, ΔH = +40. kJ: C → A + B · 2A + 2B → 2C · ½A + ½B → ½C · 3C → 3A + 3B · A + B → D · D → A + B · 2D → 2C · 2A + 2B → 2D
cards.a:
C → A + B → +100. kJ (reversed)
2A + 2B → 2C → −200. kJ (× 2)
½A + ½B → ½C → −50. kJ (× ½)
3C → 3A + 3B → +300. kJ (reversed, × 3)
A + B → D → −60. kJ (sum of the two)
D → A + B → +60. kJ (sum, reversed)
2D → 2C → −80. kJ (second reversed, × 2)
2A + 2B → 2D → −120. kJ (sum, × 2)
cards.h: → reverse: flip sign; × c: × c; add: add
cards.n: Flipping the sign when an equation is only scaled, or scaling without flipping when it is also reversed, is the usual slip; apply each rule separately.

cards.q: Determine ΔH for H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(g), given H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8 kJ, and H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +44.0 kJ.
cards.a: ΔH = −241.8 kJ. The target is formation of liquid water followed by its vaporization: adding the two equations cancels H₂O(l), leaving H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(g). ΔH = −285.8 + 44.0 = −241.8 kJ. Less energy is released because the vapor keeps the energy that condensing would have released.
cards.h: → add the two steps, cancel H₂O(l)
cards.n: Subtracting 44.0 (−329.8 kJ) treats vaporization as releasing energy; vaporizing absorbs energy, so it makes ΔH less negative.

cards.q: Represent on an enthalpy diagram the formation of CO₂ from C(s) and O₂(g) both directly (ΔH = −393.5 kJ) and in two steps via CO(g): C + ½ O₂ → CO, ΔH = −110.5 kJ; then CO + ½ O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ.
cards.a: Vertical axis: enthalpy (kJ). Top level: C(s) + O₂(g), set at 0. Middle level: CO(g) + ½ O₂(g), at −110.5 kJ. Bottom level: CO₂(g), at −393.5 kJ. One long downward arrow from top to bottom labeled −393.5 kJ; beside it two shorter downward arrows, top → middle (−110.5 kJ) and middle → bottom (−283.0 kJ). The two short arrows together span exactly the long one.
cards.h: → three levels, one long arrow, two short arrows
cards.n: Drawing the two-step route ending at a different level from the direct route shows the steps summing to a different ΔH, which contradicts Hess's law.

cards.q: Explain why Hess's law allows enthalpies of individual steps to be added even if the reaction does not actually occur via that pathway.
cards.a: Energy is conserved. If the steps, added together, turn the same reactants into the same products, the net energy transferred to or from the surroundings must equal the sum of the steps' transfers; otherwise, running one route forward and the other backward would create or destroy energy.
cards.h: → steps sum to the same overall change → energy conserved → net heat = sum of step heats, real path or not
cards.n: 'Because the reaction really happens in those steps' earns nothing: the steps can be hypothetical; only their sum must match the target.
o: Each step's ΔH reflects the potential-energy difference between its starting and ending species, and chaining steps adds those differences, which depend only on where the chain starts and ends.
A route giving a different ΔH could be run forward with the other route backward to make energy from nothing, violating the first law.

w.a: Hess's law works because the reaction actually goes through those steps in the flask.
w.why: the steps may be hypothetical

w.a: Hess's law works because all reactions release the same amount of heat.
w.why: false, and irrelevant to adding steps

w.a: Hess's law works because the steps happen at the same temperature.
w.why: temperature is not the reason; conservation of energy is

cards.q: Explain why reversing a chemical equation reverses the sign of ΔH but keeps its magnitude.
cards.a: The reverse reaction moves between the same two energy levels in the opposite direction. If the forward reaction releases 100 kJ, running it backward must absorb exactly 100 kJ to return to the start; any other amount would mean energy was created or destroyed over the round trip.
cards.h: → same two levels, opposite direction → round trip must net zero → equal magnitude, opposite sign
cards.n: 'Reversing makes it endothermic because going backward is harder' earns nothing: the magnitude is identical; only the direction changes.
o: Forward plus reverse is no net change, so ΔH(forward) + ΔH(reverse) = 0 by conservation of energy.
The bonds broken in the forward direction are the bonds formed in the reverse direction, so the same energy terms appear with opposite signs.

w.a: The reverse reaction has a different magnitude of ΔH because it has a different activation energy.
w.why: Ea differs, ΔH does not

w.a: Reversing the equation keeps the same sign because it is the same reaction.
w.why: the direction of energy flow reverses

cards.q: Explain why H₂O(l) in one equation cannot cancel H₂O(g) in another when equations are added in a Hess's law calculation.
cards.a: H₂O(l) and H₂O(g) are at different energies: the vapor is 44.0 kJ/mol higher because the attractions between the molecules have been overcome. Cancelling them would silently drop a vaporization step and its ΔH, so the sum of the steps would no longer describe the target process.
cards.h: → liquid and gas differ in energy (ΔH_vap) → cancelling them drops a real energy change → wrong total
cards.n: 'They are the same compound, so they cancel' earns nothing: in enthalpy bookkeeping the phase is part of a species' identity.
o: To cancel them legitimately you must add the step H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) with its own ΔH; leaving it out loses 44.0 kJ per mole.
Species cancel only when they are identical, including phase, because only then do they carry identical energies.

w.a: H₂O(l) and H₂O(g) cancel because they have the same formula.
w.why: different phases have different energies

w.a: They cannot cancel because liquids never appear in thermochemical equations.
w.why: liquids appear routinely

cards.q: Explain how Hess's law allows ΔH for graphite → diamond to be found even though the conversion cannot be carried out in a calorimeter at ordinary conditions.
cards.a: Both forms can be burned to CO₂ in a calorimeter (ΔH = −393.5 and −395.4 kJ/mol). Graphite → CO₂ followed by the reverse of diamond → CO₂ adds up to graphite → diamond, so ΔH = −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ/mol; the steps need only sum to the target, not actually occur that way.
cards.h: → measure the combustion of each → graphite → CO₂ then CO₂ → diamond → add ΔH values
cards.n: Reversing the graphite equation instead of the diamond one gives −1.9 kJ/mol, as if diamond were lower in energy than graphite.
o: Measurable reactions (the two combustions) are combined so that CO₂ and O₂ cancel, leaving the unmeasurable reaction with ΔH = sum of the steps.
Diamond releases 1.9 kJ/mol more on burning than graphite, so it must be 1.9 kJ/mol higher in energy.

w.a: Hess's law lets us find it because graphite slowly turns into diamond on its own.
w.why: no real conversion is needed; the steps can be hypothetical

w.a: ΔH is zero because graphite and diamond are both pure carbon.
w.why: the two forms differ in energy by 1.9 kJ/mol

cards.q: Explain why the enthalpy of sublimation of ice at 0 °C equals the enthalpy of fusion plus the enthalpy of vaporization at 0 °C.
cards.a: Sublimation (solid → gas) can be written as two steps with the same start and end: melting (solid → liquid, ΔH_fus) and then vaporizing (liquid → gas, ΔH_vap). The liquid cancels, and because energy is conserved, ΔH for the overall process equals the sum of the steps' ΔH values.
cards.h: → solid → liquid → gas adds to solid → gas → liquid cancels → ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap
cards.n: Adding ΔH_vap at 100 °C (40.7) to ΔH_fus at 0 °C mixes temperatures; the sum is exact only with both steps at the same temperature.
o: The physical process is broken into steps just like a reaction, and Hess's law adds their enthalpy changes.
Going solid → gas directly or via the liquid transfers the same total energy, so ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap.

w.a: ΔH_sub equals ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap because ice melts before it sublimes.
w.why: ice can sublime directly; the steps need not occur

w.a: ΔH_sub is smaller than the sum because sublimation skips the liquid.
w.why: skipping the liquid does not change the total energy

cards.q: Define dynamic equilibrium for a reversible chemical reaction.
cards.a: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in which the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates, so there is no net change: the concentrations (or partial pressures) of every species stay constant, reactants and products are both present, and both reactions keep occurring at the particle level. Nothing observable changes, but the reaction has not stopped.
cards.h: → equal rates, constant amounts, still running
cards.n: 'The reaction stops' or 'reactants and products are equal' earns nothing: equal RATES, not equal amounts, and both processes continue.

cards.q: Identify three reversible physical processes and, for each, name the pair of opposing changes.
cards.a: (1) Evaporation and condensation: liquid water ⇌ water vapor in a sealed flask. (2) Absorption and desorption of a gas: CO₂ dissolving into and escaping from a liquid, or a gas binding to and leaving a solid surface. (3) Dissolution and precipitation: a salt dissolving into its ions while ions rejoin the solid, as in a saturated solution over undissolved solid. Each reaches equilibrium when the two opposing rates are equal.
cards.h: → three pairs of opposing processes
cards.n: Naming one direction only ('evaporation') earns nothing; the point is that each process has a reverse that runs at the same time.

cards.q: Identify the two kinds of reversible chemical process that the CED singles out, and give one example of each.
cards.a: Proton transfer (acid-base) and electron transfer (redox). Proton transfer: HF(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq), where H₃O⁺ can hand the proton back to F⁻. Electron transfer: Fe³⁺(aq) + Cu⁺(aq) ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu²⁺(aq), where the electron can move back. Both are dynamic: the transfer runs in both directions at once, and equilibrium is reached when the two rates match.
cards.h: → two transfer types + one equation each
cards.n: Writing a one-way arrow, or calling a weak-acid ionization 'complete', earns nothing; the reverse process is the whole point.

cards.q: Describe what an observer measures once a closed system has reached equilibrium, and what species are present in the container.
cards.a: Every measurable property (concentration, partial pressure, color, total pressure, mass of undissolved solid) has stopped changing and stays constant. Both reactants and products are present at the same time, in amounts that are usually unequal and are fixed by K and the starting amounts. The constancy is the macroscopic sign of equal forward and reverse rates, not of a reaction that has ended.
cards.h: → constant measurables + both sides present
cards.n: 'All the reactant has been used up' earns nothing: a reversible reaction at equilibrium always holds some of every species.

cards.q: Explain how the forward and reverse reaction rates change as a reaction that starts with pure reactants approaches equilibrium.
cards.a: The forward rate starts at its maximum and falls, because reactant concentrations fall as reactant is consumed; the reverse rate starts at zero (no product yet) and rises as product accumulates. The gap between them shrinks until the two rates become equal; from that moment they stay equal and constant, and the concentrations stop changing. That is the establishment of equilibrium.
cards.h: → one falls, one rises, they meet and stay
cards.n: Curves that both drop to zero earn nothing: at equilibrium both rates are equal and nonzero.

cards.q: Draw the concentration-versus-time graph for A(g) ⇌ B(g) in a rigid flask that starts with 0.80 M A and no B, given that [A] = 0.20 M at equilibrium. Describe your graph in words.
cards.a: Axes: time (s) on x, concentration (M) on y. [A] starts at 0.80 M and falls steeply at first, then more slowly (concave up), leveling to a horizontal line at 0.20 M. [B] starts at 0 and rises as the mirror image of [A], leveling at 0.60 M (every A lost is a B gained: 0.80 − 0.20). The curves cross at 0.40 M before equilibrium. Both go flat at the same time and stay flat at different heights; the flat region is equilibrium.
cards.h: → two mirror curves, plateaus at 0.20 and 0.60
cards.n: Plateaus at equal heights, or curves that go flat at different times, earn nothing; [B] must end at 0.60 M by mass balance.

cards.q: Draw the forward-rate and reverse-rate curves versus time for a reaction started with reactants only, and mark where equilibrium is reached. Describe your graph in words.
cards.a: Axes: time on x, rate (M/s) on y. The forward-rate curve starts high at t = 0 and decreases, leveling off; the reverse-rate curve starts at zero and increases, leveling off. The two curves approach each other and merge into a single horizontal line at a nonzero rate. Mark equilibrium at the time they first coincide; after it both rates are equal and constant.
cards.h: → falling curve meets rising curve, one flat line
cards.n: Curves that cross and then separate, or that meet at zero, earn nothing; after equilibrium the two rates stay equal and nonzero.

cards.q:
Determine the time at which this system reaches equilibrium, for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) in a rigid flask (concentrations in M):
time (s) · [NO₂] · [N₂O₄]
0 · 0.100 · 0
20 · 0.060 · 0.020
40 · 0.044 · 0.028
60 · 0.040 · 0.030
80 · 0.040 · 0.030
100 · 0.040 · 0.030
cards.a: Equilibrium is reached by t = 60 s (at some time between 40 s and 60 s; 60 s is the first reading that shows it): from 60 s onward both concentrations are constant, [NO₂] = 0.040 M and [N₂O₄] = 0.030 M. Before 60 s both were still changing. The data are consistent: the NO₂ consumed is twice the N₂O₄ formed (0.100 − 0.040 = 0.060 = 2 × 0.030).
cards.h: → first time the rows stop changing, with a check
cards.n: Picking 20 s because 'most of the change happened by then' earns nothing; equilibrium is where change stops, not where it slows.

cards.q: Identify how equilibrium appears on a concentration-versus-time graph.
cards.a: Every curve becomes horizontal and stays horizontal, usually at different heights. The earliest time at which all curves are flat marks the establishment of equilibrium; after it the concentrations are constant though the reaction continues in both directions. Before it, reactant curves fall and product curves rise, with slopes in the ratio of the coefficients.
cards.h: → all curves flat, unequal heights
cards.n: Reading the point where two curves cross as 'equilibrium' earns nothing; crossing only means two concentrations happen to be equal.

cards.q: Identify what a graph of forward and reverse reaction rates versus time shows at the moment equilibrium is reached.
cards.a: The two rate curves meet: the falling forward-rate curve and the rising reverse-rate curve become equal, and from that instant they stay equal and constant at a nonzero value. Equal rates mean no net change in concentration, even though both reactions keep running. The concentrations at that moment need not be equal; they are whatever values satisfy K.
cards.h: → the two curves merge into one flat line
cards.n: Saying the rates 'drop to zero' or that the curves 'cross and continue' earns nothing.

cards.q: Justify the claim that a saturated AgCl solution over excess solid is a dynamic equilibrium, using this experiment: solid AgCl containing radioactive silver is added to a saturated, non-radioactive AgCl solution, and after some time the solution is radioactive even though [Ag⁺] never changed.
cards.a: The equilibrium is dynamic: dissolution and precipitation both keep occurring at equal rates. Radioactive Ag⁺ can only enter the solution if solid keeps dissolving; because [Ag⁺] stayed constant, an equal amount of Ag⁺ must have been precipitating at the same time. A static system (nothing dissolving, nothing precipitating) would leave the solution non-radioactive.
cards.h: → claim, then what the tracer proves about each direction
cards.n: 'The solution was already saturated so nothing dissolved' earns nothing; the tracer shows that dissolving continued and was matched by precipitation.

cards.q:
Identify whether each observation shows a system AT equilibrium, NOT YET at equilibrium, or gives NO INFORMATION about equilibrium:
(1) the brown color of an NO₂/N₂O₄ flask has stopped changing
(2) the pressure in a sealed flask of reacting gases is still rising
(3) in a sealed flask of a reversible reaction, one reactant has just been completely used up
(4) the forward rate equals the reverse rate
(5) the concentrations of reactant and product are equal
(6) a saturated solution sits over undissolved solid whose mass is constant
(7) the flask is at the same temperature as the room
(8) [product] has been constant for several minutes
(9) the reverse rate is zero
(10) a catalyst was added a moment ago
cards.a:
(1) → AT equilibrium (a measurable property has stopped changing)
(2) → NOT YET (a property is still changing)
(3) → NOT YET: with that reactant at zero the forward rate is zero while the reverse rate is not, so net reverse change must follow; an equilibrium mixture holds some of every species
(4) → AT equilibrium (the defining condition)
(5) → NO INFORMATION (equal amounts are not the criterion; equal rates are)
(6) → AT equilibrium (dissolution and precipitation balanced)
(7) → NO INFORMATION (thermal equilibrium with the room says nothing about the reaction)
(8) → AT equilibrium
(9) → NOT YET (no product yet, so net forward change must follow)
(10) → NO INFORMATION (a catalyst changes how fast equilibrium is reached, not whether it has been)
cards.h: → ten verdicts, each with the criterion it uses
cards.n: Case (5) is the trap: equal concentrations are neither necessary nor sufficient for equilibrium.

cards.q: Explain why macroscopic properties like concentration and color remain constant at equilibrium even though the forward and reverse reactions continue.
cards.a: Because the forward and reverse rates are equal. Reactant is converted to product exactly as fast as product is converted back, so the two changes cancel and there is no net change in any concentration; a property such as color that tracks concentration therefore holds constant while both reactions keep running.
cards.h: → equal rates → changes cancel → no net change → constant color
cards.n: 'The reaction has stopped' earns nothing; the reaction continues in both directions and only the NET change is zero.
o: At equilibrium the rate of the forward process equals the rate of the reverse, so each species is made as fast as it is consumed and its concentration cannot drift.
Color depends on concentration; concentration is constant because the net rate (forward minus reverse) is zero, not because either rate is zero.

w.a: The reaction has finished, so nothing is left to change the color.
w.why: the reaction continues in both directions; only the net change is zero

w.a: The reactants and products have reached equal concentrations, so the color settles.
w.why: equilibrium is equal rates, not equal concentrations

w.a: The forward reaction slows down until it stops, so the color stops changing.
w.why: the forward rate levels off at a nonzero value equal to the reverse rate

cards.q: Explain why water in an open beaker never reaches evaporation-condensation equilibrium, while water in a sealed flask does.
cards.a: In a sealed flask the vapor accumulates, so the condensation rate (which rises with vapor concentration) climbs until it equals the evaporation rate and the vapor pressure holds constant. In an open beaker the vapor escapes, condensation never catches up with evaporation, and the water keeps evaporating away.
cards.h: → sealed: vapor builds → condensation rate rises → matches evaporation; open: vapor lost → never matches
cards.n: 'Equilibrium needs a closed system' with no mention of the reverse process (condensation) catching up earns nothing.
o: Equilibrium requires the reverse process to run as fast as the forward one; condensation depends on vapor being present, and only a closed container keeps the vapor.
In the open beaker there is a net loss of vapor to the room, so the system can never reach a state of no net change.

w.a: The open beaker is at a lower temperature, so the water cannot evaporate fast enough to reach equilibrium.
w.why: temperature is not the issue; the vapor escapes so condensation never matches evaporation

w.a: Equilibrium requires a closed system, and the beaker is open.
w.why: restates the rule without the mechanism (vapor escapes, reverse rate never catches up)

w.a: In the sealed flask evaporation stops once the air is saturated.
w.why: evaporation continues; it is balanced by condensation at the same rate

cards.q: Explain why the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium are not, in general, equal to each other.
cards.a: Equilibrium is the condition of equal forward and reverse RATES, not equal amounts. The concentrations at which the two rates match are fixed by K and the starting amounts, and K can be any positive number; only in a special case such as A ⇌ B with K = 1 would the two concentrations be equal.
cards.h: → equilibrium = equal rates → ratio fixed by K → amounts usually unequal
cards.n: Any answer that treats 'equilibrium' as 'balanced amounts' earns nothing; the balance is between rates.
o: A reaction with a large K reaches equal rates only when product concentrations are much larger than reactant concentrations, so the amounts are far from equal.
The forward rate depends on reactant concentrations and the reverse rate on product concentrations; they can be equal at very different concentrations because the rate constants differ.

w.a: At equilibrium the system is balanced, so there are equal amounts of reactants and products.
w.why: confuses equal rates with equal amounts

w.a: The concentrations are unequal because the reaction has not quite finished.
w.why: equilibrium is not an incomplete reaction; the amounts are fixed by K

w.a: They are unequal only for reactions with different coefficients on each side.
w.why: even A ⇌ B has unequal amounts unless K happens to be 1

cards.q: Explain why the reverse rate is zero at the instant a reaction starts with pure reactants, yet nonzero at equilibrium.
cards.a: The reverse rate depends on product concentration. At t = 0 there is no product, so nothing can react backwards and the reverse rate is zero. As product accumulates the reverse rate grows, and at equilibrium it equals the forward rate, which is still nonzero because reactant remains.
cards.h: → reverse rate depends on [product] → zero at start → grows → equals forward rate
cards.n: Borrows the rate-concentration link from Unit 5. 'The reverse reaction has not started yet' without tying it to product concentration earns nothing.
o: No product molecules exist at t = 0, so no reverse collisions can occur; once product forms, reverse collisions happen at a rate set by its concentration.
The reverse rate tracks product concentration, which rises from zero to its equilibrium value.

w.a: The reverse rate is zero at the start because the reaction is not yet at equilibrium.
w.why: being away from equilibrium does not make the reverse rate zero; the absence of product does

w.a: The reverse rate is always smaller than the forward rate, and it is zero at the beginning.
w.why: at equilibrium the rates are equal, and after a disturbance the reverse rate can exceed the forward

w.a: The reverse rate stays at zero until the forward reaction has finished.
w.why: the reverse rate starts rising as soon as any product exists

cards.q: Determine the direction of net change in a mixture where the forward rate is 3.2 × 10⁻³ M/s and the reverse rate is 1.1 × 10⁻³ M/s, and state what happens to each rate as the system approaches equilibrium.
cards.a: Net conversion of reactants to products: the forward rate exceeds the reverse rate, so product is made faster than it is unmade (net rate 3.2 × 10⁻³ − 1.1 × 10⁻³ = 2.1 × 10⁻³ M/s toward products). As the reaction proceeds, reactant concentrations fall so the forward rate decreases, and product concentrations rise so the reverse rate increases, until the two are equal and net change stops.
cards.h: → direction from the comparison, then both trends
cards.n: 'Shifts right' with no comparison of the two rates earns nothing; the direction follows from forward rate > reverse rate.

cards.q: Determine the direction of net change when a flask is prepared with products only and no reactants, and describe how the two rates behave until equilibrium.
cards.a: Net conversion of products to reactants. At t = 0 the forward rate is zero (no reactant present) while the reverse rate is at its maximum, so reverse > forward. The reverse rate falls as product is consumed and the forward rate rises from zero as reactant forms, until the two are equal; the same equilibrium condition (equal rates) is reached from the product side.
cards.h: → reverse > forward at start, then converge
cards.n: Claiming 'no reaction occurs because there are no reactants' earns nothing; the reverse reaction runs and makes reactants.

cards.q:
Determine the direction of net change (toward products, toward reactants, or no net change) for each situation:
(1) forward 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, reverse 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ M/s
(2) forward = reverse = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s
(3) forward 0, reverse 1.2 × 10⁻³ M/s
(4) forward 4.0 × 10⁻³ M/s, reverse 4.0 × 10⁻² M/s
(5) a flask holding only reactants at t = 0
(6) a flask holding only products at t = 0
(7) the forward rate has been falling and the reverse rate rising, and they have just become equal
(8) the reverse rate is half the forward rate
(9) forward = reverse = 6 × 10⁻⁵ M/s, but [product] is much larger than [reactant]
(10) forward 3.0 × 10⁻² M/s, reverse 2.9 × 10⁻² M/s
cards.a:
(1) → toward products (forward > reverse)
(2) → no net change (equilibrium)
(3) → toward reactants (only the reverse process runs; there is no reactant)
(4) → toward reactants (the reverse rate is ten times the forward rate)
(5) → toward products (reverse rate = 0 at t = 0)
(6) → toward reactants (forward rate = 0 at t = 0)
(7) → no net change from now on; equilibrium has just been established
(8) → toward products
(9) → no net change; equal rates mean equilibrium however unequal the concentrations are
(10) → toward products, slowly (net rate 1 × 10⁻³ M/s, close to equilibrium)
cards.h: → compare the two rates every time
cards.n: Case (9) is the trap: unequal concentrations with equal rates is equilibrium; the direction is never read off the concentrations.

cards.q: Explain how the equilibrium constant is related to the rate constants of an elementary reversible reaction.
cards.a: For a single elementary step, K = $k_{f}/k_{r}$. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so $k_{f}$ × (reactant concentration terms) = $k_{r}$ × (product concentration terms); rearranging gives (products)/(reactants) = $k_{f}/k_{r}$, which is the mass-action expression, so K equals the ratio of the rate constants. A large K means $k_{f}$ ≫ $k_{r}$: products are favored.
cards.h: → equate the two rate laws, then rearrange
cards.n: Borrows elementary rate laws from Unit 5. It holds only for an elementary step, not for an overall multistep equation.

cards.q: For an elementary reversible reaction with forward rate constant $k_f = 4.0\times10^{-2}$ and reverse rate constant $k_r = 2.0\times10^{-3}$, compute K.
cards.a: K = 20. For an elementary step the equilibrium condition (forward rate = reverse rate) gives K = $k_{f}/k_{r}$ = (4.0 × 10⁻²)/(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 20. Because K > 1 the forward rate constant is the larger one, so at equilibrium the product terms outweigh the reactant terms.
cards.h: → one ratio
cards.n: Dividing the other way ($k_{r}/k_{f}$ = 0.050) gives K for the reverse reaction. Borrows Unit 5 rate constants; valid for an elementary step only.

cards.q: Predict how the forward rate changes over time for the elementary reversible reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g), whose forward rate is $k_{f}$[A], when a rigid flask starts with 1.0 M A and no B, and state the value it settles at.
cards.a: The forward rate falls continuously from its starting value $k_{f}$ × 1.0 M because [A] decreases as A is converted to B, and the decrease slows as the system nears equilibrium. It settles at a constant nonzero value, $k_{f}$[A] at equilibrium, which is exactly equal to the reverse rate $k_{r}$[B]; it does not fall to zero because A is never used up.
cards.h: → falls with [A], levels off equal to the reverse rate
cards.n: Borrows the rate law from Unit 5. 'The forward rate drops to zero at equilibrium' earns nothing.

cards.q:
Determine, from these rates for a reversible reaction started with pure reactant, when equilibrium is reached and the direction and size of the net change at t = 10 s (rates in 10⁻³ M/s):
time (s) · forward rate · reverse rate
0 · 8.0 · 0
10 · 4.0 · 1.0
20 · 2.5 · 1.8
30 · 2.0 · 2.0
40 · 2.0 · 2.0
cards.a: Equilibrium is reached by t = 30 s, the first reading at which the forward and reverse rates are equal (2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s each); they stay equal afterwards. At t = 10 s the forward rate (4.0 × 10⁻³ M/s) exceeds the reverse rate (1.0 × 10⁻³ M/s), so there is net conversion of reactants to products at 4.0 − 1.0 = 3.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises throughout because [reactant] falls and [product] rises.
cards.h: → first equal-rate row, then a subtraction
cards.n: Reading 'equilibrium at 40 s' (the row after the rates are already equal) or 'the reaction ends at 30 s' earns nothing.

cards.q: Justify, using reaction rates rather than Le Châtelier's principle, why a system at equilibrium that receives an injection of reactant undergoes net conversion to products.
cards.a: The injection raises the reactant concentration, so the forward rate (which depends on reactant concentration) jumps above the reverse rate, which is momentarily unchanged because product concentrations have not changed. With forward rate > reverse rate there is net conversion of reactants to products. As reactant is consumed and product forms, the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal again at a new equilibrium.
cards.h: → forward rate jumps, reverse unchanged, then reconverge
cards.n: Borrows rate-concentration dependence from Unit 5. 'The system shifts to relieve the stress' earns no rate-based credit.

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with very fast forward and reverse rates can still have a small equilibrium constant.
cards.a: K reflects the ratio of the rate constants (K = $k_{f}/k_{r}$ for an elementary step), not their size. If both are large but $k_{r}$ is much larger than $k_{f}$, equilibrium is reached quickly yet lies toward reactants, so K is small. Speed (kinetics) and position (K) are independent.
cards.h: → K = kf/kr → ratio, not magnitude → fast but reactant-favored
cards.n: Borrows rate constants from Unit 5. 'Fast reactions have large K' earns nothing; rate and extent are unrelated.
o: Equal rates can be reached at low product concentration if the reverse rate constant is large, so the equilibrium mixture is mostly reactant even though both processes are fast.
How quickly the rates become equal says nothing about the concentrations at which they become equal.

w.a: A fast reaction always has a large K because it makes product quickly.
w.why: rate and equilibrium position are independent

w.a: The equilibrium constant is small because the reaction reaches equilibrium before much product forms.
w.why: K is set by the ratio of rate constants, not by how soon equilibrium arrives

w.a: If the reverse reaction is fast the reaction cannot reach equilibrium, so K is small.
w.why: a fast reverse reaction does not prevent equilibrium; it places it toward reactants

cards.q: Explain why the forward and reverse rates settle at an equal nonzero value at equilibrium rather than both falling to zero.
cards.a: Both reactant and product remain present, and each keeps reacting at a rate set by its concentration, so neither rate can be zero. Net change stops only because the two rates are equal, not because reactions cease; the rates level off where forward conversion is exactly balanced by reverse conversion.
cards.h: → both species present → both rates nonzero → equal → no net change
cards.n: 'The reaction stops when it runs out of reactant' earns nothing; a reversible reaction never exhausts either side.
o: Zero rates would require zero concentration of reactant and of product, which cannot both hold; equilibrium is reached instead when the two nonzero rates match.
Isotope-tracer experiments show that exchange continues at equilibrium, so both rates are nonzero.

w.a: Both rates fall to zero because the reaction is complete at equilibrium.
w.why: the reaction is not complete; both species persist and both rates continue

w.a: The rates become equal because the concentrations become equal.
w.why: equal rates occur at concentrations fixed by K, which are usually unequal

w.a: The forward rate becomes zero and the reverse rate becomes zero at different times.
w.why: neither rate reaches zero; they converge to the same nonzero value

cards.q: Explain why the net rate of change of [product] falls steadily to zero as a reaction started from pure reactants approaches equilibrium.
cards.a: The net rate is the forward rate minus the reverse rate. From t = 0 the forward rate falls (reactant is consumed) while the reverse rate rises from zero (product builds up), so their difference shrinks steadily; it reaches zero exactly when the two rates are equal, which is equilibrium.
cards.h: → net = forward − reverse → one falls, one rises → difference → 0
cards.n: 'The reaction slows down and stops' earns nothing; only the NET rate goes to zero while both individual rates remain.
o: On a concentration-time graph the product curve's slope is the net rate; the slope flattens to zero as the reverse process catches up with the forward one.
Each forward conversion is increasingly matched by a reverse conversion, so the surplus of product formation per second shrinks to nothing.

w.a: The net rate falls because the reactant runs out.
w.why: reactant is not exhausted; the forward rate merely falls while the reverse rate rises

w.a: The net rate falls to zero because the catalyst is used up.
w.why: no catalyst is involved and catalysts are not consumed

w.a: The net rate becomes zero when the product concentration stops increasing because the forward reaction has stopped.
w.why: the forward reaction continues at a rate equal to the reverse

cards.q: State the equilibrium constant expression Kc for the general reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD.
cards.a: $K_{c} = \frac{[C]^{c}[D]^{d}}{[A]^{a}[B]^{b}}$: products over reactants, each equilibrium molar concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation (the law of mass action). The identical expression evaluated with the concentrations at any moment is Qc; only at equilibrium does Qc = Kc.
cards.h: → products over reactants, coefficients as exponents
cards.n: Coefficients become exponents, never multipliers: writing 2[C] for [C]², or adding terms instead of multiplying them, earns nothing.

cards.q: State the equilibrium constant expression Kp for a gas-phase reaction.
cards.a: For aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g), $K_{p} = \frac{(P_{C})^{c}(P_{D})^{d}}{(P_{A})^{a}(P_{B})^{b}}$, built from the equilibrium partial pressures (usually in atm) of the gaseous species only, each raised to its coefficient. Qp has the same form with the partial pressures at any moment.
cards.h: → same form, partial pressures
cards.n: Mixing partial pressures and molarities in one expression earns nothing. Kc-to-Kp conversion is excluded from the exam; just use the constant the question names.

cards.q: Identify which species are left out of an equilibrium constant expression.
cards.a: Pure solids and pure liquids, including water when it is the solvent, are left out, because their concentrations do not depend on how much of them is present. Gases (as concentrations or partial pressures) and dissolved (aq) species are included. Example: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) gives Kp = P(CO₂).
cards.h: → two phases excluded, with the reason
cards.n: Writing [H₂O(l)] or [CaCO₃(s)] into K is the classic lost point; but water as a gas, H₂O(g), does appear.

cards.q: State the convention AP Chemistry uses for the units of an equilibrium constant.
cards.a: Equilibrium constants are reported as pure numbers, without units. Each concentration or partial pressure in the expression is effectively a ratio to a standard reference (1 M or 1 atm), so the units cancel: write Kc = 25, not 25 M⁻¹. The same holds for Q and for Ksp.
cards.h: → one convention plus the reason
cards.n: Tacking M⁻¹ or atm² onto K is not expected; released scoring guidelines report K as a unitless number.

cards.q: Define the reaction quotient Q.
cards.a: Q is the mass-action expression (products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, solids and pure liquids omitted) evaluated with the concentrations or partial pressures present at any moment, at equilibrium or not. It has exactly the same form as K; Q changes as the reaction proceeds, tends toward K, and equals K only at equilibrium.
cards.h: → same expression as K, values at any moment
cards.n: 'Q is K before equilibrium' is muddled: K is one fixed number at a given temperature; Q is whatever the current mixture gives.

cards.q: Define the equilibrium constant K and state what distinguishes it from the reaction quotient Q.
cards.a: K is the value of the mass-action expression when the system is at equilibrium; it is constant at a given temperature whatever the starting amounts. Q is the same expression evaluated at any instant: it varies as the reaction proceeds and equals K only once equilibrium is reached.
cards.h: → definition plus the one distinction
cards.n: Writing K when the mixture is not at equilibrium (or Q for an equilibrium value) is a frequent point-losing mix-up.

cards.q: Identify the correct Kc expression for the heterogeneous equilibrium $CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$.
cards.a: Kc = [CO₂]. CaCO₃ and CaO are pure solids whose concentrations do not depend on their amounts, so both are left out; only the gas remains. In pressure form, Kp = P(CO₂).
cards.h: → one term
cards.n: Writing [CaO][CO₂]/[CaCO₃] earns nothing; only species whose concentration can change appear.

cards.q: Predict the shift when additional solid $CaCO_3$ is added to $CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$ at constant temperature.
cards.a: No shift. Q = P(CO₂), since both solids are omitted, and adding solid CaCO₃ does not change P(CO₂); Q therefore still equals K, and the CO₂ pressure and the amount of CaO stay the same. Only the mass of CaCO₃ in the container increases.
cards.h: → no shift, justified through Q
cards.n: 'More reactant, so it shifts right' earns nothing: a pure solid is not in Q, so adding it cannot make Q differ from K.

cards.q: State why the equilibrium constant expression uses equilibrium concentrations raised to the stoichiometric coefficients, not initial concentrations.
cards.a: K is defined as the value the mass-action expression takes at equilibrium. Only when the concentrations have stopped changing does the ratio reach the same constant value in every trial at that temperature, and only the form with each concentration raised to its coefficient stays constant. Initial concentrations give Q at t = 0, not K.
cards.h: → definition, then why the exponents
cards.n: Substituting initial concentrations gives Q at t = 0, which usually differs from K; that substitution earns nothing as K.

cards.q:
Write the equilibrium expression asked for each reaction (Kc unless Kp is named):
(1) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
(2) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), Kp
(3) 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
(4) PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
(5) C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g)
(6) CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), Kp
(7) NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g), Kp
(8) HF(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq)
(9) NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
(10) Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq)
(11) Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq)
(12) H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂O(g), Kp
(13) 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) ⇌ 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g)
(14) CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
(15) Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) ⇌ Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
cards.a:
(1) → [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³)
(2) → P(NH₃)²/(P(N₂)·P(H₂)³)
(3) → [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂])
(4) → [PCl₃][Cl₂]/[PCl₅]
(5) → [CO][H₂]/[H₂O] (C(s) omitted; H₂O is a gas, so it stays)
(6) → P(CO₂)
(7) → P(NH₃)·P(HCl)
(8) → [H₃O⁺][F⁻]/[HF]
(9) → [NH₄⁺][OH⁻]/[NH₃]
(10) → [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻]
(11) → [FeSCN²⁺]/([Fe³⁺][SCN⁻])
(12) → P(H₂O)
(13) → [NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶/([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵)
(14) → [CH₃COO⁻]/([CH₃COOH][OH⁻])
(15) → [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]
cards.h: → fifteen expressions, solids and liquids dropped
cards.n: Writing H₂O(l) into (8), (9), (14) or a solid into (5), (6), (7), (10), (15) earns nothing; (5), (12) and (13) keep water because it is a gas.

cards.q: Calculate Qc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at a moment when [N₂] = 0.50 M, [H₂] = 0.20 M, and [NH₃] = 0.10 M, and state what else you would need to know to decide which way the mixture reacts.
cards.a: Qc = 2.5. Qc = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) = (0.10)²/((0.50)(0.20)³) = 0.010/(0.50 × 0.0080) = 0.010/0.0040 = 2.5. You also need Kc at the same temperature: if Kc > 2.5 the mixture makes more NH₃ (Q rises toward K); if Kc < 2.5 NH₃ decomposes; if Kc = 2.5 it is already at equilibrium.
cards.h: → substitute, cube, then name the missing value
cards.n: (0.20)³ = 0.0080; tripling 0.20 instead of cubing it, or declaring a direction from Q alone, earns nothing.

cards.q: Draw a graph of Q versus time for a mixture that starts with Q = 0.50 and reaches equilibrium, for a reaction with K = 20, continuing for a while after equilibrium is reached. Describe your graph in words.
cards.a: Axes: time on x; Q (no units) on y, running from 0 to about 25. Draw a horizontal dashed reference line at Q = K = 20. The Q curve starts at 0.50 at t = 0, rises steeply at first and then more and more slowly (concave down), and meets the dashed line; from then on it lies flat on the line at 20. It never overshoots above 20, since Q moves toward K and stops there.
cards.h: → rising curve that merges with a dashed line at K
cards.n: A Q curve that overshoots K, or a K line that moves while Q changes, earns nothing: K is fixed at a given temperature and Q approaches it.

cards.q: Describe how Kc and Kp differ for a gas-phase reaction, and state which of the two can be written for a reaction in which every species is aqueous.
cards.a: Kc is built from molar concentrations (mol/L); Kp is built from partial pressures (atm) and applies only to gaseous species. Both describe the same equilibrium and have the same mass-action form, but for a given reaction they are in general different numbers, so a question that gives pressures wants Kp and one that gives molarities wants Kc. An all-aqueous reaction has only Kc.
cards.h: → what each is built from + which applies to aq
cards.n: Converting one into the other with (RT)^Δn is excluded from the AP Exam; the point is noticing which constant the question uses.

cards.q: Explain why pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in an equilibrium constant expression.
cards.a: A pure solid or liquid has a fixed concentration (its density divided by its molar mass) that does not change with how much is present. Adding or removing some of it therefore changes neither Q nor the equilibrium mixture, so its constant term is folded into K and it is left out of both Q and K.
cards.h: → concentration set by density → independent of amount → constant → left out of Q and K
cards.n: 'Solids do not react' earns nothing: they do react; only their effective concentration is constant.
o: The moles per liter of a pure solid are its density over its molar mass, a constant at a given temperature, so the term is absorbed into K.
Because the amount of a pure solid or liquid does not affect Q, it cannot affect the equilibrium position, so writing it in would add nothing.

w.a: Solids and liquids are left out because they do not take part in the reaction.
w.why: they do react; the point is their constant concentration

w.a: Solids are omitted because their concentration in the solution is zero.
w.why: a solid's concentration is constant, not zero

w.a: Solids and liquids are left out because they are always present in excess.
w.why: excess is not the reason; constant concentration independent of amount is

cards.q: Explain why H₂O is left out of K for HF(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq) but included in K for CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g).
cards.a: In the aqueous reaction water is the solvent: a nearly pure liquid whose concentration (about 55.5 M) barely changes, so it is constant and omitted. In the gas-phase reaction H₂O is a gas whose partial pressure depends on how much is present and changes as the reaction proceeds, so it must appear.
cards.h: → liquid solvent: constant → omitted; gas: pressure varies → included
cards.n: 'Water never goes in K' earns nothing: the rule is about phase, and H₂O(g) is always written in.
o: Only species whose concentrations change as the reaction proceeds appear in K; solvent water's concentration is effectively fixed, gaseous water's is not.
The (l) and (g) labels decide it: H₂O(l) is a pure liquid, H₂O(g) is one gas in a mixture of gases.

w.a: Water is left out of every equilibrium expression because it is only a solvent.
w.why: gaseous water is a reacting gas and must be included

w.a: Water is left out of the HF reaction because it is a product.
w.why: water is a reactant there, and products are not omitted anyway

w.a: Water is included in the gas reaction because it has a coefficient of 1.
w.why: the coefficient is irrelevant; the phase decides

cards.q: Explain why, for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at a fixed temperature, the equilibrium pressure of CO₂ is the same whether the container holds 10 g or 100 g of CaCO₃.
cards.a: Both solids are omitted, so Kp = P(CO₂). At a fixed temperature Kp is a constant, so the equilibrium CO₂ pressure must equal that one value whatever the amount of solid, as long as both CaCO₃ and CaO are present.
cards.h: → solids omitted → Kp = P(CO₂) → Kp fixed at fixed T → same pressure
cards.n: 'More solid makes more CO₂ gas' earns nothing; the amount of solid is not in the expression. (Both solids must be present for equilibrium.)
o: The mass of CaCO₃ does not appear in Q, so it cannot change the pressure at which Q equals K.
The equilibrium CO₂ pressure is fixed by temperature alone, like the vapor pressure of a liquid.

w.a: The larger sample produces more CO₂, so the pressure is higher with 100 g.
w.why: more solid does not change Q, so the equilibrium pressure is the same

w.a: The pressure is the same because both samples decompose completely.
w.why: at equilibrium the solids are not used up; both are still present

w.a: The pressure is the same because K has no units.
w.why: units are irrelevant; the solids are simply absent from the expression

cards.q: Compute Kc for H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) when the equilibrium concentrations are [H2] = 0.020 M, [I2] = 0.020 M, and [HI] = 0.10 M.
cards.a: Kc = 25. Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = (0.10)²/((0.020)(0.020)) = 0.010/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 25. The coefficient 2 on HI becomes the exponent, and K is reported without units.
cards.h: → one substitution, no units
cards.n: Writing 2[HI] instead of [HI]² gives 5.0 × 10² and earns nothing; every value substituted must be an equilibrium value.

cards.q: Compute Kc for $PCl_5(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g)$ given equilibrium concentrations $[PCl_5]=0.30$ M, $[PCl_3]=0.20$ M, $[Cl_2]=0.20$ M.
cards.a: Kc = 0.13. Kc = [PCl₃][Cl₂]/[PCl₅] = (0.20)(0.20)/0.30 = 0.040/0.30 = 0.13 (two significant figures, as in the data). A value between 0.1 and 10 means appreciable amounts of reactant and products coexist at equilibrium.
cards.h: → products over reactant, two sig figs
cards.n: Inverting the ratio gives 7.5, which is K for the reverse reaction, not this one.

cards.q: Compute Kc for $2NO(g)+O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)$ given [NO]=0.020 M, $[O_2]=0.010$ M, $[NO_2]=0.40$ M at equilibrium.
cards.h: → square two terms, then divide
cards.n: Dropping the square on [NO] gives 8.0 × 10² (or on [NO₂] 1.0 × 10⁵); the exponents change the answer by orders of magnitude.

cards.q: Compute Kc for $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)$ given equilibrium concentrations $[SO_2]=0.20$ M, $[O_2]=0.10$ M, $[SO_3]=0.60$ M.
cards.h: → [SO₃]² over [SO₂]²[O₂]
cards.n: O₂ carries the power 1; squaring it too gives 900, and forgetting the square on [SO₂] gives 18.

cards.q: Explain how to find Kc when you are given initial concentrations and only one equilibrium concentration.
cards.a: Use an ICE table. Enter the initial concentrations; write each change as its coefficient times x (minus for the side being consumed); set the one known equilibrium value equal to its I + C entry and solve for x; fill in every other equilibrium concentration; substitute the equilibrium row into the Kc expression. Example: for 2A ⇌ B from 1.00 M A with [B] = 0.20 M at equilibrium, x = 0.20, [A] = 0.60 M, Kc = 0.20/0.60² = 0.56.
cards.h: → ICE steps, then one worked example
cards.n: Putting the initial concentrations straight into Kc, or changing every species by x regardless of its coefficient, earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate Kp for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) given the equilibrium partial pressures P(N₂O₄) = 0.40 atm and P(NO₂) = 0.60 atm.
cards.a: Kp = 0.90. Kp = P(NO₂)²/P(N₂O₄) = (0.60)²/0.40 = 0.36/0.40 = 0.90, a pure number built from partial pressures in atm.
cards.h: → square the product pressure, divide
cards.n: (0.60)/(0.40) = 1.5 forgets the square; and using the total pressure anywhere in Kp earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate Kc for 2SO₃(g) ⇌ 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) given that 0.100 mol of SO₃ alone is placed in a 1.00 L flask at a fixed temperature and the equilibrium concentration of O₂ is 0.012 M.
cards.h: → ICE with x from the O₂ value, then substitute
cards.n: Subtracting only x (not 2x) from SO₃, or using 0.100 M as the equilibrium [SO₃], earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate Kp for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) given that pure N₂O₄ at 1.00 atm is sealed in a rigid flask and, at equilibrium at the same temperature, the total pressure is 1.30 atm.
cards.h: → total pressure fixes x, then Kp
cards.n: Setting P(NO₂) = 0.30 atm (the rise in total pressure) earns nothing: each N₂O₄ lost makes two NO₂, so P(NO₂) = 2x.

cards.q: Calculate Kp for NH₄HS(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + H₂S(g) given that solid NH₄HS is placed in an evacuated flask and, at equilibrium with solid still present, the total gas pressure is 0.660 atm.
cards.a: Kp = 0.109. The solid is omitted, so Kp = P(NH₃)·P(H₂S). The two gases form in a 1:1 ratio from the solid alone, so each has half the total: 0.330 atm. Kp = (0.330)(0.330) = 0.109.
cards.h: → split the total pressure, multiply
cards.n: Writing Kp = (0.660)², or including NH₄HS in the denominator, earns nothing.

cards.q:
Calculate Kc for each trial of H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at one temperature, and describe what the results show (equilibrium concentrations, M):
trial · [H₂] · [I₂] · [HI]
1 · 0.0020 · 0.0020 · 0.014
2 · 0.0040 · 0.0010 · 0.014
3 · 0.0050 · 0.0020 · 0.022
cards.a: Kc = 49, 49 and 48. Trial 1: (0.014)²/((0.0020)(0.0020)) = 1.96 × 10⁻⁴/4.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 49; trial 2: 1.96 × 10⁻⁴/4.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 49; trial 3: 4.84 × 10⁻⁴/1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 48. The equilibrium concentrations differ, but K is the same within rounding: K depends only on the reaction and T. The ratio without the exponent ([HI]/([H₂][I₂]) = 3500, 3500, 2200) is not constant.
cards.h: → three substitutions, then the pattern
cards.n: Concluding that K depends on the starting amounts because the concentrations differ earns nothing; only the ratio with exponents is constant.

cards.q: Calculate Kc for Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) given that a solution is prepared with initial [Fe³⁺] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ M and [SCN⁻] = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ M, and its absorbance at equilibrium, read against a calibration curve, shows [FeSCN²⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ M.
cards.h: → subtract the complex from each ion, then Kc
cards.n: Borrows the Beer's-law calibration from Unit 3. Using the initial ion concentrations in the denominator gives 125 and earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain why trials that start with different amounts of H₂, I₂ and HI at the same temperature all give the same value of Kc.
cards.a: K depends only on the reaction and the temperature. Each trial settles at its own equilibrium concentrations, but in every trial the forward and reverse rates balance only when the ratio [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) reaches the same value, so the calculated Kc agrees within experimental error.
cards.h: → K set by reaction + T → every trial reaches the same ratio → same Kc
cards.n: 'Because the concentrations are the same' earns nothing: the concentrations differ from trial to trial; only the ratio is constant.
o: Starting amounts decide where each trial ends up, but not the value of the mass-action ratio at the end, which is fixed at a given temperature.
Only a change in temperature changes K; changing starting amounts changes the equilibrium concentrations and leaves K alone.

w.a: All three trials reach the same equilibrium concentrations, so Kc is the same.
w.why: the concentrations differ; only the ratio is constant

w.a: Kc is the same because the same amount of HI forms in every trial.
w.why: different amounts of HI form; K does not depend on amount

w.a: Kc is the same because the reaction always goes to completion.
w.why: the reaction reaches equilibrium, not completion

cards.q: Explain why substituting initial concentrations into the equilibrium expression does not give K.
cards.a: K is defined by the concentrations at equilibrium. Initial concentrations describe a mixture that is still undergoing net reaction, so the ratio they give is Q at t = 0, which generally differs from K; only after the concentrations stop changing does the ratio equal K.
cards.h: → initial mixture still reacting → ratio is Q → Q ≠ K until concentrations stop changing
cards.n: Calling the initial ratio 'K before the reaction' earns nothing: it is Q, and K is defined only at equilibrium.
o: At t = 0 the mixture may hold no product at all, giving a ratio of zero, while K is a fixed positive number.
The initial ratio is the Q that tells you which way the mixture will react, not where it ends up.

w.a: Initial concentrations give K because K does not depend on concentration.
w.why: K is independent of starting amounts only when evaluated with equilibrium values

w.a: Initial concentrations are fine as long as you raise them to the coefficients.
w.why: the exponents are right, but non-equilibrium values give Q, not K

w.a: Initial concentrations do not work because they have units.
w.why: units are not the issue; the mixture is not at equilibrium

cards.q: Explain why a ratio calculated from equilibrium data without the coefficient exponents changes from trial to trial, while the true K expression does not.
cards.a: Only the mass-action expression, with each concentration raised to its coefficient, is constant at equilibrium at a given temperature. Dropping the exponents gives a function that is not constant: for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, [HI]/([H₂][I₂]) gave 3500 and 2200 in two trials while [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) gave 49 and 48.
cards.h: → only the exponent form is constant → other ratios drift → the data test the expression
cards.n: 'The exponents do not matter because they cancel' earns nothing; the trial data show directly that they do not.
o: The law of mass action is an experimental result: the exponent form is the combination of concentrations that stays constant across trials.
Changing the exponents changes the math, so the ratio no longer describes the equilibrium state.

w.a: The ratio changes because the trials were at different temperatures.
w.why: the trials were at one temperature; the missing exponent is the cause

w.a: The ratio changes because K is different for each trial.
w.why: K is the same; the incorrect expression is what varies

w.a: Leaving out the exponents only changes the units of K, not its value.
w.why: it changes the value and makes it inconsistent between trials

cards.q: Explain what the magnitude of K tells you about a reaction mixture at equilibrium.
cards.a: K ≫ 1: at equilibrium the product terms far exceed the reactant terms, so the mixture is mostly products and the reaction proceeds essentially to completion. K ≪ 1: the mixture is mostly reactants and the reaction barely proceeds, though some product is always present. K near 1: appreciable amounts of both. K describes how far the reaction goes, not how fast.
cards.h: → three magnitude cases, extent not rate
cards.n: 'K ≪ 1 means no reaction' earns nothing (a little product always forms), and neither does reading a large K as 'fast'.

cards.q: Rank these equilibria by how far each lies toward products: K = 1x10⁻¹⁰, K = 1, K = 1x10¹².
cards.a: K = 1 × 10¹² > K = 1 > K = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰. With K = 10¹² the products overwhelmingly dominate and the reaction is essentially complete; with K = 1 reactants and products are both present in appreciable amounts (the exact split depends on the stoichiometry and starting amounts); with K = 10⁻¹⁰ the reaction barely proceeds and reactants dominate.
cards.h: → ordered list, one clause each
cards.n: The ranking says nothing about speed: the 10¹² reaction could be the slowest of the three.

cards.q: Predict whether a reaction with K = 3.0×10⁸ goes nearly to completion or barely proceeds, and justify.
cards.a: It goes nearly to completion. K = 3.0 × 10⁸ ≫ 1 means that at equilibrium the product terms exceed the reactant terms by a factor of about 10⁸, so essentially all of the limiting reactant is converted and only a trace of it remains.
cards.h: → verdict, then what K ≫ 1 means for the mixture
cards.n: A large K describes the equilibrium position, not the rate; the reaction could still be slow to get there.

cards.q: Predict whether a reaction with $K = 4.0\times10^{-9}$ goes nearly to completion or barely proceeds, and justify.
cards.a: It barely proceeds. K = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ ≪ 1 means that at equilibrium the product terms are only about a billionth of the reactant terms, so the mixture is essentially the starting reactants, with a very small but nonzero amount of product.
cards.h: → verdict, then what K ≪ 1 means for the mixture
cards.n: 'No reaction occurs' earns nothing: every species is present at equilibrium, some product just in tiny amounts.

cards.q: Estimate the equilibrium concentration of B, and the percent of A that reacts, when 0.25 M A(g) reaches equilibrium in A(g) ⇌ 2B(g), Kc = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰.
cards.a: [B] ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M; about 0.0020% of A reacts. Because K is tiny, x ≪ 0.25, so [A] ≈ 0.25 M: Kc = (2x)²/0.25 = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ → 4x² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ → x = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ M, [B] = 2x = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M. Percent reacted = (5.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.25) × 100 = 0.0020%, which confirms the approximation.
cards.h: → drop x beside 0.25, solve, then check
cards.n: Writing (2x)² as 2x² gives [B] = 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ M and earns nothing; the coefficient is squared along with x.
