cards.q: Estimate the equilibrium concentrations of A, B and C when 0.20 M A and 0.20 M B are mixed for A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq), Kc = 1.0 × 10¹⁰.
cards.a: [C] ≈ 0.20 M; [A] = [B] ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ M. Because K is huge, let the reaction go to completion (0.20 M C, no A or B), then let a small amount x react back: Kc = (0.20 − x)/x² ≈ 0.20/x² = 1.0 × 10¹⁰, so x² = 2.0 × 10⁻¹¹ and x = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ M.
cards.h: → run to completion, then back off by x
cards.n: Solving forward from 0.20 M with a tiny x in the denominator makes the algebra blow up; and '[A] = 0' earns nothing, since some A always remains.

cards.q:
Identify, for each value of K, whether the reaction essentially goes to completion, barely proceeds, or leaves appreciable amounts of both reactants and products:
(1) K = 1.0 × 10⁻³⁰
(2) K = 6.0 × 10⁴⁰
(3) K = 1.2
(4) K = 0.35
(5) K = 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁵
(6) K = 2.4 × 10¹⁸
(7) K = 4.0
(8) the reverse of a reaction whose K is 1.0 × 10²⁰
(9) the reverse of a reaction whose K is 1.0 × 10⁻²⁵
(10) K = 1.0
cards.a:
(1) → barely proceeds (mostly reactants)
(2) → essentially complete (mostly products)
(3) → appreciable amounts of both
(4) → appreciable amounts of both
(5) → barely proceeds
(6) → essentially complete
(7) → appreciable amounts of both
(8) → K(reverse) = 1.0 × 10⁻²⁰: barely proceeds
(9) → K(reverse) = 1.0 × 10²⁵: essentially complete
(10) → appreciable amounts of both (not necessarily equal amounts)
cards.h: → ten verdicts from the size of K
cards.n: The CED sets no exact cut-off for 'appreciable amounts of both'; the clear calls are the very large and very small K values.

cards.q: Predict how far the reaction proceeds when a flask holding only the products of a reaction with K = 5.0 × 10¹⁵ is left to reach equilibrium.
cards.a: Almost no reactant forms: the products barely convert back. For the reverse reaction K = 1/(5.0 × 10¹⁵) = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ ≪ 1, so the equilibrium reached from the product side is the same product-rich mixture, holding only a trace of reactants.
cards.h: → invert K, then judge its size
cards.n: 'The products convert back until the amounts are equal' earns nothing; the same equilibrium is reached from either side.

cards.q: Justify treating the neutralization H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) as going to completion in a titration calculation, given that its K is 1.0 × 10¹⁴ at 25 °C.
cards.a: Because K = 1.0 × 10¹⁴ ≫ 1, the equilibrium lies overwhelmingly on the product side: at equilibrium [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] must fall to 1/K = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, so whichever ion is limiting is consumed essentially entirely. Treating the reaction as complete therefore introduces negligible error in the stoichiometry.
cards.h: → K ≫ 1 → product-favored → limiting ion used up
cards.n: Borrows Kw from Unit 8 (K here is 1/Kw). 'Strong acids react completely' without using the size of K earns no equilibrium credit.

cards.q: Explain why a very large equilibrium constant does not guarantee that a reaction will be observed to occur.
cards.a: K measures only where equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached. A reaction with a huge K can have an activation energy so high that its rate at room temperature is negligible, so no product appears on a practical timescale: a mixture of H₂ and O₂ has an enormous K for forming water yet sits unchanged until sparked.
cards.h: → K = extent → rate set by activation energy → large K can still be too slow to see
cards.n: Borrows activation energy from Unit 5. 'The reaction does not happen because K is too big' earns nothing; the barrier is kinetic.
o: Thermodynamics (K) and kinetics (rate) are independent: K says where the reaction ends up, the activation energy says how quickly.
A catalyst can make a large-K reaction observable without changing K, which shows the obstacle was the rate, not the equilibrium.

w.a: A large K means the reaction is fast, so it will always be observed.
w.why: K says nothing about rate

w.a: The reaction is not observed because the reactants are more stable than the products.
w.why: a large K means the products are favored at equilibrium

w.a: A large K means the reaction needs a lot of energy to start.
w.why: K does not measure the activation energy

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with K ≪ 1 cannot be described as 'no reaction occurs'.
cards.a: K ≪ 1 means the equilibrium mixture is mostly reactants, but K is a positive number, so the product terms cannot be zero: some product must form for Q to rise from 0 to K. The reaction runs in both directions at equal rates at equilibrium; it simply stops at a very small extent.
cards.h: → K > 0 → products present → reaction proceeds slightly → dynamic equilibrium
cards.n: 'K is small so nothing happens' earns nothing; the correct claim is 'barely proceeds' or 'reactant-favored'.
o: If no product formed, Q would stay at zero, which is less than any K, so net forward reaction must occur until Q reaches K.
Weak-acid ionization (Ka ≪ 1) still gives a measurable pH change, showing that a small-K reaction does occur.

w.a: When K is very small the reaction does not happen at all.
w.why: product is present at equilibrium, only in a small amount

w.a: A small K means the reaction is too slow to happen.
w.why: K describes extent, not rate

w.a: K ≪ 1 means the products react back completely so none are left.
w.why: products are at a small nonzero equilibrium concentration

cards.q: Explain why K = 1 for A ⇌ 2B does not mean that [A] and [B] are equal at equilibrium.
cards.a: K = [B]²/[A] = 1 requires [A] = [B]², not [A] = [B]. For example [A] = 0.25 M and [B] = 0.50 M gives 0.50²/0.25 = 1. Because the exponents differ, a K of 1 fixes a relation between the concentrations, not equality; equal values would occur only at 1 M each.
cards.h: → K expression has unequal exponents → K = 1 means [A] = [B]² → usually unequal
cards.n: 'K = 1 means half reactants, half products' earns nothing unless the expression is a simple ratio of equal powers.
o: Substituting numbers shows it: [A] = 0.040 M and [B] = 0.20 M also give K = 1 with [B] five times [A].
Only for a reaction like A ⇌ B, where both terms have exponent 1, does K = 1 force equal concentrations.

w.a: K = 1 always means reactants and products are present in equal amounts.
w.why: the exponents make K = 1 a relation, not equality

w.a: K = 1 means the reaction is exactly halfway to completion.
w.why: K does not measure fraction converted

w.a: With K = 1 neither side is favored, so [A] = [B].
w.why: 'neither favored' is loose; [A] = [B]² is the actual condition

cards.q: State what happens to the equilibrium constant when a reaction is written in reverse.
cards.a: The new constant is the reciprocal of the original: K(reverse) = 1/K(forward). Reversing the equation swaps the numerator and denominator of the mass-action expression. Example: K = 4.0 × 10⁻³ forward gives K = 1/(4.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.5 × 10² for the reverse.
cards.h: → reciprocal
cards.n: Writing −K, or leaving K unchanged, earns nothing; an equilibrium constant is never negative.

cards.q: State what happens to K when every coefficient in a balanced equation is multiplied by n.
cards.a: K is raised to the power n: K′ = Kⁿ. Multiplying every coefficient by n multiplies every exponent in the expression by n, which raises the whole expression to the nth power. Halving the coefficients gives K^½ = √K. Example: K = 3.0 for the original becomes 3.0² = 9.0 for the doubled equation.
cards.h: → raise to a power
cards.n: Multiplying K by n (3.0 → 6.0) earns nothing; coefficients are exponents, so the operation is a power.

cards.q: State how to obtain K for an overall reaction formed by adding two reactions together.
cards.a: Multiply the individual constants: K(overall) = K₁ × K₂. When the equations are added, the overall mass-action expression is the product of the two expressions (any species that appears on opposite sides cancels), so the constants multiply.
cards.h: → multiply the constants
cards.n: K₁ + K₂ earns nothing: equations add, constants multiply (it is ΔG° values that add, which is Unit 9).

cards.q: Apply the rules for manipulating K: given A ⇌ B with K1 = 4.0 and B ⇌ C with K2 = 3.0, find K for 2C ⇌ 2A.
cards.a: K = 6.9 × 10⁻³. Add: A ⇌ C has K = K₁ × K₂ = 4.0 × 3.0 = 12. Reverse: C ⇌ A has K = 1/12 = 0.083. Double the coefficients: 2C ⇌ 2A has K = (1/12)² = 6.9 × 10⁻³.
cards.h: → add, reverse, then square
cards.n: Doubling 1/12 to 1/6 instead of squaring it, or adding 4.0 + 3.0, earns nothing.

cards.q: Given $A \rightleftharpoons B$, K1 = 2.0x10² and $B \rightleftharpoons 2C$, K2 = 5.0x10⁻³, compute K for $A \rightleftharpoons 2C$.
cards.a: K = 1.0. The two equations add directly (B cancels), so K = K₁ × K₂ = (2.0 × 10²)(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.0.
cards.h: → add the equations, multiply the constants
cards.n: Multiply for added reactions, invert for a reversed one, raise to a power for a scaled one; mixing the rules up is the usual loss.

cards.q: Reaction 1: $2X \rightleftharpoons Y$, K = 25. Reaction 2: $Y \rightleftharpoons 2Z$, K = 0.20. Compute the equilibrium constant for $2Z \rightleftharpoons 2X$.
cards.a: K = 0.20. Reverse reaction 2: 2Z ⇌ Y, K = 1/0.20 = 5.0. Reverse reaction 1: Y ⇌ 2X, K = 1/25 = 0.040. Adding them gives 2Z ⇌ 2X, so K = (5.0)(0.040) = 0.20.
cards.h: → reverse both, then multiply
cards.n: Multiplying 25 × 0.20 = 5.0 gives K for 2X ⇌ 2Z, the reverse of what was asked.

cards.q: Given $A \rightleftharpoons B$ with K = 0.25, compute K for $3B \rightleftharpoons 3A$.
cards.a: K = 64. Reverse: B ⇌ A has K = 1/0.25 = 4.0. Triple the coefficients: 3B ⇌ 3A has K = (4.0)³ = 64.
cards.h: → invert, then cube
cards.n: 3 × 4.0 = 12 multiplies instead of cubing and earns nothing.

cards.q:
Determine K (or Q) for each new equation, given 2A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g) with K = 16 at this temperature:
(1) 2C ⇌ 2A + B
(2) A + ½B ⇌ C
(3) 4A + 2B ⇌ 4C
(4) C ⇌ A + ½B
(5) 6A + 3B ⇌ 6C
(6) 4C ⇌ 4A + 2B
(7) at one moment Q = 4.0 for the original equation: Q for 2C ⇌ 2A + B at that moment, and which way the mixture reacts
(8) at the same moment: Q for A + ½B ⇌ C, and which way the mixture reacts
cards.a:
(1) → 1/16 = 0.063 (reversed)
(2) → 16^½ = 4.0 (halved)
(3) → 16² = 2.6 × 10² (doubled)
(4) → 1/4.0 = 0.25 (halved and reversed)
(5) → 16³ = 4.1 × 10³ (tripled)
(6) → 1/256 = 3.9 × 10⁻³ (doubled and reversed)
(7) → Q = 1/4.0 = 0.25, which is greater than K = 0.063 for this equation, so it runs in reverse: toward C, the same as Q = 4.0 < 16 for the original
(8) → Q = 4.0^½ = 2.0 < K = 4.0, so it runs forward: toward C again
cards.h: → invert for reversing, power for scaling; same rules for Q
cards.n: Cases (7) and (8) are the point of 7.6.A.4: Q transforms exactly like K, so every way of writing the equation predicts the same physical direction.

cards.q: Represent the overall equilibrium expression for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) as the product of the expressions for its two steps: step 1, 2NO(g) ⇌ N₂O₂(g) with K₁; step 2, N₂O₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) with K₂.
cards.a: K₁ = [N₂O₂]/[NO]² and K₂ = [NO₂]²/([N₂O₂][O₂]). Their product is K₁K₂ = ([N₂O₂]/[NO]²) × ([NO₂]²/([N₂O₂][O₂])) = [NO₂]²/([NO]²[O₂]), which is the expression for the overall reaction: the intermediate N₂O₂ cancels, so K(overall) = K₁ × K₂.
cards.h: → two step expressions, multiply, cancel the intermediate
cards.n: Leaving N₂O₂ in the overall expression earns nothing; an intermediate appears in the numerator of one step and the denominator of the next.

cards.q: Calculate K for N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) and for NO₂(g) ⇌ ½N₂(g) + O₂(g) at a temperature where N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) has K₁ = 4.0 × 10⁻³¹ and 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) has K₂ = 2.5 × 10¹².
cards.a: K = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁸, then 1.0 × 10⁹. Adding the two equations (2NO cancels) gives N₂ + 2O₂ ⇌ 2NO₂, so K = K₁K₂ = (4.0 × 10⁻³¹)(2.5 × 10¹²) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁸. Reversing and halving it gives NO₂ ⇌ ½N₂ + O₂, so K = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁸)^(−½) = 1/(1.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 1.0 × 10⁹.
cards.h: → multiply, then invert and square-root
cards.n: The K values here are illustrative; the steps are what matter. Halving means a square root, not division by 2.

cards.q: Calculate K for 2HI(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + I₂(g) and for HI(g) ⇌ ½H₂(g) + ½I₂(g), given that H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) has K = 49 at the same temperature.
cards.a: 0.020 and 0.14. Reversing: K = 1/49 = 0.020. Reversing and halving: K = (1/49)^½ = 1/7.0 = 0.14.
cards.h: → invert, then square-root
cards.n: Halving the reversed equation gives 1/49 ÷ 2 = 0.010 if you divide instead of taking the root; that earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain why doubling every coefficient in an equation squares its equilibrium constant rather than doubling it.
cards.a: Coefficients are exponents in the mass-action expression. Doubling every coefficient doubles every exponent, and raising each factor to twice the power is the same as squaring the whole expression, so the new K is K², not 2K.
cards.h: → coefficients are exponents → exponents doubled → whole expression squared
cards.n: 'Twice the amount of reaction, so twice the K' earns nothing; K is not proportional to the coefficients.
o: Writing the doubled equation as the original added to itself gives K × K = K² by the addition rule.
Example: [C]/[A] becomes [C]²/[A]², which is ([C]/[A])².

w.a: Doubling the coefficients doubles K because twice as much product forms.
w.why: coefficients enter as exponents, so K is squared

w.a: K stays the same because the reaction is the same reaction.
w.why: the expression changes when the equation is rewritten

w.a: Doubling the coefficients halves K because there are more reactant molecules.
w.why: no rule halves K; the exponents are doubled on both sides

cards.q: Explain why the equilibrium constant of an overall reaction is the product, not the sum, of the constants for the steps that add up to it.
cards.a: Each step's K is a ratio of concentration terms. Multiplying the step expressions cancels every species that is a product of one step and a reactant of the next (such as an intermediate), leaving exactly the overall expression. So the overall K is K₁ × K₂; a sum of ratios has no such meaning.
cards.h: → each K is a ratio → multiply ratios → shared species cancel → overall expression
cards.n: Adding K values earns nothing; it is the free energies (Unit 9), which are logarithms of K, that add.
o: Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, adding equations adds ΔG° values, and adding logarithms multiplies the constants.
Writing out 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ and N₂O₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO₂ shows [N₂O₂] canceling when the two expressions are multiplied.

w.a: You add the K values because you are adding the equations.
w.why: adding equations multiplies their expressions

w.a: The overall K is the larger of the two step constants because that step dominates.
w.why: every step contributes as a factor

w.a: The overall K is the average of the step constants.
w.why: there is no averaging rule; the constants multiply

cards.q: Explain why comparing Q with K predicts the same direction of reaction whether the equation is written forward, reversed, or with doubled coefficients.
cards.a: Q and K have the same mathematical form, so any rewrite transforms both identically: reversing inverts both, and doubling squares both. The inequality between them flips or holds consistently, so every version predicts the same physical change, such as more C forming.
cards.h: → Q and K same form → same transformation → same physical direction
cards.n: 'Reversing the equation reverses the direction the mixture moves' earns nothing; the mixture does one physical thing however it is written.
o: If Q < K, then 1/Q > 1/K for the reversed equation, which means 'run in reverse', making the same products as before.
Squaring both sides of Q < K keeps the inequality because both are positive.

w.a: Reversing the equation makes Q greater than K, so the reaction goes the other way.
w.why: the reversed equation's reverse is the same physical change

w.a: Only K changes when the equation is rewritten; Q stays the same.
w.why: Q transforms exactly as K does

w.a: The prediction only works if the equation is written with the smallest whole-number coefficients.
w.why: any consistent way of writing it gives the same answer

cards.q: Explain the purpose and structure of an ICE table.
cards.a: An ICE table organizes the calculation of equilibrium amounts from initial conditions and K. The I row holds initial concentrations (or partial pressures); the C row holds each change as its coefficient times x, negative for the side being consumed; the E row is I + C. The E row is then substituted into the K expression and solved for x.
cards.h: → three labeled rows and what each holds
cards.n: Changes that ignore the coefficients (x for every species), or moles in the table when the volume is not 1 L, earn nothing.

cards.q: Compute the equilibrium [B] when 0.20 M A is allowed to reach equilibrium for A(aq) ⇌ B(aq) + C(aq) with Kc = 1.0×10⁻⁵.
cards.a: [B] = 1.4 × 10⁻³ M. ICE: A 0.20 − x; B x; C x. Kc = x²/(0.20 − x) ≈ x²/0.20 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵, so x² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ and x = 1.4 × 10⁻³ M. Check: 1.4 × 10⁻³/0.20 = 0.7%, well under 5%, so dropping x beside 0.20 is justified.
cards.h: → ICE, small-x approximation, check
cards.n: Leaving out the check, or using 0.20 M as [B], earns nothing; x is the amount of B formed.

cards.q: State the 5% approximation rule used in equilibrium calculations.
cards.a: When K is small, you may replace (initial − x) by the initial value if the x you then find is less than 5% of that initial value. Always check afterwards: (x ÷ initial concentration) × 100% < 5%. If the check fails, solve the full equation (for example with the quadratic formula).
cards.h: → threshold percentage plus a check
cards.n: Dropping x without checking, or dropping it from a numerator term such as (2x)², earns nothing; x is only neglected beside a much larger number.

cards.q: Decide the direction a reaction mixture shifts by comparing Q to K.
cards.a: Q < K: net forward reaction (reactants consumed, products formed) until Q rises to K. Q > K: net reverse reaction (products consumed, reactants formed) until Q falls to K. Q = K: already at equilibrium; forward and reverse rates are equal and there is no net change.
cards.h: → three inequality cases
cards.n: 'The reaction shifts' without comparing Q to K and naming the direction earns nothing; the comparison IS the justification.

cards.q: Compute Q and predict the shift for A ⇌ 2B (Kc = 0.50) when [A] = 0.40 M and [B] = 0.20 M.
cards.a: Q = 0.10; the mixture reacts forward, making more B. Q = [B]²/[A] = (0.20)²/0.40 = 0.040/0.40 = 0.10. Since Q (0.10) < K (0.50), net forward reaction occurs: [A] falls and [B] rises until Q = K.
cards.h: → number plus a direction
cards.n: Guessing the direction from which species 'looks' more abundant earns nothing; compute Q first.

cards.q: Set up the ICE table entries (do not solve) for 1.00 M $N_2O_4$ decomposing as $N_2O_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)$, starting with no product.
cards.a: I: [N₂O₄] = 1.00, [NO₂] = 0. C: −x, +2x. E: 1.00 − x, 2x. Then Kc = (2x)²/(1.00 − x). The 1:2 stoichiometry fixes the change row before any value of K is used.
cards.h: → three rows of entries
cards.n: Writing +x for NO₂, or x² instead of (2x)² in the expression, earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the equilibrium concentrations for $2A(g) \rightleftharpoons B(g)$ if x = 0.030 M of B forms, starting from [A] = 0.50 M and [B] = 0 M.
cards.h: → apply the mole ratio to x
cards.n: Here x is the amount of B formed, so A falls by 2x; subtracting only 0.030 from A gives 0.47 M and earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate the equilibrium concentrations when 1.00 M H₂ and 1.00 M I₂ are placed in a flask for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = 49.
cards.h: → perfect square: take the root, solve linearly
cards.n: Using the small-x approximation here earns nothing: K is large and x is 78% of the start; the perfect square avoids the quadratic.

cards.q: Calculate the equilibrium partial pressures when NO₂ alone, at 1.00 atm, is sealed in a rigid flask, for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) with Kp = 0.90 at that temperature. First determine the direction of reaction.
cards.a: P(N₂O₄) = 0.259 atm, P(NO₂) = 0.483 atm. With no N₂O₄, Q is infinite (> K), so the reaction runs in reverse. ICE (atm): NO₂ 1.00 − 2x; N₂O₄ +x. Kp = (1.00 − 2x)²/x = 0.90 → 4x² − 4.90x + 1.00 = 0 → x = 0.259 (the other root, 0.966, makes P(NO₂) negative). P(NO₂) = 1.00 − 0.518 = 0.483 atm. Check: 0.483²/0.259 = 0.90.
cards.h: → Q vs K for direction, ICE in reverse, quadratic
cards.n: Setting up the change row forward (NO₂ + 2x) when only NO₂ is present earns nothing; Q vs K sets the signs.

cards.q:
Determine, for each mixture of N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) with Kc = 4.0 × 10⁻³, whether it reacts toward NO₂ (forward), toward N₂O₄ (reverse), or is at equilibrium ([N₂O₄], [NO₂] in M):
(1) 0.10, 0.010
(2) 0.050, 0.020
(3) 0.10, 0.020
(4) 0.40, 0
(5) 0, 0.050
(6) 0.0010, 0.0020
(7) 1.0, 0.050
(8) 0.010, 0.010
(9) 0.90, 0.060
(10) 0.020, 0.0080
cards.a:
Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄]:
(1) → Q = 1.0 × 10⁻³ < K: forward
(2) → Q = 8.0 × 10⁻³ > K: reverse
(3) → Q = 4.0 × 10⁻³ = K: at equilibrium
(4) → Q = 0 < K: forward
(5) → no N₂O₄, Q undefined (infinitely large) > K: reverse
(6) → Q = 4.0 × 10⁻³ = K: at equilibrium, even at these low concentrations
(7) → Q = 2.5 × 10⁻³ < K: forward
(8) → Q = 1.0 × 10⁻² > K: reverse
(9) → Q = 4.0 × 10⁻³ = K: at equilibrium
(10) → Q = 3.2 × 10⁻³ < K: forward
cards.h: → compute Q each time, then compare with K
cards.n: Deciding from which concentration is larger (e.g. calling (8) 'at equilibrium' because the values are equal) earns nothing; only Q against K decides.

cards.q: Explain the conditions under which the 5% approximation is likely to fail.
cards.a: It fails when x is not small beside the starting concentration: when K is not small (roughly above 10⁻³) or when the initial concentration is very low, so that a large fraction reacts. Then (initial − x) cannot be replaced by the initial value, and the full equation must be solved.
cards.h: → K not small or start very dilute → x large fraction → approximation invalid
cards.n: 'It fails when K is large' alone is half the answer; a very dilute start with a small K can fail the check too.
o: The approximation assumes x ≪ initial; the ratio K/initial concentration controls how big x is relative to the start, so a large K or a tiny start both break it.
If the percent reacted computed from the approximate x exceeds 5%, the assumption was false and must be replaced by an exact solution.

w.a: The 5% approximation fails whenever there are coefficients larger than 1.
w.why: coefficients do not decide it; the size of x relative to the start does

w.a: It fails when the concentration is high because more reacts.
w.why: high concentration makes the fraction reacted smaller, not larger

w.a: The 5% approximation always works if K is less than 1.
w.why: K near 1 or a very dilute start can still give x above 5%

cards.q: Explain why a very large K value lets you assume a reaction goes essentially to completion before setting up an ICE table in reverse.
cards.a: With a very large K the equilibrium lies almost entirely on the product side, so running the reaction to completion puts you very close to equilibrium. Letting a small amount x react back then makes x tiny beside the product amounts, so the algebra simplifies with negligible error.
cards.h: → K ≫ 1 → equilibrium ≈ completion → small back-reaction x → simple algebra
cards.n: Starting from the reactant side with a huge K leaves an unworkable tiny denominator; run the limiting reactant to completion first.
o: The same equilibrium is reached from either side, so it is legitimate to start from the nearly complete state and approach equilibrium in reverse.
Near completion the reactant concentrations are the small unknowns, so they become x and the large product values stay nearly unchanged.

w.a: A large K means the reaction is fast, so it finishes before equilibrium.
w.why: K says nothing about rate, and equilibrium is still reached

w.a: With a large K no reactant is left at all, so no ICE table is needed.
w.why: a small nonzero amount of reactant remains and is what x finds

w.a: You assume completion because large K reactions are irreversible.
w.why: the reaction is reversible; it is just product-favored

cards.q: Explain why the change row of an ICE table must be written in the ratio of the balanced coefficients.
cards.a: The changes come from the reaction itself: each time the reaction occurs once, the species change in the ratio of their coefficients. So if A changes by −x in aA + bB ⇌ cC, B must change by −(b/a)x and C by +(c/a)x; any other ratio would create or destroy atoms.
cards.h: → reaction events consume and form in fixed ratios → changes ∝ coefficients → mass balance
cards.n: 'Every species changes by x' earns nothing unless all coefficients are 1.
o: The change row is just stoichiometry applied to an unknown amount of reaction, so the mole ratio from the balanced equation must be used.
For N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ each N₂O₄ that breaks apart makes two NO₂, so the changes are −x and +2x.

w.a: All species change by the same amount x at equilibrium.
w.why: species change in the ratio of their coefficients

w.a: The change row uses the equilibrium constant to set each change.
w.why: K is used only after the E row; the ratio comes from the equation

w.a: The coefficients go in the exponents, so the change row does not need them.
w.why: the coefficients appear in both the change row and the exponents

cards.q: Explain why a mixture with Q < K undergoes net forward reaction rather than net reverse reaction.
cards.a: To reach equilibrium Q must rise to equal K. Q increases only when product concentrations (numerator) rise and reactant concentrations (denominator) fall, which is net forward reaction. Net reverse reaction would lower Q further from K.
cards.h: → Q must rise to K → numerator up, denominator down → forward
cards.n: 'Q < K so it shifts left' is the most common reversal; tie the direction to what makes Q grow.
o: When Q < K the forward rate exceeds the reverse rate, giving net conversion of reactants to products until the rates are equal at Q = K.
Q < K means there is too little product relative to the equilibrium ratio, so product forms.

w.a: When Q < K the reaction shifts left to increase Q.
w.why: shifting left lowers Q

w.a: Q < K means there are more reactants than products, so reactants form.
w.why: the comparison is to K, and reactants are consumed

w.a: Q < K means the system is at equilibrium on the reactant side.
w.why: equilibrium requires Q = K

cards.q: Identify what a particulate diagram of a reaction mixture at equilibrium should show when K is very large ($K \ge 10^{8}$).
cards.a: Almost all product particles. With K ≥ 10⁸ the reactant fraction is far below one particle in a drawing of a few dozen particles, so the box shows the products (with atoms conserved from the start) and at most a stray reactant particle; a trace of reactant still exists but is too small to draw.
cards.h: → mostly products, reactant too scarce to draw
cards.n: A diagram with comparable numbers of reactant and product particles earns nothing; that fits K near 1.

cards.q: Calculate Kc for A₂(g) ⇌ 2A(g) from this description of an equilibrium mixture: a 1.0 L box holds 4 A₂ molecules (two joined spheres) and 6 A atoms (single spheres), and each particle drawn represents 0.10 mol.
cards.h: → count, convert to M, substitute
cards.n: Using raw counts (6²/4 = 9.0) earns nothing here: the reaction changes the number of gas particles, so the mol-per-particle scale does not cancel.

cards.q: Determine whether this mixture is at equilibrium, and if not which way it reacts, for X(g) + Y(g) ⇌ XY(g) with Kc = 5.0: a 1.0 L box holds 3 X, 3 Y and 2 XY particles, each particle representing 0.10 mol.
cards.a: Not at equilibrium; net forward reaction occurs, forming more XY. [X] = [Y] = 0.30 M, [XY] = 0.20 M, so Q = 0.20/(0.30 × 0.30) = 2.2. Since Q (2.2) < K (5.0), X and Y combine: the box will end with fewer X and Y and more XY.
cards.h: → counts to M, Q, compare with K
cards.n: 'Not at equilibrium because the numbers are unequal' earns nothing; only Q compared with K decides.

cards.q:
Identify the earliest snapshot that shows equilibrium, and calculate K, for 2AB(g) ⇌ A₂(g) + B₂(g) followed in a sealed box (particle counts):
snapshot · AB · A₂ · B₂
t₁ · 8 · 0 · 0
t₂ · 4 · 2 · 2
t₃ · 2 · 3 · 3
t₄ · 2 · 3 · 3
cards.a: Equilibrium is shown by t₃ (it was reached at some point between t₂ and t₃): t₃ and t₄ have identical counts, so there is no net change. K = [A₂][B₂]/[AB]² = (3)(3)/(2)² = 2.25 ≈ 2.3. Counts can be used directly because the moles of gas are equal on both sides, so the particle-to-molarity factors cancel. Atoms are conserved throughout: 8 A and 8 B in every snapshot.
cards.h: → first repeated snapshot, then K from counts
cards.n: Choosing t₄, or t₂ because 'half the AB is gone', earns nothing; the first snapshot matched by the next is the evidence.

cards.q: Draw a particulate diagram of the equilibrium mixture for A(g) ⇌ B(g), K = 3.0, reached in a box that started with 12 A particles and no B. Describe your drawing in words.
cards.a: A box containing 3 A particles (for example open circles) and 9 B particles (filled circles), scattered at random through the box, 12 particles in all. Reasoning: particles are conserved, A + B = 12, and at equilibrium [B]/[A] = 3.0, so B = 9 and A = 3; since K has no volume dependence here, counts work directly.
cards.h: → counts from conservation + K, then the picture
cards.n: A drawing with 0 A particles (reaction 'complete') or 6 and 6 earns nothing; K = 3 fixes a 3:1 ratio of B to A.

cards.q: Identify which reaction has the larger K, and estimate each K, from two equilibrium boxes of equal volume at the same temperature: box 1, for A ⇌ B, holds 2 A and 10 B; box 2, for C ⇌ D, holds 9 C and 3 D.
cards.a: Reaction 1 (A ⇌ B) has the larger K. K₁ = [B]/[A] = 10/2 = 5.0; K₂ = [D]/[C] = 3/9 = 0.33. Both are 1:1 reactions with the same volume, so particle ratios equal concentration ratios. Box 1 is product-rich, box 2 reactant-rich.
cards.h: → product:reactant ratio in each box
cards.n: Comparing total particle counts, or which box has 'more particles', earns nothing; K is the product-to-reactant ratio.

cards.q: Predict the particle counts after 8 more A particles are added to a box at equilibrium for A(g) ⇌ B(g), K = 3.0, that holds 3 A and 9 B, once equilibrium is restored.
cards.a: 5 A and 15 B. Just after the addition the box holds 11 A and 9 B, so Q = 9/11 = 0.82 < K = 3.0 and net forward reaction occurs. Particles are conserved (20 in all) and at the new equilibrium B/A = 3.0, so A = 5 and B = 15: both counts end higher than before the addition.
cards.h: → Q after the addition, then conservation + ratio
cards.n: 'All 8 added A turn into B' (3 A, 17 B) earns nothing: that gives Q = 5.7, above K.

cards.q: Describe a particulate diagram of saturated AgCl solution in contact with undissolved solid AgCl at equilibrium, including what is happening at the surface of the solid.
cards.a: At the bottom, a block of solid drawn as an ordered lattice of alternating Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Above it, water molecules fill the solution with only a few dissolved ions, equal numbers of Ag⁺ and Cl⁻, each surrounded by water. At the surface, arrows show ions leaving the lattice and other ions rejoining it at the same rate, so the numbers of dissolved ions stay constant.
cards.h: → lattice + few hydrated ions + two-way arrows
cards.n: Drawing AgCl units floating in solution earns nothing: dissolved AgCl is present as separate hydrated ions, and in equal numbers.

cards.q: Explain why two consecutive particulate snapshots with identical counts of every species indicate equilibrium but do not show that the reactions have stopped.
cards.a: Identical counts mean no net change, the observable sign of equilibrium. But individual particles can still be reacting: if forward and reverse events happen at equal rates, each species is formed as often as it is destroyed, so the counts stay fixed while particles keep changing identity.
cards.h: → same counts → no net change → equal forward and reverse rates → reactions continue
cards.n: 'Nothing is reacting any more' earns nothing; a snapshot cannot distinguish a stopped system from a dynamic one, and chemistry says it is dynamic.
o: A constant count is what equal forward and reverse rates look like in a picture: each forward event that removes an AB is matched by a reverse event that makes one.
Isotope-labeling experiments show atoms continuing to swap between species at equilibrium, so identical snapshots hide ongoing reaction.

w.a: The counts are the same because the reaction has finished.
w.why: equilibrium is dynamic; only the net change is zero

w.a: The counts are the same because the reactant has been used up.
w.why: reactant is still present in the snapshots

w.a: Identical snapshots show that the forward reaction has stopped and only the reverse reaction continues.
w.why: both reactions continue at equal rates

cards.q: Explain why particle counts can be put straight into K for 2AB(g) ⇌ A₂(g) + B₂(g) without converting them to molarities, but not for A₂(g) ⇌ 2A(g).
cards.a: For 2AB ⇌ A₂ + B₂ the numerator and denominator each contain two concentration factors, so the conversion factor (mol per particle ÷ volume) cancels. For A₂ ⇌ 2A there are two factors on top and one below, so one factor survives and raw counts give the wrong K.
cards.h: → equal numbers of factors top and bottom → conversion cancels; unequal → it does not
cards.n: 'Counts are always the same as concentrations' earns nothing; it holds only when the total exponents on top and bottom match.
o: Doubling the box volume halves every concentration: that leaves K for 2AB ⇌ A₂ + B₂ unchanged but halves [A]²/[A₂], so counts alone cannot give K for the dissociation.
In the dissociation the value computed from counts depends on the arbitrary mol-per-particle scale, so it cannot be the constant K.

w.a: You can always use counts because concentration is just the number of particles.
w.why: concentration is particles per volume, and the scale cancels only in some expressions

w.a: Counts cannot be used for A₂ ⇌ 2A because A₂ is a molecule and A is an atom.
w.why: the issue is the unequal exponents, not atoms versus molecules

w.a: Counts work for 2AB ⇌ A₂ + B₂ because it has more particles.
w.why: it works because the exponents balance, not because of particle number

cards.q: Explain why an equilibrium box showing equal numbers of A₂ molecules and A atoms does not mean that K = 1 for A₂(g) ⇌ 2A(g).
cards.a: K = [A]²/[A₂], so equal concentrations give K = [A], not 1. With 4 A₂ and 4 A in a 1.0 L box at 0.10 mol per particle, [A₂] = [A] = 0.40 M and K = 0.40²/0.40 = 0.40. Equal counts mean K = 1 only when the exponents are equal.
cards.h: → unequal exponents → equal counts give K = [A] → depends on scale, not 1
cards.n: 'Same number of each, so K = 1' earns nothing unless the reaction is of the A ⇌ B type.
o: If the box were half as large, the same counts would give concentrations twice as high and a different ratio, so equal counts cannot pin K at 1.
Only a reaction whose K expression has equal total exponents top and bottom turns equal amounts into K = 1.

w.a: Equal numbers of reactant and product particles always mean K = 1.
w.why: the squared term makes K depend on the actual concentration

w.a: K = 1 because the box is at equilibrium.
w.why: equilibrium means Q = K, whatever K is

w.a: K is 2 because each A₂ makes two A atoms.
w.why: the coefficient is an exponent on [A], not a multiplier of K

cards.q: State Le Chatelier's principle.
cards.a: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed (by adding or removing a species, changing the temperature, changing the volume or pressure of a gas-phase system, or diluting a solution), it undergoes net reaction in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance, until a new equilibrium is established.
cards.h: → disturbance, partial counteraction, new equilibrium
cards.n: The shift only partly offsets the stress; saying the system 'returns to the original concentrations' earns nothing.

cards.q: Predict the effect of adding more of a reactant to a system at equilibrium.
cards.a: Net forward reaction (a shift toward products). The added reactant makes Q < K, so reactants are consumed and products formed until Q = K again. At the new equilibrium the products and the added reactant are both higher than before the addition, the other reactants are lower, and K is unchanged.
cards.h: → direction, what rises and falls, K unchanged
cards.n: Saying K increases earns nothing: only temperature changes K. The added reactant is only partly consumed, never all of it.

cards.q: Predict the effect of continuously removing a product from an equilibrium mixture.
cards.a: Continuous net forward reaction: every removal makes Q < K, so more reactant converts to product to restore Q = K. Because the product is never allowed to build up, the reaction keeps being pulled forward and can go far beyond its normal equilibrium extent, even when K is small.
cards.h: → repeated Q < K, reaction pulled forward
cards.n: This is how removing NH₃ as a liquid raises Haber-process yield; K itself does not change.

cards.q: Predict the effect of decreasing the volume of a gaseous equilibrium mixture at constant temperature.
cards.a: Net reaction toward the side with fewer moles of gas. Compression raises every partial pressure, and reacting toward fewer gas molecules partly counteracts that rise; in terms of Q, the side with more gas moles carries more factors, so Q moves away from K in its favor. K is unchanged. If both sides have equal moles of gas, there is no shift.
cards.h: → toward fewer gas moles, K unchanged
cards.n: Count only gas-phase coefficients; solids, liquids and aqueous species do not count toward either side.

cards.q: Predict the effect of raising the temperature of an exothermic equilibrium.
cards.a: Net reverse reaction (a shift toward reactants), and K decreases. Treat heat as a product: adding heat is like adding product, so the system consumes some of it by running the endothermic reverse reaction. Unlike a concentration change, this changes the value of K.
cards.h: → shift toward reactants, K decreases
cards.n: Saying 'K stays the same' earns nothing here: temperature is the one stress that changes K.

cards.q: Predict the effect of raising the temperature of an endothermic equilibrium.
cards.a: Net forward reaction (a shift toward products), and K increases. Treat heat as a reactant: adding heat is like adding reactant, so the system absorbs some of it by running the endothermic forward reaction further.
cards.h: → shift toward products, K increases
cards.n: Writing heat into the equation on the correct side (reactant for ΔH > 0) turns every temperature question into a concentration question.

cards.q: Predict the shift when $2SO_2(g)+O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)$ at equilibrium has its container volume suddenly halved.
cards.a: Net forward reaction, toward SO₃ (3 mol of gas on the left, 2 on the right). Halving the volume doubles every concentration, so Q = (2)²/((2)²(2)) × K = K/2 < K, and SO₂ and O₂ react to form SO₃ until Q = K again. K is unchanged.
cards.h: → direction plus the gas-mole count or Q
cards.n: Adding an inert gas at constant volume would NOT shift this system: only a change in the reacting gases' concentrations moves Q.

cards.q: Predict the shift in $N_2(g)+3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$ (exothermic) when both temperature and pressure are raised together.
cards.a: The net direction cannot be predicted from Le Châtelier's principle alone. Raising the pressure by compression favors NH₃ (4 mol of gas → 2), while raising the temperature favors N₂ and H₂ because the forward reaction is exothermic (and K decreases). The two stresses oppose each other; the outcome depends on their sizes.
cards.h: → two opposing effects, no net prediction
cards.n: Picking one direction without data earns nothing; say both effects and that they oppose. (Pressure raised by adding an inert gas would have no effect at all.)

cards.q:
Predict the response (direction of net reaction, and any change in K) of N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol, at equilibrium in a rigid container unless stated, to each stress:
(1) N₂ is added
(2) NH₃ is removed
(3) NH₃ is added
(4) H₂ is removed
(5) the temperature is raised
(6) the temperature is lowered
(7) the volume is halved
(8) the volume is doubled
(9) argon is added at constant volume
(10) argon is added at constant total pressure
(11) an iron catalyst is added
(12) for Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq): the solution is diluted with water
cards.a:
(1) → forward (toward NH₃); K unchanged
(2) → forward; K unchanged
(3) → reverse (toward N₂ and H₂); K unchanged
(4) → reverse; K unchanged
(5) → reverse; K decreases (exothermic forward)
(6) → forward; K increases
(7) → forward (4 mol gas → 2 mol); K unchanged
(8) → reverse (toward more gas moles); K unchanged
(9) → no shift: reacting partial pressures unchanged, Q = K
(10) → reverse: the container expands, as in (8)
(11) → no shift; equilibrium is reached faster; K unchanged
(12) → reverse (toward more dissolved particles): FeSCN²⁺ partly dissociates, K unchanged
cards.h: → twelve directions, K changes only with temperature
cards.n: Cases (9) and (11) are the traps: an inert gas at constant volume and a catalyst leave Q = K, so there is no shift.

cards.q: Predict the color change for [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) (pink) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq) (blue) + 6H₂O(l), forward reaction endothermic, when (a) the solution is heated, (b) it is cooled in ice, (c) concentrated HCl is added, (d) AgNO₃ is added, precipitating AgCl, (e) water is added.
cards.a: (a) Bluer: heat acts as a reactant, so net forward reaction forms [CoCl₄]²⁻ (and K increases). (b) Pinker: net reverse reaction. (c) Bluer: added Cl⁻ makes Q < K, net forward reaction. (d) Pinker: removing Cl⁻ as AgCl makes Q > K, net reverse reaction. (e) Pinker: dilution lowers the total dissolved-particle concentration, so the system shifts toward the side with more dissolved particles (5 on the left, 1 on the right).
cards.h: → five color predictions, each with its direction
cards.n: For (e), 'water is a product, so adding it shifts left' earns nothing: H₂O(l) is not in Q; the shift comes from diluting the ions.

cards.q: Predict how the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid, CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq), changes when solid sodium acetate is dissolved in it, and justify.
cards.a: The pH rises. Dissolving sodium acetate adds CH₃COO⁻, a product of the ionization, so Q > K and net reverse reaction occurs: acetate combines with H₃O⁺ to re-form acetic acid. [H₃O⁺] falls, so the pH increases.
cards.h: → direction of pH, then Q vs K via the added ion
cards.n: Borrows weak-acid equilibria from Unit 8. 'Sodium acetate is a salt, so pH stays at 7-ish' earns nothing; name the acetate ion and the shift.

cards.q: Predict the temperature change inside an insulated, rigid flask holding N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol, at equilibrium when more H₂ is injected at the same temperature.
cards.a: The temperature rises. The added H₂ makes Q < K, so net forward reaction occurs, and the forward reaction is exothermic; in an insulated flask the heat it releases stays in the gas and raises its temperature. (The warming lowers K slightly, which limits how far the forward shift goes.)
cards.h: → direction of shift, then the heat it releases
cards.n: 'Temperature stays constant because only concentration changed' earns nothing: the shift itself releases heat that the insulated flask keeps.

cards.q: Explain when a change in volume produces no shift in a gaseous equilibrium.
cards.a: When both sides have the same number of moles of gas. Changing the volume multiplies every concentration by the same factor, and with equal total exponents in the numerator and denominator of Q that factor cancels, so Q still equals K. Example: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
cards.h: → equal gas moles → factor cancels in Q → Q = K → no shift
cards.n: Counting solids or liquids toward the mole total earns nothing; only gas-phase coefficients count.
o: No shift occurs when neither direction of reaction changes the total moles of gas, so reacting cannot counteract a pressure change.
With Δn(gas) = 0 the equilibrium position does not depend on volume, because the volume terms cancel in the K expression.

w.a: A volume change never shifts an equilibrium because K stays the same.
w.why: K stays the same, but Q changes whenever the gas moles differ

w.a: There is no shift when the reactants and products have the same number of atoms.
w.why: atoms are always conserved; moles of gas is the test

w.a: There is no shift when the gases have equal partial pressures.
w.why: equal pressures are not the condition; equal gas moles on each side are

cards.q: Explain why adding an inert gas at constant volume does not shift a gaseous equilibrium.
cards.a: At constant volume, adding argon changes neither the amount nor the volume of any reacting gas, so their concentrations and partial pressures are unchanged. Q is therefore unchanged and still equals K. Only the total pressure rises, and the total pressure does not appear in Q or K.
cards.h: → reacting partial pressures unchanged → Q unchanged → Q = K → no shift
cards.n: 'Pressure increased, so it shifts to fewer moles' earns nothing: pressure shifts an equilibrium only when it changes the reacting gases' partial pressures.
o: Each gas's partial pressure is its own moles × RT/V, and none of those change when argon is added at fixed V.
The inert gas does not take part in the reaction and is not in the K expression, so it cannot change Q.

w.a: Adding argon raises the pressure, so the reaction shifts toward fewer moles of gas.
w.why: the reacting gases' partial pressures, and so Q, do not change

w.a: Argon dilutes the gases, so the reaction shifts toward more moles of gas.
w.why: at constant volume no reacting concentration changes

w.a: The argon collides with the molecules and slows both reactions equally, so there is no shift.
w.why: the reason is unchanged Q, not collision rates

cards.q: Explain why adding a catalyst does not change the position of an equilibrium.
cards.a: A catalyst provides a lower-energy pathway that speeds the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor. It changes no concentration, so Q is unchanged, and it leaves K unchanged; the system simply reaches the same equilibrium sooner.
cards.h: → both rates sped equally → no change in Q or K → same equilibrium, sooner
cards.n: Borrows catalysis from Unit 5. 'The catalyst shifts it toward products' earns nothing; a catalyst changes how fast, never how far.
o: The catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions by the same amount, so the ratio of the rate constants, and hence K, is unchanged.
A catalyst is not in the K expression and does not change any concentration, so Q still equals K.

w.a: A catalyst speeds up the forward reaction, so more product forms.
w.why: it speeds both directions equally

w.a: The catalyst is used up, so it cannot change the equilibrium.
w.why: catalysts are not consumed; the reason is equal rate enhancement

w.a: A catalyst increases K by lowering the activation energy.
w.why: K is set by temperature, not by the pathway

cards.q: Explain why heating a sealed flask containing 2NO₂(g) (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) (colorless), ΔH° = −57 kJ/mol, makes the gas a darker brown.
cards.a: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat acts as a product. Raising the temperature lowers K, so Q > K and net reverse reaction occurs: N₂O₄ dissociates into brown NO₂. More NO₂ means a darker brown color.
cards.h: → exothermic → heating lowers K → Q > K → reverse → more brown NO₂
cards.n: 'Heat makes molecules move faster, so the color darkens' earns nothing; the color follows [NO₂], which rises by the shift.
o: By Le Châtelier's principle, the system absorbs added heat by running the endothermic direction, which is N₂O₄ → 2NO₂.
The color is a direct measure of [NO₂]; any change that favors the reverse reaction deepens it.

w.a: Heating speeds up the forward reaction, so more colorless N₂O₄ forms.
w.why: heating favors the endothermic reverse reaction

w.a: The color darkens because heating increases the pressure, which shifts toward NO₂.
w.why: in a sealed rigid flask the concentrations do not change on heating; the change in K causes the shift

w.a: K stays the same when the flask is heated, so only the rate changes.
w.why: temperature changes K

cards.q: Identify the only disturbance that changes the numerical value of an equilibrium constant.
cards.a: A change in temperature. Changes in concentration, volume or pressure, dilution, an inert gas, or a catalyst leave K unchanged; the concentration and volume changes alter Q instead, and the system reacts until Q returns to the same K.
cards.h: → one variable
cards.n: If a question says K changed, the temperature changed; 'adding reactant increases K' earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain a Le Chatelier shift using the reaction quotient rather than the principle itself.
cards.a: A change in concentration, volume or pressure alters Q so that Q ≠ K; a temperature change alters K instead. If Q < K, net forward reaction occurs; if Q > K, net reverse reaction occurs; the concentrations redistribute until Q = K again at a new equilibrium. Example: adding product raises Q above K, so net reverse reaction follows.
cards.h: → stress moves Q (or K), then Q vs K gives direction
cards.n: 'The system shifts to relieve the stress' with no Q-versus-K comparison earns less than the Q argument on free response.

cards.q: Predict the shift when the volume of a gaseous equilibrium is increased at constant temperature, for a reaction with equal moles of gas on both sides.
cards.a: No shift. For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), doubling the volume halves every concentration: Q = (½[HI])²/((½[H₂])(½[I₂])) = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = K, so Q still equals K and no net reaction occurs.
cards.h: → Q unchanged, so no shift
cards.n: Counting solids, liquids or aqueous species when tallying the two sides earns nothing; equal moles of GAS is the test.

cards.q: Predict the shift when the temperature of an equilibrium mixture is lowered for a reaction with ΔH° = 0.
cards.a: No shift is expected. The temperature rule works through the sign of ΔH°: with ΔH° = 0, heat is neither a reactant nor a product, so K does not change with temperature and Q (unchanged by cooling) still equals K.
cards.h: → ΔH° = 0 → K unchanged → Q = K
cards.n: AP uses only the sign of ΔH°; the exact temperature dependence of K (van 't Hoff) is beyond the course.

cards.q: Predict the effect of adding an inert gas to a gaseous equilibrium held at constant total pressure.
cards.a: Net reaction toward the side with more moles of gas, as for any expansion. To keep the total pressure constant the container must expand, which lowers every reacting gas's partial pressure. If the gas moles differ between sides, Q ≠ K: for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Q = P(NH₃)²/(P(N₂)P(H₂)³) rises above K, so net reverse reaction follows.
cards.h: → container expands → Q changes → toward more gas moles
cards.n: Constant pressure and constant volume give opposite answers here; an inert gas at constant VOLUME causes no shift.

cards.q: Calculate Q immediately after the volume is halved for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at equilibrium with [N₂O₄] = 0.040 M and [NO₂] = 0.020 M, and determine the direction of the resulting net reaction.
cards.a: Q = 0.020 = 2K; net reverse reaction, toward N₂O₄. K = (0.020)²/0.040 = 0.010. Halving the volume doubles both concentrations: [N₂O₄] = 0.080 M, [NO₂] = 0.040 M, so Q = (0.040)²/0.080 = 0.0016/0.080 = 0.020. Since Q > K, NO₂ combines to form N₂O₄ (the side with fewer gas moles) until Q = K.
cards.h: → K first, then Q with doubled concentrations
cards.n: Doubling [NO₂] without squaring the factor gives Q = K and 'no shift', which earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate the new equilibrium concentrations after 0.50 M of extra A is added to A(aq) ⇌ B(aq), K = 4.0, at equilibrium with [A] = 0.20 M and [B] = 0.80 M.
cards.a: [A] = 0.30 M, [B] = 1.20 M. Just after the addition [A] = 0.70 M, so Q = 0.80/0.70 = 1.1 < K = 4.0: net forward reaction. ICE: A 0.70 − x, B 0.80 + x; (0.80 + x)/(0.70 − x) = 4.0 → 0.80 + x = 2.80 − 4.0x → x = 0.40. Check: 1.20/0.30 = 4.0. [A] ends above its old 0.20 M but well below 0.70 M.
cards.h: → Q after the addition, then an ICE from the new start
cards.n: Starting the ICE from the old equilibrium values (ignoring the added 0.50 M) or letting all the added A react earns nothing.

cards.q: Determine the direction of net reaction when an equilibrium mixture of Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) is diluted to twice its volume with water, by comparing Q with K.
cards.a: Net reverse reaction: FeSCN²⁺ partly dissociates. Doubling the volume halves each concentration, so Q = (½[FeSCN²⁺])/((½[Fe³⁺])(½[SCN⁻])) = 2 × [FeSCN²⁺]/([Fe³⁺][SCN⁻]) = 2K. Since Q > K, the reverse reaction, toward the side with more dissolved particles, occurs until Q = K. The red color fades by more than dilution alone would cause.
cards.h: → halve every term, Q = 2K, reverse
cards.n: 'Water is a solvent so dilution does nothing' earns nothing: water is not in Q, but diluting the ions changes Q.

cards.q: Draw concentration-versus-time curves for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), K = 49, starting at equilibrium with [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.10 M and [HI] = 0.70 M, when H₂ is injected at time t₁ so that [H₂] jumps to 0.30 M. Describe your graph in words, including the new plateau values.
cards.a: Before t₁ all three lines are flat: H₂ and I₂ at 0.10 M, HI at 0.70 M. At t₁ [H₂] jumps vertically to 0.30 M. Then [H₂] curves down to a new plateau at 0.25 M, [I₂] curves down to 0.052 M, and [HI] curves up to 0.80 M, the HI rise twice the H₂ drop. Solving (0.70 + 2x)²/((0.30 − x)(0.10 − x)) = 49 gives x = 0.048.
cards.h: → one vertical jump, then smooth curves to new plateaus
cards.n: Showing [I₂] or [HI] jumping at t₁ earns nothing: only the injected species changes instantly; the others change gradually as the reaction shifts.

cards.q: Draw concentration-versus-time curves for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH° < 0, at equilibrium in a rigid flask, when the flask is heated at time t₁ to a new constant temperature. Describe your graph in words.
cards.a: Before t₁ both lines are flat. At t₁ there is no vertical jump in either concentration, because heating a rigid flask changes no concentration. After t₁ [NO₂] rises smoothly and [N₂O₄] falls smoothly, the rise in [NO₂] twice the fall in [N₂O₄], until both level off at new plateaus: NO₂ higher, N₂O₄ lower. Heating lowered K, making Q > K, so net reverse reaction occurred.
cards.h: → no jump, smooth 2:1 changes to new plateaus
cards.n: A vertical jump at t₁ earns nothing for a temperature change; only adding or removing a species (or a volume change) produces one.

cards.q: Determine whether the forward reaction is endothermic or exothermic given that its K is 1.2 × 10⁻² at 300 K and 3.5 × 10⁻¹ at 400 K.
cards.a: Endothermic. K increases as the temperature rises, so higher temperature favors products. By Le Châtelier's principle heat must then act as a reactant, which means the forward reaction absorbs heat (ΔH° > 0).
cards.h: → direction of K with T, then the sign of ΔH
cards.n: 'K increased, so the reaction is exothermic because it gives off more product' earns nothing; rising K with rising T means ΔH° > 0.

cards.q:
Determine, for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH° < 0, at equilibrium, whether each change alters Q or K, how Q then compares with K, and the direction of net reaction:
(1) O₂ is added
(2) SO₃ is removed
(3) SO₃ is added
(4) the temperature is raised
(5) the temperature is lowered
(6) the volume is halved
(7) the volume is doubled
(8) helium is added at constant volume
(9) a catalyst is added
(10) helium is added at constant total pressure
cards.a:
(1) → Q falls; Q < K; forward
(2) → Q falls; Q < K; forward
(3) → Q rises; Q > K; reverse
(4) → K falls (exothermic), Q unchanged; Q > K; reverse
(5) → K rises, Q unchanged; Q < K; forward
(6) → Q halves; Q < K; forward
(7) → Q doubles; Q > K; reverse
(8) → neither changes; Q = K; no shift
(9) → neither changes; Q = K; no shift (equilibrium reached sooner)
(10) → container expands, Q rises; Q > K; reverse
cards.h: → which one moves, the inequality, the direction
cards.n: Cases (4) and (5) are the point: a temperature change moves K, not Q; saying 'Q changes when heated' earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain why adding more reactant to a system at equilibrium makes Q momentarily less than K, and connect this to the resulting shift.
cards.a: Reactant concentrations are in the denominator of Q. Adding reactant enlarges the denominator while the numerator is momentarily unchanged, so Q drops below K. With Q < K, net forward reaction occurs, consuming reactants and forming products until Q rises back to K.
cards.h: → reactant in denominator → Q falls below K → net forward until Q = K
cards.n: 'Adding reactant raises K' earns nothing: K is fixed at constant temperature; Q is what moves.
o: The added reactant raises the forward rate above the unchanged reverse rate, giving net forward reaction until the rates are equal again.
Q < K means the mixture holds too little product relative to the equilibrium ratio, so products form.

w.a: Adding reactant increases Q, so the reaction shifts forward.
w.why: adding reactant decreases Q

w.a: Adding reactant increases K, so more product forms.
w.why: K is unchanged; Q falls below it

w.a: Q becomes less than K, so the reaction shifts toward the reactants.
w.why: Q < K means net forward reaction

cards.q: Explain how decreasing the volume of a gaseous equilibrium with unequal moles of gas on each side changes Q relative to K, and use that to justify the resulting shift.
cards.a: Compression multiplies every concentration by the same factor, but the side with more moles of gas carries more factors in Q, so its terms grow more. For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, halving V makes Q = K/2 < K, so net reaction toward the side with fewer gas moles occurs until Q = K.
cards.h: → all concentrations × factor → more-moles side grows more → Q ≠ K → toward fewer moles
cards.n: 'Higher pressure pushes toward fewer moles' without showing how Q changes earns less than the Q argument.
o: Reacting toward fewer gas moles lowers the total pressure, partly counteracting the compression.
For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, Q scales with V, so halving V halves Q and net forward reaction follows.

w.a: Decreasing the volume increases K, so the reaction shifts toward products.
w.why: K is unchanged; Q changes

w.a: Compression raises all concentrations equally, so Q does not change.
w.why: with unequal gas moles the factors do not cancel

w.a: The system shifts toward the side with more moles to fill the smaller space.
w.why: it shifts toward fewer gas moles

cards.q: Explain why heating an equilibrium mixture in a rigid container causes a shift even though no concentration changes at the moment of heating.
cards.a: A temperature change alters K, not Q. The concentrations, and so Q, are the same just after heating, but K has a new value, so Q ≠ K. The system then reacts in whichever direction brings Q to the new K: toward the endothermic side as the temperature rises.
cards.h: → T changes K → Q unchanged → Q ≠ new K → net reaction to the new K
cards.n: 'Heating changes Q' earns nothing; in a rigid container heating leaves every concentration, and Q, unchanged at first.
o: Other stresses move Q away from a fixed K; temperature moves K away from a fixed Q, with the same result: Q ≠ K.
Heating speeds the endothermic direction more than the exothermic one, so the rates become unequal until a new equilibrium forms.

w.a: Heating increases all concentrations, so Q changes and the system shifts.
w.why: in a rigid container heating does not change concentrations

w.a: Heating shifts the equilibrium but K stays the same.
w.why: temperature is the stress that changes K

w.a: Heating speeds up both reactions equally, so the shift comes from the faster collisions.
w.why: the rates change unequally because K changes

cards.q: Explain why, after extra reactant is added and equilibrium is restored, that reactant's concentration is higher than it was before the addition.
cards.a: The net forward reaction that follows only brings Q back to K; it does not undo the addition. If it consumed all the added reactant, the products would be higher while the reactants returned to their old values, making Q > K. So only part of the added reactant reacts, and its concentration ends higher than before.
cards.h: → products rise → Q = K needs reactant above its old value → added reactant only partly used
cards.n: 'The system uses up all the added reactant' earns nothing; Le Châtelier shifts only partly counteract a stress.
o: In the A ⇌ B example, 0.50 M A added to 0.20 M ends at 0.30 M: above 0.20 M, below 0.70 M.
Because K = [B]/[A] is fixed and [B] rises, [A] must also end higher to keep the ratio.

w.a: The added reactant is completely used up, so its concentration returns to the original value.
w.why: that would leave Q above K

w.a: The reactant concentration ends lower than before because the reaction shifts forward.
w.why: it ends between its old value and its value just after the addition

w.a: The reactant concentration ends higher because K increased.
w.why: K is unchanged at constant temperature

cards.q: Define the solubility product constant Ksp.
cards.a: Ksp is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a slightly soluble ionic solid into its aqueous ions, for example AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. It equals the product of the ion concentrations in a saturated solution, each raised to its coefficient; the solid is omitted. Like any K it depends only on temperature.
cards.h: → dissolution equilibrium, product of ion terms
cards.n: Ksp describes a saturated solution in contact with solid; ion concentrations in an unsaturated solution give Q, not Ksp.

cards.q: State the Ksp expression for Ca3(PO4)2(s) ⇌ 3Ca²⁺(aq) + 2PO4³⁻(aq).
cards.a: Ksp = [Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]². The solid is omitted. With molar solubility s, [Ca²⁺] = 3s and [PO₄³⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = (3s)³(2s)² = 27s³ × 4s² = 108s⁵.
cards.h: → two bracketed ion terms with exponents
cards.n: (3s)³ is 27s³, not 3s³; forgetting to raise the 3 and the 2 to their powers is the most common molar-solubility error.

cards.q: Define molar solubility.
cards.a: Molar solubility (s) is the number of moles of a solid that dissolve per liter of solution to make a saturated solution, in mol/L. It is related to Ksp through the dissolution stoichiometry: for AgCl, Ksp = s²; for CaF₂, Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³.
cards.h: → moles dissolved per liter at saturation
cards.n: Molar solubility and Ksp are different quantities; setting s equal to Ksp earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water given Ksp = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰.
cards.a: s = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻; each mole that dissolves gives s of each ion, so Ksp = s² = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M.
cards.h: → one square root
cards.n: The square-root shortcut works only for 1:1 salts; other formulas need the full stoichiometry.

cards.q: Compute Ksp for PbI2 given that its molar solubility is 1.5×10⁻³ M.
cards.h: → 4s³ form
cards.n: The 2 in 2I⁻ appears twice, as a multiplier inside the bracket and as the exponent; (1.5 × 10⁻³)(1.5 × 10⁻³)² earns nothing.

cards.q: Decide whether a precipitate forms when two solutions are mixed.
cards.a: Compute Q (the ion product) from the ion concentrations immediately after mixing, each corrected for dilution into the combined volume, and compare it with Ksp. Q > Ksp: a precipitate forms until Q falls to Ksp. Q = Ksp: exactly saturated. Q < Ksp: no precipitate.
cards.h: → dilute, compute Q, compare to Ksp
cards.n: Using the concentrations of the stock solutions, before dilution by mixing, earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the molar solubility of $CaF_2$ given $K_{sp}=3.9\times10^{-11}$.
cards.a: s = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M. CaF₂(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻, so [Ca²⁺] = s and [F⁻] = 2s: Ksp = (s)(2s)² = 4s³ = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹, so s³ = 9.75 × 10⁻¹² and s = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M.
cards.h: → set up with the 1:2 ion ratio
cards.n: Writing Ksp = s(2s) or s³ undercounts the fluoride and earns nothing.

cards.q: Decide whether a precipitate forms when 50.0 mL of 0.0020 M $Pb^{2+}$ is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.0020 M $Cl^{-}$, given $K_{sp}(PbCl_2)=1.7\times10^{-5}$.
cards.a: No precipitate forms. Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration: [Pb²⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 0.0010 M. Q = [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]² = (0.0010)(0.0010)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹, far below Ksp = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵, so the solution is unsaturated.
cards.h: → dilute first, then Q vs Ksp
cards.n: Forgetting to square [Cl⁻], or skipping the dilution, changes Q but here still gives Q < Ksp; the method, not luck, earns the point.

cards.q: $Ag_2CrO_4$ has $K_{sp}=1.1\times10^{-12}$. Compute its molar solubility in pure water.
cards.a: s = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M. Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻, so [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s: Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹², s³ = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³, s = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
cards.h: → 2:1 ion stoichiometry gives 4s³
cards.n: Note that Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble than AgCl (1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M) despite its smaller Ksp; Ksp alone cannot rank salts of different formula types.

cards.q:
Write the Ksp expression for each salt, and Ksp in terms of its molar solubility s in pure water:
(1) AgBr
(2) BaSO₄
(3) CaCO₃
(4) CaF₂
(5) PbI₂
(6) Ag₂CO₃
(7) Mg(OH)₂
(8) PbCl₂
(9) Cu(IO₃)₂
(10) Al(OH)₃
(11) Ag₃PO₄
(12) Ca₃(PO₄)₂
cards.a:
(1) → [Ag⁺][Br⁻] = s²
(2) → [Ba²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = s²
(3) → [Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻] = s²
(4) → [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² = 4s³
(5) → [Pb²⁺][I⁻]² = 4s³
(6) → [Ag⁺]²[CO₃²⁻] = 4s³
(7) → [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² = 4s³
(8) → [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]² = 4s³
(9) → [Cu²⁺][IO₃⁻]² = 4s³
(10) → [Al³⁺][OH⁻]³ = 27s⁴
(11) → [Ag⁺]³[PO₄³⁻] = 27s⁴
(12) → [Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]² = 108s⁵
cards.h: → twelve expressions, then the s form
cards.n: These s forms ignore any reaction of the anion with water (CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻); that pH effect belongs to Unit 8, not this calculation.

cards.q: Rank AgCl (Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰), Ag₂CrO₄ (Ksp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹²) and CaF₂ (Ksp = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹) from most to least soluble in water, by molar solubility.
cards.a: CaF₂ > Ag₂CrO₄ > AgCl. AgCl: s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M. Ag₂CrO₄: 4s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹², s = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M. CaF₂: 4s³ = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹, s = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M. The order is not the Ksp order, because AgCl is a 1:1 salt and the others are 1:2.
cards.h: → convert each Ksp to s, then rank
cards.n: Ranking straight from Ksp (AgCl first) earns nothing when the formula types differ.

cards.q: Calculate Ksp for Ag₂SO₄ given that a saturated solution contains 4.5 g of dissolved Ag₂SO₄ per liter (molar mass 311.8 g/mol).
cards.a: Ksp = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵. Molar solubility s = 4.5 g/L ÷ 311.8 g/mol = 1.44 × 10⁻² M. Ag₂SO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + SO₄²⁻, so [Ag⁺] = 2s = 2.89 × 10⁻² M and [SO₄²⁻] = 1.44 × 10⁻² M. Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³ = 4(1.44 × 10⁻²)³ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵.
cards.h: → g/L to mol/L, then 4s³
cards.n: Using grams per liter directly in Ksp, or [Ag⁺] = s, earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate Ksp for Mg(OH)₂ given that a saturated solution in pure water has [OH⁻] = 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ M.
cards.h: → the other ion from stoichiometry, then substitute
cards.n: Setting [Mg²⁺] = [OH⁻] gives 1.1 × 10⁻¹¹ and earns nothing; each Mg²⁺ comes with two OH⁻.

cards.q: Explain why you cannot rank the solubility of two salts by comparing their Ksp values when their formulas have different ion ratios.
cards.a: Ksp is a product of ion concentrations raised to powers set by the formula, so the same Ksp corresponds to different molar solubilities for a 1:1 salt (Ksp = s²) and a 1:2 salt (Ksp = 4s³). Each Ksp must be converted to s before ranking; Ag₂CrO₄ has the smaller Ksp but dissolves more than AgCl.
cards.h: → Ksp formula depends on ion ratio → same Ksp, different s → convert, then rank
cards.n: Direct Ksp comparison is valid only among salts with the same ion ratio, such as AgCl, AgBr and AgI.
o: Molar solubility is s = √Ksp for a 1:1 salt but (Ksp/4)^⅓ for a 1:2 salt; the cube root of a tiny number is far larger than its square root.
The exponents in Ksp come from stoichiometry, so Ksp is not a direct measure of how many moles dissolve.

w.a: The salt with the smaller Ksp is always less soluble.
w.why: true only for salts with the same ion ratio

w.a: You cannot compare them because Ksp values have different units.
w.why: units are not the issue; the exponents are

w.a: Salts with more ions in the formula are always more soluble.
w.why: solubility depends on Ksp and the formula together

cards.q: Explain why salts that the solubility rules call soluble, such as NaCl and KNO₃, have Ksp values greater than 1, while AgCl and BaSO₄ have Ksp ≪ 1.
cards.a: Ksp measures the extent of dissolution. A soluble salt dissolves until its ions reach high concentrations (several molar for NaCl), so their product exceeds 1. AgCl and BaSO₄ stop dissolving at about 10⁻⁵ M of each ion, so their ion products are near 10⁻¹⁰: 'insoluble' means Ksp ≪ 1, not zero.
cards.h: → Ksp = extent of dissolution → high ion concentrations → Ksp > 1; tiny ones → Ksp ≪ 1
cards.n: 'Insoluble salts have Ksp = 0' earns nothing; every salt dissolves to some small extent. (NaCl's Ksp near 37 is approximate.)
o: The solubility rules are a qualitative summary of Ksp: Ksp > 1 corresponds to salts listed as soluble.
A large Ksp means the dissolution equilibrium lies far toward the aqueous ions, which is what 'soluble' means.

w.a: Soluble salts have no Ksp because they dissolve completely.
w.why: soluble salts also reach a saturated equilibrium, with Ksp > 1

w.a: AgCl has a small Ksp because it dissolves slowly.
w.why: Ksp measures extent, not rate

w.a: NaCl has a large Ksp because it is made of small ions.
w.why: the point is how far dissolution goes, which the rules summarize

cards.q: Explain why adding more solid AgCl to a saturated AgCl solution does not increase the concentration of Ag⁺ in solution.
cards.a: The solution is already at equilibrium, with Q = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = Ksp. The solid is not in the Ksp expression, so adding more of it does not change Q; no net dissolution occurs, and the extra solid simply sits at the bottom while dissolving and precipitating continue at equal rates.
cards.h: → saturated: Q = Ksp → solid not in Q → Q unchanged → no net dissolution
cards.n: 'More solid means more dissolves' earns nothing once the solution is saturated.
o: At saturation the ion concentrations are fixed by Ksp at that temperature, whatever the amount of excess solid.
Adding solid increases both the dissolving and the precipitating surfaces equally, so the rates stay balanced.

w.a: More solid dissolves, raising [Ag⁺] until the solid runs out.
w.why: the solution is saturated; Q already equals Ksp

w.a: [Ag⁺] increases because Ksp increases with more solid.
w.why: Ksp depends only on temperature

w.a: The added solid stops all dissolving, so [Ag⁺] stays the same.
w.why: dissolving continues, balanced by precipitation

cards.q: Explain why mixing solutions that contain Pb²⁺ and Cl⁻ does not always produce a PbCl₂ precipitate, even though PbCl₂ is only slightly soluble.
cards.a: A precipitate forms only when the ion product Q = [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]² after mixing exceeds Ksp. If the diluted concentrations are small enough that Q < Ksp, the solution is unsaturated: dissolved PbCl₂ is below its solubility limit, so no solid appears.
cards.h: → precipitate needs Q > Ksp → dilute solutions give Q < Ksp → unsaturated → no solid
cards.n: 'Slightly soluble salts always precipitate' earns nothing; the comparison of Q with Ksp decides.
o: Every slightly soluble salt still has a nonzero solubility; below that concentration its ions stay dissolved.
Precipitation is the reverse of dissolution and runs net only when Q > Ksp.

w.a: No precipitate forms because PbCl₂ is soluble according to the rules.
w.why: PbCl₂ is slightly soluble; the concentrations are simply too low

w.a: The precipitate forms but is too small to see.
w.why: with Q < Ksp no solid forms at all

w.a: No precipitate forms because the ions have not had time to collide.
w.why: the reason is Q < Ksp, not rate

cards.q: Explain the common-ion effect on the solubility of a slightly soluble salt.
cards.a: A slightly soluble salt is less soluble in a solution that already contains one of its ions. The common ion is already present in the Ksp expression, so less of the salt has to dissolve before Q reaches Ksp; adding the ion to a saturated solution makes Q > Ksp and some salt precipitates. The molar solubility falls, while Ksp is unchanged.
cards.h: → common ion in Q → less dissolves; Ksp unchanged
cards.n: Arguing 'the solution is already full of ions' without naming the common ion and its effect on Q earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the molar solubility of AgCl (Ksp = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰) in 0.10 M NaCl.
cards.a: s = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M. [Cl⁻] = 0.10 + s ≈ 0.10 M, so Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = s(0.10) and s = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, about 7,000 times less than in pure water (1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M).
cards.h: → divide Ksp by the common-ion concentration
cards.n: Using s² = Ksp (the pure-water answer) ignores the 0.10 M chloride and earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the molar solubility of $CaF_2$ ($K_{sp}=3.9\times10^{-11}$) in 0.10 M NaF solution.
cards.a: s = 3.9 × 10⁻⁹ M. [F⁻] = 0.10 + 2s ≈ 0.10 M, so Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² = s(0.10)² and s = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹/0.010 = 3.9 × 10⁻⁹ M, about 50,000 times less than in pure water (2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M).
cards.h: → fix [F⁻] at 0.10 M, square it, solve for s
cards.n: Forgetting to square the 0.10 gives 3.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ M; the common ion enters with its exponent.

cards.q: Predict whether the molar solubility of $CaF_2$ increases, decreases, or stays the same when solid $Ca(NO_3)_2$ is added to a saturated $CaF_2$ solution.
cards.a: It decreases. Ca(NO₃)₂ dissolves completely and raises [Ca²⁺], an ion that CaF₂ shares, so Q = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² exceeds Ksp and CaF₂ precipitates until Q = Ksp again. Less CaF₂ can remain dissolved; Ksp is unchanged.
cards.h: → the common ion here is Ca²⁺, not F⁻
cards.n: Common-ion problems can add either ion of the salt; nitrate is a spectator, and calling the effect 'more ions, less room' earns nothing.

cards.q: Calculate the molar solubility of CaF₂ (Ksp = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹) in 0.010 M Ca(NO₃)₂, and compare it with its solubility in pure water (2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M).
cards.a: s = 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ M, about 7 times lower than in pure water. [Ca²⁺] = 0.010 + s ≈ 0.010 M and [F⁻] = 2s: Ksp = (0.010)(2s)² = 0.040s² = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹, so s² = 9.75 × 10⁻¹⁰ and s = 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ M. Check: s is 0.3% of 0.010 M, so the approximation holds.
cards.h: → fix [Ca²⁺], keep (2s)², solve
cards.n: Writing (s)² instead of (2s)² gives 6.2 × 10⁻⁵ M; each dissolved CaF₂ still releases two F⁻.

cards.q: Calculate Ksp for Ag₂CrO₄ given that its measured molar solubility in 0.050 M AgNO₃ is 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ M.
cards.a: Ksp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹². [CrO₄²⁻] = s = 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ M and [Ag⁺] = 0.050 + 2s ≈ 0.050 M, so Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] = (0.050)²(4.4 × 10⁻¹⁰) = (2.5 × 10⁻³)(4.4 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹², the same Ksp as in pure water.
cards.h: → [Ag⁺] from the AgNO₃, [CrO₄²⁻] = s
cards.n: Using 4s³ (the pure-water formula) gives 3.4 × 10⁻²⁸ and earns nothing: most of the Ag⁺ comes from the AgNO₃.

cards.q:
Identify whether the molar solubility of CaF₂ in each 0.10 M solution is lower than, or about the same as, its solubility in pure water, naming any common ion:
(1) NaF
(2) CaCl₂
(3) NaNO₃
(4) KF
(5) Ca(NO₃)₂
(6) NaCl
(7) KBr
(8) NH₄F
cards.a:
(1) → lower: common ion F⁻
(2) → lower: common ion Ca²⁺
(3) → about the same: no common ion
(4) → lower: common ion F⁻
(5) → lower: common ion Ca²⁺
(6) → about the same: no common ion
(7) → about the same: no common ion
(8) → lower: common ion F⁻
At equal concentration, an F⁻ source lowers the solubility far more (s = 3.9 × 10⁻⁹ M in 0.10 M NaF) than a Ca²⁺ source (s = 9.9 × 10⁻⁶ M in 0.10 M CaCl₂), because [F⁻] is squared in Ksp.
cards.h: → spot the shared ion in each
cards.n: 'About the same' ignores small ionic-strength effects that AP does not test. NH₄⁺ can react as a weak acid, but the F⁻ it brings dominates here.

cards.q: Predict what happens to the mass of undissolved AgCl, to [Ag⁺], and to Ksp when solid NaCl is dissolved in a saturated AgCl solution that sits over excess solid AgCl.
cards.a: The mass of solid AgCl increases, [Ag⁺] decreases, and Ksp is unchanged. The added Cl⁻ makes Q = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] > Ksp, so AgCl precipitates until Q = Ksp again; that removes Ag⁺ from solution, so the final [Ag⁺] is lower, while [Cl⁻] is much higher than before.
cards.h: → three predictions from Q > Ksp
cards.n: 'Ksp decreases because less dissolves' earns nothing: the solubility falls, the constant does not.

cards.q: Explain how the Ksp a student calculates for Ca(OH)₂ is affected if the saturated solution is accidentally prepared in 0.010 M CaCl₂ instead of water, the [OH⁻] is measured correctly, and the student still assumes [Ca²⁺] = ½[OH⁻].
cards.a: The calculated Ksp is too small. The common ion Ca²⁺ lowers the solubility of Ca(OH)₂, so the measured [OH⁻] is lower than in water. The true [Ca²⁺] is 0.010 M plus ½[OH⁻], but the student uses only ½[OH⁻], so both factors in Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]² are underestimated. The true Ksp has not changed.
cards.h: → lower [OH⁻] + missing Ca²⁺ → Ksp too low
cards.n: 'Ksp is lower in CaCl₂ solution' earns nothing: Ksp is a constant; the error is in the assumed [Ca²⁺].

cards.q: Explain why a common ion lowers the molar solubility of a salt but does not change its Ksp.
cards.a: Ksp is an equilibrium constant, fixed at a given temperature. The common ion is already part of the ion product, so less of the salt needs to dissolve before [cation]ˣ[anion]ʸ reaches Ksp. The amount dissolved (the solubility) falls; the constant it must reach does not.
cards.h: → Ksp fixed by T → common ion already in Q → less salt dissolves to reach Ksp
cards.n: 'Ksp decreases because the salt dissolves less' earns nothing; solubility and Ksp are different quantities.
o: Adding the common ion to a saturated solution makes Q > Ksp, so precipitation occurs until Q = Ksp again: the same Ksp is restored at a lower solubility.
Only temperature changes Ksp; the common ion changes how the ion product is shared between the two ions.

w.a: The common ion lowers Ksp, so less salt dissolves.
w.why: Ksp is unchanged; only the solubility falls

w.a: The common ion takes up space in the water, leaving less room for the salt.
w.why: the effect is equilibrium through Q, not space

w.a: Ksp stays the same because the common ion does not affect the salt at all.
w.why: it does affect the salt: it lowers the solubility

cards.q: Explain why dissolving NaNO₃ in a saturated AgCl solution does not lower the solubility of AgCl, while dissolving NaCl does.
cards.a: NaCl supplies Cl⁻, which appears in Q = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻], so Q exceeds Ksp and AgCl precipitates. NaNO₃ supplies Na⁺ and NO₃⁻, neither of which is in the expression, so Q is unchanged, still equals Ksp, and the solubility stays essentially the same.
cards.h: → common ion appears in Q → Q > Ksp → precipitation; no common ion → Q unchanged
cards.n: 'Any added salt lowers solubility' earns nothing; the ion must be one of the salt's own ions.
o: By Le Châtelier's principle, only adding a product of the dissolution (Ag⁺ or Cl⁻) shifts the equilibrium back toward the solid.
Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions for AgCl's dissolution equilibrium.

w.a: Both salts lower the solubility because both add ions to the solution.
w.why: only an ion in the Ksp expression shifts the equilibrium

w.a: NaNO₃ does not lower solubility because nitrates are always soluble.
w.why: NaNO₃'s own solubility is not the point; it shares no ion with AgCl
