w.a: NaCl lowers solubility because Na⁺ reacts with Ag⁺.
w.why: the common ion is Cl⁻, not Na⁺

cards.q: Explain why 0.10 M NaF lowers the solubility of CaF₂ far more than 0.10 M CaCl₂ does.
cards.a: In Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]², fluoride is squared. Fixing [F⁻] at 0.10 M puts 0.010 into the expression, leaving s = Ksp/0.010 = 3.9 × 10⁻⁹ M. Fixing [Ca²⁺] at 0.10 M leaves (2s)² = Ksp/0.10, so s = 9.9 × 10⁻⁶ M: the squared ion suppresses solubility much more.
cards.h: → F⁻ is squared in Ksp → fixing it removes more of the product → s much smaller
cards.n: 'Fluoride ions are smaller so they fit better' earns nothing; the exponent in Ksp is the reason.
o: With F⁻ fixed, s is inversely proportional to [F⁻]²; with Ca²⁺ fixed, s is inversely proportional only to the square root of [Ca²⁺].
The calculation shows s differs by a factor of about 2,500 between the two solutions.

w.a: Both lower the solubility equally because both are 0.10 M.
w.why: the ions enter Ksp with different exponents

w.a: CaCl₂ lowers it more because Ca²⁺ has a larger charge.
w.why: the charge is not the factor; the exponent on F⁻ is

w.a: NaF lowers it more because NaF is more soluble than CaCl₂.
w.why: both dissolve fully; the exponent decides

cards.q: Explain why the s in (0.10 + s) can be dropped when calculating the solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl.
cards.a: AgCl's solubility is tiny even in pure water (1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M), and the common ion lowers it further, to about 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M. Adding that to 0.10 M changes it by far less than 5%, so [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.10 M, and s is then found exactly from s = Ksp/0.10.
cards.h: → s tiny (small Ksp + common ion) → 0.10 + s ≈ 0.10 → check < 5%
cards.n: Dropping s in the Ag⁺ term as well ([Ag⁺] ≈ 0) earns nothing; s is only negligible beside 0.10.
o: Nearly all the chloride comes from the NaCl; the dissolving AgCl adds a negligible amount.
A check afterwards (1.8 × 10⁻⁹/0.10 = 2 × 10⁻⁸ = 0.000002%) confirms the approximation.

w.a: You drop s because AgCl does not dissolve in NaCl solution.
w.why: it dissolves slightly; s is small, not zero

w.a: You can drop s because Ksp is always much smaller than 0.10.
w.why: the comparison is between s and 0.10, and should be checked

w.a: s cancels out because it appears on both sides of the equation.
w.why: s does not cancel; it is negligible beside 0.10

cards.q: State the definitions of pH and pOH and the relationship between them at 25 °C.
cards.a: pH = −log[H3O⁺] and pOH = −log[OH⁻], so [H3O⁺] = $10^{-pH}$ and [OH⁻] = $10^{-pOH}$. Taking −log of Kw = [H3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ gives pH + pOH = pKw = 14.00 at 25 °C. At 25 °C only, pH below 7.00 is acidic and above 7.00 is basic.
cards.h: → two log definitions, then the Kw sum
cards.n: Stating 'pH + pOH = 14' as a law of nature earns nothing: it is Kw at 25 °C in log form, and at other temperatures the sum is that temperature's pKw.

cards.q: Explain the autoionization of water and write its equilibrium constant.
cards.a: Water molecules transfer protons to one another: H2O(l) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), one acting as acid and one as base. Kw = [H3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; liquid water is left out of the expression. The tiny K means pure water holds only 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M of each ion, about 2 ions per 10⁹ water molecules.
cards.h: → equation, then the constant and its value
cards.n: Writing Kw = [H3O⁺][OH⁻]/[H2O]² loses the point: pure liquids are omitted. Kw holds in every aqueous solution, not only in pure water.

cards.q: Explain how Kw and the pH of pure water change when the temperature is raised above 25 °C.
cards.a: Kw increases and the pH of pure water falls below 7.00, but the water stays neutral. Autoionization is endothermic (ΔH° ≈ +56 kJ/mol), so a higher temperature shifts it toward the ions. At 50 °C, Kw = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴, so [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻] = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ M and pH = pOH = 6.63. Neutral means [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻], which still holds.
cards.h: → direction of Kw, new pH, then the neutrality check
cards.n: 'Hot water is acidic' earns nothing: pH 7 marks neutral only at 25 °C. Borrows Unit 7's rule that heating an endothermic equilibrium raises K.

cards.q: Explain the significant-figure rule for a pH value.
cards.a: The number of decimal places in a pH equals the number of significant figures in [H3O⁺]. The digits before the decimal point only locate the power of ten, so they are not counted. So 0.025 M (2 significant figures) gives pH 1.60, and pH 4.30 converts back to 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ M (2 significant figures).
cards.h: → decimal places ↔ significant figures
cards.n: Counting the 1 in pH 1.60 as significant, then writing 1.602 or 1.6, is the slip; the digit before the point is just the exponent of ten.

cards.q: Compute [H3O⁺] in a solution whose pH is 4.30.
cards.a: [H3O⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ M. [H3O⁺] = $10^{-pH}$ = $10^{-4.30}$ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ M; the two decimal places in 4.30 give two significant figures. The solution is acidic, since 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ M is greater than 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M at 25 °C.
cards.h: → one antilog
cards.n: Typing 10^4.30 or −10^4.30 is the slip: a pH between 4 and 5 must give a concentration between 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁴ M.

cards.q: Compute the pOH of a solution with pH = 9.40 at 25 °C.
cards.a: pOH = 4.60. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = pKw = 14.00, so pOH = 14.00 − 9.40 = 4.60. That is [OH⁻] = $10^{-4.60}$ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ M, larger than [H3O⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ M, so the solution is basic.
cards.h: → one subtraction
cards.n: The 14.00 is Kw at 25 °C; at 50 °C (pKw = 13.26) the same pH would give pOH = 3.86, not 4.60.

cards.q: Compute $[OH^{-}]$ in a solution whose pOH is 5.60.
cards.h: → one antilog
cards.n: Reading pOH 5.60 as acidic because it is below 7 is the trap: a pOH below 7 means [OH⁻] > 10⁻⁷ M, a basic solution.

cards.q: Define an amphiprotic species and give an example.
cards.a: An amphiprotic species can either donate a proton (act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid) or accept one (act as a base), depending on its partner. Water is the key example: in autoionization one H2O donates H⁺ and another accepts it, H2O + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + OH⁻. HCO3⁻, H2PO4⁻ and HPO4²⁻ are also amphiprotic.
cards.h: → definition + an example reaction
cards.n: Having an H is not enough: NH4⁺ cannot accept a proton, so it is not amphiprotic. The Brønsted–Lowry definitions are Unit 4 (4.8) content.

cards.q: Calculate [OH⁻] and the pH of a solution at 25 °C in which [H3O⁺] = 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ M, and classify the solution as acidic, basic, or neutral.
cards.a: [OH⁻] = 3.1 × 10⁻⁶ M, pH = 8.49, basic. [OH⁻] = Kw/[H3O⁺] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)/(3.2 × 10⁻⁹) = 3.1 × 10⁻⁶ M, and pH = −log(3.2 × 10⁻⁹) = 8.49. The solution is basic because [OH⁻] > [H3O⁺] (pH above 7.00 at 25 °C).
cards.h: → Kw division, one log, one label
cards.n: Getting 9.49 or 8.51 is the usual log slip; [H3O⁺] between 10⁻⁹ and 10⁻⁸ M must give a pH between 8 and 9.

cards.q: Calculate the pH of pure water at 0 °C, where Kw = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, and state whether the water is acidic, basic, or neutral.
cards.a: pH = 7.48, and the water is neutral. In pure water [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻] = x, so x² = Kw = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ and x = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ M; pH = −log(3.3 × 10⁻⁸) = 7.48, and pOH = 7.48 as well. It is neutral because [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻], even though the pH is above 7.
cards.h: → square root of Kw, then −log
cards.n: Calling cold water basic because its pH exceeds 7 earns nothing; the 7.00 benchmark belongs to 25 °C only.

cards.q: Determine the factor by which [H3O⁺] changes when the pH of a solution falls from 6.40 to 4.10.
cards.a: [H3O⁺] increases by a factor of about 2.0 × 10² (200). Because [H3O⁺] = $10^{-pH}$, a drop of 2.30 pH units multiplies [H3O⁺] by $10^{2.30}$ = 2.0 × 10²: from 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ M to 7.9 × 10⁻⁵ M.
cards.h: → 10 raised to the pH difference
cards.n: 'About 2.3 times' or 'about 1.6 times' (6.40 ÷ 4.10) treats pH as linear; each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H3O⁺].

cards.q: Identify what the symbols H⁺(aq) and H3O⁺(aq) stand for in AP Chemistry, and state whether pH may be written as −log[H⁺].
cards.a: Both stand for the same species, the aqueous hydrogen ion: the CED uses 'hydrogen ion' and 'hydronium ion', H⁺(aq) and H3O⁺(aq), interchangeably. So pH = −log[H⁺] = −log[H3O⁺]. H3O⁺ is the more realistic picture, since a proton in water is always bonded to a water molecule, but either symbol is used on the exam.
cards.h: → same species, two symbols
cards.n: Treating [H⁺] and [H3O⁺] as different quantities, or adding them together, is the error; they are one concentration written two ways.

cards.q:
Calculate, for each solution at 25 °C, the missing values among [H3O⁺], [OH⁻], pH and pOH, and label it acidic, basic or neutral:
[H3O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M
[H3O⁺] = 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ M
[OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻² M
[OH⁻] = 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ M
pH = 7.00
pH = 2.70
pH = 11.52
pOH = 3.15
pOH = 12.40
pH = 6.20
[H3O⁺] = 0.50 M
[OH⁻] = 2.0 M
cards.h: → Kw links the ions; pH + pOH = 14.00 links the logs
cards.n: pH can be negative or above 14 for concentrated solutions; the idea that pH must lie between 0 and 14 is a trap.

cards.q: Explain why pure water at 50 °C is neutral even though its pH is 6.63.
cards.a: Neutral means [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻], and autoionization makes the two ions one-for-one. At 50 °C the larger Kw (5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) raises both to 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = pOH = 6.63. The pH-7 benchmark marks neutral only at 25 °C, where pKw = 14.00.
cards.h: → 2H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + OH⁻ makes ions 1:1 → [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻] at any T → larger Kw lowers pH and pOH equally
cards.n: 'Its pH is under 7 but no acid was added' restates the puzzle without the reason; the point needs [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻].
o: For any pure water pH = pOH = ½ pKw; at 50 °C pKw = 13.26, so the neutral pH there is 6.63.
Acidic means [H3O⁺] > [OH⁻], and nothing in pure water produces an extra H3O⁺ without an OH⁻ partner.

w.a: Water at 50 °C is slightly acidic because its pH is below 7.
w.why: applies the 25 °C benchmark at the wrong temperature

w.a: Heating water releases extra H⁺ ions, so it becomes acidic but only weakly.
w.why: ignores that every H3O⁺ formed comes with an OH⁻

w.a: It is neutral because pH + pOH still equals 14.
w.why: false: at 50 °C pH + pOH = pKw = 13.26

cards.q: Explain why a 0.10 M HCl solution still contains hydroxide ions.
cards.a: Water's autoionization equilibrium is present in every aqueous solution, so [H3O⁺][OH⁻] = Kw must still hold. With [H3O⁺] = 0.10 M, [OH⁻] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)/0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ M. The added H3O⁺ shifts 2H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + OH⁻ to the left, lowering [OH⁻] but never to zero.
cards.h: → Kw holds in every aqueous solution → [OH⁻] = Kw/[H3O⁺] → 10⁻¹³ M: tiny but not zero
cards.n: 'An acid has no OH⁻' is the trap; questions ask for [OH⁻] in acid solutions precisely to test Kw.
o: An equilibrium constant can be satisfied only if every species in it is present, so [OH⁻] cannot be zero while Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
By Le Châtelier's principle, added H3O⁺ pushes autoionization left, cutting [OH⁻] to 10⁻¹³ M without removing it.

w.a: An acid solution contains only H3O⁺ ions, so [OH⁻] is zero.
w.why: contradicts Kw, which holds in every aqueous solution

w.a: The HCl neutralizes all the OH⁻, so none can be left.
w.why: neutralization lowers [OH⁻] to Kw/[H3O⁺], not to zero

w.a: It has OH⁻ because HCl contains some basic impurities.
w.why: invents a cause; water itself supplies the OH⁻

cards.q: Explain why pH + pOH = 14.00 for every aqueous solution at 25 °C.
cards.a: Every aqueous solution at 25 °C is at autoionization equilibrium, so [H3O⁺][OH⁻] = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Taking −log of both sides turns the product into a sum: −log[H3O⁺] + (−log[OH⁻]) = −log Kw, that is, pH + pOH = pKw = 14.00.
cards.h: → [H3O⁺][OH⁻] = Kw → −log of a product is a sum of −logs → pH + pOH = pKw = 14.00
cards.n: Quoting the equation as its own reason ('because pH + pOH = 14') is circular and earns nothing; start from Kw.
o: pKw is defined as −log Kw, and the log of a product is the sum of the logs, so pH + pOH must equal pKw, which is 14.00 at 25 °C.
Raising [H3O⁺] tenfold must lower [OH⁻] tenfold to keep the product at Kw, so pH falls by 1 exactly as pOH rises by 1.

w.a: Because the pH scale runs from 0 to 14.
w.why: circular, and false: pH can lie outside 0 to 14

w.a: Because acids and bases always cancel out to give 14.
w.why: no such cancellation exists; the sum comes from Kw

w.a: Because pure water has pH 7 and pOH 7, which add to 14.
w.why: true for one case only; it does not explain every solution

cards.q: Explain why the value of Kw increases as the temperature of water increases.
cards.a: Autoionization, 2H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + OH⁻, is endothermic (ΔH° ≈ +56 kJ/mol, the reverse of exothermic neutralization). Heating favors the endothermic direction, so more ions form at equilibrium and Kw grows: 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ at 0 °C, 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 50 °C.
cards.h: → neutralization is exothermic → autoionization is endothermic → heat shifts it right → more ions → Kw rises
cards.n: 'Molecules move faster, so more ionize' is a rate argument and earns nothing; K changes with T through ΔH°. Borrows Unit 7's temperature effect on K.
o: Neutralization releases about 56 kJ per mole of water formed, so its reverse, autoionization, absorbs that energy; heating an endothermic equilibrium increases K.
The Kw values rise steadily with temperature, which is the signature of an endothermic reaction under Le Châtelier's principle.

w.a: Higher temperature makes molecules collide faster, so more water ionizes.
w.why: speed changes the rate, not the equilibrium position

w.a: Heating evaporates water, so the ions become more concentrated.
w.why: Kw is a property of the liquid and does not depend on evaporation

w.a: Kw increases because hot water is more acidic.
w.why: hot pure water is neutral; this reverses cause and effect

cards.q: State the seven strong acids that ionize essentially completely in water.
cards.a: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, HClO4 and H2SO4 (first proton only) are the six the CED names; HClO3, chloric acid, is the usual seventh and is also strong. Each ionizes completely, HA + H2O → H3O⁺ + A⁻, so [H3O⁺] equals the acid's initial concentration.
cards.h: → list of formulas, then what 'strong' means
cards.n: HF is weak even though HCl, HBr and HI are strong; H2SO4's second proton (HSO4⁻, Ka ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻²) is only weakly acidic.

cards.q: State which bases are treated as strong bases in AP Chemistry.
cards.a: The group 1 hydroxides (LiOH, NaOH, KOH, RbOH, CsOH) and the group 2 hydroxides, of which Ca(OH)2, Sr(OH)2 and Ba(OH)2 dissolve well enough to be used as solutions. What dissolves dissociates completely, so [OH⁻] equals the concentration of a group 1 hydroxide and twice the concentration of a group 2 hydroxide.
cards.h: → two families, then the OH⁻ count for each
cards.n: NH3 and amines are weak bases, not strong ones. Forgetting to double [OH⁻] for Ba(OH)2 or Ca(OH)2 is the standard pH error.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.025 M HNO3.
cards.a: pH = 1.60. HNO3 is a strong acid, HNO3 + H2O → H3O⁺ + NO3⁻, so [H3O⁺] = [NO3⁻] = 0.025 M and pH = −log(0.025) = 1.60. Essentially no HNO3 molecules remain, and [OH⁻] = Kw/0.025 = 4.0 × 10⁻¹³ M.
cards.h: → one log
cards.n: Setting up an ICE table with a Ka for HNO3 signals a misclassification; for a strong acid [H3O⁺] is simply the stated concentration.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.010 M Ba(OH)2 at 25 °C.
cards.h: → double the molarity, then pOH, then pH
cards.n: Skipping the factor of 2 gives 12.00; reporting −log(0.020) = 1.70 as the pH forgets that this log gives pOH.

cards.q: Calculate the pH after 10.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl is diluted with water to a total volume of 500.0 mL at 25 °C.
cards.a: pH = 2.70. Moles HCl = 0.0100 L × 0.100 M = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol, now in 0.5000 L, so [H3O⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.5000 L = 2.00 × 10⁻³ M (HCl stays completely ionized). pH = −log(2.00 × 10⁻³) = 2.70.
cards.h: → dilute the concentration, then one log
cards.n: Scaling the pH itself (pH 1.00 × 50) is meaningless; dilute the concentration first (M1V1 = M2V2), then take the log.

cards.q: Calculate the concentrations of H3O⁺, Cl⁻, OH⁻ and un-ionized HCl in 0.040 M HCl at 25 °C, and give the pH and pOH.
cards.a: [H3O⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 0.040 M, [HCl] ≈ 0, [OH⁻] = 2.5 × 10⁻¹³ M; pH = 1.40, pOH = 12.60. HCl ionizes completely (HCl + H2O → H3O⁺ + Cl⁻), turning every molecule into one H3O⁺ and one Cl⁻. Then [OH⁻] = Kw/[H3O⁺] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)/0.040, and pOH = 14.00 − 1.40.
cards.h: → complete ionization, then Kw for the minor ion
cards.n: Listing HCl molecules as a major species treats a strong acid as weak; the only HCl-derived species are H3O⁺ and Cl⁻.

cards.q: Calculate the pH at 25 °C of a solution made by dissolving 0.300 g of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) in enough water to make 250.0 mL of solution.
cards.a: pH = 12.48. n = 0.300 g ÷ 40.00 g/mol = 7.50 × 10⁻³ mol, and [NaOH] = 7.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.2500 L = 0.0300 M = [OH⁻], since NaOH dissociates completely. pOH = −log(0.0300) = 1.52; pH = 14.00 − 1.52 = 12.48.
cards.h: → grams → moles → molarity → pOH → pH
cards.n: Dividing by 250.0 instead of 0.2500 L, or stopping at the pOH, are the usual losses; a base's pH must come out above 7.

cards.q: Determine the molar concentration of a Sr(OH)2 solution whose pH is 12.60 at 25 °C.
cards.h: → pH → pOH → [OH⁻] → halve
cards.n: Reporting 0.040 M gives the hydroxide concentration, not the base's; for a group 2 hydroxide halve [OH⁻].

cards.q: Represent a particulate view of a small volume of 0.050 M Ba(OH)2(aq), drawn as if 4 formula units of Ba(OH)2 had dissolved (omit water molecules).
cards.a: The box holds 4 Ba²⁺ ions and 8 OH⁻ ions, all separate and scattered, with no intact Ba(OH)2 units and no ion pairs. The 1 Ba²⁺ : 2 OH⁻ count shows complete dissociation and the doubled [OH⁻] (0.10 M). No H3O⁺ is drawn, since [H3O⁺] = Kw/0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ M is far too small to appear.
cards.h: → counts of each particle, then what the counts show
cards.n: Drawing Ba(OH)2 units, or each Ba²⁺ attached to its OH⁻, shows incomplete dissociation and earns nothing.

cards.q:
Calculate the pH at 25 °C of each strong acid or strong base solution:
0.10 M HCl
0.0050 M HBr
1.0 M HNO3
2.5 × 10⁻³ M HClO4
0.035 M HI
3.2 × 10⁻⁵ M HNO3
2.0 M HCl
0.10 M NaOH
0.0020 M KOH
0.0075 M Ca(OH)2
5.0 × 10⁻⁴ M Ba(OH)2
0.25 M LiOH
0.0400 M Sr(OH)2
cards.h: → [H3O⁺] or [OH⁻] = C (×2 for group 2), then logs
cards.n: A negative pH (2.0 M HCl) is correct, not an error; and a strong base's pH is never −log of its molarity.

cards.q: Explain why [H3O⁺] in a strong acid solution equals the initial concentration of the acid.
cards.a: A strong acid ionizes completely: HA + H2O → H3O⁺ + A⁻ proceeds until no measurable HA remains. Each molecule produces exactly one H3O⁺, so 0.050 M HCl gives 0.050 M H3O⁺. Water's own H3O⁺ (at most 10⁻⁷ M, and suppressed further by the acid) is negligible beside it.
cards.h: → ionization is complete → 1 HA gives 1 H3O⁺ → [H3O⁺] = C; water's 10⁻⁷ M is negligible
cards.n: 'Because strong acids are concentrated' confuses strength with concentration and earns nothing; strength is the extent of ionization.
o: Its conjugate base (Cl⁻, NO3⁻) is too weak to take a proton back, so the reaction lies entirely on the product side and the 1:1 ratio gives [H3O⁺] = C.
No equilibrium table is needed: ionization of a strong acid goes to completion like a limiting-reactant problem.

w.a: Strong acids are more concentrated, so their [H3O⁺] is high.
w.why: strength is extent of ionization, not concentration

w.a: Every acid gives [H3O⁺] equal to its concentration.
w.why: false for weak acids, which ionize only a few percent

w.a: The H3O⁺ comes from the water, which the strong acid ionizes.
w.why: the H3O⁺ comes from the acid's protons; water's share is negligible

cards.q: Explain why 0.010 M Ba(OH)2 has a higher pH than 0.010 M NaOH.
cards.a: Both are strong bases that dissociate completely, but each Ba(OH)2 releases two OH⁻ (Ba(OH)2 → Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻) while each NaOH releases one. So [OH⁻] is 0.020 M versus 0.010 M: pOH 1.70 versus 2.00, and pH 12.30 versus 12.00.
cards.h: → both dissociate fully → 2 OH⁻ vs 1 OH⁻ per formula unit → [OH⁻] doubled → lower pOH, higher pH
cards.n: 'Ba(OH)2 is a stronger base' earns nothing; both are fully dissociated. The difference is the number of OH⁻ per formula unit.
o: At equal molarity the group 2 hydroxide supplies twice the OH⁻, and doubling [OH⁻] lowers pOH by log 2 = 0.30, raising pH by 0.30.
Dissociation stoichiometry, not base strength, sets [OH⁻] = 2C for Ba(OH)2 and C for NaOH.

w.a: Ba(OH)2 is a stronger base than NaOH, so its pH is higher.
w.why: both are strong; the extent of dissociation is the same

w.a: Barium is heavier than sodium, so Ba(OH)2 is more basic.
w.why: mass has nothing to do with [OH⁻]

w.a: Ba²⁺ reacts with water to make extra OH⁻.
w.why: Ba²⁺ is a spectator; the extra OH⁻ is the second hydroxide in the formula

cards.q: Explain why diluting a strong acid solution tenfold raises its pH by 1 unit.
cards.a: In a strong acid [H3O⁺] equals the acid concentration, and the acid stays fully ionized on dilution, so a tenfold dilution divides [H3O⁺] by exactly 10. Since pH = −log[H3O⁺] and −log(C/10) = −log C + 1, the pH rises by 1.00: 0.10 M HCl (pH 1.00) becomes 0.010 M (pH 2.00).
cards.h: → volume ×10 → [H3O⁺] ÷10 (still fully ionized) → −log adds 1 → pH rises 1.00
cards.n: The rule fails for very dilute acid (near 10⁻⁶ M), where water's own H3O⁺ matters; diluting an acid never pushes its pH above 7.
o: Each factor of 10 in [H3O⁺] is one pH unit, and complete ionization means [H3O⁺] changes by exactly the dilution factor.
A weak acid's pH rises only about 0.5 per tenfold dilution because its percent ionization increases; a strong acid has no such offset.

w.a: Adding water adds OH⁻, which neutralizes some of the acid.
w.why: water supplies equal H3O⁺ and OH⁻; the acid is simply spread out

w.a: Diluting weakens the acid, so it ionizes less.
w.why: dilution does not change strength; a strong acid stays fully ionized

w.a: The pH goes up by 10 because the volume is 10 times larger.
w.why: pH is logarithmic; a factor of 10 is one unit

cards.q: State the acid dissociation constant expression for a weak acid HA in water.
cards.a: HA(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq), with $K_{a} = \frac{[H_{3}O^{+}][A^{-}]}{[HA]}$ written with equilibrium concentrations; water, the solvent, is left out. pKa = −log Ka, so a larger Ka (smaller pKa) means a larger fraction ionized and a stronger weak acid.
cards.h: → equation, then products over reactant
cards.n: Putting initial concentrations or [H2O] into Ka, or writing the expression upside down, earns nothing.

cards.q: State the base ionization constant expression for a weak base B in water.
cards.a: B(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ HB⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), with $K_{b} = \frac{[HB^{+}][OH^{-}]}{[B]}$; water is omitted. For ammonia, NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻ and Kb = [NH4⁺][OH⁻]/[NH3] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. pKb = −log Kb.
cards.h: → equation, then products over the base
cards.n: Solving a Kb problem gives [OH⁻] and pOH first; reporting −log x as the pH skips the pOH step and is the classic slip.

cards.q: State the relationship between Ka and Kb for a conjugate acid-base pair.
cards.a: Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pKa + pKb = 14.00. Adding HA + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + A⁻ to A⁻ + H2O ⇌ HA + OH⁻ gives 2H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + OH⁻, and adding reactions multiplies their K values. Example: Ka(HF) = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴ gives Kb(F⁻) = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹.
cards.h: → product equals Kw, with the reason
cards.n: It holds only for a conjugate pair (HF/F⁻, NH4⁺/NH3), never for two unrelated species. The multiply-K rule for summed reactions is Unit 7.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid, Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵.
cards.a: pH = 2.87. CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + CH3COO⁻; with x = [H3O⁺] = [CH3COO⁻], Ka = x²/(0.10 − x) ≈ x²/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, so x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.3 × 10⁻³ M and pH = −log(1.34 × 10⁻³) = 2.87. x is 1.3% of 0.10 M, so dropping it from 0.10 − x was justified.
cards.h: → ICE, x² over C, square root, −log
cards.n: Treating acetic acid as strong ([H3O⁺] = 0.10 M, pH 1.00) is the trap; a weak acid is only slightly ionized.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.10 M NH3, Kb = 1.8×10⁻⁵.
cards.h: → ICE for OH⁻, pOH, then pH
cards.n: Reporting 2.87 as the pH forgets that x is [OH⁻]; a weak base solution must have a pH above 7.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.50 M HF, given $K_a=7.2\times10^{-4}$.
cards.a: pH = 1.72. HF + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + F⁻; x²/(0.50 − x) ≈ x²/0.50 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴, so x = √(3.6 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.019 M = [H3O⁺] and pH = −log(0.019) = 1.72. x is 3.8% of 0.50 M, under 5%, so the approximation holds (the quadratic gives 0.0186 M, pH 1.73).
cards.h: → x = √(Ka·C), check 5%, −log
cards.n: HF is weak despite being a hydrogen halide; setting [H3O⁺] = 0.50 M (pH 0.30) treats it as strong.

cards.q: Define percent ionization of a weak acid and state how to calculate it.
cards.a: Percent ionization = ([A⁻]eq ÷ [HA]initial) × 100%, which for a weak acid alone equals ([H3O⁺]eq ÷ [HA]initial) × 100%: the percentage of the acid molecules originally added that have donated a proton. It is found from Ka and the initial concentration (solve for x), or from the initial concentration and any one measured equilibrium concentration, such as [H3O⁺] from the pH.
cards.h: → ionized over initial, times 100
cards.n: Dividing by the equilibrium [HA] instead of the initial concentration, or dividing by Ka, gives a number with no meaning.

cards.q: Compute the percent ionization of a 0.050 M weak acid with $K_a=2.0\times10^{-4}$.
cards.a: About 6.3% (6.1% by the quadratic). x = √(Ka·C) = √((2.0 × 10⁻⁴)(0.050)) = 3.2 × 10⁻³ M, and (3.2 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.050) × 100% = 6.3%. Because 6.3% is above the 5% guideline, the quadratic x² + (2.0 × 10⁻⁴)x − 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 0 is more exact: x = 3.1 × 10⁻³ M, 6.1%.
cards.h: → x = √(Ka·C), then x ÷ C × 100
cards.n: Percent ionization falls as C rises, so a more concentrated weak acid ionizes a smaller percentage despite its lower pH.

cards.q: Explain how the percent ionization of a weak acid changes as the solution is diluted.
cards.a: Percent ionization increases on dilution, even though [H3O⁺] falls and the pH rises. With x ≈ √(Ka·C), percent ionization ≈ √(Ka/C) × 100%, which grows as C shrinks: 0.10 M acetic acid is 1.3% ionized, 0.0010 M about 12.5%. Diluting lowers Q = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] below Ka (two factors shrink on top, one below), so ionization shifts forward.
cards.h: → direction, then the √(Ka/C) or Q < K reason
cards.n: Dilution raises percent ionization but never makes a weak acid strong, and Ka itself does not change; only temperature changes Ka.

cards.q: Compute Ka for a 0.20 M weak acid whose measured pH is 3.00.
cards.a: Ka = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶. [H3O⁺] = $10^{-3.00}$ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M = [A⁻], since each ionization makes one of each. [HA] = 0.20 − 0.0010 = 0.199 M ≈ 0.20 M. Ka = (1.0 × 10⁻³)²/0.199 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ (the acid is 0.50% ionized).
cards.h: → pH gives x, then Ka = x²/(C − x)
cards.n: Using [HA] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M, or writing Ka = x/C, are the usual setup errors; the pH fixes x and the recipe fixes C.

cards.q: Rank three weak acids by the pH of their 0.10 M solutions, given $K_a$ values $1.8\times10^{-5}$, $6.3\times10^{-3}$, and $4.0\times10^{-8}$.
cards.a: Lowest to highest pH: Ka = 6.3 × 10⁻³ (pH ≈ 1.65) < Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ (pH 2.87) < Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ (pH 4.20). At the same starting concentration a larger Ka means a larger fraction ionized and more H3O⁺ ([H3O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C)), so a lower pH. The first acid is 22% ionized, so its value comes from the quadratic.
cards.h: → ordered list, lowest pH first, then one reason
cards.n: Equal 0.10 M concentrations make Ka the only variable; at different concentrations a larger Ka need not give the lower pH.

cards.q: State the definition of pKa and how it relates to acid strength.
cards.a: pKa = −log Ka, so Ka = $10^{-pKa}$. A smaller pKa means a larger Ka and a stronger acid, and each 1-unit drop in pKa is a 10-fold rise in Ka. Example: HF (pKa 3.14, Ka 7.2 × 10⁻⁴) is a stronger acid than acetic acid (pKa 4.74, Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵).
cards.h: → negative log, inverse ordering
cards.n: Ranking acids as if a higher pKa meant a stronger acid reverses the order; the strongest acid has the lowest pKa.

cards.q: Compute the $pK_b$ of the conjugate base of a weak acid with $pK_a = 4.60$.
cards.a: pKb = 9.40. For a conjugate pair at 25 °C, pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.00, so pKb = 14.00 − 4.60 = 9.40, i.e., Kb = $10^{-9.40}$ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. The acid (Ka = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵) therefore has a much weaker conjugate base.
cards.h: → one subtraction from 14.00
cards.n: The relationship holds only for a genuine conjugate pair at 25 °C, not for any acid and base you happen to be given.

cards.q: Predict which is the stronger acid: one with $pK_a = 3.2$ or one with $pK_a = 8.1$.
cards.a: The acid with pKa 3.2 is stronger. Ka = $10^{-pKa}$ gives Ka ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁴ versus ≈ 8 × 10⁻⁹, so the lower-pKa acid ionizes further and gives a lower pH at equal concentration. The two Ka values differ by $10^{4.9}$, about 8 × 10⁴.
cards.h: → which acid, plus the Ka comparison
cards.n: '8.1 is bigger, so that acid is stronger' reads pKa as if it were Ka; the lower pKa is the larger Ka and the stronger acid.

cards.q: Rank the equilibrium concentrations of CH3COOH, H3O⁺, CH3COO⁻ and OH⁻ in 0.10 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) at 25 °C, from highest to lowest.
cards.a: [CH3COOH] ≈ 0.099 M > [H3O⁺] = [CH3COO⁻] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ M > [OH⁻] = 7.5 × 10⁻¹² M. Only 1.3% of the acid ionizes, so almost all of it stays as molecules; each ionization makes one H3O⁺ and one CH3COO⁻ (water's own H3O⁺ is negligible); and [OH⁻] = Kw/[H3O⁺] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)/(1.34 × 10⁻³).
cards.h: → ordered list with values, then why each sits there
cards.n: Ranking CH3COO⁻ above CH3COOH treats the acid as mostly ionized; a weak acid solution is mostly un-ionized molecules.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, particulate views of equal volumes of 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M HF, each drawn as if 10 acid molecules had been dissolved (omit water molecules).
cards.a: HCl box: no HCl molecules; 10 H3O⁺ and 10 Cl⁻ ions, separate and scattered. HF box: 9 intact H–F molecules plus 1 H3O⁺ and 1 F⁻ (0.10 M HF is about 8% ionized, Ka = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴). The HCl box shows complete ionization and the HF box shows that most weak-acid molecules stay un-ionized; each box has equal numbers of H3O⁺ and anions.
cards.h: → particle counts for each box, then what they show
cards.n: Drawing some HCl molecules left intact, or HF mostly ionized, earns nothing; the two boxes must differ in the fraction ionized.

cards.q: Calculate the percent ionization and the value of Ka for a 0.150 M solution of a weak acid HA whose equilibrium [A⁻] is 2.1 × 10⁻³ M.
cards.h: → ratio × 100, then Ka from the same numbers
cards.n: Dividing 2.1 × 10⁻³ by the equilibrium [HA] instead of the initial 0.150 M, or squaring [HA], are the setup errors.

cards.q:
Calculate the pH at 25 °C of each weak acid or weak base solution (use x ≈ √(K·C) and check that x is under 5% of C):
0.20 M HCOOH, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴
0.050 M HCN, Ka = 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰
0.10 M HOCl, Ka = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸
0.10 M C6H5COOH, Ka = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵
1.0 M HNO2, Ka = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴
0.30 M CH3COOH, pKa = 4.74
0.080 M HA, pKa = 5.00
0.040 M HF, Ka = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴
0.50 M CH3NH2, Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴
0.20 M NH3, pKb = 4.74
0.15 M C5H5N, Kb = 1.7 × 10⁻⁹
0.25 M N2H4, Kb = 1.3 × 10⁻⁶
cards.h: → x = √(K·C) → [H3O⁺] or [OH⁻] → pH
cards.n: All twelve are weak: setting [H3O⁺] = C, as for a strong acid, is the trap. For the bases x is [OH⁻], so find pOH first.

cards.q: Explain why 0.10 M HF has a higher pH than 0.10 M HCl.
cards.a: HCl is a strong acid and ionizes completely, so [H3O⁺] = 0.10 M (pH 1.00). HF is weak (Ka = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴): its equilibrium lies to the left and only about 8% of the molecules ionize, so [H3O⁺] ≈ 8 × 10⁻³ M (pH ≈ 2.1). Less H3O⁺ means a higher pH.
cards.h: → HCl ionizes fully → HF's equilibrium lies left (small Ka) → less H3O⁺ from HF → higher pH
cards.n: 'HF is weaker' with no link to how much H3O⁺ each makes restates the claim; the point needs extent of ionization → [H3O⁺].
o: At equal concentration [H3O⁺] = C for the strong acid but only about √(Ka·C) for the weak one, and less H3O⁺ is a higher pH.
Cl⁻ cannot hold a proton while F⁻ recaptures protons, so most HF stays as molecules and fewer H3O⁺ ions form.

w.a: HF has a higher pH because it is less concentrated than HCl.
w.why: both are 0.10 M; the difference is extent of ionization

w.a: HF has fewer hydrogen atoms available, so it makes fewer H⁺ ions.
w.why: each molecule has one H; the issue is how many donate it

w.a: HF has a higher pH because fluorine is more electronegative and holds its H tighter.
w.why: electronegativity would predict the opposite; the evidence is HF's small Ka

cards.q: Explain why [OH⁻] in 0.10 M NH3 is far lower than 0.10 M.
cards.a: NH3 is a weak base: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻ has Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, so the equilibrium lies far to the left. Only about 1.3% of the NH3 molecules accept a proton from water, giving [OH⁻] ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ M; the other 98.7% remain as NH3 molecules.
cards.h: → NH3 must take H⁺ from water → small Kb → equilibrium lies left → only ~1% forms OH⁻
cards.n: 'NH3 has no OH in its formula' misses the mechanism; it makes OH⁻ by taking protons from water, just not many.
o: Unlike NaOH, NH3 contains no hydroxide; it makes OH⁻ only by proton transfer from water, and the small Kb means few transfers occur.
Solving Kb = x²/0.10 gives x = 1.3 × 10⁻³ M, so [OH⁻] is about 1% of the base's concentration.

w.a: NH3 is a strong base, so [OH⁻] equals 0.10 M.
w.why: misclassifies NH3; only group 1 and 2 hydroxides are strong

w.a: Most of the OH⁻ reacts with NH4⁺ as soon as it forms, so none is left.
w.why: the reverse reaction balances the forward one; it does not remove all OH⁻

w.a: The NH3 escapes from the solution as a gas before it can react.
w.why: irrelevant; the limit is the small equilibrium constant

cards.q: Explain why, at equal concentrations, the weak acid with the larger Ka gives the lower pH.
cards.a: Ka = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] measures how far ionization goes at equilibrium. From the same starting concentration C, a larger Ka means a larger fraction of HA ionized ([H3O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C)), so more H3O⁺ in solution, and more H3O⁺ is a lower pH.
cards.h: → larger Ka → equilibrium further toward ions → more H3O⁺ at the same C → lower pH
cards.n: 'A bigger Ka is a stronger acid' without the H3O⁺ link skips the step that connects K to pH.
o: With equal C, [H3O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C) depends only on Ka, and pH = −log[H3O⁺] falls as that root grows.
A larger Ka means a weaker conjugate base that recaptures fewer protons, leaving more H3O⁺ free.

w.a: The acid with the larger Ka has more hydrogen atoms, so it gives more H⁺.
w.why: Ka is not a count of H atoms

w.a: A larger Ka makes the acid ionize faster, so the pH drops.
w.why: Ka describes how far the equilibrium lies, not the rate

w.a: The acid with the larger Ka is more concentrated.
w.why: the concentrations are stated to be equal

cards.q: Explain why x can usually be dropped from (C − x) when calculating the pH of a weak acid solution.
cards.a: A weak acid with a small Ka ionizes only slightly, so x (the amount ionized) is tiny next to C: 0.10 − 0.0013 ≈ 0.10 M for acetic acid. Dropping it changes the answer by less than the data's precision. The check is x/C ≤ 5%; if it fails (0.040 M HF, 13%), solve the quadratic.
cards.h: → small Ka → only a few % ionizes → x ≪ C → C − x ≈ C; verify x/C ≤ 5% afterward
cards.n: Claiming x is always negligible earns nothing; the justification is the size of x relative to C, checked after solving.
o: Because x/C is only a few percent, C − x differs from C by less than the uncertainty in C, so the shortcut costs no significant figures.
The shortcut is safe when C/Ka is above about 400; a very dilute or fairly strong weak acid breaks it.

w.a: x is always zero because weak acids do not ionize.
w.why: weak acids do ionize; x is small, not zero

w.a: x can be dropped because Ka is small, whatever the concentration is.
w.why: at low C the ionized fraction grows and the shortcut fails

w.a: x cancels because it appears on both sides of the equation.
w.why: nothing cancels; x is neglected, not cancelled

cards.q: Explain why pKa + pKb = 14.00 for a conjugate acid-base pair at 25 °C.
cards.a: The acid's reaction (HA + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + A⁻, Ka) plus its conjugate base's reaction (A⁻ + H2O ⇌ HA + OH⁻, Kb) add up to 2H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + OH⁻. Adding reactions multiplies their constants, so Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, and taking −log gives pKa + pKb = 14.00.
cards.h: → Ka reaction + Kb reaction = autoionization → the K values multiply → Ka·Kb = Kw → −log gives 14.00
cards.n: Asserting 'an acid and a base always make 14' earns nothing; the two reactions must be summed. Borrows Unit 7's rules for K.
o: Multiplying the Ka and Kb expressions cancels [HA] and [A⁻], leaving [H3O⁺][OH⁻], which is Kw.
Because the product is fixed at Kw, a stronger acid (larger Ka) must have a weaker conjugate base (smaller Kb).

w.a: Because every acid and base together add up to pH 14.
w.why: confuses pKa and pKb with pH and pOH; the reason is Kw

w.a: Because Ka and Kb are always both equal to 10⁻⁷.
w.why: false; only their product is fixed

w.a: It holds for any acid and any base in the same solution.
w.why: only for a conjugate pair, whose reactions sum to autoionization

cards.q: Predict whether a salt formed from a strong acid and a strong base gives an acidic, basic, or neutral solution.
cards.a: Neutral: pH 7.00 at 25 °C. The ions, e.g., Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from NaOH + HCl, are the conjugates of a strong base and a strong acid: Cl⁻ is too weak a base and Na⁺ too weak an acid to react with water, so [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻] as in pure water. The same reasoning puts a strong acid–strong base equivalence point at pH 7.
cards.h: → one word plus a reason about each ion
cards.n: Group 1 and heavy group 2 cations and the anions of strong acids (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻, NO3⁻, ClO4⁻) never change the pH.

cards.q: Predict the acid-base character of a solution of sodium acetate, NaC2H3O2.
cards.a: Basic. Na⁺ is a spectator, but C2H3O2⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HC2H3O2 (Kb = Kw/Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰), so C2H3O2⁻ + H2O ⇌ HC2H3O2 + OH⁻ makes a little OH⁻. This is the solution present at the equivalence point when acetic acid is titrated with NaOH.
cards.h: → one word plus the hydrolysis equation
cards.n: 'Basic because it contains sodium' earns nothing; Na⁺ is a spectator and the acetate ion does the work.

cards.q: Predict the acid-base character of a solution of ammonium chloride, NH4Cl.
cards.a: Acidic. Cl⁻ is a spectator (the conjugate base of a strong acid), but NH4⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH3 (Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰): NH4⁺ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O⁺. This is the solution present at the equivalence point when NH3 is titrated with HCl.
cards.h: → one word plus the hydrolysis equation
cards.n: Writing NH4⁺ + OH⁻, or saying Cl⁻ makes it acidic, misassigns the ion; the weak acid NH4⁺ gives H⁺ to water.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.10 M NaF given Ka(HF) = 7.2×10⁻⁴.
cards.h: → Kb from Ka, then a weak-base ICE
cards.n: Using Ka directly on the F⁻ ion (and getting an acidic pH) is the classic mistake; the anion is a base, so convert to Kb first.

cards.q: Predict whether a solution of $NH_4F$ is acidic, basic, or neutral, given $K_a(NH_4^+)=5.6\times10^{-10}$ and $K_b(F^-)=1.4\times10^{-11}$.
cards.a: Acidic. Both ions react with water: NH4⁺ as a weak acid (Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, making H3O⁺) and F⁻ as a weak base (Kb = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹, making OH⁻). Since Ka(NH4⁺) is about 40 times Kb(F⁻), more H3O⁺ forms than OH⁻ and the solution is slightly acidic.
cards.h: → compare Ka of the cation with Kb of the anion
cards.n: Naming only one ion's reaction is incomplete when both are weak; the explicit Ka versus Kb comparison is what earns the point.

cards.q: Predict whether an aqueous solution of $Na_2CO_3$ tests as acidic, basic, or neutral, and identify the ion responsible.
cards.a: Basic; the carbonate ion is responsible. CO3²⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HCO3⁻ (Ka2 = 4.7 × 10⁻¹¹), so Kb = Kw/Ka2 = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ and CO3²⁻ + H2O ⇌ HCO3⁻ + OH⁻ produces OH⁻. Na⁺ does not react with water.
cards.h: → verdict, the ion, and its hydrolysis equation
cards.n: Using Ka1 of H2CO3 (4.3 × 10⁻⁷) to get Kb of CO3²⁻ pairs it with the wrong acid; CO3²⁻ is the conjugate base of HCO3⁻.

cards.q: Identify two laboratory ways to prepare a buffer of a given pH.
cards.a: (1) Mix a weak acid with a soluble salt of its conjugate base (e.g., CH3COOH + NaCH3COO) in the mole ratio Henderson–Hasselbalch gives for the target pH. (2) Partly neutralize a weak acid with less than one equivalent of strong base (or a weak base with less strong acid): HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O goes to completion and leaves both HA and A⁻, e.g., 0.10 mol CH3COOH + 0.050 mol NaOH gives 0.050 mol of each.
cards.h: → two methods, each naming what is mixed
cards.n: In method 2 the strong reagent must be limiting; adding one full equivalent leaves only A⁻, which is not a buffer.

cards.q: Identify the products when $HSO_3^-$ reacts as an acid with $OH^-$, and as a base with $H_3O^+$.
cards.a: As an acid: HSO3⁻ + OH⁻ → SO3²⁻ + H2O. As a base: HSO3⁻ + H3O⁺ → H2SO3 + H2O. Both proton transfers go essentially to completion because OH⁻ and H3O⁺ are the strongest base and acid that can exist in water, just as any weak acid reacts completely with a strong base and any weak base with a strong acid.
cards.h: → two balanced equations
cards.n: Sulfur stays +4 in both products; writing SO4²⁻ or H2SO4 turns a proton transfer into a redox reaction.

cards.q: Identify the two Bronsted-Lowry conjugate acid-base pairs in $HCO_3^{-}+H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3+OH^{-}$.
cards.a: H2CO3/HCO3⁻ and H2O/OH⁻. HCO3⁻ acts as the base: it gains H⁺ to become its conjugate acid, H2CO3. H2O acts as the acid: it loses H⁺ to become its conjugate base, OH⁻. Each pair differs by exactly one H⁺; the reaction has the weak acid + weak base form HA + B ⇌ A⁻ + HB⁺, with water as HA.
cards.h: → two paired formulas, with the role of each
cards.n: Pairing HCO3⁻ with OH⁻, or H2O with H2CO3, is the error: partners differ by exactly one H⁺. The definitions are Unit 4 content.

cards.q: Define a conjugate acid-base pair.
cards.a: Two species whose formulas differ by exactly one H⁺ (and one unit of charge): an acid HA and the base A⁻ it becomes after donating a proton, or a base B and the acid HB⁺ it becomes after accepting one. In HA + B ⇌ A⁻ + HB⁺ there are two pairs, HA/A⁻ and HB⁺/B; the stronger the acid of a pair, the weaker its partner base.
cards.h: → differ by one proton
cards.n: H2SO4 and SO4²⁻ differ by two protons, so they are not a conjugate pair; neither are NH4⁺ and NH2⁻. Definition from Unit 4 (4.8).

cards.q: Calculate the pH at 25 °C after 40.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH is mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.120 M HCl.
cards.h: → moles, react, excess ÷ total volume, then pH
cards.n: Dividing by one solution's volume instead of the 65.0 mL total, or averaging the two starting pH values, loses the point.

cards.q: Calculate the pH after 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH is added to 50.0 mL of 0.100 M HNO2 (Ka = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴).
cards.a: pH = 3.52. HNO2 + OH⁻ → NO2⁻ + H2O goes to completion: 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol HNO2 − 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻ leaves 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol HNO2 and forms 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol NO2⁻. The weak acid is in excess, so the mixture is a buffer: pH = pKa + log(3.00/2.00) = 3.35 + 0.18 = 3.52.
cards.h: → react in moles, then Henderson–Hasselbalch
cards.n: This mixing calculation is in scope (8.4.A.2); what is excluded is computing the pH change when acid or base is added to an existing buffer.

cards.q: Calculate the pH after 25.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl is added to 25.0 mL of 0.200 M NH3 (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵).
cards.a: pH = 5.13. NH3 + H3O⁺ → NH4⁺ + H2O is complete and the amounts are equal (5.00 × 10⁻³ mol each), leaving 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol NH4⁺ in 0.0500 L = 0.100 M. NH4⁺ is a weak acid with Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, so [H3O⁺] = √((5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰)(0.100)) = 7.5 × 10⁻⁶ M and pH = 5.13.
cards.h: → react to completion, then treat NH4⁺ as a weak acid
cards.n: Calling the equimolar mixture neutral (pH 7) ignores that NH4⁺ is a weak acid; forgetting the doubled volume gives 0.200 M and pH 4.98.

cards.q: Calculate the equilibrium constant for CH3COOH(aq) + NH3(aq) ⇌ CH3COO⁻(aq) + NH4⁺(aq), given Ka(CH3COOH) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and Kb(NH3) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, and state which side is favored.
cards.a: K = 3.2 × 10⁴, so products are favored. The reaction is the sum of CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + CH3COO⁻ (Ka) and NH3 + H3O⁺ ⇌ NH4⁺ + H2O (K = Kb/Kw), so K = Ka·Kb/Kw = (1.8 × 10⁻⁵)(1.8 × 10⁻⁵)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 3.2 × 10⁴. K > 1 because CH3COOH is a stronger acid than NH4⁺ (Ka 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰).
cards.h: → add two reactions, multiply their K values
cards.n: Multiplying Ka × Kb without dividing by Kw gives 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ and the wrong side; weak acid + weak base reaches equilibrium, not completion.

cards.q:
Write the net ionic equation for the reaction that occurs when each pair of solutions is mixed:
HCl + NaOH
HNO3 + Ba(OH)2
CH3COOH + NaOH
HF + KOH
HCN + NaOH
NH3 + HCl
CH3NH2 + HNO3
NaF + HCl
NaCH3COO + HBr
NH4Cl + NaOH
HNO2 + NH3
CH3COOH + NaF
cards.a:
HCl + NaOH → (H3O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H2O)
HNO3 + Ba(OH)2 → (H3O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H2O)
CH3COOH + NaOH → (CH3COOH + OH⁻ → CH3COO⁻ + H2O)
HF + KOH → (HF + OH⁻ → F⁻ + H2O)
HCN + NaOH → (HCN + OH⁻ → CN⁻ + H2O)
NH3 + HCl → (NH3 + H3O⁺ → NH4⁺ + H2O)
CH3NH2 + HNO3 → (CH3NH2 + H3O⁺ → CH3NH3⁺ + H2O)
NaF + HCl → (F⁻ + H3O⁺ → HF + H2O)
NaCH3COO + HBr → (CH3COO⁻ + H3O⁺ → CH3COOH + H2O)
NH4Cl + NaOH → (NH4⁺ + OH⁻ → NH3 + H2O)
HNO2 + NH3 → (HNO2 + NH3 ⇌ NO2⁻ + NH4⁺, an equilibrium with K ≈ 8 × 10⁵)
CH3COOH + NaF → (CH3COOH + F⁻ ⇌ CH3COO⁻ + HF, an equilibrium with K ≈ 0.025)
cards.h: → weak species stay whole; strong ones split into ions
cards.n: Writing a weak acid as H⁺ + A⁻, or keeping Na⁺ and Cl⁻ spectators, loses the point; weak + strong goes to completion (→), weak + weak to equilibrium (⇌).

cards.q:
Classify each 0.10 M salt solution as acidic, basic, or neutral:
KCl
NaF
NH4NO3
NaNO3
K2CO3
NaCH3COO
CH3NH3Cl
LiBr
NaCN
KClO4
Ca(NO3)2
NaHCO3
Na3PO4
KNO2
NaHSO4
C5H5NHCl
NaOCl
BaCl2
NH4CN
cards.a:
KCl → neutral (both ions are spectators)
NaF → basic (F⁻ is a weak base)
NH4NO3 → acidic (NH4⁺ is a weak acid)
NaNO3 → neutral
K2CO3 → basic (CO3²⁻, Kb 2.1 × 10⁻⁴)
NaCH3COO → basic (acetate)
CH3NH3Cl → acidic (CH3NH3⁺ is a weak acid)
LiBr → neutral
NaCN → basic (CN⁻, Kb 1.6 × 10⁻⁵)
KClO4 → neutral
Ca(NO3)2 → neutral
NaHCO3 → basic (HCO3⁻: Kb 2.3 × 10⁻⁸ > Ka2 4.7 × 10⁻¹¹)
Na3PO4 → basic (PO4³⁻ is a fairly strong weak base)
KNO2 → basic (NO2⁻)
NaHSO4 → acidic (HSO4⁻, Ka 1.2 × 10⁻²)
C5H5NHCl → acidic (pyridinium, Ka 5.9 × 10⁻⁶)
NaOCl → basic (OCl⁻, Kb 3.3 × 10⁻⁷)
BaCl2 → neutral
NH4CN → basic (Kb of CN⁻ 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ > Ka of NH4⁺ 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰)
cards.h: → each ion: conjugate of a strong species or of a weak one?
cards.n: Judging by an H or OH in the formula fails (NaHCO3 is basic); ask what each ion does with water, and compare Ka with Kb when both react.

cards.q: Explain why adding 0.050 mol NaOH to 0.10 mol CH3COOH in water produces a buffer.
cards.a: OH⁻ is the limiting reactant and reacts completely, CH3COOH + OH⁻ → CH3COO⁻ + H2O, turning 0.050 mol of acid into 0.050 mol CH3COO⁻ and leaving 0.050 mol CH3COOH. The solution now holds comparable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base, which is a buffer (here pH = pKa = 4.74).
cards.h: → OH⁻ is limiting → reacts completely → half the HA becomes A⁻ → weak acid + its conjugate base = buffer
cards.n: 'NaOH neutralizes the acid' misses the point: only half is neutralized, and the leftover HA with the new A⁻ is the buffer.
o: Partial neutralization by a strong base is a standard way to make a buffer: the base's moles become A⁻ and the rest of the weak acid stays as HA.
After reaction the mixture is identical to one made from 0.050 mol CH3COOH and 0.050 mol NaCH3COO, a textbook buffer.

w.a: Adding a strong base to a weak acid neutralizes it, so the solution becomes neutral.
w.why: only half the acid reacts; the leftover HA and new A⁻ buffer near pH 4.74

w.a: It is a buffer because NaOH and CH3COOH are a conjugate pair.
w.why: they are not a pair; the pair is CH3COOH/CH3COO⁻

w.a: NaOH is itself a buffer because it absorbs added acid.
w.why: a strong base alone has no conjugate acid to absorb added base

cards.q: Explain why the reaction of a weak acid with a strong base goes essentially to completion.
cards.a: HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O is the reverse of the conjugate base's Kb reaction, so K = 1/Kb = Ka/Kw. For acetic acid K = (1.8 × 10⁻⁵)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.8 × 10⁹, enormous, because OH⁻ is a far stronger base than CH3COO⁻. So essentially every OH⁻ added removes one HA.
cards.h: → reverse of A⁻'s Kb reaction → K = Ka/Kw ≈ 10⁹ → OH⁻ is a far stronger base than A⁻ → complete
cards.n: 'Strong bases always win' names no evidence; the size of K, or the base-strength comparison, is what earns it.
o: Proton transfer favors the weaker acid and base: OH⁻ is a much stronger base than A⁻ and H2O a much weaker acid than HA, so products dominate.
Even very weak HCN gives K = Ka/Kw = 6.2 × 10⁴ with OH⁻, still large enough to treat the reaction as complete.

w.a: The reaction is complete because the weak acid ionizes fully in water.
w.why: a weak acid is barely ionized; completeness comes from the OH⁻ reaction

w.a: It goes to completion because water is a product that cannot react.
w.why: the reason is the size of K, not water's stability alone

w.a: Weak acids and strong bases always stop at an equilibrium about halfway.
w.why: K ≈ 10⁹ puts the equilibrium essentially all the way to products

cards.q: Explain why a solution of NH4CN is basic even though NH4⁺ is an acid.
cards.a: Both ions react with water: NH4⁺ as a weak acid (Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) and CN⁻ as a weak base (Kb = Kw/Ka(HCN) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵). Kb(CN⁻) exceeds Ka(NH4⁺) about 3 × 10⁴-fold, so CN⁻ makes far more OH⁻ than NH4⁺ makes H3O⁺, and the solution is basic.
cards.h: → both ions react → compare Kb(CN⁻) with Ka(NH4⁺) → Kb ≫ Ka → more OH⁻ than H3O⁺ → basic
cards.n: Naming only one ion, or declaring every salt of a weak acid and weak base neutral, earns nothing; the Ka versus Kb comparison decides.
o: Since Kb(CN⁻) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ is about 30 000 times Ka(NH4⁺), the reaction CN⁻ + H2O ⇌ HCN + OH⁻ controls the pH.
In NH4F the comparison reverses (Ka 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ > Kb 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹), which is why NH4F is acidic while NH4CN is basic.

w.a: NH4CN is acidic because it contains the NH4⁺ ion.
w.why: ignores the much larger basic reaction of CN⁻

w.a: NH4CN is neutral because its weak acid and weak base cancel out.
w.why: they cancel only if Ka = Kb; here Kb is far larger

w.a: It is basic because cyanide is a strong base.
w.why: CN⁻ is a weak base; the point is that its Kb exceeds NH4⁺'s Ka

cards.q: Explain why a solution of NaCl is neutral while a solution of NaF is basic.
cards.a: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl, too weak a base to take protons from water, so NaCl leaves [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻]. F⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HF (Kb = Kw/Ka = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹), so F⁻ + H2O ⇌ HF + OH⁻ proceeds slightly and [OH⁻] > [H3O⁺]. Na⁺ is a spectator in both.
cards.h: → HCl strong → Cl⁻ a negligible base; HF weak → F⁻ a weak base → F⁻ + H2O makes OH⁻ → basic
cards.n: 'F is more electronegative' does not explain basicity; the point is the strength of each anion's conjugate acid.
o: The weaker the parent acid, the stronger its conjugate base: HF has a measurable Ka, so F⁻ has a measurable Kb, while Cl⁻ has effectively none.
H3O⁺ added to Cl⁻ forms no HCl molecules, but H3O⁺ added to F⁻ forms HF; that same proton affinity lets F⁻ pull protons from water.

w.a: NaF is basic because it contains Na⁺, which makes NaOH.
w.why: Na⁺ is a spectator in both salts

w.a: Both are neutral because salts are always neutral.
w.why: salts of weak acids or weak bases change the pH

w.a: NaF is basic because fluoride is more electronegative than chloride.
w.why: electronegativity does not decide it; the strength of the conjugate acid does

cards.q: Explain why the equilibrium HNO2(aq) + NH3(aq) ⇌ NO2⁻(aq) + NH4⁺(aq) lies far to the right.
cards.a: Proton transfer favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base. HNO2 (Ka = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴) is a far stronger acid than NH4⁺ (Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰), so K = Ka(HNO2)/Ka(NH4⁺) ≈ 8 × 10⁵ ≫ 1 and the products dominate.
cards.h: → compare the two acids' Ka → HNO2 ≫ NH4⁺ → K = Ka(HNO2)/Ka(NH4⁺) ≫ 1 → products favored
cards.n: Calling it complete like a strong-acid reaction overstates it; weak + weak reaches an equilibrium whose K is set by the two Ka values.
o: K = Ka(HNO2)·Kb(NH3)/Kw = (4.5 × 10⁻⁴)(1.8 × 10⁻⁵)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 8.1 × 10⁵, so products greatly outweigh reactants.
NH3 is a far stronger base than NO2⁻ (Kb 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ versus 2.2 × 10⁻¹¹), so the proton ends up on NH3.

w.a: It lies right because HNO2 is a strong acid.
w.why: HNO2 is weak; its comparison with NH4⁺ decides

w.a: It lies right because ions are always favored over molecules.
w.why: ionic products are not automatically favored; relative acid strength is

w.a: It lies right because NH3 is a strong base.
w.why: NH3 is weak; it is only stronger than NO2⁻

cards.q: Describe the shape of a strong acid-strong base titration curve.
cards.a: For 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl titrated with 0.100 M NaOH (pH 0–14 against mL of NaOH): the curve starts at pH 1.00, rises slowly (1.95 at 20.0 mL), then almost vertically from pH 3.70 at 24.9 mL to 10.30 at 25.1 mL; the equivalence point, 25.0 mL at pH 7.00, is the midpoint of that jump. Beyond it the curve flattens toward 12–12.5 (12.22 at 35.0 mL).
cards.h: → start, slow rise, vertical jump through pH 7, plateau
cards.n: Only the strong acid–strong base case has its equivalence point at pH 7.00; drawing every titration through 7 is the trap.

cards.q: Describe the shape of a weak acid-strong base titration curve.
cards.a: For 25.0 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH with 0.100 M NaOH: starts at pH 2.87 (above a strong acid's 1.00), rises quickly, then slowly through a buffer region centered on the half-equivalence point (12.5 mL, pH = pKa = 4.74); jumps steeply from about 7.1 (24.9 mL) to 10.3 (25.1 mL) through the equivalence point at 25.0 mL, pH 8.72; then follows the same excess-OH⁻ plateau near 12.2–12.5.
cards.h: → start, pKa plateau, shorter jump, basic equivalence
cards.n: Putting the equivalence point at pH 7, or the half-equivalence pH anywhere but pKa, are the two marks this sketch is graded on.

cards.q: State what is true about the pH at the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration.
cards.a: pH = pKa. Halfway to the equivalence volume, OH⁻ has converted exactly half of the original HA into A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻]; in Ka = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] the two cancel, leaving Ka = [H3O⁺], that is, pH = pKa. For acetic acid this is pH 4.74.
cards.h: → pH equals a constant, with the [HA] = [A⁻] reason
cards.n: Stating pH = pKa at the equivalence point instead of halfway to it is the usual misplacement.

cards.q: Explain why the equivalence point of a weak base-strong acid titration falls below pH 7.
cards.a: At the equivalence point every B has been converted to its conjugate acid HB⁺ (NH3 + H3O⁺ → NH4⁺ + H2O), so NH4⁺ and Cl⁻ are the major species. NH4⁺ is a weak acid (Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰): NH4⁺ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O⁺ makes [H3O⁺] > [OH⁻]. For 0.050 M NH4⁺ the pH is 5.28.
cards.h: → what is left at equivalence, then its reaction with water
cards.n: 'Because HCl is a strong acid' earns nothing; the HCl is all used up at equivalence, and the leftover NH4⁺ sets the pH.

cards.q: Compute the molarity of an HCl solution if 25.0 mL requires 32.5 mL of 0.100 M NaOH to reach the equivalence point.
cards.a: [HCl] = 0.130 M. mol NaOH = 0.0325 L × 0.100 M = 3.25 × 10⁻³ mol. At the equivalence point of a monoprotic acid, mol titrant = mol analyte (H3O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H2O is 1:1), so mol HCl = 3.25 × 10⁻³ mol and M = 3.25 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.130 M.
cards.h: → moles of titrant = moles of analyte, then ÷ volume
cards.n: M1V1 = M2V2 works only for 1:1 reactions; with H2SO4 or Ba(OH)2 the mole ratio changes. Titration stoichiometry is Unit 4 content.

cards.q: Describe the titration curve of a diprotic weak acid with a strong base.
cards.a: Two buffer regions and two steep rises. The first equivalence point comes at volume V1 (all H2A → HA⁻) and the second at 2V1 (all HA⁻ → A²⁻), because each proton needs the same moles of OH⁻. The half-equivalence points at ½V1 and 1½V1 give pH ≈ pKa1 and pKa2, and the second equivalence point lies at a higher, basic pH (A²⁻ is a base).
cards.h: → two plateaus, two jumps, at volumes V1 and 2V1
cards.n: Distinct steps need Ka1/Ka2 of about 10³ or more. Computing species concentrations along a polyprotic curve is excluded; reading it qualitatively is not.

cards.q: Explain why the successive Ka values of a polyprotic acid decrease sharply.
cards.a: Each proton is removed from a more negatively charged species: H3PO4 (neutral) → H2PO4⁻ → HPO4²⁻. Pulling a positive proton off a more negative ion is harder because of the stronger Coulombic attraction, so Ka1 ≫ Ka2 ≫ Ka3: for H3PO4, 7.5 × 10⁻³, 6.2 × 10⁻⁸ and 4.8 × 10⁻¹³, about 10⁵ apart.
cards.h: → growing negative charge holds H⁺ more tightly
cards.n: 'The acid runs out of protons' earns nothing; the reason is the growing negative charge. The Coulombic reasoning is from Unit 1.

cards.q: Identify the pH region on a weak acid-strong base titration curve where the solution acts as an effective buffer.
cards.a: The flat middle stretch of the curve, from shortly after the start to shortly before the equivalence point, centered on the half-equivalence point; roughly pH = pKa ± 1. For 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid titrated with 0.100 M NaOH it runs from about 2.3 mL (pH 3.7) to 22.7 mL (pH 5.7), where [A⁻]/[HA] goes from 1:10 to 10:1.
cards.h: → a region between two landmarks
cards.n: Buffering is strongest at half-equivalence, where the ratio is 1, and it ends once the equivalence point is passed and no HA remains.

cards.q: Compute the pH at the half-equivalence point of a titration of a weak acid with $K_a = 4.5\times10^{-4}$.
cards.a: pH = 3.35. At the half-equivalence point [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa = −log(4.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.35. No concentration or volume is needed.
cards.h: → a single pH value
cards.n: Neither the acid's concentration nor the titrant volume enters; Ka alone fixes the half-equivalence pH (for a fairly strong weak acid a measured value can drift slightly).

cards.q: Identify the titration-curve feature used to read off pKa directly, without any calculation.
cards.a: The pH at the half-equivalence point. Find the equivalence volume from the midpoint of the steep vertical section, halve it, and read the pH at that volume: it equals pKa because [HA] = [A⁻] there. Example: equivalence at 25.0 mL → read the pH at 12.5 mL.
cards.h: → equivalence volume, halve it, read the pH
cards.n: Reading the pH at the equivalence point itself gives the pH of the A⁻ solution, not pKa.

cards.q: Compute the pH at the equivalence point of titrating 0.10 M $CH_3COOH$ with NaOH if the resulting acetate concentration is 0.050 M ($K_b=5.6\times10^{-10}$).
cards.a: pH = 8.72. At equivalence acetate is the only acid-base active species, and it is a weak base: CH3COO⁻ + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH⁻. [OH⁻] = √(Kb·C) = √((5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰)(0.050)) = 5.3 × 10⁻⁶ M, pOH = 5.28, pH = 14.00 − 5.28 = 8.72.
cards.h: → treat the conjugate base as a weak base
cards.n: Calling the equivalence point pH 7.00 is the classic error; the conjugate base of a weak acid makes the solution basic.

cards.q: Explain why the pH jump near the equivalence point is smaller for a weak acid-strong base titration than for a strong acid-strong base titration.
cards.a: The jump starts higher but ends at the same place. Before equivalence the weak-acid mixture is a buffer near pKa, so just before equivalence (24.9 of 25.0 mL) acetic acid's curve is already at pH 7.1, versus 3.7 for HCl; just after (25.1 mL) both are at 10.3, set by the same excess OH⁻. So the vertical section spans about 3 pH units instead of about 6.6.
cards.h: → buffering raises the start of the jump; the end is shared
cards.n: The equivalence point is still where moles match; a smaller jump does not mean less base is needed.

cards.q: Identify the conjugate acid and the conjugate base of HCO3⁻.
cards.a: Conjugate acid: H2CO3 (HCO3⁻ + H⁺). Conjugate base: CO3²⁻ (HCO3⁻ − H⁺). HCO3⁻ is the intermediate species of diprotic carbonic acid: it is the major species at the first equivalence point when H2CO3 is titrated with a strong base, and it predominates between pH ≈ 6.4 (pKa1) and 10.3 (pKa2).
cards.h: → one gains H⁺, one loses H⁺
cards.n: Answering CO2 for the conjugate acid, or HCO3 with no charge, loses it; conjugate partners differ by exactly one H⁺ and one charge.

cards.q: Predict the acid-base character of a solution of $NaH_2PO_4$.
cards.a: Slightly acidic. H2PO4⁻ can donate a proton (Ka2 = 6.2 × 10⁻⁸) or accept one (Kb = Kw/Ka1 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/7.5 × 10⁻³ = 1.3 × 10⁻¹²). Since Ka2 ≫ Kb, donation wins and [H3O⁺] > [OH⁻]. H2PO4⁻ is the major species at the first equivalence point of an H3PO4 titration, which is why that point is acidic.
cards.h: → one word, then Ka versus Kb of the ion
cards.n: Using Ka1 as the ion's acid constant, or Kw/Ka2 as its base constant, pairs the wrong species; Na2HPO4 run the same way comes out basic.

cards.q: Represent the titration curve for 20.0 mL of 0.100 M NH3 (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) titrated with 0.100 M HCl, giving the pH at the start, at the half-equivalence point, at the equivalence point and after 30.0 mL of HCl.
cards.a: Axes: pH (0–14) against mL of HCl (0–30). The curve starts high at pH 11.13, falls quickly, then slowly through a buffer region with pH = pKa(NH4⁺) = 9.26 at 10.0 mL; it drops almost vertically from about 7.0 (19.9 mL) to 3.6 (20.1 mL), with the equivalence point at 20.0 mL, pH 5.28 (0.050 M NH4⁺); then it flattens toward pH 1.70 at 30.0 mL.
cards.h: → axes, four labeled points, the shape between them
cards.n: Drawing it rising like an acid titrated with base, or through pH 7 at equivalence, are the errors; half-equivalence gives pKa of NH4⁺, not pKb.

cards.q: Identify the major species containing A at each point in the titration of 20.0 mL of a weak diprotic acid H2A with NaOH, where the first equivalence point is at 15.0 mL: 0 mL, 7.5 mL, 15.0 mL, 22.5 mL, 30.0 mL and 35.0 mL.
cards.a: 0 mL: H2A. 7.5 mL (first half-equivalence): H2A and HA⁻ in equal amounts, pH ≈ pKa1. 15.0 mL (first equivalence): HA⁻. 22.5 mL (second half-equivalence): HA⁻ and A²⁻ equal, pH ≈ pKa2. 30.0 mL (second equivalence): A²⁻. 35.0 mL: A²⁻ plus excess OH⁻. Na⁺ is present throughout as a spectator.
cards.h: → one or two species per point, in order
cards.n: This qualitative reading is in scope; computing each species' concentration along a polyprotic curve is excluded from the exam.

cards.q:
Calculate the pH at each volume of 0.100 M NaOH added to 25.0 mL of 0.100 M formic acid, HCOOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, pKa = 3.74):
0 mL
5.0 mL
12.5 mL
20.0 mL
25.0 mL
30.0 mL
40.0 mL
cards.a:
0 mL → weak acid alone: [H3O⁺] = √((1.8 × 10⁻⁴)(0.100)) = 4.2 × 10⁻³ M, pH 2.37
5.0 mL → buffer, 0.50 mmol HCOO⁻ and 2.00 mmol HCOOH: pH = 3.74 + log(0.25) = 3.14
12.5 mL → half-equivalence: pH = pKa = 3.74
20.0 mL → buffer, 2.00 mmol HCOO⁻ and 0.50 mmol HCOOH: pH = 3.74 + log 4 = 4.35
25.0 mL → equivalence, 0.0500 M HCOO⁻ with Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹¹: [OH⁻] = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ M, pOH 5.78, pH 8.22
30.0 mL → excess OH⁻, 0.50 mmol in 55.0 mL = 9.1 × 10⁻³ M: pOH 2.04, pH 11.96
40.0 mL → excess OH⁻, 1.50 mmol in 65.0 mL = 0.023 M: pOH 1.64, pH 12.36
cards.h: → pick the region, then its method, at each volume
cards.n: Using Henderson–Hasselbalch at 0 mL or 25.0 mL (no A⁻, or no HA) and calling the equivalence pH 7 are the traps this drill targets.

cards.q: Explain why the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is above pH 7.
cards.a: At equivalence all the HA has been converted to A⁻ (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O), so A⁻ is the major species besides Na⁺ and water. A⁻ is a weak base: A⁻ + H2O ⇌ HA + OH⁻ produces OH⁻, so [OH⁻] > [H3O⁺] and pH > 7 (8.72 for 0.050 M acetate).
cards.h: → all HA becomes A⁻ at equivalence → A⁻ is a weak base → A⁻ + H2O makes OH⁻ → pH above 7
cards.n: 'Because NaOH is a strong base' earns nothing; at equivalence no excess NaOH remains, so the conjugate base must be named.
o: The solution at equivalence is simply a solution of the salt NaA, and a salt of a weak acid and a strong base is basic because A⁻ reacts with water.
Na⁺ is a spectator, so the only species that changes [OH⁻] is A⁻, whose Kb = Kw/Ka is small but not zero.

w.a: The pH is above 7 because excess NaOH is present at the equivalence point.
w.why: there is no excess at equivalence; that describes the region after it

w.a: It is above 7 because equal moles of acid and base always give a basic solution.
w.why: equal moles of HCl and NaOH give pH 7; the weak acid's conjugate base matters

w.a: It is above 7 because Na⁺ makes the solution basic.
w.why: Na⁺ is a spectator ion

cards.q: Explain why the pH equals pKa at the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration.
cards.a: By the half-equivalence point, OH⁻ has converted exactly half the original HA into A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻]. Substituting into Ka = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] cancels the equal terms, leaving Ka = [H3O⁺]; taking −log gives pH = pKa.
cards.h: → half the HA neutralized → [HA] = [A⁻] → they cancel in Ka → Ka = [H3O⁺] → pH = pKa
cards.n: 'Because it is halfway' names the point, not the reason; the [HA] = [A⁻] step is what earns credit.
o: In Henderson–Hasselbalch form, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pKa + log 1 = pKa.
Half the required OH⁻ has been added, so the moles of A⁻ formed equal the moles of HA left, and since they share one volume their concentrations are equal.

w.a: The pH equals pKa because half of the acid has dissociated in water.
w.why: the HA was converted by added OH⁻, not by dissociating on its own

w.a: At the half-equivalence point the acid and base have completely neutralized each other.
w.why: that describes the equivalence point

w.a: The pH equals pKa because the solution is neutral there.
w.why: the pH there is pKa, which is usually far from 7

cards.q: Explain why 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl and 25.0 mL of 0.10 M CH3COOH need the same volume of 0.10 M NaOH to reach their equivalence points.
cards.a: The equivalence point depends on moles of acid, not on acid strength. Both samples contain 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol of a monoprotic acid, and OH⁻ reacts completely with either one, 1:1 (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O). So both need 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻, which is 25 mL of 0.10 M NaOH.
cards.h: → same moles of monoprotic acid → each reacts 1:1 and completely with OH⁻ → same moles of OH⁻ → same volume
cards.n: 'The weak acid needs less base because it is weaker' is the trap; un-ionized HA still reacts with OH⁻.
o: As OH⁻ removes acetic acid's few H3O⁺ ions, Le Châtelier's principle drives more CH3COOH to ionize, so all of it is eventually neutralized.
K for CH3COOH + OH⁻ is about 10⁹, so every mole of acetic acid consumes one mole of OH⁻, exactly like HCl.

w.a: The weak acid needs less NaOH because only a few percent of it is ionized.
w.why: the un-ionized HA also reacts with OH⁻

w.a: The strong acid needs less NaOH because it is already fully ionized.
w.why: the degree of ionization does not change the moles of acid

w.a: They need the same volume because both solutions have the same pH.
w.why: their pH values differ (1.00 and 2.87); the moles are what match

cards.q: Explain why the titration curve of a weak diprotic acid shows two equivalence points.
cards.a: The two protons are removed one at a time because Ka1 ≫ Ka2: OH⁻ first converts all H2A to HA⁻ (first equivalence point), and only then converts HA⁻ to A²⁻ (second). Each step consumes the same moles of OH⁻, so the second equivalence volume is twice the first.
cards.h: → Ka1 ≫ Ka2 → protons removed in sequence → one jump per proton → second at twice the first volume
cards.n: 'Because it has two H atoms' is incomplete: jumps count acidic protons only when the Ka values are well separated and each is large enough to show.
o: Each acidic proton gives its own buffer region and its own steep rise, so the number of equivalence points reveals the number of acidic protons.
HA⁻ is a much weaker acid than H2A, so added OH⁻ reacts with H2A first; only when H2A is used up does HA⁻ begin to react.

w.a: It has two equivalence points because the acid has two hydrogen atoms.
w.why: acetic acid has four H atoms but one acidic proton; only acidic protons count

w.a: Both protons are removed at the same time, which makes two jumps.
w.why: simultaneous removal would give one jump

w.a: The second equivalence point comes from water reacting with the NaOH.
w.why: water is not titrated; the second jump is HA⁻ → A²⁻

cards.q: Explain why the pH at the equivalence point of a strong acid–strong base titration is 7.00 at 25 °C.
cards.a: At equivalence H3O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H2O has consumed both completely, leaving only spectator ions (e.g., Na⁺ and Cl⁻), the conjugates of a strong base and a strong acid, which do not react with water. So [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M, as in pure water: pH 7.00.
cards.h: → H3O⁺ and OH⁻ fully consumed → only spectator ions remain → no reaction with water → pure-water pH 7.00
cards.n: 'Acid and base cancel' earns nothing unless the leftover ions are shown not to react with water.
o: The solution at equivalence is NaCl(aq), the salt of a strong acid and a strong base, which is neutral.
Neither Na⁺ nor Cl⁻ has a measurable Ka or Kb, so autoionization alone sets [H3O⁺] = √Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.

w.a: The pH is 7 because all equivalence points are at pH 7.
w.why: false for weak acid or weak base titrations

w.a: The pH is 7 because the moles of acid and base are equal.
w.why: equal moles give pH 7 only when neither leftover ion reacts with water

w.a: The pH is 7 because NaCl is a neutral molecule.
w.why: NaCl is ionic; the reason is that its ions do not react with water

cards.q: Explain the trend in binary acid strength (HX) down a group and across a period.
cards.a: Down group 17 acid strength rises, HF < HCl < HBr < HI: the halogen is larger, so the H–X bond is longer and weaker and the negative charge of X⁻ is spread over a bigger ion, making X⁻ a weaker base. Across period 2 it rises CH4 < NH3 < H2O < HF: the atoms are similar in size, and a more electronegative atom better stabilizes the negative charge of the conjugate base.
cards.h: → two trends, each with its reason
cards.n: Using electronegativity for the group trend predicts HF as strongest, the wrong order; down a group, size and bond strength dominate.

cards.q: Explain how the number of terminal oxygen atoms affects the strength of an oxyacid.
cards.a: More terminal (non-OH) oxygens make the acid stronger. Each electronegative O pulls electron density away from the central atom and the O–H bond (an inductive effect), and in the conjugate base the negative charge is delocalized by resonance over more oxygens, stabilizing the anion: HClO (Ka 3.0 × 10⁻⁸) < HClO2 (1.1 × 10⁻²) < HClO3 < HClO4 (both strong).
cards.h: → more oxygens, stronger acid, with two reasons
cards.n: 'More O means more H to donate' is wrong: each of these acids has one acidic H; the extra O atoms stabilize the anion.

cards.q: Explain the inductive effect on acid strength using CH3COOH and CCl3COOH.
cards.a: CCl3COOH is the much stronger acid (pKa about 0.7, versus 4.74 for CH3COOH). The three electronegative Cl atoms withdraw electron density through the σ bonds (inductive effect), weakening the O–H bond and spreading the negative charge of the carboxylate conjugate base, which stabilizes it.
cards.h: → electron withdrawal stabilizes the anion
cards.n: Any acid-strength argument should end at the stability of the conjugate base; 'Cl is electronegative' alone is only the start.

cards.q: Rank HClO, HClO2, HClO3, and HClO4 from weakest to strongest acid and justify the order.
cards.a: HClO < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4. All share the H–O–Cl core, so the only variable is the number of terminal O atoms (0, 1, 2, 3). Each added O withdraws more electron density from the O–H bond and delocalizes the conjugate base's charge over more atoms, stabilizing ClO⁻ < ClO2⁻ < ClO3⁻ < ClO4⁻.
cards.h: → ordered list plus one structural reason
cards.n: Ranking by the number of O atoms without the conjugate-base stability reason earns the order but not the justification.

cards.q: Rank $HClO_4$, $HClO_3$, and $HClO_2$ by acid strength, and justify using terminal oxygen atoms.
cards.a: HClO4 > HClO3 > HClO2, with 3, 2 and 1 terminal O atoms on Cl. Terminal oxygens pull electron density away from the O–H bond, and in the anion the negative charge is shared by resonance over 4, 3 or 2 O atoms, so ClO4⁻ is the most stable, weakest conjugate base.
cards.h: → ordered list plus the terminal-O reason
cards.n: Arguing from chlorine's oxidation number alone is acceptable only if it is tied to electron withdrawal and anion stability.

cards.q: Predict which is the stronger acid, $H_2SO_3$ or $H_2SO_4$, using the number of terminal oxygens on sulfur.
cards.a: H2SO4. Written (HO)2SO2 and (HO)2SO, it has two terminal O atoms on S versus one. More terminal O withdraw more electron density from the O–H bonds and delocalize the charge of HSO4⁻ over three O atoms instead of two in HSO3⁻, so H2SO4 ionizes completely (a strong acid) while H2SO3 is weak (Ka1 about 10⁻²).
cards.h: → one formula plus the terminal-O reason
cards.n: Both acids have two H atoms, so counting hydrogens explains nothing; the extra terminal oxygen is the difference.

cards.q: Explain the relationship between the strength of an acid and the strength of its conjugate base.
cards.a: Inverse: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. For weak acids Ka × Kb = Kw, so a larger Ka means a smaller Kb: HF (Ka 7.2 × 10⁻⁴) → F⁻ (Kb 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹), HCN (6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰) → CN⁻ (1.6 × 10⁻⁵). The conjugate bases of strong acids (Cl⁻, NO3⁻, ClO4⁻) are too weak to react with water, and the conjugate acids of strong bases (Na⁺, K⁺) likewise.
cards.h: → inverse relationship, with Ka·Kb = Kw
cards.n: 'A strong acid has a strong conjugate base' is the reversed claim; a stable, weak conjugate base is what makes the acid strong.

cards.q: Identify which hydrogen atom or atoms in acetic acid, CH3COOH, are acidic, and justify the choice from the structure.
cards.a: Only the hydrogen on the –COOH oxygen (the carboxyl O–H) is acidic; the three C–H hydrogens are not. The O–H bond is highly polar (O is very electronegative), and losing that proton gives acetate, CH3COO⁻, whose negative charge is shared by resonance over two O atoms. Removing a C–H proton would leave the charge on carbon with no such stabilization.
cards.h: → which H, then bond polarity and anion stability
cards.n: 'All four H atoms are acidic' leads to treating CH3COOH as tetraprotic; only the carboxyl H is ever counted.

cards.q:
Classify each species as a strong acid, weak acid, strong base, weak base, or neither (negligible acid-base behavior in water):
HCl
HF
HNO3
HNO2
H2SO4
HClO4
HI
HCOOH
CH3COOH
HCN
NH4⁺
NaOH
Ba(OH)2
NH3
CH3NH2
C5H5N
CH3COO⁻
F⁻
CO3²⁻
Cl⁻
NO3⁻
K⁺
cards.a:
HCl → strong acid
HF → weak acid
HNO3 → strong acid
HNO2 → weak acid
H2SO4 → strong acid (first proton)
HClO4 → strong acid
HI → strong acid
HCOOH → weak acid (carboxylic acid)
CH3COOH → weak acid (carboxylic acid)
HCN → weak acid
NH4⁺ → weak acid (conjugate acid of NH3)
NaOH → strong base
Ba(OH)2 → strong base
NH3 → weak base (lone pair on N)
CH3NH2 → weak base (amine)
C5H5N → weak base (pyridine N)
CH3COO⁻ → weak base (carboxylate)
F⁻ → weak base
CO3²⁻ → weak base
Cl⁻ → neither (conjugate of a strong acid)
NO3⁻ → neither (conjugate of a strong acid)
K⁺ → neither (conjugate of a strong base)
cards.h: → strong list from memory, then structure for the rest
cards.n: HF is the classic misclassification (weak, not strong); Cl⁻ and NO3⁻ are not weak bases in water, they are negligible ones.

cards.q: Identify the atom that accepts a proton when methylamine, CH3NH2, acts as a base, and write the equation for its reaction with water.
cards.a: The nitrogen atom, through its lone pair: CH3NH2(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ CH3NH3⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴. Nitrogenous bases such as NH3 and the amines are the common weak bases because N carries a lone pair that can bond to H⁺; the C–H and N–H hydrogens play no part.
cards.h: → the atom and its lone pair, then the equation
cards.n: Writing CH3NH2 → CH3NH⁻ + H⁺ makes it an acid; amines accept a proton on N. Lone pairs from Lewis structures are Unit 2 content.

cards.q: Rank HOCl, HOBr and HOI in order of increasing acid strength, and justify the order from their structures.
cards.a: HOI < HOBr < HOCl (Ka about 2 × 10⁻¹¹, 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ and 3.0 × 10⁻⁸). All have the same H–O–X structure, so the variable is the halogen's electronegativity (I 2.7 < Br 3.0 < Cl 3.2). A more electronegative X pulls more electron density from the O–H bond and better stabilizes the negative charge of OX⁻, so the acid is stronger.
cards.h: → ordered list, then electronegativity → anion stability
cards.n: Borrowing the HX size trend (HI strongest) reverses the order: in oxyacids the H sits on O, so the halogen's electronegativity decides.

cards.q: Identify the functional group that marks a carboxylic acid, and give three examples with their Ka values to show that they are weak acids.
cards.a: The carboxyl group, –COOH: a carbon double-bonded to one O and single-bonded to an O–H, whose hydrogen is the acidic one. Examples: formic acid HCOOH (Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁴), acetic acid CH3COOH (1.8 × 10⁻⁵) and benzoic acid C6H5COOH (6.3 × 10⁻⁵). All ionize only partly, so carboxylic acids are the CED's common class of weak acid.
cards.h: → the group, then three named examples with Ka
cards.n: Counting every H in the formula as acidic, or calling an alcohol (an O–H on carbon with no C=O) a carboxylic acid, loses the point.

cards.q: Explain why acetic acid, CH3COOH, is a far stronger acid than ethanol, CH3CH2OH, even though both lose a proton from an O–H group.
cards.a: The conjugate bases differ. In acetate, CH3COO⁻, the negative charge is delocalized by resonance over two electronegative O atoms; in ethoxide, CH3CH2O⁻, it sits on one O. The more stable acetate means CH3COOH gives up H⁺ far more readily (pKa 4.74 versus about 16).
cards.h: → compare conjugate bases → acetate's charge shared by resonance over 2 O → more stable → stronger acid
cards.n: 'Acetic acid has more oxygen' is half an idea; the point is that the C=O oxygen lets the charge be delocalized.
o: The C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond and, after deprotonation, shares the negative charge, so carboxylate is a much weaker base than ethoxide.
A stable, weak conjugate base means a strong acid; ethoxide is a strong base, so ethanol is a very weak acid.

w.a: Acetic acid is stronger because it has more hydrogen atoms.
w.why: ethanol has more H atoms; hydrogen count is irrelevant

w.a: Acetic acid is stronger because it is a larger molecule.
w.why: molecular size is not the reason; resonance in the anion is

w.a: Ethanol is weaker because its O–H bond is not polar.
w.why: both O–H bonds are polar; the difference is conjugate-base stability

cards.q: Explain why HClO4 is a strong acid while HOCl is a weak acid.
cards.a: In HClO4 three terminal O atoms withdraw electron density from the O–H bond, and in ClO4⁻ the negative charge is spread by resonance over four O atoms, making it a very stable, very weak base. HOCl has no terminal O; OCl⁻ carries its charge on one O, so it holds H⁺ well (Ka 3.0 × 10⁻⁸).
cards.h: → terminal O atoms withdraw density and delocalize the anion's charge → ClO4⁻ very stable → HClO4 strong
cards.n: Citing chlorine's oxidation number (+7 versus +1) earns credit only if linked to electron withdrawal and anion stability.
