o: Strong acids have very weak conjugate bases stabilized by electronegativity and resonance; ClO4⁻ fits that description and OCl⁻ does not.
The more oxygens around Cl, the more electron-poor the O–H bond and the more easily H⁺ leaves.

w.a: HClO4 is strong because it has more oxygen atoms to donate.
w.why: oxygens are not donated; they stabilize the anion

w.a: HClO4 is strong because it contains more hydrogen.
w.why: each acid has one acidic H

w.a: HOCl is weak because chlorine is less electronegative than oxygen.
w.why: true but does not compare the two acids; the terminal oxygens do

cards.q: Explain why HCl is a strong acid in water but HF is a weak acid.
cards.a: F is small, so the H–F bond is short and very strong (about 565 kJ/mol) and F⁻ packs its charge into a tiny ion that holds H⁺ well; HF ionizes only partly (Ka 7.2 × 10⁻⁴). Cl is larger, the H–Cl bond is longer and weaker (about 431 kJ/mol), and Cl⁻ spreads its charge over a bigger ion, a very weak base.
cards.h: → F small → strong H–F bond, concentrated charge on F⁻ → F⁻ holds H⁺ → HF weak; larger Cl → the reverse
cards.n: Arguing that F is more electronegative predicts the wrong result here; down a group, size and bond strength override electronegativity.
o: Cl⁻ is a far weaker base than F⁻ because its charge is spread over a larger volume, so HCl's proton is not recaptured.
Going down group 17 the H–X bond weakens as X grows, so acid strength rises from HF to HI.

w.a: HF is weak because fluorine is the most electronegative element.
w.why: electronegativity would predict HF as the strongest; size and bond strength decide

w.a: HF is weak because it does not dissolve well in water.
w.why: HF is very soluble; solubility is not the issue

w.a: HCl is strong because chlorine atoms are heavier.
w.why: mass is irrelevant; bond strength and anion size are

cards.q: Explain why NH3 acts as a base in water while CH4 does not.
cards.a: NH3's nitrogen has a lone pair that can form a bond to H⁺ taken from water: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻. In CH4 all four of carbon's electron pairs are C–H bonds, so there is no lone pair to bind a proton, and CH4 shows no basic behavior.
cards.h: → N has a lone pair → it bonds H⁺ taken from water → OH⁻ forms; C in CH4 has no lone pair → not a base
cards.n: 'NH3 contains nitrogen, which is basic' names an element, not a mechanism; the lone pair is the point. Lone pairs come from Unit 2.
o: A Brønsted–Lowry base must accept a proton, which needs an unshared electron pair; NH3 has one on N and CH4 has none.
Amines such as CH3NH2 behave like NH3 because they keep the N lone pair, which is why nitrogenous compounds are the common weak bases.

w.a: NH3 is a base because it contains OH⁻ ions.
w.why: NH3 has no hydroxide; it makes OH⁻ by taking H⁺ from water

w.a: CH4 is not a base because it is a gas.
w.why: NH3 is also a gas; the lone pair is what differs

w.a: NH3 is a base because nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon.
w.why: electronegativity alone is not the mechanism; the lone pair is

cards.q: Predict which form of a conjugate pair predominates when the solution pH is below, equal to, or above the pKa.
cards.a: pH < pKa: the protonated acid form HA predominates. pH = pKa: [HA] = [A⁻]. pH > pKa: the deprotonated base form A⁻ predominates. From Ka = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], [A⁻]/[HA] = Ka/[H3O⁺] = $10^{pH - pKa}$, so each pH unit away from pKa is a factor of 10: at pKa + 2 the ratio is 100:1.
cards.h: → three comparisons, then the ratio rule
cards.n: Reversing it (base form below pKa) is the common slip; low pH means plenty of H3O⁺, so the protonated form wins.

cards.q: Compute the pKa of a weak acid with $K_a=6.3\times10^{-5}$.
cards.a: pKa = 4.20: −log(6.3 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.20, two decimal places for Ka's two significant figures. Ka between 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁴ must give a pKa between 4 and 5. This is the benchmark for the acid's protonation state: HA predominates below pH 4.20 and A⁻ above it.
cards.h: → one negative log
cards.n: A pKa of −4.20 or 5.80 is a sign or log slip; a Ka between 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁴ has to give a pKa between 4 and 5.

cards.q: Compute the Ka of a weak acid whose pKa is 3.75.
cards.a: Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴. Ka = $10^{-pKa}$ = $10^{-3.75}$ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ (two decimal places in pKa give two significant figures). The acid is half in each form at pH 3.75, mostly HA below that pH and mostly A⁻ above it.
cards.h: → one antilog, in scientific notation
cards.n: The negative exponent is easy to lose: it is $10^{-3.75}$, not $10^{3.75}$, since a weak acid's Ka is far below 1.

cards.q: Define an acid-base indicator and state its useful pH range.
cards.a: An acid-base indicator is a weak acid, HIn, whose protonated form HIn and deprotonated form In⁻ have different colors: HIn + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + In⁻. Its color responds to pH and changes over roughly pH = pKa(HIn) ± 1, where [In⁻]/[HIn] goes from about 1:10 (acid color) to 10:1 (base color).
cards.h: → a weak acid with two colored forms, plus a range
cards.n: Because the indicator is itself a weak acid, only a couple of drops are used, so it consumes no measurable titrant.

cards.q: Decide how to choose an appropriate indicator for a titration.
cards.a: Choose an indicator whose pKa is close to the pH at the equivalence point, so its color change falls in the steep part of the curve and the endpoint coincides with equivalence: pKa ≈ 7 (bromothymol blue) for strong acid–strong base, above 7 (phenolphthalein, pKa ≈ 9) for weak acid–strong base, below 7 (methyl red, pKa ≈ 5) for weak base–strong acid.
cards.h: → match pKa to the equivalence-point pH
cards.n: Picking pKa 7 for every titration, or matching the indicator to the analyte acid's pKa, gives an early or late endpoint.

cards.q: Identify a suitable indicator for the titration of acetic acid with NaOH and justify the choice.
cards.a: Phenolphthalein, colorless below about pH 8.2 and pink above about 10.0 (pKa ≈ 9). The equivalence point of acetic acid titrated with NaOH is basic, pH ≈ 8.7 for 0.050 M acetate, which lies inside that range and inside the steep jump (about 7.1 to 10.3), so the first lasting pink marks equivalence.
cards.h: → one indicator, plus its range against the equivalence pH
cards.n: Methyl orange (pKa ≈ 3.5) would change color early in the buffer region and give far too small a titrant volume.

cards.q: Define the equivalence point of a titration and contrast it with the endpoint.
cards.a: The equivalence point is where the moles of titrant added exactly equal the moles of analyte (for a monoprotic acid, mol OH⁻ = mol HA): a stoichiometric point. The endpoint is where the indicator changes color, the point the experimenter observes. With an indicator whose pKa is near the equivalence-point pH, the endpoint falls in the steep jump and the two agree within a drop.
cards.h: → theoretical versus observed
cards.n: Treating the two terms as synonyms loses the point; a poorly chosen indicator separates them. Basic titration vocabulary is from Unit 4.

cards.q:
Predict the predominant form of each conjugate pair at the stated pH:
acetic acid (pKa 4.74) at pH 7.4
acetic acid (pKa 4.74) at pH 2.0
NH4⁺ (pKa 9.26) at pH 7.0
NH4⁺ (pKa 9.26) at pH 11.0
HF (pKa 3.14) at pH 3.14
HOCl (pKa 7.52) at pH 8.5
HCN (pKa 9.21) at pH 7.0
formic acid (pKa 3.74) at pH 1.5
CH3NH3⁺ (pKa 10.64) at pH 7.4
H2CO3 (pKa1 6.37) at pH 7.4
HCO3⁻ (pKa2 10.33) at pH 7.4
H2PO4⁻ (pKa2 7.21) at pH 7.4
C5H5NH⁺ (pKa 5.23) at pH 7.0
an indicator HIn (pKa 9.3) at pH 7.0
cards.a:
acetic acid, pH 7.4 → CH3COO⁻ (base : acid ≈ 460 : 1)
acetic acid, pH 2.0 → CH3COOH (acid : base ≈ 550 : 1)
NH4⁺, pH 7.0 → NH4⁺ (≈ 180 : 1)
NH4⁺, pH 11.0 → NH3 (≈ 55 : 1)
HF, pH 3.14 → neither: HF and F⁻ are equal
HOCl, pH 8.5 → OCl⁻ (≈ 10 : 1)
HCN, pH 7.0 → HCN (≈ 160 : 1)
formic acid, pH 1.5 → HCOOH (≈ 170 : 1)
CH3NH3⁺, pH 7.4 → CH3NH3⁺ (≈ 1700 : 1)
H2CO3, pH 7.4 → HCO3⁻ (≈ 11 : 1)
HCO3⁻, pH 7.4 → HCO3⁻ (CO3²⁻ is only ≈ 1 : 850)
H2PO4⁻, pH 7.4 → HPO4²⁻, slightly (≈ 1.5 : 1)
C5H5NH⁺, pH 7.0 → C5H5N (≈ 59 : 1)
HIn, pH 7.0 → HIn (≈ 200 : 1), so the acid color shows
cards.h: → compare pH with pKa; ratio = 10^(pH − pKa)
cards.n: Each line needs only the pH-versus-pKa comparison; for ammonium and amines use the pKa of the conjugate acid, never the base's pKb.

cards.q: Calculate the ratio [C6H5COO⁻]/[C6H5COOH] for benzoic acid (pKa = 4.20) in a solution buffered at pH 5.50, and the percentage of the acid present as benzoate.
cards.a: The ratio is about 20, and about 95% is benzoate. [A⁻]/[HA] = $10^{pH - pKa}$ = $10^{5.50 - 4.20}$ = $10^{1.30}$ = 20. The fraction present as A⁻ is 20/(20 + 1) = 0.95, i.e., 95%. The pH is above pKa, so the base form predominates, as expected.
cards.h: → 10^(pH − pKa), then ratio → percentage
cards.n: Writing the ratio as $10^{pKa - pH}$ inverts it (0.050); the base form must win when the pH is above pKa.

cards.q: Predict whether methylamine exists mainly as CH3NH2 or as CH3NH3⁺ in blood at pH 7.4, given Kb(CH3NH2) = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴.
cards.a: Mainly as CH3NH3⁺. pKb = −log(4.4 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.36, so the conjugate acid has pKa = 14.00 − 3.36 = 10.64. The pH, 7.4, is well below 10.64, so the protonated form predominates: [CH3NH2]/[CH3NH3⁺] = $10^{7.4 - 10.64}$ ≈ 1/1700.
cards.h: → pKb → pKa of the conjugate acid → compare with pH
cards.n: Comparing the pH with pKb (3.36) instead of the conjugate acid's pKa gives the opposite, wrong answer.

cards.q: Identify the color of bromothymol blue (pKa ≈ 7.1; HIn yellow, In⁻ blue) in solutions of pH 4.0, 7.1 and 10.0.
cards.a: pH 4.0: yellow. pH 7.1: green. pH 10.0: blue. At pH 4.0, about three units below pKa, HIn outnumbers In⁻ roughly 1000:1, so the acid color shows; at pH = pKa the two forms are equal and yellow mixed with blue looks green; at pH 10.0 In⁻ outnumbers HIn roughly 800:1.
cards.h: → three colors, each from pH versus pKa
cards.n: 'Blue in acid' reverses the forms; the protonated HIn shows at low pH. Green at the pKa is a mixture, not a third species.

cards.q: Identify the best indicator for titrating aqueous NH3 with HCl (equivalence-point pH ≈ 5.3) from methyl orange (pKa ≈ 3.5), methyl red (pKa ≈ 5.0), bromothymol blue (pKa ≈ 7.1) and phenolphthalein (pKa ≈ 9.3), and justify the choice.
cards.a: Methyl red. Its pKa (≈ 5.0) is closest to the equivalence-point pH of about 5.3, so its color change (roughly pH 4.4–6.2) happens inside the steep drop at equivalence. Phenolphthalein and bromothymol blue would change in the buffer region, before equivalence, and methyl orange only after it.
cards.h: → one name, then pKa versus equivalence pH
cards.n: Choosing phenolphthalein because it is 'the usual indicator' ignores that this equivalence point is acidic.

cards.q: Estimate the pKa of an indicator that is red at pH 4.4 and below and yellow at pH 6.2 and above, and state its color at pH 5.3.
cards.a: pKa ≈ 5.3, and the indicator is orange at pH 5.3. The color change spans roughly pKa ± 1, so the pKa sits near the middle of the 4.4–6.2 range: (4.4 + 6.2)/2 = 5.3. At pH = pKa the red HIn and yellow In⁻ are present in equal amounts, and the mixture looks orange.
cards.h: → midpoint of the range, then the mixed color
cards.n: Taking an end of the range (4.4 or 6.2) as the pKa misreads it; the pKa is where the two forms are equal, mid-range.

cards.q: Explain why an acid-base indicator changes color over a range of about 2 pH units centered on its pKa.
cards.a: The color seen depends on [In⁻]/[HIn] = $10^{pH - pKa}$. The eye sees one form's color only when it outnumbers the other about 10:1, which happens at pH ≤ pKa − 1 (acid color) or pH ≥ pKa + 1 (base color). In between, both colors mix, so the change spans about pKa ± 1.
cards.h: → color set by [In⁻]/[HIn] → ratio = 10^(pH − pKa) → one color dominates only past 10:1 → pKa ± 1
cards.n: 'Indicators change color at their pKa' is incomplete; the question is why the change takes about two pH units.
o: Going from pH = pKa − 1 to pKa + 1 moves [In⁻]/[HIn] from 0.1 to 10, a 100-fold swing, which is what the eye needs to see one pure color give way to the other.
At pH = pKa the forms are equal and the color is a mixture; about one unit either side one form reaches roughly 90% and its color dominates.

w.a: The indicator changes over 2 units because it has two colors.
w.why: the number of colors does not set the width of the range

w.a: It changes over 2 units because the indicator reacts slowly with H3O⁺.
w.why: proton transfer is fast; the range comes from the concentration ratio

w.a: The color changes exactly at pH 7 for every indicator.
w.why: each indicator changes near its own pKa

cards.q: Explain why an indicator's pKa should be close to the pH at the equivalence point of the titration.
cards.a: The indicator changes color near pH = pKa. If that pH lies in the steep jump at equivalence, one drop of titrant carries the solution across the whole color range, so the endpoint matches the equivalence point. A distant pKa changes color before or after equivalence, giving a wrong titrant volume.
cards.h: → color change near pH = pKa → pKa inside the steep jump → one drop spans the range → endpoint = equivalence
cards.n: 'So the colors look right' earns nothing; the point is that the endpoint volume must match the equivalence volume.
o: Near the equivalence point the pH changes by several units per drop, so any indicator whose range lies inside that jump flips within one drop of equivalence.
If the range lies in a buffer region the pH changes slowly, so the color drifts over many mL and the endpoint is both unclear and misplaced.

w.a: The indicator's pKa should equal 7 so that it shows neutrality.
w.why: equivalence points are not always at pH 7

w.a: The indicator's pKa should match the analyte acid's pKa.
w.why: that indicator would change at half-equivalence, not at equivalence

w.a: Any indicator works because all of them change color eventually.
w.why: a mismatched indicator gives a wrong titrant volume

cards.q: Explain why using methyl orange (pKa ≈ 3.5) as the indicator gives a low result for the concentration of acetic acid titrated with NaOH.
cards.a: Methyl orange changes color near pH 3.5, which the acetic acid solution passes early in the buffer region, after only about 5% of the NaOH actually needed. The student stops far short of the equivalence volume, so the moles of NaOH, and the calculated acid concentration, come out too low.
cards.h: → color change near pH 3.5 → reached early in the buffer region → volume too small → moles and concentration too low
cards.n: 'The indicator was the wrong color' names no direction; the answer must say the volume, and so the concentration, comes out too low.
o: The equivalence point is near pH 8.7, but methyl orange has finished changing below about pH 4.4, so the endpoint comes well before equivalence.
Too little titrant volume means too few moles of OH⁻, and since mol HA = mol OH⁻ at the endpoint used, the calculated [HA] is too small.

w.a: The result is too high because methyl orange reacts with the NaOH.
w.why: a few drops of indicator consume negligible base, and the direction is wrong

w.a: The result is unaffected because the indicator does not take part in the reaction.
w.why: the indicator decides where the student stops, which sets the volume

w.a: The result is low because methyl orange changes color after the equivalence point.
w.why: it changes before equivalence; a late change would give a high result

cards.q: Explain why the protonated form HA predominates when the solution pH is below the acid's pKa.
cards.a: From Ka = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] = Ka/[H3O⁺]. When pH < pKa, [H3O⁺] > Ka, so the ratio is less than 1 and HA outnumbers A⁻. Equivalently, the high [H3O⁺] pushes HA ⇌ H3O⁺ + A⁻ to the left.
cards.h: → [A⁻]/[HA] = Ka/[H3O⁺] → pH < pKa means [H3O⁺] > Ka → ratio < 1 → HA predominates
cards.n: Restating the rule ('below pKa means acid form') without the ratio or the Le Châtelier reason earns nothing.
o: By Henderson–Hasselbalch, log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pH − pKa, which is negative when pH < pKa, so [A⁻] < [HA].
Abundant H3O⁺ readily protonates A⁻, so at low pH the acid keeps its proton.

w.a: HA predominates below pKa because the acid is strongest at low pH.
w.why: Ka does not change with pH; the ratio of the forms does

w.a: Below pKa the acid has not had time to ionize.
w.why: this is an equilibrium, not a rate effect

w.a: HA predominates because a low pH means more of the acid was added.
w.why: any source of H3O⁺ sets the pH, and the pair's ratio follows from it

cards.q: Define a buffer solution and state the two components required to make one.
cards.a: A buffer is a solution that resists a change in pH when small amounts of strong acid or strong base are added. It needs large, comparable concentrations of both members of a conjugate pair: a weak acid and its conjugate base (CH3COOH/CH3COO⁻) or a weak base and its conjugate acid (NH3/NH4⁺). The conjugate base consumes added acid; the weak acid consumes added base.
cards.h: → what it does, then the two components
cards.n: A strong acid with its conjugate base (HCl/Cl⁻) cannot buffer, because Cl⁻ is far too weak a base to accept protons.

cards.q: Explain at the particle level how a buffer resists a change in pH.
cards.a: Each component neutralizes one kind of addition. Added H3O⁺ is consumed by the conjugate base, A⁻ + H3O⁺ → HA + H2O; added OH⁻ is consumed by the weak acid, HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O. Both go essentially to completion, so the strong acid or base is replaced by a weak one and [H3O⁺] barely changes.
cards.h: → two neutralization equations, one per component
cards.n: Full credit needs both reactions written; saying the buffer 'absorbs' or 'soaks up' the acid names no chemistry.

cards.q: Explain why a solution made only from $NH_4Cl$ is not a buffer, even though $NH_4^+$ is a weak acid.
cards.a: NH4Cl supplies only the weak acid NH4⁺ (with spectator Cl⁻); there is essentially no NH3 to react with added H3O⁺. Added strong acid would stay as H3O⁺ and the pH would fall sharply. A buffer needs both NH4⁺ and NH3 in comparable amounts.
cards.h: → the missing component and what it would have done
cards.n: Adding NH3, or half-neutralizing the NH4⁺ with strong base, makes the same solution a buffer; 'NH4Cl is a salt' is not the reason.

cards.q:
Write the net ionic equation for the reaction that occurs when each small addition is made to the buffer named:
HCl added to CH3COOH/NaCH3COO
NaOH added to CH3COOH/NaCH3COO
HNO3 added to NH3/NH4Cl
KOH added to NH3/NH4Cl
HCl added to HF/NaF
NaOH added to HF/NaF
H3O⁺ added to blood (H2CO3/HCO3⁻)
OH⁻ added to blood (H2CO3/HCO3⁻)
HCl added to NaH2PO4/Na2HPO4
NaOH added to NaH2PO4/Na2HPO4
cards.a:
HCl, acetate buffer → (CH3COO⁻ + H3O⁺ → CH3COOH + H2O)
NaOH, acetate buffer → (CH3COOH + OH⁻ → CH3COO⁻ + H2O)
HNO3, ammonia buffer → (NH3 + H3O⁺ → NH4⁺ + H2O)
KOH, ammonia buffer → (NH4⁺ + OH⁻ → NH3 + H2O)
HCl, fluoride buffer → (F⁻ + H3O⁺ → HF + H2O)
NaOH, fluoride buffer → (HF + OH⁻ → F⁻ + H2O)
H3O⁺, blood → (HCO3⁻ + H3O⁺ → H2CO3 + H2O)
OH⁻, blood → (H2CO3 + OH⁻ → HCO3⁻ + H2O)
HCl, phosphate buffer → (HPO4²⁻ + H3O⁺ → H2PO4⁻ + H2O)
NaOH, phosphate buffer → (H2PO4⁻ + OH⁻ → HPO4²⁻ + H2O)
cards.h: → added acid meets the base form; added base meets the acid
cards.n: Writing H3O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H2O for a buffer addition misses the point: the buffer's own component, not water, consumes the addition.

cards.q:
Classify each mixture, all in 1.0 L of solution, as a buffer or not a buffer:
0.20 mol HF + 0.20 mol NaF
0.20 mol HCl + 0.20 mol NaCl
0.30 mol NH3 + 0.20 mol NH4Cl
0.10 mol CH3COOH + 0.050 mol NaOH
0.10 mol CH3COOH + 0.10 mol NaOH
0.10 mol CH3COOH + 0.20 mol NaOH
0.20 mol NH3 + 0.10 mol HCl
0.10 mol HNO3 + 0.10 mol KNO3
0.10 mol HCOOH + 0.10 mol NaHCOO
0.10 mol NaH2PO4 + 0.10 mol Na2HPO4
0.10 mol CH3COOH + 0.10 mol HCl
0.20 mol NaF + 0.10 mol HCl
0.10 mol NaCN alone
0.10 mol NH3 + 0.10 mol NaOH
0.50 mol CH3COOH + 0.0010 mol NaCH3COO
cards.a:
HF + NaF → buffer (weak acid + conjugate base)
HCl + NaCl → not a buffer (Cl⁻ cannot accept protons)
NH3 + NH4Cl → buffer
0.10 CH3COOH + 0.050 NaOH → buffer (0.050 mol of each after reaction)
0.10 CH3COOH + 0.10 NaOH → not (only CH3COO⁻ remains)
0.10 CH3COOH + 0.20 NaOH → not (excess OH⁻, no acid left)
0.20 NH3 + 0.10 HCl → buffer (0.10 mol NH3, 0.10 mol NH4⁺)
HNO3 + KNO3 → not (strong acid)
HCOOH + NaHCOO → buffer
NaH2PO4 + Na2HPO4 → buffer (H2PO4⁻/HPO4²⁻)
CH3COOH + HCl → not (no conjugate base)
0.20 NaF + 0.10 HCl → buffer (0.10 mol HF, 0.10 mol F⁻)
NaCN alone → not (base form only)
NH3 + NaOH → not (no conjugate acid)
0.50 CH3COOH + 0.0010 NaCH3COO → not a useful buffer (500:1, not comparable)
cards.h: → react first, then ask: are both members of a pair present?
cards.n: Judging a mixture before letting its strong acid or base react is the trap; do the stoichiometry, then look for a weak conjugate pair.

cards.q: Represent a particulate view of an acetate buffer drawn with 6 CH3COOH molecules, 6 CH3COO⁻ ions and 6 Na⁺ ions (water omitted), and then the same box after 2 H3O⁺ ions (added as HCl, with 2 Cl⁻) have been added and have reacted.
cards.a: Before: 6 CH3COOH, 6 CH3COO⁻, 6 Na⁺. After: 8 CH3COOH, 4 CH3COO⁻, 6 Na⁺ and 2 Cl⁻, with no H3O⁺ drawn, because each added H3O⁺ gave its proton to an acetate ion (CH3COO⁻ + H3O⁺ → CH3COOH + H2O). The acid : base count moves only from 6:6 to 8:4, and the charges still balance: 6 Na⁺ = 4 CH3COO⁻ + 2 Cl⁻.
cards.h: → two sets of particle counts, then the reaction
cards.n: Leaving the 2 H3O⁺ unreacted in the after box shows no buffering; so does dropping the Na⁺ or making molecules vanish.

cards.q: Predict the direction and relative size of the pH change when 1.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl is added to 100 mL of an acetate buffer (0.10 M in each component) and when it is added to 100 mL of pure water.
cards.a: Both pH values fall, but the buffer's only slightly (it stays near its original 4.74) while the water's falls from 7.00 to 2.00. In water the 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol H3O⁺ remains: 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.101 L = 9.9 × 10⁻³ M, pH 2.00. In the buffer it is converted to CH3COOH by the 0.010 mol of acetate, using up only a tenth of it, so [A⁻]/[HA] barely moves.
cards.h: → direction for both, then why the sizes differ
cards.n: Computing the buffer's new pH is excluded from the exam (8.9); the qualitative comparison with water is what this card asks.

cards.q: Explain why a buffer must contain both a weak acid and its conjugate base in comparable amounts.
cards.a: Each component handles one kind of addition: the conjugate base consumes added H3O⁺ (A⁻ + H3O⁺ → HA + H2O) and the weak acid consumes added OH⁻ (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O). If either is missing or tiny, that kind of addition goes unneutralized and the pH changes sharply; comparable amounts resist both.
cards.h: → A⁻ removes added acid, HA removes added base → both must be present → comparable amounts protect both ways
cards.n: 'It needs both to be balanced' names no reaction; the point is which component consumes which addition.
o: With comparable amounts, [A⁻]/[HA] is near 1, and small additions change that ratio, and so the pH, only slightly.
A weak acid alone has almost no A⁻ to absorb added acid, and its conjugate base alone has almost no HA to absorb added base.

w.a: A buffer needs both so that they can neutralize each other.
w.why: HA and A⁻ do not neutralize each other; they react with the additions

w.a: Only the weak acid is needed because it keeps the solution acidic.
w.why: without A⁻, added acid is not consumed

w.a: The two components are needed to make the solution neutral.
w.why: a buffer holds any pH near its pKa, not only 7

cards.q: Explain why a mixture of HCl and NaCl cannot act as a buffer.
cards.a: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and is far too weak a base to accept protons, so added H3O⁺ is not consumed and simply adds to [H3O⁺]. HCl is fully ionized, so there is no reservoir of weak-acid molecules to hold the pH steady as base is added; the pH just tracks the amount of strong acid.
cards.h: → Cl⁻ is a negligible base → added H3O⁺ is not consumed → no weak-acid reservoir → no buffering
cards.n: 'HCl is a strong acid' alone is incomplete; the point is that Cl⁻ cannot consume added acid.
o: A buffer needs a weak conjugate pair; HCl/Cl⁻ is a strong-acid pair, and Cl⁻ has effectively zero Kb.
Adding H3O⁺ to Cl⁻ forms no HCl molecules, because HCl ionizes completely, so nothing removes the added acid.

w.a: It cannot buffer because NaCl is a neutral salt that does nothing.
w.why: true of Na⁺, but the key is that Cl⁻ cannot accept protons

w.a: It is a buffer because it contains an acid and its conjugate base.
w.why: the pair must be weak; Cl⁻ is a negligible base

w.a: It cannot buffer because the solution is too acidic.
w.why: acidity is not the issue; many buffers are acidic

cards.q: Explain why adding a small amount of HCl to an NH3/NH4Cl buffer changes its pH only slightly.
cards.a: The NH3 in the buffer consumes the added acid completely: NH3 + H3O⁺ → NH4⁺ + H2O. The strong acid is replaced by the weak acid NH4⁺, and because NH3 and NH4⁺ are both present in large amounts, converting a little NH3 to NH4⁺ barely changes [NH3]/[NH4⁺], so [H3O⁺] and the pH barely change.
cards.h: → NH3 consumes the H3O⁺ → strong acid replaced by weak NH4⁺ → ratio barely moves → pH barely changes
cards.n: Saying the buffer 'neutralizes the acid' without naming NH3 as the reacting species earns nothing.
o: Only a small fraction of the large NH3 reserve is used, so the conjugate pair's ratio, which sets the pH, is almost unchanged.
Nearly all the added H3O⁺ ends up as NH4⁺, a very weak acid (Ka 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰), so almost none remains as free H3O⁺.

w.a: The Cl⁻ from HCl reacts with NH4⁺, so the pH stays the same.
w.why: Cl⁻ is a spectator; NH3 is the reacting species

w.a: NH4⁺ reacts with the HCl to neutralize it.
w.why: NH4⁺ is an acid and cannot neutralize added acid

w.a: The pH does not change at all because a buffer's pH is fixed.
w.why: the pH changes slightly; buffers resist change, they do not prevent it

cards.q: Explain why the weak acid and the conjugate base in a buffer do not neutralize each other.
cards.a: A weak acid and its own conjugate base can only exchange a proton to give the same two species back: HA + A⁻ ⇌ A⁻ + HA, with K = 1 and no net change. So both stay at the amounts mixed, ready to consume added base (HA) and added acid (A⁻).
cards.h: → proton transfer between HA and A⁻ just regenerates HA and A⁻ → no net reaction → both remain available
cards.n: 'They are both weak, so they cannot react' is not the reason; they do exchange protons, but the exchange changes nothing.
o: Neutralization needs a stronger acid meeting a stronger base; HA and A⁻ are the same pair, so there is no driving force either way.
Any proton A⁻ takes from HA makes one new HA and one new A⁻, leaving both amounts unchanged.

w.a: They do neutralize each other, which is why a buffer's pH is near 7.
w.why: no net reaction occurs, and a buffer's pH is set by pKa, not 7

w.a: They cannot meet because they stay in separate layers of the solution.
w.why: they are mixed in one solution

w.a: The conjugate base is too weak to react with anything.
w.why: it reacts readily with added H3O⁺

cards.q: State the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation and the conditions under which it applies.
cards.a: $pH = pK_{a} + \log\frac{[A^{-}]}{[HA]}$, where pKa belongs to the weak acid of the pair. It applies to a buffer, a solution with appreciable, comparable amounts of both HA and A⁻ (ratio roughly 0.1 to 10), so the amounts mixed can stand in for the equilibrium amounts. It is the Ka expression rearranged in log form.
cards.h: → pKa plus a log ratio, then when it applies
cards.n: Using it on a weak acid alone ([A⁻] ≈ 0) or at an equivalence point ([HA] ≈ 0) is the classic misuse; deriving it is excluded, using it is not.

cards.q: Compute the pH of a buffer that is 0.20 M in HC2H3O2 and 0.40 M in NaC2H3O2, given Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵.
cards.a: pH = 5.04. pKa = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.74. pH = pKa + log([C2H3O2⁻]/[HC2H3O2]) = 4.74 + log(0.40/0.20) = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04. More conjugate base than acid puts the pH above the pKa, as it should.
cards.h: → pKa, then add the log of base over acid
cards.n: Putting acid over base inverts the log (4.44); a 2:1 base-to-acid ratio always lands 0.30 above the pKa.

cards.q: Compute the pH of a buffer containing 0.20 M acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$) and 0.30 M sodium acetate.
cards.h: → Henderson–Hasselbalch in one line
cards.n: The ratio inside the log is [conjugate base]/[acid], not the reverse; inverting it gives 4.56, below pKa, which cannot be right here.

cards.q: Predict the pH of a buffer in which the weak acid and its conjugate base are present in equal concentrations.
cards.a: pH = pKa. With [A⁻] = [HA] the ratio is 1 and log 1 = 0, so pH = pKa + 0. Equal amounts also give the buffer its greatest capacity against both added acid and added base.
cards.h: → pH equals a constant
cards.n: It is equal moles (or concentrations) that matter, not equal volumes of stock solutions with different molarities.

cards.q: Compute the pH of a buffer made from 0.30 mol $NH_3$ and 0.20 mol $NH_4Cl$ in 1.00 L, given $K_b(NH_3)=1.8\times10^{-5}$.
cards.a: pH = 9.43. Henderson–Hasselbalch needs the pKa of the acid, NH4⁺: pKb(NH3) = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.74, so pKa = 14.00 − 4.74 = 9.26. pH = 9.26 + log([NH3]/[NH4⁺]) = 9.26 + log(0.30/0.20) = 9.26 + 0.18 = 9.43 (carrying the unrounded pKa, 9.255; rounding it first gives 9.44).
cards.h: → convert Kb to pKa first, then H–H
cards.n: Plugging pKb (4.74) straight into the equation gives pH 4.92 for a basic buffer; a base buffer needs the conjugate acid's pKa.

cards.q: Compute the ratio $[A^-]/[HA]$ needed to buffer a solution at pH = 5.20 using an acid with pKa = 4.70.
cards.h: → rearrange for the ratio, then one antilog
cards.n: A ratio above 1 means more conjugate base than acid, matching a pH above pKa; a ratio of 0.32 means the subtraction was reversed.

cards.q: 500. mL of 0.200 M $CH_3COOH$ needs $NaC_2H_3O_2$ added to reach pH = 5.05 (pKa = 4.745). Compute the mass of $NaC_2H_3O_2$ (M = 82.0 g/mol) needed.
cards.a: 16.6 g. mol CH3COOH = 0.500 L × 0.200 M = 0.100 mol. The required ratio is [A⁻]/[HA] = $10^{5.05 - 4.745}$ = $10^{0.305}$ = 2.02, so mol NaC2H3O2 = 2.02 × 0.100 mol = 0.202 mol, and the mass is 0.202 mol × 82.0 g/mol = 16.6 g.
cards.h: → H–H for the ratio, then moles → mass
cards.n: The 500. mL cancels because both species share it, so the ratio applies to moles directly; dividing by the volume again is a wasted step.

cards.q: Calculate the pH of a solution made by mixing 40.0 mL of 0.20 M HCOOH with 60.0 mL of 0.15 M NaHCOO (Ka of HCOOH = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴).
cards.h: → moles of each, then H–H with the mole ratio
cards.n: Using the stock molarities (0.15/0.20) instead of moles ignores the different volumes and gives 3.62.

cards.q: Determine the pKa and Ka of a weak acid HA, given that a buffer 0.15 M in HA and 0.25 M in NaA has a measured pH of 6.02.
cards.a: pKa = 5.80; Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶. Rearranging Henderson–Hasselbalch: pKa = pH − log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 6.02 − log(0.25/0.15) = 6.02 − 0.22 = 5.80, and Ka = $10^{-5.80}$ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶.
cards.h: → rearrange H–H for pKa, then one antilog
cards.n: Adding the log term instead of subtracting it (6.24) is the sign slip; with more A⁻ than HA the pKa must lie below the pH.

cards.q: Estimate, without a calculator, the pH of three buffers of a weak acid with pKa = 7.20: one with 10 times as much A⁻ as HA, one with 10 times as much HA as A⁻, and one with twice as much A⁻ as HA.
cards.a: 8.20, 6.20 and 7.50. log 10 = 1 and log 0.1 = −1, so a 10:1 ratio puts the pH one unit above or below the pKa; log 2 ≈ 0.30, so a 2:1 base-to-acid ratio puts it 0.30 above: 7.20 + 0.30 = 7.50.
cards.h: → three values from log 10, log 0.1 and log 2
cards.n: Moving the pH ten units for a tenfold ratio treats the log as linear; each factor of 10 in the ratio is one pH unit.

cards.q:
Calculate the pH of each buffer:
0.10 M CH3COOH + 0.10 M CH3COO⁻ (pKa 4.74)
0.10 M HF + 0.25 M F⁻ (Ka 7.2 × 10⁻⁴)
0.50 M NH4⁺ + 0.25 M NH3 (pKa 9.26)
0.020 mol HOCl + 0.060 mol NaOCl in 500 mL (Ka 3.0 × 10⁻⁸)
0.30 M HCOOH + 0.15 M HCOO⁻ (pKa 3.74)
0.10 M H2PO4⁻ + 0.10 M HPO4²⁻ (pKa 7.21)
0.040 M H2CO3 + 0.40 M HCO3⁻ (pKa 6.37)
0.12 M C6H5COOH + 0.080 M C6H5COO⁻ (pKa 4.20)
0.25 M CH3NH2 + 0.50 M CH3NH3⁺ (Kb 4.4 × 10⁻⁴)
0.15 M HCN + 0.60 M CN⁻ (pKa 9.21)
cards.h: → pKa of the acid form + log(base/acid), each line
cards.n: The amine line needs the conjugate acid's pKa (10.64), not the base's pKb; in every line the base form goes on top of the ratio.

cards.q: Explain why moles can be used in place of concentrations in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a buffer.
cards.a: Both members of the pair are in the same solution volume V, so [A⁻]/[HA] = (n(A⁻)/V)/(n(HA)/V) = n(A⁻)/n(HA); the volume cancels. The pH therefore depends only on the mole ratio, not on the total volume.
cards.h: → both species share one volume → V cancels in the ratio → mole ratio = concentration ratio
cards.n: 'Because moles and molarity are the same thing' earns nothing; the cancellation of the shared volume is the reason.
o: Diluting a buffer changes both concentrations by the same factor, leaving the ratio and the pH unchanged; the same cancellation lets moles stand in.
Only a ratio enters the log term, and a ratio of two amounts in one volume is the same in moles or in molarity.

w.a: Moles and concentration are the same quantity.
w.why: molarity is moles per liter; the two agree only in exactly 1 L

w.a: Moles can be used because a buffer's volume is always 1.00 L.
w.why: the volume cancels whatever its value

w.a: Using moles is an approximation that makes the pH less accurate.
w.why: it is exact for the ratio, since V cancels

cards.q: Explain why the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation cannot be used to find the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid on its own.
cards.a: With no acetate added, the only A⁻ comes from the acid's own slight ionization, which is the unknown being solved for; setting [A⁻] ≈ 0 makes log([A⁻]/[HA]) undefined. The equation assumes known, comparable amounts of HA and A⁻. For the acid alone, solve Ka = x²/(C − x): pH 2.87.
cards.h: → no added A⁻ → [A⁻] is the unknown, not a given → the log ratio is undefined → use the Ka equilibrium instead
cards.n: Using H–H outside the buffer region (plain weak acid, or at equivalence) is a named trap; the plain acid's pH is not its pKa.
o: In a buffer the large added amounts of HA and A⁻ barely change on reaching equilibrium; in a plain weak acid [A⁻] starts at zero, so that assumption fails.
The log term blows up as [A⁻] approaches 0, a sign that the solution is not a buffer and the Ka equilibrium must be solved directly.

w.a: The pH of 0.10 M acetic acid equals its pKa, 4.74.
w.why: pH = pKa only when [HA] = [A⁻]; the plain acid is at pH 2.87

w.a: Henderson–Hasselbalch works if you set [A⁻] = [HA] = 0.10 M.
w.why: no acetate was added, so [A⁻] is not 0.10 M

w.a: It cannot be used because acetic acid is a strong acid.
w.why: acetic acid is weak; the problem is the missing conjugate base

cards.q: Explain, using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, why adding a small amount of strong acid to a buffer changes its pH only slightly.
cards.a: The pH depends on log([A⁻]/[HA]). A small amount of H3O⁺ converts an equally small amount of A⁻ into HA; when both are present in large amounts, their ratio barely changes, and the log of a nearly unchanged ratio changes even less. So the pH shifts only slightly.
cards.h: → H3O⁺ turns a little A⁻ into HA → large amounts barely change the ratio → its log barely moves → small pH change
cards.n: The qualitative argument is what is tested; computing the exact new pH after the addition is excluded from the AP exam.
o: Without the buffer the added H3O⁺ would stay free and change [H3O⁺] by orders of magnitude; in the buffer it is traded for weak acid, altering only the log term.
Because the pH follows the logarithm of a ratio, even a 10% change in that ratio moves the pH by only a few hundredths.

w.a: The pH does not change because the buffer absorbs the H⁺ ions.
w.why: 'absorbs' names no reaction, and the pH does change slightly

w.a: The pH changes only slightly because the pKa shifts to compensate.
w.why: pKa is a constant; the ratio is what changes

w.a: The added acid is diluted by the buffer's water, so it has little effect.
w.why: dilution alone would still lower the pH a lot; the reaction with A⁻ is the reason

cards.q: Explain why a buffer's pH is above the pKa of its weak acid when the buffer contains more conjugate base than acid.
cards.a: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). With [A⁻] > [HA] the ratio is greater than 1 and its log is positive, so pH > pKa. Chemically, the extra A⁻ pushes HA ⇌ H3O⁺ + A⁻ to the left, holding [H3O⁺] below Ka.
cards.h: → [A⁻] > [HA] → ratio > 1 → log is positive → pH above pKa
cards.n: 'More base means more basic' is not enough: such a buffer can still be acidic (acetate at 2:1 is pH 5.04); it is above pKa, not above 7.
o: From Ka = [H3O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], [H3O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻], which is less than Ka when [A⁻] > [HA], so pH > pKa.
Each doubling of [A⁻]/[HA] raises the pH by 0.30 relative to the pKa.

w.a: The pH is above pKa because the solution is basic.
w.why: an acetate buffer with extra A⁻ is still acidic, just above 4.74

w.a: The pH is above pKa because the conjugate base raises the Ka.
w.why: Ka is constant; only the ratio changes

w.a: More conjugate base makes the acid stronger, so the pH is higher.
w.why: acid strength is unchanged, and a stronger acid would lower the pH

cards.q: Define buffer capacity.
cards.a: Buffer capacity is the amount of strong acid or strong base a buffer can neutralize before its pH changes significantly. It depends on the amounts (concentrations) of the weak acid and conjugate base present, not on their ratio alone: the ratio sets the pH, the amounts set the capacity.
cards.h: → what it measures and what it depends on
cards.n: Two buffers can share a pH yet differ tenfold in capacity; equating a 'good buffer' with the 'right pH' is the confusion.

cards.q: Explain what conditions maximize buffer capacity.
cards.a: High concentrations of both components, and a [A⁻]/[HA] ratio close to 1, i.e., a pH close to the pKa. More of both means more acid and base can be neutralized; a ratio near 1 means neither component runs out first. Capacity in one direction falls off sharply once the ratio passes about 10:1.
cards.h: → two conditions, each with its reason
cards.n: Naming only 'high concentration' misses the ratio condition; a concentrated but 20:1 buffer is weak against one kind of addition.

cards.q: Decide how to choose a weak acid to prepare a buffer of a target pH.
cards.a: Choose a weak acid whose pKa is within about 1 unit of the target pH (as close as possible), then set the [A⁻]/[HA] ratio with Henderson–Hasselbalch. A pKa near the target keeps the ratio near 1, so the buffer has good capacity against both added acid and added base.
cards.h: → match pKa to the target pH, then fine-tune the ratio
cards.n: A pKa far from the target forces an extreme ratio, leaving too little of one component, so the buffer fails quickly in one direction.

cards.q: Explain why diluting a buffer with water barely changes its pH.
cards.a: Dilution lowers [HA] and [A⁻] by the same factor, so their ratio, and therefore the log term in Henderson–Hasselbalch, is unchanged: the pH stays essentially constant. But fewer moles per liter of each component remain to react with additions, so the buffer capacity per liter drops.
cards.h: → ratio unchanged, capacity per liter falls
cards.n: 'Water is neutral, so the pH stays' misses both halves; dilution shows that pH follows the ratio while capacity follows the amounts.

cards.q: Predict which buffer has the greater capacity: one with 0.10 mol each of HA and A⁻, or one with 1.0 mol each of HA and A⁻ in the same volume.
cards.a: The 1.0 mol buffer has the greater capacity, about ten times greater. Both have [A⁻]/[HA] = 1 and the same pH (= pKa), but the 1.0 mol buffer has ten times as much A⁻ to consume added acid and ten times as much HA to consume added base before either runs low.
cards.h: → which buffer, plus the amounts reason
cards.n: Capacity depends on the moles of buffer components present, not on the pH they set; 'same pH, same buffer' is the trap.

cards.q: Explain what happens to a buffer's ability to resist pH change once enough strong acid has been added to consume nearly all its conjugate base.
cards.a: The buffer loses its ability to resist added acid. With little or no A⁻ left, further H3O⁺ is not consumed and stays in solution, so each addition now lowers the pH sharply, as it would in unbuffered water. The buffer can still resist added base, since plenty of HA remains.
cards.h: → what is gone, then what further acid does
cards.n: A buffer works only while both components remain in significant amounts; 'it stops working completely' ignores that it still resists base.

cards.q: Predict which buffer has greater overall capacity: a large excess of conjugate base over acid, or equal amounts of each, at equal total concentration.
cards.a: The buffer with equal amounts has the greater overall capacity, against both acid and base. The base-rich buffer has extra A⁻, so it resists added acid well, but its small amount of HA is used up quickly by added base.
cards.h: → which buffer, plus the direction-by-direction reason
cards.n: A base-heavy buffer still buffers acid well; balanced protection against both acid and base needs a ratio near 1.

cards.q: Calculate the maximum amount, in moles, of HCl that 500. mL of a buffer 0.20 M in CH3COOH and 0.30 M in NaCH3COO can neutralize before its conjugate base is used up, and the maximum amount of NaOH it can neutralize before its weak acid is used up.
cards.a: 0.15 mol HCl and 0.10 mol NaOH. mol CH3COO⁻ = 0.500 L × 0.30 M = 0.15 mol, each consuming one H3O⁺ (CH3COO⁻ + H3O⁺ → CH3COOH + H2O); mol CH3COOH = 0.500 L × 0.20 M = 0.10 mol, each consuming one OH⁻. With more base than acid, this buffer has the greater capacity for added acid.
cards.h: → moles of each component, one-to-one with the addition
cards.n: These are stoichiometric limits, not the excluded pH-after-addition calculation; in practice buffering fails somewhat before a component is used up.

cards.q: Predict which buffer can absorb more added NaOH before its pH rises sharply: Buffer X, 0.40 M HA and 0.10 M A⁻, or Buffer Y, 0.10 M HA and 0.40 M A⁻ (same weak acid, same volume).
cards.a: Buffer X. Added OH⁻ is consumed by the weak acid (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O), and X has four times as much HA as Y. Y, rich in A⁻, would instead absorb more added acid. X's pH is lower (pKa − 0.60) and Y's higher (pKa + 0.60), but the direction of greater capacity follows the larger component.
cards.h: → which buffer, then which component meets OH⁻
cards.n: Choosing Y because it is 'more basic' reverses the logic: a base-leaning buffer resists added acid, not added base.

cards.q: Explain how a student's error of making a buffer 0.050 M in both NH3 and NH4Cl, instead of the intended 0.50 M in both, affects the buffer's measured pH and its performance when 0.020 mol HCl is added to 1.00 L.
cards.a: The pH is unaffected, still pKa = 9.26, because the ratio [NH3]/[NH4⁺] is still 1. The capacity is ten times smaller: 0.020 mol HCl uses up 40% of the 0.050 mol NH3 (versus 4% of 0.50 mol), so the NH3 : NH4⁺ ratio shifts from 1 to 0.030 : 0.070 and the pH drops noticeably instead of barely.
cards.h: → effect on pH, then effect on capacity, with numbers
cards.n: Saying the dilute buffer 'has the wrong pH' misreads the error: the pH is right and the capacity suffers. Its new pH is an excluded computation.

cards.q: Explain why a buffer that is 1.0 M in both HA and A⁻ has the same pH as one that is 0.10 M in both, but a greater buffer capacity.
cards.a: pH depends only on the ratio [A⁻]/[HA], which is 1 in both, so both have pH = pKa. Capacity depends on the amounts available to react: the 1.0 M buffer has ten times as much A⁻ to consume added acid and HA to consume added base, so it takes ten times more to shift its ratio, and pH, as far.
cards.h: → ratio sets pH (same) → amounts set capacity → 10× more of each → 10× more acid or base absorbed
cards.n: 'The stronger buffer has a lower pH' confuses capacity with pH; concentration changes capacity, the ratio fixes pH.
o: Henderson–Hasselbalch contains only the ratio, so scaling both components by 10 leaves the pH alone while multiplying each reserve by 10.
A fixed addition of acid is a ten times smaller fraction of the 1.0 M buffer's A⁻, so its ratio and pH move ten times less.

w.a: The 1.0 M buffer has a lower pH because it is more concentrated.
w.why: the ratio is the same, so the pH is the same

w.a: Both buffers have the same capacity because they have the same pH.
w.why: capacity depends on the amounts, not the pH

w.a: The 1.0 M buffer is better because its acid is stronger.
w.why: it is the same weak acid; only the amounts differ

cards.q: Explain why a buffer with more conjugate base than weak acid has a greater capacity for added acid than for added base.
cards.a: Added acid is consumed by A⁻ (A⁻ + H3O⁺ → HA + H2O) and added base by HA (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O). With more A⁻ than HA, more H3O⁺ can be neutralized before A⁻ runs out than OH⁻ before HA runs out; the smaller component, HA, sets the limit for added base.
cards.h: → acid consumed by A⁻, base by HA → more A⁻ than HA → acid absorbed longer → greater capacity for acid
cards.n: 'More base means it handles base better' reverses the logic; the base form neutralizes added acid.
o: Each mole of A⁻ neutralizes one mole of added H3O⁺, so the component in excess sets the larger capacity, and here that is A⁻, the acid-consuming component.
Added base quickly shrinks the small [HA], so [A⁻]/[HA] and the pH climb fast; added acid changes the large [A⁻] only a little.

w.a: A base-rich buffer resists added base better because it is already basic.
w.why: the base form consumes acid, not base

w.a: The capacity is the same both ways because the pKa is fixed.
w.why: capacity in each direction depends on the amount of the consuming component

w.a: A base-rich buffer cannot resist added acid at all.
w.why: it resists acid best; it is weak against added base

cards.q: Explain why a useful buffer's pH should lie within about 1 unit of its weak acid's pKa.
cards.a: pH − pKa = log([A⁻]/[HA]), so a pH 1 unit from pKa already means a 10:1 ratio. Beyond that, one component is so scarce that a modest addition of the matching acid or base uses it up, and capacity in that direction collapses.
cards.h: → pH − pKa = log(ratio) → 1 unit means 10:1 → beyond that one component is scarce → it runs out quickly
cards.n: 'Because Henderson–Hasselbalch only works near pKa' names a limit but not its cause; the cause is the scarce component.
o: At pH = pKa ± 2 the ratio is 100:1, so the minor component is only about 1% of the pair and is exhausted by a small addition.
Buffer capacity is greatest at pH = pKa, where both components are equal, and falls steadily as the ratio becomes lopsided.

w.a: The pH must be near pKa or the weak acid becomes a strong acid.
w.why: the acid's strength never changes

w.a: A buffer more than 1 unit from pKa has no conjugate base at all.
w.why: it has some, just too little to give useful capacity

w.a: The pH must be near pKa because pKa is always near 7.
w.why: pKa values range widely; the point is the ratio

cards.q: Explain why a buffer prepared at the correct pH could still fail to hold that pH during an experiment that produced more acid than expected.
cards.a: The pH was right because the ratio was right, but the buffer capacity was too small: once the acid produced exceeded the moles of conjugate base present, no A⁻ remained to consume H3O⁺, and further acid lowered the pH sharply. More concentrated components at the same ratio would have prevented it.
cards.h: → ratio set the pH, amounts set the capacity → acid exceeded the A⁻ present → no A⁻ left → pH falls sharply
cards.n: Blaming a 'wrong pKa' or 'wrong pH' misreads the failure; the pH was right, and the amount of conjugate base was too small.
o: Capacity scales with the moles of A⁻; an experiment that makes more H3O⁺ than that exhausts the buffer whatever its starting pH.
A more concentrated buffer, or a more base-rich ratio, would raise the capacity for acid without changing the chosen weak acid.

w.a: The buffer failed because its pH was calculated wrongly.
w.why: the pH was correct; the capacity was the problem

w.a: Buffers only work for a few minutes before they wear out.
w.why: buffers do not decay with time; they are used up by additions

w.a: The buffer failed because the weak acid became stronger as acid was added.
w.why: Ka does not change; the conjugate base ran out

cards.q: Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility of a salt containing a basic anion.
cards.a: Lowering the pH increases the salt's solubility. The added H3O⁺ reacts with the basic anion (for example F⁻ + H3O⁺ → HF + H2O), removing it from solution. That lowers Q = [M⁺][A⁻] below Ksp, so the dissolution equilibrium MA(s) ⇌ M⁺ + A⁻ shifts right and more solid dissolves.
cards.h: → direction, the anion-removing reaction, then Q < Ksp
cards.n: 'Le Châtelier' with no reaction named earns little; identify the removed ion. Ksp and Q are Unit 7, and the effect is qualitative only.

cards.q: Identify which slightly soluble salts have a solubility that is essentially independent of pH.
cards.a: Salts whose anions are the conjugate bases of strong acids: chlorides, bromides and iodides (AgCl, AgBr, PbI2), plus nitrates and perchlorates, which are soluble anyway. Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻ are negligibly basic, so added H3O⁺ does not react with them and does not shift the dissolution equilibrium.
cards.h: → the anion family, then why H3O⁺ ignores it
cards.n: Listing CaF2 or CaCO3 here is the error; F⁻ and CO3²⁻ are weak bases, so those salts dissolve more in acid.

cards.q: Predict whether the solubility of $Mg(OH)_2$ increases or decreases as the solution pH is lowered, and explain.
cards.a: Solubility increases. Mg(OH)2(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2OH⁻; added H3O⁺ removes OH⁻ (H3O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H2O), lowering Q below Ksp, so by Le Châtelier's principle more Mg(OH)2 dissolves to replace the hydroxide.
cards.h: → direction, then the reaction that removes OH⁻
cards.n: Name the neutralization that removes OH⁻ rather than only citing Le Châtelier; a numerical solubility at a given pH is excluded.

cards.q: Predict whether the molar solubility of $CaCO_3$ increases or decreases as the solution pH is lowered, and explain.
cards.a: Molar solubility increases. CO3²⁻ is a basic anion: added H3O⁺ converts it to HCO3⁻ and then H2CO3 (which releases CO2), removing CO3²⁻ from CaCO3(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + CO3²⁻. Q falls below Ksp, so the dissolution equilibrium shifts forward and more CaCO3 dissolves.
cards.h: → direction, then the reaction that removes CO3²⁻
cards.n: Saying acid 'breaks down' limestone without the CO3²⁻ + H3O⁺ reaction earns nothing; the removed ion must be named.

cards.q: Explain why the solubility of AgCl is essentially unaffected by the solution's pH.
cards.a: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl, so it is far too weak a base to react with H3O⁺, and AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ is not disturbed when acid is added. Neither ion is a weak acid, a weak base or OH⁻, so changing the pH has no meaningful effect on AgCl's solubility.
cards.h: → Cl⁻ is a spectator, not a base
cards.n: Adding HCl does lower AgCl's solubility, but through the common ion Cl⁻, not through pH; don't confuse the two effects.

cards.q: Predict how [Ca²⁺], [F⁻] and [HF] change when HNO3 is added to a saturated solution of CaF2 in contact with excess solid.
cards.a: [HF] increases, [Ca²⁺] increases, and [F⁻] decreases. H3O⁺ converts F⁻ to HF (F⁻ + H3O⁺ → HF + H2O), so Q < Ksp and more CaF2 dissolves, raising [Ca²⁺]. At the new equilibrium Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² still holds, so with [Ca²⁺] higher, [F⁻] must be lower than before.
cards.h: → three directions, then the Ksp check
cards.n: Saying [F⁻] rises because more CaF2 dissolves overlooks that the new F⁻ becomes HF; Ksp forces [F⁻] down when [Ca²⁺] goes up.

cards.q:
Classify each slightly soluble salt as more soluble in acidic solution than in pure water, or essentially unaffected by pH:
AgCl
CaCO3
BaF2
Mg(OH)2
PbI2
Ca3(PO4)2
AgBr
Fe(OH)3
CaC2O4
Zn(OH)2
PbCl2
AgCH3COO
AgI
Cu(OH)2
Ag2CO3
cards.a:
AgCl → unaffected (Cl⁻ comes from a strong acid)
CaCO3 → more soluble in acid (CO3²⁻ is basic)
BaF2 → more soluble (F⁻ is a weak base)
Mg(OH)2 → more soluble (OH⁻ is neutralized)
PbI2 → unaffected (I⁻)
Ca3(PO4)2 → more soluble (PO4³⁻ is basic)
AgBr → unaffected (Br⁻)
Fe(OH)3 → more soluble (OH⁻)
CaC2O4 → more soluble (oxalate is a weak base)
Zn(OH)2 → more soluble (OH⁻)
PbCl2 → unaffected (Cl⁻)
AgCH3COO → more soluble (acetate is a weak base)
AgI → unaffected (I⁻)
Cu(OH)2 → more soluble (OH⁻)
Ag2CO3 → more soluble (CO3²⁻)
cards.h: → is the anion a weak base or OH⁻, or from a strong acid?
cards.n: How soluble the salt is in pure water is irrelevant here; only whether H3O⁺ reacts with the anion decides. No numerical solubility is expected.

cards.q:
Identify which salt contains a basic anion from these measured molar solubilities at 25 °C, and justify the choice:
pH · salt P (M) · salt Q (M)
3.0 · 1.2 × 10⁻² · 1.3 × 10⁻⁵
5.0 · 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ · 1.3 × 10⁻⁵
7.0 · 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ · 1.3 × 10⁻⁵
cards.a: Salt P. Its solubility rises about sixtyfold as the pH falls from 7.0 to 3.0, the signature of an anion that H3O⁺ protonates and removes from the dissolution equilibrium (a weak base or OH⁻). Salt Q's solubility is the same at every pH, so its anion is the conjugate base of a strong acid, such as Cl⁻, which H3O⁺ leaves alone.
cards.h: → which salt, then the trend that shows it
cards.n: Picking Q because it is less soluble reads the wrong feature; the change with pH, not the size of the solubility, reveals the basic anion.

cards.q: Predict how the solubility of Ni(OH)2 changes when the pH of its saturated solution is raised from 7 to 10, and justify the prediction.
cards.a: Solubility decreases. Ni(OH)2(s) ⇌ Ni²⁺ + 2OH⁻; raising the pH from 7 to 10 raises [OH⁻] a thousandfold, from 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁴ M. OH⁻ is a product ion, so Q exceeds Ksp and the equilibrium shifts left, precipitating Ni(OH)2: the common-ion effect of the hydroxide ion.
cards.h: → direction, then [OH⁻] as a common ion
cards.n: Arguing that 'base dissolves things' reverses the effect for a hydroxide salt; OH⁻ is a product, so more of it suppresses dissolving.

cards.q: Write the net ionic equation for the reaction that dissolves solid Fe(OH)3 in excess nitric acid, and state what it shows about the effect of pH on the solubility of Fe(OH)3.
cards.a: Fe(OH)3(s) + 3H3O⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + 6H2O(l), or Fe(OH)3(s) + 3H⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + 3H2O(l); NO3⁻ is a spectator. The acid consumes the hydroxide completely, so the lower the pH, the more Fe(OH)3 dissolves: hydroxide salts are far more soluble in acid.
cards.h: → balanced net ionic equation, then one sentence on pH
cards.n: Splitting the solid into ions, or keeping NO3⁻ in the equation, loses the point; the solid is written whole. Net ionic rules are Unit 4.

cards.q: Explain why adding HCl dissolves a precipitate of calcium oxalate, CaC2O4, while adding the same amount of NaCl does not.
cards.a: Oxalate, C2O4²⁻, is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so H3O⁺ from HCl converts it to HC2O4⁻, removing it from CaC2O4(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + C2O4²⁻; Q < Ksp and the solid dissolves. NaCl supplies only Na⁺ and Cl⁻, neither of which reacts with Ca²⁺ or C2O4²⁻, so the equilibrium is undisturbed.
cards.h: → HCl supplies H3O⁺ → H3O⁺ protonates C2O4²⁻ → Q < Ksp → dissolves; NaCl's ions react with neither ion
cards.n: 'Both add Cl⁻' misses the point; the H3O⁺ of HCl, not its Cl⁻, does the work. Ksp and Q are Unit 7 ideas.
o: The acid lowers [C2O4²⁻] by forming HC2O4⁻ and H2C2O4, and Le Châtelier's principle replaces the lost oxalate by dissolving more solid; NaCl lowers nothing.
Only an added species that reacts with one of the salt's ions can shift the dissolution equilibrium, and only H3O⁺ reacts with oxalate here.

w.a: HCl dissolves it because acids dissolve all solids.
w.why: acid has no effect on salts such as AgCl; the anion must be basic

w.a: NaCl should dissolve it too because it is also a salt.
w.why: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ react with neither ion of CaC2O4

w.a: The Cl⁻ from HCl forms CaCl2, which pulls Ca²⁺ out of the solid.
w.why: CaCl2 is soluble and forms no product; the H3O⁺ removes oxalate

cards.q: Explain why silver acetate, AgCH3COO, is more soluble in a solution at pH 3 than in one at pH 8.
cards.a: At pH 3, below acetic acid's pKa (4.74), H3O⁺ converts most CH3COO⁻ to CH3COOH, removing it from AgCH3COO(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + CH3COO⁻ and shifting dissolution right. At pH 8, above the pKa, acetate stays as CH3COO⁻, so nothing removes it and less solid dissolves.
cards.h: → pH 3 < pKa → acetate protonated → removed → Q < Ksp → more dissolves; pH 8 > pKa → no removal
cards.n: 'Acid dissolves things' is not the reason; comparing the pH with acetic acid's pKa shows which form of the anion dominates.
o: The salt's anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so the lower the pH, the more of it is tied up as CH3COOH and the further dissolution proceeds.
At pH 8 the ratio [CH3COO⁻]/[CH3COOH] is about 1800:1, so almost no acetate is removed, while at pH 3 it is about 1:55.

w.a: Silver acetate is more soluble at pH 3 because Ag⁺ reacts with H3O⁺.
w.why: Ag⁺ does not react with H3O⁺; the acetate ion does

w.a: It is more soluble at pH 8 because bases dissolve metal salts.
w.why: at pH 8 the acetate is not removed, so the solubility is lower

w.a: pH does not matter because silver acetate is an ionic compound.
w.why: its anion is a weak base, so pH matters

cards.q: Explain why tooth enamel, hydroxyapatite Ca5(PO4)3OH, dissolves faster when bacteria in the mouth produce acid.
cards.a: Both of enamel's anions are bases: H3O⁺ converts OH⁻ to H2O and PO4³⁻ to HPO4²⁻. Removing these ions lowers Q below Ksp for Ca5(PO4)3OH(s) ⇌ 5Ca²⁺ + 3PO4³⁻ + OH⁻, so the dissolution equilibrium shifts right and the enamel dissolves.
cards.h: → acid produced → H3O⁺ removes OH⁻ and PO4³⁻ → Q < Ksp → equilibrium shifts right → enamel dissolves
cards.n: 'Acid eats teeth' names no chemistry; the answer must identify the basic ions consumed and the resulting shift.
o: Hydroxyapatite contains the hydroxide ion and the basic phosphate ion, so it belongs to the class of salts that are more soluble at low pH.
Fluoride treatment helps partly because fluorapatite, Ca5(PO4)3F, swaps OH⁻ for F⁻, a much weaker base, so acid attacks it less.

w.a: Acid dissolves enamel because Ca²⁺ reacts with the acid.
w.why: Ca²⁺ is not basic; the anions react

w.a: The bacteria eat the enamel directly.
w.why: the bacteria make acid; the acid shifts the equilibrium

w.a: Enamel dissolves because acid lowers its Ksp.
w.why: Ksp is constant at a given temperature; Q is what drops

cards.q: Define entropy in terms of the dispersal of matter and energy.
cards.a: Entropy (S) measures how dispersed a system's matter and energy are: the more ways its particles and their energy can be arranged, the greater S. Matter disperses when particles gain space or freedom of motion (melting, vaporizing, a gas expanding); energy disperses when the particles' kinetic energy is spread over a broader range of speeds, as happens on heating.
cards.h: → matter dispersal + energy dispersal, one clause each
cards.n: 'Entropy is disorder' alone earns little; the CED's language is dispersal of matter and of energy, argued from particle freedom, phase, volume and moles of gas.

cards.q: Identify the changes that increase the entropy of a chemical system.
cards.a: Entropy increases when (1) a solid melts, a liquid vaporizes or a solid sublimes; (2) a gas expands into a larger volume at constant temperature; (3) a reaction forms more moles of gas than it consumes; (4) the temperature rises, broadening the spread of particle kinetic energies. Each disperses matter (more space, more freedom of motion) or energy (a wider range of speeds).
cards.h: → four kinds of change, each tied to dispersal
cards.n: Listing 'dissolving' as always raising S is risky: a gas dissolving lowers S, and small, highly charged ions can make ΔS° of dissolution negative (9.6).

cards.q: Identify two examples of processes that decrease the entropy of a chemical system.
cards.a: Condensing steam to liquid water (the particles lose freedom of motion and occupy far less volume) and N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) (4 mol of gas become 2 mol, so matter is less dispersed). Others that also qualify: freezing, compressing a gas at constant T, cooling a sample, a precipitate forming from dissolved ions, a gas dissolving in a liquid.
cards.h: → two processes, each with a dispersal reason
cards.n: 'Entropy can never decrease' confuses the system with the universe and earns nothing; a system's entropy falls in every process listed here.

cards.q: Rank solid, liquid, and gas phases of the same substance by molar entropy.
cards.a: S(gas) ≫ S(liquid) > S(solid). Solid particles only vibrate about fixed positions; liquid particles also move past one another; gas particles move freely through a volume roughly 1000 times larger. For water at 298 K, S°(H₂O(l)) = 70.0 and S°(H₂O(g)) = 188.8 J/(mol·K), so the liquid-to-gas step is by far the largest.
cards.h: → three-term inequality + particle-freedom reason
cards.n: Putting liquid above gas because liquid particles 'move around more' misreads dispersal; the gas occupies far more volume and wins by a wide margin.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° for 2NO2(g) → N2O4(g) and justify it.
cards.a: ΔS° < 0. Two moles of gas-phase reactant become one mole of gas-phase product, so fewer independent particles move through the container and matter is less dispersed. (With tabulated S° values, ΔS° = 304.3 − 2(240.1) = −175.9 J/(mol·K).)
cards.h: → sign + gas-mole count
cards.n: 'N₂O₄ is a bigger, more complex molecule, so S rises' earns nothing; the change in moles of gas decides the sign.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° for $CaCO_3(s) \to CaO(s)+CO_2(g)$ and justify.
cards.a: ΔS° > 0. The reactant side has no gas and the product side has 1 mol of CO₂(g); gas molecules move freely through a large volume, so matter becomes far more dispersed. (Tabulated values give ΔS° ≈ +161 J/(mol·K).)
cards.h: → sign + gas-mole count (0 → 1)
cards.n: 'One reactant becomes two products' is weaker than the gas argument; the scoring point is that 0 mol of gas becomes 1 mol of gas.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° when a gas dissolves into a liquid solvent, such as $CO_2(g) \to CO_2(aq)$.
cards.a: ΔS° < 0. Gas molecules that moved freely through a large volume become confined among solvent molecules in the solution, so the CO₂ is much less dispersed. This is why dissolving a gas becomes less favored as temperature rises: the −TΔS° term grows more positive.
cards.h: → sign + loss of the gas's freedom
cards.n: Treating every 'dissolving' as ΔS > 0 fails here: the gas losing its freedom of motion outweighs any mixing with the solvent.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° for $2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \to 2H_2O(l)$ and justify.
cards.a: ΔS° < 0. Three moles of gas become zero moles of gas: every product particle is in the liquid, where it occupies far less volume and has less freedom of motion, so matter is much less dispersed (ΔS° = −327 J/(mol·K) from tabulated S° values).
cards.h: → sign + gas-mole count (3 → 0)
cards.n: Counting '3 molecules → 2 molecules' undersells it; the product is liquid, so the gas count goes from 3 to 0.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS for each process (+, −, or ≈ 0 if it cannot be decided by counting): H₂O(s) → H₂O(l) · H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) · CO₂(s) → CO₂(g) · I₂(g) → I₂(s) · a gas expands from 1.0 L to 5.0 L at constant T · Ne(g) heated from 300 K to 400 K at constant volume · N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) · 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) · C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) · C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g) · Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) · 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g) · NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s) · CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) · H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)
cards.a:
H₂O(s) → H₂O(l) → + (particles freed from fixed sites)
H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) → − (gas condenses)
CO₂(s) → CO₂(g) → + (solid to gas)
I₂(g) → I₂(s) → − (gas to solid)
gas expands 1.0 → 5.0 L → + (more volume)
Ne heated 300 → 400 K → + (broader KE distribution)
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ → − (4 → 2 mol gas)
2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) → + (0 → 1 mol gas)
propane → CO₂ + H₂O(l) → − (6 → 3 mol gas)
propane → CO₂ + H₂O(g) → + (6 → 7 mol gas)
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) → − (free ions → ordered solid)
2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ → + (0 → 3 mol gas)
NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl(s) → − (2 → 0 mol gas)
CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃ → − (1 → 0 mol gas)
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl → ≈ 0 (2 → 2 mol gas; tabulated +20 J/(mol·K))
cards.h: → phase? moles of gas? volume? temperature?
cards.n: Arguing from 'complexity' or 'number of product species' instead of phase, gas moles, volume and temperature earns nothing; Δn(gas) = 0 allows no confident call.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS when 1.00 mol of helium at 300 K expands from 10.0 L to 20.0 L with its temperature held constant, and justify it at the particulate level.
cards.a: ΔS > 0. At constant temperature the distribution of particle kinetic energies is unchanged, but each He atom can now move through twice the volume, so there are more positions available to the atoms and the matter is more dispersed.
cards.h: → sign + one volume-based reason
cards.n: 'Entropy is unchanged because T and the number of moles did not change' misses the volume argument that 9.1.A.1 states outright.

cards.q: Describe how the distribution of molecular speeds of a sample of N₂(g) changes when it is heated from 300 K to 600 K at constant volume, and identify which temperature gives the sample the higher entropy.
cards.a: At 600 K the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve is lower and broader: its peak shifts to a higher speed and the molecules are spread over a wider range of speeds (the area under both curves is the same, since the number of molecules is unchanged). The kinetic energy is dispersed over more energy states, so the 600 K sample has the higher entropy.
cards.h: → curve shape at higher T + which sample has greater S
cards.n: 'The molecules move faster, so they are more disordered' earns nothing; the point is the broader distribution of kinetic energy. The distribution curve is Unit 3 content.

cards.q: Determine the sign of ΔS for a process shown in two particulate diagrams: before, a box holds 6 X₂ molecules spread throughout the box, far apart and moving in random directions; after, the same 6 X₂ molecules are packed side by side in a regular array at the bottom of the box, each touching its neighbors.
cards.a: ΔS < 0. The molecules go from a gas, moving freely through the whole box, to a regular solid array in which each only vibrates about a fixed position; the matter occupies far less volume and has fewer possible arrangements, so it is less dispersed. The diagrams show deposition (gas → solid).
cards.h: → sign + what changed in phase and space
cards.n: Counting molecules (6 before, 6 after) and concluding ΔS = 0 misses the phase change the diagram shows.

cards.q: Rank these reactions from most positive to most negative ΔS°: (1) 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g); (2) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g); (3) H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
cards.a: (1) > (3) > (2). Reaction 1 creates 1 mol of gas from none, so ΔS° is large and positive (+126 J/(mol·K) from tables); reaction 3 has 2 mol of gas on each side, so ΔS° is small (+20 J/(mol·K)); reaction 2 turns 4 mol of gas into 2 mol, so ΔS° is large and negative (−199 J/(mol·K)).
cards.h: → ordered list + Δn(gas) for each
cards.n: Ranking reaction 3 last because 'two molecules combine' ignores that Δn(gas) = 0 there; only reaction 2 loses gas.

cards.q: Explain why the entropy of a substance increases when it melts.
cards.a: In the solid, each particle only vibrates about a fixed lattice position; in the liquid, particles are free to move past one another. Matter is therefore more dispersed: each particle can occupy many more positions, and the sample has many more possible arrangements, so S increases.
cards.h: → fixed lattice sites → particles free to move past one another → more arrangements → S increases
cards.n: 'Melting absorbs heat, so entropy goes up' confuses ΔH with ΔS; the point is the particles' freedom of motion.
o: Solid particles are locked into one site each, while liquid particles translate through the sample, so matter is more dispersed.
The liquid has many more accessible arrangements of the same particles than the ordered crystal, so S(l) > S(s).

w.a: Melting increases entropy because heat is added to the substance.
w.why: names an energy input, not the dispersal of matter

w.a: Melting increases entropy because the molecules break apart into atoms.
w.why: melting breaks no covalent bonds; the same molecules just move more freely

w.a: Melting increases entropy because the liquid takes up much more volume than the solid.
w.why: volume barely changes on melting (ice even shrinks); the gain is freedom of motion

cards.q: Explain why the entropy of a gas increases when its temperature is raised at constant volume.
cards.a: By kinetic molecular theory, raising T broadens the distribution of particle kinetic energies: the particles spread over a wider range of speeds and energy states. Energy is therefore more dispersed among the particles, so the entropy rises even though the volume is unchanged.
cards.h: → higher T → broader kinetic-energy distribution → energy more dispersed → S increases
cards.n: 'The particles move faster' alone is incomplete; the scoring idea is the broader spread of energies, not the higher average. KMT is Unit 3 content.
o: At higher temperature the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve flattens and widens, so the energy is shared over more states.
More energy states are populated at the higher temperature, so there are more ways to distribute the total energy among the particles.

w.a: The entropy increases because the gas takes up more space when it is heated.
w.why: the volume is fixed here; the argument must be energy dispersal

w.a: The entropy increases because hot molecules hit the walls harder.
w.why: describes pressure, not the distribution of energy

w.a: The entropy does not change because the number of particles and the volume stay the same.
w.why: ignores 9.1.A.2: energy dispersal rises with temperature

cards.q: Explain why vaporizing a liquid produces a much larger entropy increase than melting the same substance's solid.
cards.a: On melting, particles gain freedom to move past one another but stay in contact in about the same volume. On vaporizing, they separate completely and move through a volume roughly 1000 times larger, so matter disperses far more: for water ΔS(vap) ≈ +109 J/(mol·K) versus ΔS(fus) ≈ +22 J/(mol·K).
cards.h: → liquid keeps particles in contact → gas spreads them over ~1000× the volume → far more dispersal
cards.n: 'Boiling takes more heat than melting' argues from ΔH, not ΔS; the scored reasoning is the change in volume and freedom of the particles.
o: The liquid-to-gas step changes the volume available to each particle enormously, while melting barely changes it.
Gas particles move essentially independently, while liquid particles are still held together by intermolecular forces, so the gas has many more arrangements.

w.a: Vaporization has the bigger entropy change because it happens at a higher temperature.
w.why: the temperature of the change is not a dispersal argument

w.a: Vaporization has the bigger entropy change because it needs more heat than melting.
w.why: ΔH is not ΔS; the reason is volume and freedom

w.a: Vaporization and melting have the same entropy change because both are phase changes.
w.why: false; the gas is far more dispersed than the liquid

cards.q: Explain why the change in the number of moles of gas usually decides the sign of ΔS° for a reaction.
cards.a: Gas particles move freely through a volume about 1000 times larger than the same particles in a liquid or solid, so gases hold most of a system's matter dispersal. Changing the moles of gas changes how many particles move freely, which outweighs changes among condensed phases.
cards.h: → gas particles far more dispersed → Δn(gas) changes the number of free particles → dominates ΔS°
cards.n: Say why gas dominates (freedom and volume); 'more moles means more entropy' without 'of gas' is wrong for solids and liquids.
o: Standard molar entropies of gases (about 130 to 300 J/(mol·K)) are much larger than those of most liquids and solids, so the gas terms dominate the sum.
Each mole of gas gained adds a large amount of positional freedom, while forming solids or liquids adds comparatively little.

w.a: The moles of gas decide ΔS° because gases are the lightest substances.
w.why: mass is irrelevant to dispersal

w.a: More moles of any product always mean a higher entropy.
w.why: only moles of gas count reliably; 2 mol of solid from 1 mol of gas is still a decrease

w.a: Gases have more entropy because they have more energy.
w.why: asserts energy, not the particle freedom and volume that make up dispersal

cards.q: Explain why ΔS° is negative when Ag⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq) combine to form solid AgCl.
cards.a: The dissolved ions move independently throughout the whole solution; in AgCl(s) they are locked into fixed lattice positions where they can only vibrate. Matter becomes less dispersed, so ΔS° < 0 (tabulated: about −33 J/(mol·K)).
cards.h: → free ions in solution → fixed lattice sites → matter less dispersed → ΔS° < 0
cards.n: The value is modest because water released from the ions' hydration shells gains freedom (the 9.6 story); arguing from enthalpy or mass earns nothing.
o: Two independently moving solute particles become part of one ordered solid, so the number of possible arrangements drops.
The reverse process, AgCl dissolving, disperses the ions into solution with ΔS° > 0, so the precipitation must have ΔS° < 0.

w.a: ΔS° is negative because forming a precipitate is always exothermic.
w.why: argues from enthalpy, not dispersal

w.a: ΔS° is negative because AgCl is heavier than either ion.
w.why: mass is not a dispersal argument

w.a: ΔS° is negative because there are fewer moles of gas in the products.
w.why: no gas appears in this equation; the argument is about ions and a solid

cards.q: State how to calculate the standard entropy change of a reaction from absolute entropies.
cards.a: ΔS°rxn = ΣnS°(products) − ΣnS°(reactants): multiply each standard molar entropy by its coefficient in the balanced equation, add the products, add the reactants, and subtract. The result is in J/(mol·K) per mole of reaction as written, and every species, elements included, contributes a nonzero S°.
cards.h: → products minus reactants, each × coefficient
cards.n: Leaving out O₂ 'because it is an element' is the classic loss; that shortcut belongs to ΔH°f and ΔG°f, not to absolute S°.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l) given S° values of 131, 205, and 70. J/(mol·K).
cards.a: ΔS° = −327 J/(mol·K). ΔS° = [2(70.)] − [2(131) + 205] = 140 − 467 = −327 J/(mol·K) per mole of reaction as written. The sign agrees with the particle picture: 3 mol of gas become liquid.
cards.h: → one line of products minus reactants, with units
cards.n: Dropping a coefficient of 2 (e.g. 70 − 336) is the usual slip; multiply every S° by its coefficient before adding.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $N_2(g)+3H_2(g) \to 2NH_3(g)$ given S° = 192, 131, and 193 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.a: ΔS° = −199 J/(mol·K). ΔS° = 2(193) − [192 + 3(131)] = 386 − 585 = −199 J/(mol·K). The value is negative, as 4 mol of gas becoming 2 mol predicts.
cards.h: → one line with coefficients, then a sign check
cards.n: Reversing the subtraction (reactants minus products) gives +199, a sign that contradicts the gas count; always check against Δn(gas).

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \to 2SO_3(g)$ given S° = 248, 205, and 257 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.a: ΔS° = −187 J/(mol·K). ΔS° = 2(257) − [2(248) + 205] = 514 − 701 = −187 J/(mol·K). Three moles of gas become two, so a negative value is expected.
cards.h: → one line with coefficients, then a sign check
cards.n: Omitting O₂'s 205 because O₂ is an element gives +18 J/(mol·K) and the wrong sign; elements have real, positive S° values.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $CaCO_3(s) \to CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$ given S° = 92.9, 39.8, and 213.7 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.a: ΔS° = +160.6 J/(mol·K). ΔS° = (39.8 + 213.7) − 92.9 = 253.5 − 92.9 = +160.6 J/(mol·K). It is large and positive because a gas (CO₂) is produced from a solid.
cards.h: → one line, products minus reactants
cards.n: Reporting +253.5 by leaving out the reactant is a common slip; the solid CaCO₃ still has S° = 92.9 J/(mol·K).

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $N_2O_4(g) \to 2NO_2(g)$ given S° = 304 and 240 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.a: ΔS° = +176 J/(mol·K). ΔS° = 2(240) − 304 = 480 − 304 = +176 J/(mol·K). One mole of gas becomes two, so the positive sign is expected.
cards.h: → one line, remembering the coefficient 2
cards.n: Using 240 once instead of 2 × 240 gives −64 J/(mol·K) and the wrong sign; the coefficient multiplies NO₂'s molar entropy.

cards.q: Calculate ΔS° for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), given S° values in J/(mol·K): CH₄(g) 186.3, O₂(g) 205.2, CO₂(g) 213.8, H₂O(l) 70.0.
cards.a: ΔS° = −242.9 J/(mol·K). Products: 213.8 + 2(70.0) = 353.8; reactants: 186.3 + 2(205.2) = 596.7; ΔS° = 353.8 − 596.7 = −242.9 J/(mol·K). Negative, consistent with 3 mol of gas becoming 1 mol of gas plus liquid water.
cards.h: → sum products, sum reactants, subtract
cards.n: Using S° of H₂O(g) (188.8) instead of H₂O(l) gives about −5 J/(mol·K); the phase label on each species selects its S° value.

cards.q: Calculate ΔS° for the vaporization H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 298 K, given S°(H₂O(l)) = 70.0 J/(mol·K) and S°(H₂O(g)) = 188.8 J/(mol·K), and state whether the sign agrees with a particulate prediction.
cards.a: ΔS° = +118.8 J/(mol·K). ΔS° = 188.8 − 70.0 = +118.8 J/(mol·K). The sign agrees: liquid particles in contact with one another become gas particles moving freely through a far larger volume, so matter is more dispersed.
cards.h: → one subtraction + a one-sentence sign check
cards.n: The same S° equation applies to a physical change as to a reaction; treating 'no reaction' as ΔS° = 0 earns nothing.

cards.q: Determine the standard molar entropy of NO₂(g), given that ΔS° = −146.6 J/(mol·K) for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), S°(NO(g)) = 210.8 J/(mol·K) and S°(O₂(g)) = 205.2 J/(mol·K).
cards.h: → set up the sum, solve for the one unknown
cards.n: Forgetting to divide by the coefficient 2 at the end reports 480.2, the entropy of 2 mol of NO₂, not its molar entropy.

cards.q: Determine ΔS° for NH₃(g) → ½N₂(g) + 3/2 H₂(g), given that ΔS° = −199 J/(mol·K) for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
cards.a: ΔS° = +99.5 J/(mol·K). Reversing the reaction changes the sign (+199 J/(mol·K)), and halving every coefficient halves the value (+199 ÷ 2 = +99.5 J/(mol·K)), because ΔS°rxn is summed over the coefficients of the equation as written.
cards.h: → reverse (sign), then scale (÷ 2)
cards.n: Keeping −199 or −99.5 ignores the reversal: ΔS°, like ΔH°, flips sign when the equation is reversed and scales with its coefficients.

cards.q: Describe what the unit J/(mol·K) means in a reported value such as ΔS° = −199 J/(mol·K) for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
cards.a: The value is per mole of reaction as written: when 1 mol of N₂ reacts with 3 mol of H₂ to form 2 mol of NH₃, the system's entropy falls by 199 J/K.
