Reacting twice those amounts doubles the change. The per-kelvin part is why ΔS° is multiplied by T (in K) before it can be compared with ΔH° in ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
cards.h: → what 'per mol' counts + why 'per K' matters
cards.n: Reading 'per mol' as 'per mole of NH₃' halves or doubles later results; the mole is one mole of the reaction as balanced.

cards.q: Identify the error in a student's work that reports ΔS° = +327 J/(mol·K) for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), using S° values of 131 (H₂), 205 (O₂) and 70. (H₂O(l)) J/(mol·K).
cards.a: The student subtracted products from reactants: [2(131) + 205] − 2(70.) = +327. The correct order is products minus reactants, giving −327 J/(mol·K), and only the negative value agrees with 3 mol of gas becoming a liquid.
cards.h: → name the step that went wrong + the corrected value
cards.n: A sign check against Δn(gas) catches this in seconds; a positive ΔS° for a gas turning into a liquid should never be reported.

cards.q: Explain why S° of an element in its standard state is not zero, unlike ΔH°f.
cards.a: S° is an absolute quantity, measured from a zero point of a perfect crystal at 0 K; any substance at 298 K has particle motion and dispersed energy, so S° > 0. ΔH°f is relative: the change for forming a substance from its elements, which is zero when the substance is the element.
cards.h: → S° absolute (zero only at 0 K) → element at 298 K has dispersed energy → S° > 0; ΔH°f relative → 0
cards.n: 'Elements have zero energy' earns nothing; the contrast is absolute (S°) versus relative-to-the-elements (ΔH°f, ΔG°f). The 0 K reference goes slightly beyond the CED.
o: ΔH°f is defined relative to the elements themselves, so an element's is zero by definition; S° has no such reference other than a perfect crystal at 0 K.
Tabulated S° values for O₂(g) (205) or Fe(s) (27) are positive because these substances have thermal motion at 298 K.

w.a: S° of an element is not zero because elements are unstable.
w.why: stability has nothing to do with the absolute entropy scale

w.a: S° of an element is zero, just like its ΔH°f.
w.why: false; only a perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy

w.a: S° is not zero because every element is a mixture of isotopes.
w.why: isotopes are not the reason; thermal motion above 0 K is

cards.q: Explain why each standard molar entropy is multiplied by its coefficient when ΔS° for a reaction is calculated.
cards.a: S° is the entropy of one mole of a substance, and entropy is extensive: 2 mol of NH₃ has twice the entropy of 1 mol. The balanced equation states how many moles of each species react or form, so each S° must be scaled by its coefficient before the sums are subtracted.
cards.h: → S° is per mole → entropy is extensive → n mol hold n × S° → weight each term by its coefficient
cards.n: 'Because the formula says ΣnS°' restates the rule without the reason; the reason is that S° is a per-mole, extensive quantity.
o: The equation fixes the amounts per mole of reaction, and entropy adds over amounts, so 3 mol of H₂ contributes 3 × 131 J/K.
Without the coefficients the calculation would describe a different reaction from the balanced one.

w.a: Coefficients are only needed for ΔH°, not for ΔS°.
w.why: both are extensive; the same weighting applies

w.a: The coefficients are multiplied in so that the units cancel.
w.why: coefficients do not change units; the reason is amount

w.a: Coefficients matter because bigger molecules have more entropy.
w.why: molecular size is not the reason for the weighting

cards.q: Explain why the calculated ΔS° for CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) is large and positive even though one solid is simply replaced by another.
cards.a: The products include 1 mol of gas and the reactants none. CO₂(g) has a large S° (213.7 J/(mol·K)) because its molecules move freely through a large volume, while the two solids have small, similar S° values; the gas term dominates, giving +160.6 J/(mol·K).
cards.h: → 0 → 1 mol gas → gas S° far exceeds solid S° → CO₂ term dominates → large positive ΔS°
cards.n: Say where the entropy comes from, the CO₂(g) term; 'two products from one reactant' earns nothing.
o: Matter becomes much more dispersed because part of the solid is released as a freely moving gas.
S°(CaO) and S°(CaCO₃) nearly cancel, so the result is close to S°(CO₂) itself.

w.a: ΔS° is positive because one reactant forms two products.
w.why: counting species, not moles of gas, is not the dispersal argument

w.a: ΔS° is positive because the reaction is endothermic.
w.why: ΔH does not set the sign of ΔS

w.a: ΔS° is positive because CaO is a simpler compound than CaCO₃.
w.why: complexity is not the scored reasoning; the gas is

cards.q: State the Gibbs free energy equation and what each term contributes.
cards.a: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. ΔH° is the enthalpy change (kJ/mol), T the absolute temperature in kelvin, and ΔS° the entropy change (J/(mol·K), converted to kJ). A negative ΔH° and a positive ΔS° each push ΔG° negative; because the entropy term is multiplied by T, it matters more and more as the temperature rises.
cards.h: → equation + the role of each term
cards.n: Writing ΔG = ΔH + TΔS, or plugging T in °C, earns nothing; the minus sign and kelvin are part of the equation.

cards.q: Define a thermodynamically favorable process in terms of ΔG.
cards.a: A process is thermodynamically favored when ΔG° < 0: under standard conditions the products are favored and the process proceeds without a continuous outside energy source. If ΔG° > 0 the reverse process is favored; ΔG = 0 describes a system at equilibrium. Favorability says nothing about how fast the process occurs.
cards.h: → sign of ΔG° + what favored does and does not mean
cards.n: Calling a ΔG° < 0 reaction 'spontaneous, so it happens quickly' is the misunderstanding the CED names; favored never means fast or sudden.

cards.q: Identify the standard-state conditions that the degree sign in ΔG° refers to for a pure solid or liquid, a solute in solution, and a gas.
cards.a: A pure solid or liquid is in its standard state as the pure substance; a solute is at a concentration of 1.0 M; a gas is at a partial pressure of 1.0 atm (or 1.0 bar). ΔG° is the free energy change when every reactant and product is in its standard state. Temperature is not part of the definition, although tables usually report values at 298 K.
cards.h: → three phases, one condition each
cards.n: 'Standard conditions are 0 °C and 1 atm' confuses gas-law STP with thermodynamic standard states and earns nothing.

cards.q: State how to calculate ΔG°rxn from standard free energies of formation.
cards.a: ΔG°rxn = ΣnΔG°f(products) − ΣnΔG°f(reactants), each standard free energy of formation multiplied by its coefficient. ΔG°f of an element in its standard state (O₂(g), C(graphite), Fe(s)) is zero, so those terms drop out; the result is in kJ per mole of reaction.
cards.h: → products minus reactants, weighted; elements zero
cards.n: Unlike S°, ΔG°f of an element in its standard state IS zero; mixing up which tabulated quantities drop out is the usual error.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), given ΔG°f values in kJ/mol: CH₄(g) −50.8, CO₂(g) −394.4, H₂O(l) −237.1.
cards.a: ΔG° = −817.8 kJ/mol; the combustion is thermodynamically favored. Products: −394.4 + 2(−237.1) = −868.6 kJ; reactants: −50.8 + 2(0) = −50.8 kJ (O₂ is an element in its standard state); ΔG° = −868.6 − (−50.8) = −817.8 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → sum products, sum reactants, subtract
cards.n: Subtracting −50.8 as if it were +50.8 (giving −919.4) is the sign slip that costs the point; write the brackets out.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0.
cards.a: Thermodynamically favored at all temperatures. With ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0, both ΔH° and −TΔS° are negative at any T, so ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° < 0 always; no calculation is needed.
cards.h: → one verdict + both terms' signs
cards.n: 'Favored at high T' loses the point here; when both terms are negative the answer is all temperatures.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0.
cards.a: ΔG is negative only at high temperatures, where the -TΔS term becomes large enough to overcome the unfavorable positive ΔH.
cards.h: → favorable at high T
cards.n: Melting, boiling, and many dissolutions are endothermic but entropy-driven.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0.
cards.a: ΔG is negative only at low temperatures, where the favorable -ΔH term outweighs the unfavorable -TΔS term. Raising T eventually makes ΔG positive.
cards.h: → favorable at low T
cards.n: Freezing and condensation belong here: exothermic but entropy-decreasing.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0.
cards.a: ΔG is positive at all temperatures, so the reaction is never thermodynamically favorable; only the reverse reaction is favorable.
cards.h: → never favorable
cards.n: If a question shows this sign pattern, no temperature change can make the reaction go.

cards.q: State the temperatures at which a process is thermodynamically favored for each combination of signs: ΔH° < 0 with ΔS° > 0 · ΔH° > 0 with ΔS° < 0 · ΔH° < 0 with ΔS° < 0 · ΔH° > 0 with ΔS° > 0
cards.a:
ΔH° < 0, ΔS° > 0 → favored at all T (ΔH° and −TΔS° both negative; no calculation needed)
ΔH° > 0, ΔS° < 0 → favored at no T (both terms positive; the reverse process is favored at all T)
ΔH° < 0, ΔS° < 0 → favored only at low T, below T = ΔH°/ΔS°, where the enthalpy term outweighs −TΔS° (freezing, condensing)
ΔH° > 0, ΔS° > 0 → favored only at high T, above T = ΔH°/ΔS°, where −TΔS° outweighs ΔH° (melting, boiling, dissolving NaNO₃)
cards.h: → four rows: signs of the two terms, then who wins
cards.n: Swapping the two mixed cases (low T for ΔH° > 0, ΔS° > 0) is the classic slip; the entropy term is the one multiplied by T, so it wins at high T.

cards.q: Determine whether each process is thermodynamically favored at all temperatures, only at low temperatures, only at high temperatures, or at no temperature: H₂O(l) → H₂O(s) · H₂O(s) → H₂O(l) · H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) · CO₂(s) → CO₂(g) · NaNO₃(s) → Na⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) (the water cools as it dissolves) · 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), ΔH° = −196 kJ/mol · 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g), ΔH° < 0 · 3O₂(g) → 2O₃(g), ΔH° = +285 kJ/mol · N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH° = +66 kJ/mol · CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178 kJ/mol · N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol · NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s), ΔH° = −176 kJ/mol
cards.a:
freezing → ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 → low T (below 0 °C)
melting → ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 → high T (above 0 °C)
condensing → ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 → low T (below 100 °C at 1 atm)
sublimation of CO₂ → ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 → high T
NaNO₃ dissolving → ΔH > 0 (cooling), ΔS > 0 → high T (already favored at 25 °C)
2H₂O₂ → ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0 (0 → 1 mol gas) → all T
2KClO₃ → ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0 (0 → 3 mol gas) → all T
3O₂ → 2O₃ → ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0 (3 → 2) → no T
N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂ → ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0 (3 → 2) → no T
CaCO₃ → ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 (0 → 1) → high T (above ≈ 1100 K)
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ → ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 (4 → 2) → low T (below ≈ 460 K)
NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl(s) → ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 (2 → 0) → low T
cards.h: → sign of ΔH, sign of ΔS, then read the table
cards.n: Deciding from ΔH alone ('exothermic, so favored') is the trap; every verdict needs both signs, and for NaNO₃ the cooling itself says ΔH > 0 (Unit 6).

cards.q: Compute the temperature at which a reaction with ΔH° = +58.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +176 J/(mol·K) becomes thermodynamically favorable.
cards.a: T = 330. K. At the crossover ΔG° = 0, so T = ΔH°/ΔS° = (58,000 J/mol) ÷ (176 J/(mol·K)) = 330. K (about 57 °C). With ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° > 0, the reaction is favored above 330. K, where −TΔS° outweighs ΔH°. This assumes ΔH° and ΔS° do not change with temperature.
cards.h: → set ΔG° = 0, solve T = ΔH°/ΔS°, then say above/below
cards.n: Dividing 58.0 by 176 without converting kJ to J gives 0.330 K, an absurd temperature; matching units is the point.

cards.q: Compute the crossover temperature at which ΔG° = 0 for a reaction with ΔH° = -92.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -199 J/(mol·K).
cards.a: T = 462 K. T = ΔH°/ΔS° = (−92,000 J/mol) ÷ (−199 J/(mol·K)) = 462 K. With both signs negative, the reaction is favored below 462 K and not favored above it, assuming ΔH° and ΔS° stay constant with temperature.
cards.h: → T = ΔH°/ΔS° in matching units, then below/above
cards.n: 'Favored above 462 K' reverses the logic: with ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0 the entropy penalty grows with T, so high T is unfavorable.

cards.q: Compute ΔG° at 298 K for a reaction with ΔH° = -92.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -199 J/(mol·K).
cards.a: ΔG° = −32.7 kJ/mol; thermodynamically favored at 298 K. ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −92.0 kJ/mol − (298 K)(−0.199 kJ/(mol·K)) = −92.0 + 59.3 = −32.7 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → convert ΔS° to kJ, substitute, sign verdict
cards.n: Using −199 directly with −92.0 gives +59,210 and the wrong sign; divide ΔS° by 1000 (to kJ/(mol·K)) first.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG for H₂O(l) → H₂O(s) at −10 °C and at +10 °C, using ΔH = −6.01 kJ/mol and ΔS = −22.0 J/(mol·K) (assume both are constant), and state at which temperature freezing is thermodynamically favored.
cards.a: At 263 K: ΔG = −6.01 − (263)(−0.0220) = −6.01 + 5.79 = −0.22 kJ/mol, favored. At 283 K: ΔG = −6.01 + 6.23 = +0.22 kJ/mol, not favored. Freezing is favored at −10 °C, where the favorable ΔH outweighs the unfavorable −TΔS; the crossover is 6010 ÷ 22.0 = 273 K.
cards.h: → two substitutions in kelvin + verdict
cards.n: Using −10 and +10 as T gives nonsense; convert to 263 K and 283 K. The CED names freezing as a case that needs both ΔH and ΔS.

cards.q: Explain the unit precaution required when using ΔG = ΔH - TΔS.
cards.a: ΔH° is tabulated in kJ/mol but ΔS° in J/(mol·K), so one must be converted (ΔS° ÷ 1000, or ΔH° × 1000) before TΔS° is subtracted, and T must be in kelvin. Otherwise the TΔS° term is off by a factor of 1000 and can reverse the sign of ΔG°.
cards.h: → ΔH in kJ, ΔS in J → mismatch of 1000 → convert one; T in K → else the TΔS term is badly wrong
cards.n: An answer off by exactly 1000, or with a flipped sign, is the tell-tale mark of an unconverted ΔS°.
o: The two terms must share an energy unit to be subtracted, and kelvin is required because entropy is defined per kelvin.
Carrying units through every step (kJ/mol − K × kJ/(mol·K)) exposes the mismatch before it causes an error.

w.a: You have to convert ΔH to calories before using the equation.
w.why: calories are irrelevant; the J/kJ mismatch is the issue

w.a: Temperature must be in degrees Celsius because the data are for 25 °C.
w.why: the equation requires absolute temperature in kelvin

w.a: No conversion is needed because both values come from the same table.
w.why: the table gives them in different units, kJ and J

cards.q: Explain why chemists describe a process with ΔG° < 0 as 'thermodynamically favored' rather than 'spontaneous'.
cards.a: ΔG° < 0 says only that products are favored under standard conditions; it says nothing about rate. 'Spontaneous' is often heard as 'sudden' or 'without cause', yet many favored processes, such as diamond becoming graphite, are immeasurably slow; 'thermodynamically favored' avoids that misreading.
cards.h: → ΔG° measures favorability, not rate → 'spontaneous' suggests sudden → 'favored' avoids the misconception
cards.n: Any answer implying ΔG° predicts speed earns nothing; the CED's stated reason is that 'spontaneous' is misread as 'sudden' or 'without cause'.
o: Thermodynamics compares the free energies of the initial and final states and carries no information about the pathway or speed, which 'spontaneous' wrongly implies.
A favored reaction may still have to overcome a large activation energy, so it can be favored yet not observed.

w.a: 'Spontaneous' is wrong because a reaction with ΔG° < 0 happens immediately.
w.why: repeats the misconception; favored reactions can be very slow

w.a: 'Spontaneous' is avoided because it only applies to exothermic reactions.
w.why: favorability depends on ΔG°, not on ΔH° alone

w.a: The phrases differ because 'favored' means ΔG° > 0.
w.why: reverses the sign; favored means ΔG° < 0

cards.q: Explain why liquid water freezes at −10 °C but not at +10 °C, using the signs of ΔH and ΔS.
cards.a: Freezing has ΔH < 0 (favorable) and ΔS < 0 (unfavorable). In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS the opposing term, −TΔS, is positive and grows with T: at −10 °C it is smaller than |ΔH|, so ΔG < 0; at +10 °C it is larger, so ΔG > 0 and freezing is not favored.
cards.h: → ΔH < 0 favors, ΔS < 0 opposes → −TΔS grows with T → wins above 273 K → ΔG > 0
cards.n: CED 9.3.A.4 uses this exact example: an argument from ΔH alone or ΔS alone earns nothing; both terms and T are needed. Exothermic freezing is Unit 6 content.
o: Freezing is enthalpy-driven and entropy-opposed, so it is favored only where T is low enough that the entropy penalty TΔS is smaller in size than the heat released.
With ΔH = −6.01 kJ/mol and ΔS = −22.0 J/(mol·K), ΔG ≈ −0.22 kJ/mol at 263 K and ≈ +0.22 kJ/mol at 283 K.

w.a: Water freezes below 0 °C because freezing is exothermic.
w.why: ignores the entropy term that makes freezing unfavored above 0 °C

w.a: Water freezes below 0 °C because its entropy increases when it freezes.
w.why: wrong sign; freezing decreases entropy

w.a: Water freezes below 0 °C because the molecules are too slow to stay liquid.
w.why: a kinetic description, not a ΔH/ΔS argument

cards.q: Explain why sodium nitrate dissolves readily in water at 25 °C even though the solution becomes colder as it dissolves.
cards.a: The cooling shows ΔH° > 0 (endothermic), which opposes dissolving. But the ions become dispersed through the solution, so ΔS° > 0, and at 298 K −TΔS° (about −26 kJ/mol) outweighs ΔH° (about +20 kJ/mol), making ΔG° < 0: dissolving NaNO₃ is entropy-driven.
cards.h: → gets colder → ΔH° > 0 opposes → ions disperse → ΔS° > 0 → TΔS° > ΔH° at 298 K → ΔG° < 0
cards.n: The CED names this example (9.3.A.4); never mentioning ΔS° > 0 outweighing ΔH° > 0 earns nothing. Table values for NaNO₃ differ by 1 to 2 kJ/mol.
o: With ΔH° ≈ +20.5 kJ/mol and ΔS° ≈ +88.9 J/(mol·K), ΔG° = 20.5 − 298(0.0889) ≈ −6.0 kJ/mol, so dissolving is favored.
With ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° > 0, dissolving is favored above ΔH°/ΔS° ≈ 231 K, a range that includes room temperature.

w.a: NaNO₃ dissolves because dissolving it is exothermic.
w.why: contradicts the observed cooling, which means ΔH° > 0

w.a: NaNO₃ dissolves because the solution gets colder, and cold favors dissolving.
w.why: the cooling reveals ΔH° > 0; it is not a driving force

w.a: NaNO₃ dissolves because all ionic compounds are soluble in water.
w.why: false, and it offers no ΔH/ΔS reasoning

cards.q: Explain why no calculation is needed to conclude that a process with ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0 is thermodynamically favored.
cards.a: In ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, a negative ΔH° is a negative term, and with ΔS° > 0 and T always positive in kelvin, −TΔS° is negative too. The sum of two negative terms is negative, so ΔG° < 0 at every temperature.
cards.h: → ΔH° < 0 → first term negative; ΔS° > 0, T > 0 → −TΔS° negative → sum negative at any T
cards.n: CED 9.3.A.6 states this shortcut outright; the mirror case, ΔH° > 0 with ΔS° < 0, is unfavored at every temperature.
o: Both the enthalpy change and the entropy change favor the products, so neither term can oppose the process at any temperature.
ΔG° could only be positive at a negative kelvin temperature, which does not exist.

w.a: No calculation is needed because exothermic reactions are always favored.
w.why: true here only because ΔS° > 0 as well; ΔH alone does not decide

w.a: No calculation is needed because ΔS° > 0 means the reaction is fast.
w.why: entropy says nothing about rate

w.a: You still need T, because at high temperature ΔG° turns positive.
w.why: raising T only makes −TΔS° more negative here

cards.q: Contrast thermodynamic control and kinetic control of a reaction.
cards.a: Thermodynamics (ΔG°) says whether a process is favored, that is, whether products are favored at equilibrium; kinetics (activation energy, rate) says how fast the system gets there. A process is under kinetic control when it is thermodynamically favored (ΔG° < 0) but does not proceed at a measurable rate, most often because its activation energy is high.
cards.h: → what each governs + the CED definition of kinetic control
cards.n: The CED meaning is 'favored but too slow to observe'; defining kinetic control as 'the product that forms fastest wins' (an organic usage) misses it.

cards.q: Identify the quantity that determines whether a reaction is thermodynamically favored and the quantity that chiefly determines how fast it proceeds at a given temperature.
cards.a: ΔG° (the free energy difference between products and reactants) determines favorability; the activation energy Eₐ (the height of the barrier between reactants and the transition state), together with temperature and concentrations, determines the rate. The two are independent: a very negative ΔG° can pair with a very large Eₐ.
cards.h: → one quantity each + that they are independent
cards.n: 'ΔH decides both' earns nothing: favorability is ΔG°, rate is Eₐ, and neither predicts the other. Activation energy is Unit 5 content.

cards.q: Contrast a reaction that is thermodynamically favorable but kinetically slow with one that is favorable in both senses, using an everyday example.
cards.a: Paper burning in air (ΔG° < 0) is favored but under kinetic control at room temperature: its activation energy is high, so it does not occur measurably until a flame supplies that energy. H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) is also favored (ΔG° ≈ −80 kJ/mol) but has a tiny activation energy, so it is essentially instantaneous.
cards.h: → two examples, each with ΔG° sign and barrier size
cards.n: Saying paper 'is not favored until lit' is wrong; the flame only supplies activation energy, and ΔG° was negative all along.

cards.q: Determine whether a mixture of H₂(g) and O₂(g) that has sat unchanged at 25 °C for a year is at equilibrium, given ΔG° = −237 kJ/mol for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l).
cards.a: It is not at equilibrium; it is under kinetic control. ΔG° = −237 kJ/mol means K is enormous (about 10⁴¹), so at equilibrium almost no H₂ and O₂ would remain. The mixture persists only because the activation energy is so high that the rate at 25 °C is immeasurably slow; a spark makes it react explosively.
cards.h: → claim + K from ΔG° + the kinetic reason
cards.n: 'Nothing is happening, so it must be at equilibrium' is exactly what CED 9.4.A.2 warns against: no observable rate does not mean Q = K.

cards.q: Determine what a chemist can reasonably conclude about a reaction that has ΔG° = −150 kJ/mol at 25 °C but shows no measurable product after several days at 25 °C.
cards.a: The reaction is under kinetic control: it is thermodynamically favored but has a high activation energy, so its rate at 25 °C is immeasurably slow. The chemist should not conclude that the ΔG° value is wrong or that the system is at equilibrium; raising the temperature or adding a catalyst could let it proceed at a measurable rate.
cards.h: → the conclusion + two conclusions that are NOT justified
cards.n: Concluding 'ΔG° must be wrong' or 'it is at equilibrium' earns nothing; 9.4.A.2 says kinetic control is the reasonable conclusion.

cards.q: Predict the effect of adding a suitable catalyst on the rate, ΔG° and K of a thermodynamically favored reaction that is under kinetic control.
cards.a: The rate increases; ΔG° and K are unchanged. A catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed and the reaction proceeds measurably. ΔG° depends only on the free energies of the reactants and products, which the catalyst does not change, so the equilibrium position stays the same.
cards.h: → three quantities, one verdict each + the reason
cards.n: 'The catalyst makes ΔG° more negative' earns nothing; a catalyst changes the pathway, never the states at either end. Catalysis is Unit 5 content.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to sketch, a reaction energy profile for a process that is thermodynamically favored but under kinetic control.
cards.a: Axes: free energy (vertical) against reaction progress (horizontal). A flat reactant level at the left; a single very tall hump (the transition state) whose height above the reactant level is the large activation energy; a flat product level at the right drawn well BELOW the reactant level, because the process is favored. Label Eₐ from the reactant level to the peak, and ΔG° from the reactant level down to the product level.
cards.h: → axes, three features, two labeled arrows
cards.n: Products drawn above reactants show an unfavored process; kinetic control needs products lower AND a tall barrier. Energy profiles are Unit 5 content.

cards.q: Classify each process at 25 °C as (A) thermodynamically favored and fast, (B) thermodynamically favored but under kinetic control, or (C) not thermodynamically favored: C(diamond) → C(graphite), ΔG° = −2.9 kJ/mol · H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔG° = −80 kJ/mol · a mixture of H₂(g) and O₂(g) with no spark · sucrose sitting in air (combustion ΔG° ≈ −5800 kJ/mol) · natural gas and air mixed with no flame · Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s), ΔG° = −56 kJ/mol · N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), ΔG° = +173 kJ/mol · 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g), ΔG° = +474 kJ/mol · ice melting on a bench at 25 °C · 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) in a clean bottle, ΔG° = −233 kJ/mol
cards.a:
diamond → graphite → B (no observable change over lifetimes)
H⁺ + OH⁻ → A (instantaneous neutralization)
H₂ + O₂, no spark → B (explodes once ignited)
sucrose in air → B (burns only when lit, or slowly with enzymes)
natural gas + air → B (needs a flame)
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → A (precipitate forms at once)
N₂ + O₂ → 2NO → C (ΔG° > 0; air does not form NO at 25 °C)
2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ → C (needs electrolysis)
ice melting at 25 °C → A (favored above 0 °C; observable rate)
H₂O₂ decomposition → B (slow until a catalyst such as MnO₂ is added)
cards.h: → sign of ΔG° first, then: is it observably fast?
cards.n: Putting diamond in class C because 'it never changes' is the trap; no observable change does not make ΔG° positive.

cards.q: Explain why diamond does not visibly convert to graphite even though ΔG° for the conversion is negative.
cards.a: The conversion is thermodynamically favored (ΔG° ≈ −2.9 kJ/mol) but under kinetic control: it requires breaking and rearranging strong C–C covalent bonds throughout the network solid, so the activation energy is enormous and the rate at room temperature is immeasurably slow.
cards.h: → ΔG° < 0 so favored → conversion needs network C–C bonds broken → huge Eₐ → immeasurable rate
cards.n: 'Diamonds are forever' is kinetics, not thermodynamics; calling diamond the stable form contradicts the given ΔG°. Activation energy is Unit 5 content.
o: ΔG° only compares the free energies of diamond and graphite; the height of the barrier between them sets the rate, and that barrier is very high.
At very high temperatures the conversion can be observed, which shows that the barrier, not the thermodynamics, is what stops it.

w.a: Diamond does not convert because it is more stable than graphite.
w.why: contradicts ΔG° < 0; graphite is the more stable form

w.a: Diamond does not convert because the system is at equilibrium.
w.why: no measurable rate does not mean equilibrium

w.a: Diamond does not convert because ΔG° is only slightly negative.
w.why: a small negative ΔG° still means favored; the barrier explains the slowness

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with a large negative ΔG° can still proceed too slowly to observe at room temperature.
cards.a: ΔG° compares only the free energies of reactants and products; it holds no information about the pathway between them. The rate depends on the activation energy: if Eₐ is large, only a tiny fraction of collisions at room temperature have enough energy, so the reaction is favored but under kinetic control.
cards.h: → ΔG° = end states only → rate set by Eₐ → large Eₐ → few successful collisions → favored but slow
cards.n: Name the activation energy explicitly; 'the kinetics are slow' with no Eₐ earns nothing. Collision theory is Unit 5 content.
o: Favorability and rate are governed by different quantities (ΔG° versus Eₐ), so one does not predict the other.
A high activation barrier leaves the reactants kinetically trapped even though the products are much lower in free energy.

w.a: A very negative ΔG° means the reaction must be fast, so it cannot be slow.
w.why: repeats the misconception that favorability sets rate

w.a: It is slow because the reaction is already at equilibrium.
w.why: a favored reaction far from equilibrium can still be slow

w.a: It is slow because its ΔH° is positive.
w.why: ΔH° does not control rate; activation energy does

cards.q: Explain why increasing temperature reliably speeds up a reaction's rate, while its effect on thermodynamic favorability depends on the sign of ΔS°.
cards.a: Raising T increases the fraction of collisions with energy at least Eₐ, so the rate rises. Favorability follows ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°: a higher T makes ΔG° more negative only if ΔS° > 0; if ΔS° < 0, a higher T makes ΔG° less negative and can make the process unfavored.
cards.h: → higher T → more collisions exceed Eₐ → always faster; −TΔS° → sign of ΔS° sets which way ΔG° moves
cards.n: 'Higher T lowers Eₐ' describes a catalyst, not temperature, and earns nothing. Collision theory is Unit 5 content.
o: Temperature enters the rate through the energy distribution of the particles, but enters ΔG° only through the TΔS° term, whose sign depends on ΔS°.
For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ (ΔS° < 0), heating speeds the reaction yet makes it less favored.

w.a: Higher temperature always makes reactions more favorable because they go faster.
w.why: conflates rate with favorability

w.a: Higher temperature speeds reactions because it lowers the activation energy.
w.why: T does not change Eₐ; it changes the fraction of collisions exceeding it

w.a: Temperature has no effect on ΔG° because ΔG° is a standard value.
w.why: ΔG° depends on T through the TΔS° term

cards.q: Explain why adding a catalyst cannot make a thermodynamically unfavored reaction occur to any significant extent.
cards.a: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally; it does not change the free energies of reactants or products, so ΔG° and K are unchanged. A reaction with ΔG° > 0 still favors reactants, and the catalyst only helps the system reach that reactant-favored equilibrium sooner.
cards.h: → catalyst lowers Eₐ both ways → end states unchanged → ΔG° and K unchanged → still unfavored
cards.n: Driving an unfavored process needs external energy or coupling (9.7), not a catalyst. Catalysis is Unit 5 content.
o: Favorability is a property of the initial and final states, and a catalyst changes only the path between them.
Speeding up a reaction whose equilibrium lies on the reactant side just gets the system to mostly reactants faster.

w.a: A catalyst can make any reaction happen because it provides energy.
w.why: a catalyst supplies no energy; it lowers Eₐ

w.a: A catalyst makes ΔG° more negative by lowering the activation energy.
w.why: Eₐ and ΔG° are independent; ΔG° is unchanged

w.a: A catalyst shifts the equilibrium toward products.
w.why: it speeds both directions equally; K is unchanged

cards.q: State the relationship between standard free energy change and the equilibrium constant.
cards.a: ΔG° = −RT ln K, or equivalently K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T in kelvin and ΔG° in J/mol. A negative ΔG° gives ln K > 0 and K > 1 (products favored); a positive ΔG° gives K < 1 (reactants favored).
cards.h: → equation, units of R, what the sign means
cards.n: Using R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K), or ΔG° in kJ with R in J, gives a wildly wrong K; match joules to joules.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔG° from the magnitude of K.
cards.a: K > 1 → ln K > 0 → ΔG° < 0 (products favored; thermodynamically favored). K < 1 → ln K < 0 → ΔG° > 0 (reactants favored). K = 1 → ΔG° = 0. This follows from ΔG° = −RT ln K; the farther K is from 1, the larger |ΔG°|.
cards.h: → three cases keyed to K = 1
cards.n: The dividing line is K = 1, not K = 0; a K of 0.2 still means ΔG° > 0 even though some product forms.

cards.q: State the equation relating ΔG under nonstandard conditions to ΔG° and Q.
cards.a: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient of the actual mixture. When Q = 1 (every species at standard state) ΔG = ΔG°; when Q < K, ΔG < 0 and the forward reaction proceeds; at equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, which gives back ΔG° = −RT ln K.
cards.h: → equation + three cases of Q
cards.n: Not on the AP equation sheet: it is the Nernst equation multiplied by −nF. Use it qualitatively and keep ΔG and ΔG° distinct.

cards.q: Explain what ΔG equals at equilibrium and what that implies about Q.
cards.a: At equilibrium ΔG = 0: no drive remains in either direction. Substituting into ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q gives 0 = ΔG° + RT ln Q, so Q must equal K (since ΔG° = −RT ln K). ΔG° itself is a constant at a given temperature and is generally not zero at equilibrium.
cards.h: → one value, one identity, one warning about ΔG°
cards.n: 'ΔG° = 0 at equilibrium' is the classic error; only ΔG for the actual mixture is zero, and ΔG° is zero only if K = 1.

cards.q: Compute K at 298 K for a reaction with ΔG° = -22.8 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → ln K = −ΔG°/RT in joules, then e^x
cards.n: Leaving ΔG° in kJ gives ln K = 0.0092 and K ≈ 1, which misses the point; convert to 22,800 J/mol.

cards.q: Compute K at 298 K for a reaction with ΔG° = +11.4 kJ/mol.
cards.a: K = 0.010. ln K = −(11,400 J/mol) ÷ [(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K)] = −4.60; K = e^(−4.60) = 1.0 × 10⁻². ΔG° > 0, so K < 1 and reactants are favored at equilibrium.
cards.h: → solve for ln K, then exponentiate
cards.n: Dropping the minus sign gives K = 99.5, which would mean products are favored; a positive ΔG° must give K < 1.

cards.q: Compute ΔG° at 298 K for a reaction with K = 5.0×10⁻³.
cards.a: ΔG° = +13.1 kJ/mol. ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K) ln(5.0 × 10⁻³) = −(2478 J/mol)(−5.30) = +1.31 × 10⁴ J/mol = +13.1 kJ/mol. K < 1 and ΔG° > 0 agree: reactants are favored.
cards.h: → one substitution with ln, answer in kJ
cards.n: Using log instead of ln (log 0.0050 = −2.30) gives +5.7 kJ/mol; the equation uses the natural logarithm.

cards.q: Estimate K at 298 K (RT ≈ 2.48 kJ/mol) for each value of ΔG°: 0 · +2.5 kJ/mol · −1.0 kJ/mol · −5.7 kJ/mol · −11.4 kJ/mol · +11.4 kJ/mol · −57 kJ/mol · +57 kJ/mol · −100 kJ/mol · +100 kJ/mol
cards.a:
0 → K = 1 (neither side favored)
+2.5 kJ/mol → K ≈ e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37 (close to 1, reactants slightly favored)
−1.0 kJ/mol → K ≈ 1.5 (close to 1)
−5.7 kJ/mol → K ≈ 10
−11.4 kJ/mol → K ≈ 10²
+11.4 kJ/mol → K ≈ 10⁻²
−57 kJ/mol → K ≈ 10¹⁰ (essentially all products)
+57 kJ/mol → K ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ (essentially all reactants)
−100 kJ/mol → K ≈ 3 × 10¹⁷
+100 kJ/mol → K ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹⁸
Rule of thumb at 298 K: every 5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG° changes K by a factor of 10.
cards.h: → compare |ΔG°| with RT; 5.7 kJ/mol per power of 10
cards.n: When |ΔG°| is only a few kJ/mol, K stays near 1 and both sides are present in comparable amounts; calling K = 0.37 'no reaction' misreads it.

cards.q: Calculate K at 500. K for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), given ΔH° = −92.2 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −198.7 J/(mol·K), assuming both are independent of temperature.
cards.a: K ≈ 0.18. ΔG°(500 K) = −92.2 kJ/mol − (500. K)(−0.1987 kJ/(mol·K)) = −92.2 + 99.4 = +7.2 kJ/mol. ln K = −7150 J/mol ÷ [(8.314 J/(mol·K))(500. K)] = −1.72, so K = e^(−1.72) = 0.18. At 500 K the reaction is no longer favored under standard conditions (K < 1).
cards.h: → ΔG° at the new T, then ln K with the same T
cards.n: Using the 298 K value of ΔG° (−33 kJ/mol) at 500 K is the trap; ΔG° must be recomputed at the new T, and RT uses 500 K too.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K for CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq), for which Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, and state what its sign means.
cards.a: ΔG° = +27.1 kJ/mol. ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K) ln(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = −(2478 J/mol)(−10.93) = +2.71 × 10⁴ J/mol. The positive value means ionization is not favored under standard conditions: K < 1, so the un-ionized acid is favored, as expected for a weak acid.
cards.h: → ΔG° = −RT ln Ka, then interpret the sign
cards.n: A positive ΔG° does not mean 'no ionization': a 0.10 M solution is still about 1% ionized. Ka is Unit 8 content.

cards.q: Explain what value K must equal whenever ΔG° = 0, and what that special case means physically.
cards.a: K = 1. From ΔG° = −RT ln K, ΔG° = 0 requires ln K = 0, so K = 1. Physically, a mixture with every species in its standard state (Q = 1) is already at equilibrium: neither reactants nor products are favored, and there is no net reaction from that mixture.
cards.h: → ΔG° = 0 → ln K = 0 → K = 1 → the standard-state mixture (Q = 1) is already at equilibrium
cards.n: Only the standard-state mixture is at equilibrium; a mixture with Q ≠ 1 still reacts toward Q = K = 1.
o: When ΔG° = 0, products and reactants have equal standard free energies, so neither side is favored.
Q = 1 for the standard-state mixture and K = 1, so Q = K and there is no net change from that starting point.

w.a: K must equal 0, because ΔG° = 0.
w.why: e⁰ = 1, so K = 1; K = 0 would need an infinite ΔG°

w.a: If ΔG° = 0, the reaction does not happen at all.
w.why: forward and reverse still occur at equal rates at equilibrium

w.a: ΔG° = 0 means every mixture of these species is at equilibrium.
w.why: only the mixture with Q = 1 is; others shift

cards.q: Explain why a thermodynamically favored reaction (ΔG° < 0) has an equilibrium constant greater than 1.
cards.a: ΔG° = −RT ln K, and R and T are positive, so a negative ΔG° requires ln K > 0, which means K > 1. Physically, the products lie lower in standard free energy than the reactants, so at equilibrium under standard conditions products are favored over reactants.
cards.h: → ΔG° = −RT ln K → ΔG° < 0 → ln K > 0 → K > 1 → products favored at equilibrium
cards.n: CED 9.5.A.1: 'thermodynamically favored' means products are favored at equilibrium (K > 1); it says nothing about completion or speed.
o: Rearranged, K = e^(−ΔG°/RT); a negative ΔG° makes the exponent positive, so K > 1.
Favored means the equilibrium mixture lies on the product side, which is exactly what K > 1 states.

w.a: ΔG° < 0 means K < 0 because both are negative.
w.why: K is never negative; ln K > 0 gives K > 1

w.a: ΔG° < 0 means the reaction goes to completion, so K is infinite.
w.why: K is finite; products are favored, not exclusive

w.a: ΔG° < 0 means the reaction is fast, so products build up.
w.why: rate plays no part in K

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with ΔG° > 0 still forms some products when its reactants are mixed.
cards.a: ΔG° > 0 means K < 1, not K = 0. Starting from pure reactants Q = 0, which is less than K, so the forward reaction proceeds until Q = K; the equilibrium mixture is mostly reactants but contains some products. ΔG° describes the standard-state mixture, not every mixture.
cards.h: → ΔG° > 0 → K < 1 but K > 0 → Q = 0 < K → some forward reaction → mostly reactants at equilibrium
cards.n: Confusing ΔG and ΔG° is the trap: ΔG° is fixed at a given T, while ΔG changes with the composition of the mixture.
o: ΔG° > 0 says products are not favored at equilibrium under standard conditions; it does not forbid their formation.
For the actual mixture, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q is negative while Q is very small, so the forward reaction is favored at first.

w.a: A reaction with ΔG° > 0 cannot form any products.
w.why: K < 1 still means a nonzero amount of product

w.a: It forms products because it is under kinetic control.
w.why: kinetic control describes favored reactions that are slow

w.a: It forms products because ΔG° becomes negative as the reaction proceeds.
w.why: ΔG° is constant at a given T; Q and ΔG change

cards.q: Explain why a ΔG° of only a few kJ/mol gives K close to 1, while a ΔG° of tens of kJ/mol gives K far from 1.
cards.a: K = e^(−ΔG°/RT) depends exponentially on ΔG°/RT, and RT at 298 K is only about 2.5 kJ/mol. When |ΔG°| is comparable to RT the exponent is near 1 and K stays within an order of magnitude of 1; when |ΔG°| ≫ RT, K is many powers of ten above or below 1.
cards.h: → K = e^(−ΔG°/RT) → RT ≈ 2.5 kJ/mol → |ΔG°| ≈ RT gives K ≈ 1; |ΔG°| ≫ RT gives K ≫ 1 or ≪ 1
cards.n: CED 9.5.A.3 asks for exactly this estimate; comparing ΔG° with RT, not with zero, is the reasoning that scores.
o: Every 5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG° at 298 K changes K by a factor of 10, so 57 kJ/mol changes it by 10¹⁰.
ΔG° = −2.5 kJ/mol gives K ≈ 2.7, but ΔG° = −50 kJ/mol gives K ≈ 6 × 10⁸.

w.a: K is proportional to ΔG°, so a small ΔG° gives a small K.
w.why: the relation is exponential, and the sign of ΔG° decides whether K is above or below 1

w.a: K is close to 1 whenever ΔG° is negative.
w.why: a large negative ΔG° gives a K far above 1

w.a: Any nonzero ΔG° makes K either 0 or infinite.
w.why: K changes smoothly and exponentially with ΔG°

cards.q: Identify the three factors whose free energy changes combine to give ΔG° for dissolving an ionic solid in water.
cards.a: (1) Breaking the interactions that hold the solid together (the ion–ion attractions of the lattice); (2) reorganizing the solvent: separating water molecules from one another and arranging them around the dissolved ions; (3) the interaction of the dissolved ions with the solvent (ion–dipole attractions). Each factor has its own enthalpy and entropy contribution.
cards.h: → three factors, one clause each
cards.n: 'Breaking bonds and forming bonds' misses the solvent-reorganization factor, which carries the entropy cost of ordered hydration shells.

cards.q: Estimate the sign of the enthalpy and entropy contributions of each step in dissolving NaCl(s) in water: separating the ions of the lattice; separating water molecules and ordering them around the ions; forming ion–dipole attractions.
cards.a: Separating the lattice ions: ΔH > 0 (Coulombic attractions overcome), ΔS > 0 (ions become free to disperse). Reorganizing the water: ΔH > 0 (some water–water hydrogen bonds broken), ΔS < 0 (water held in ordered hydration shells). Forming ion–dipole attractions: ΔH < 0 (energy released). Net ΔH and ΔS are small differences of these terms.
cards.h: → three steps, a sign of ΔH and ΔS for each
cards.n: Giving every step ΔS > 0 because 'dissolving increases disorder' misses the ordered hydration shells that can make ΔS° of dissolution negative.

cards.q: Calculate ΔH° of dissolution for NaCl, given that separating 1 mol of NaCl(s) into gaseous ions requires +787 kJ and hydrating 1 mol of Na⁺(g) plus 1 mol of Cl⁻(g) releases 783 kJ.
cards.a: ΔH°soln ≈ +4 kJ/mol. ΔH°soln = (+787 kJ/mol) + (−783 kJ/mol) = +4 kJ/mol. Two very large terms of opposite sign nearly cancel, so dissolving NaCl is only slightly endothermic (tabulated: +3.9 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → add the two steps with their signs
cards.n: Adding 787 + 783 = 1570 kJ/mol ignores the sign of the exothermic hydration step. Lattice energy and Hess's law come from Units 2 and 6.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG° and K (the Ksp) at 298 K for AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), given ΔH° = +65.5 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +33.0 J/(mol·K) for the dissolution.
cards.a: ΔG° = +55.7 kJ/mol and Ksp ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁰. ΔG° = 65.5 − (298)(0.0330) = 65.5 − 9.8 = +55.7 kJ/mol. ln K = −55,700 ÷ [(8.314)(298)] = −22.5, so K = e^(−22.5) ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁰, close to the measured Ksp of 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. The large ΔH° outweighs the small TΔS°, so AgCl is only sparingly soluble.
cards.h: → ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, then K = e^(−ΔG°/RT)
cards.n: 'ΔS° > 0, so AgCl dissolves' ignores the size of ΔH°; the lattice-breaking cost far exceeds TΔS° here. Ksp is Unit 7 content.

cards.q: Determine ΔG° of dissolution at 298 K and whether dissolving is thermodynamically favored for each salt (ΔH° in kJ/mol, ΔS° in J/(mol·K)): NaCl +3.9, +43.4 · NH₄NO₃ +25.7, +108.7 · NaNO₃ +20.5, +88.9 · MgCl₂ −159.8, −114.7 · CaCO₃ −13.1, −202.9 · AgCl +65.5, +33.0
cards.a:
NaCl → 3.9 − 12.9 = −9.0 kJ/mol → favored (entropy-driven)
NH₄NO₃ → 25.7 − 32.4 = −6.7 kJ/mol → favored (entropy-driven; a cold pack)
NaNO₃ → 20.5 − 26.5 = −6.0 kJ/mol → favored (entropy-driven)
MgCl₂ → −159.8 + 34.2 = −125.6 kJ/mol → favored (enthalpy-driven although ΔS° < 0)
CaCO₃ → −13.1 + 60.5 = +47.4 kJ/mol → not favored (the ΔS° < 0 penalty wins; Ksp ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁹)
AgCl → 65.5 − 9.8 = +55.7 kJ/mol → not favored (large ΔH°; Ksp ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁰)
cards.h: → ΔH° − (298)(ΔS°/1000) for each, then the sign
cards.n: No single sign predicts solubility: MgCl₂ dissolves with ΔS° < 0 and AgCl fails with ΔS° > 0. Values are rounded from standard tables.

cards.q: Determine the signs of ΔH°, ΔS° and ΔG° for dissolving NH₄NO₃(s) in water, given that the salt dissolves readily and the water temperature falls from 22.0 °C to 14.5 °C.
cards.a: ΔH° > 0, ΔS° > 0, ΔG° < 0. The temperature drop shows the dissolving salt absorbs heat from the water (endothermic, ΔH° > 0). It dissolves readily, so ΔG° < 0. For ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° to be negative with ΔH° > 0, TΔS° must exceed ΔH°, so ΔS° must be positive: the dissolution is entropy-driven.
cards.h: → three signs, each tied to an observation or to ΔG°
cards.n: Reading the cooling as 'ΔH < 0 because heat left the water' mixes up system and surroundings; the dissolving salt absorbed that heat. Calorimetry is Unit 6.

cards.q: Predict how the solubility of O₂(g) in water changes as the temperature rises, using the signs of ΔH° and ΔS° for O₂(g) → O₂(aq).
cards.a: Solubility decreases. Dissolving a gas has ΔS° < 0 (the molecules lose their freedom and are confined in the solution) and ΔH° < 0 (attractions to water form while little is broken). With both negative, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° becomes less negative as T rises, so dissolution is less favored and K falls: warm water holds less O₂.
cards.h: → signs of ΔH° and ΔS°, then the −TΔS° trend
cards.n: 'Heat gives the molecules energy to escape' is a kinetic story; the scored reasoning is the −TΔS° term growing more positive as T rises. Gas solubility is Unit 3.

cards.q: Predict how the solubility of KNO₃ in water changes as the temperature rises, given that its dissolution has ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° > 0.
cards.a: Solubility increases. ΔH° > 0 opposes dissolving and ΔS° > 0 favors it; as T rises the favorable −TΔS° term grows in magnitude while ΔH° stays about the same, so ΔG° becomes more negative and K increases. KNO₃'s solubility does rise steeply with temperature.
cards.h: → verdict + how −TΔS° changes with T
cards.n: 'Heat speeds up dissolving' confuses rate with extent; the claim concerns the equilibrium amount dissolved, set by ΔG° and K.

cards.q: Represent in words a particulate diagram of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions dissolved in water, showing how the water molecules are oriented around each ion.
cards.a: Draw separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, each surrounded by a shell of about four to six water molecules, each drawn as a bent O with two H atoms. Around Na⁺ every water points its O atom (partial negative end) toward the ion, H atoms outward; around Cl⁻ every water points an H atom (partial positive end) toward the ion. The ions are far apart, not paired, and water beyond the shells is randomly arranged.
cards.h: → ions apart, shells, which end faces which ion
cards.n: Pointing H atoms at Na⁺ (or O at Cl⁻) earns nothing: the partial charge facing an ion must be opposite to the ion's charge. Solution diagrams are Unit 3.

cards.q: Explain how the free energy of dissolution is related to Ksp.
cards.a: ΔG° of dissolution and Ksp are linked by ΔG° = −RT ln Ksp, because Ksp is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution. A salt with ΔG° < 0 has Ksp > 1 (dissolving is thermodynamically favored); a sparingly soluble salt has ΔG° > 0 and Ksp < 1. For AgCl, ΔG° = +55.7 kJ/mol gives Ksp = e^(−55,700/2478) ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁰.
cards.h: → Ksp is a K, so ΔG° = −RT ln Ksp, then the two sign cases
cards.n: 'A large ΔG° means a large Ksp' reverses the sign: the more positive ΔG° of dissolution, the smaller Ksp. Ksp itself is Unit 7 content.

cards.q: Given ΔH°soln = +15.0 kJ/mol and ΔS°soln = +65.0 J/(mol·K) at 298 K, compute ΔG°soln and determine whether dissolution is spontaneous.
cards.a: ΔG° = −4.4 kJ/mol; dissolution is thermodynamically favored at 298 K. ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 15.0 kJ/mol − (298 K)(0.0650 kJ/(mol·K)) = 15.0 − 19.4 = −4.4 kJ/mol. The process is endothermic but entropy-driven: TΔS° outweighs ΔH°.
cards.h: → convert ΔS° to kJ, substitute, verdict
cards.n: The question says 'spontaneous'; answer 'thermodynamically favored'. Using 65.0 unconverted gives about −19,000 kJ/mol, a factor-of-1000 error.

cards.q: Explain why a salt can dissolve spontaneously in water even when its dissolution is endothermic $(ΔH°_soln$ > 0).
cards.a: Dissolving disperses the ions of an ordered solid throughout the solution, so ΔS° > 0. In ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, a large enough TΔS° outweighs a positive ΔH°, making ΔG° < 0: the dissolution is thermodynamically favored and entropy-driven, although it absorbs heat.
cards.h: → ions disperse → ΔS° > 0 → TΔS° > ΔH° → ΔG° < 0 → favored although endothermic
cards.n: The question says 'spontaneous'; the CED's phrase is 'thermodynamically favored'. An answer that never compares TΔS° with ΔH° earns nothing.
o: For NaCl, ΔH° = +3.9 kJ/mol but TΔS° = 298 × 0.0434 = 12.9 kJ/mol, so ΔG° ≈ −9.0 kJ/mol.
The small enthalpy cost (lattice separation barely repaid by hydration) is outweighed by the entropy gained as the ions disperse.

w.a: A salt dissolves when it is endothermic because heat helps break the ionic bonds.
w.why: heat absorbed is the cost, not the driving force

w.a: An endothermic dissolution cannot be favored, so the salt must be dissolving exothermically.
w.why: a positive ΔH° is allowed when TΔS° is larger

w.a: The salt dissolves because water is polar and like dissolves like.
w.why: a rule of thumb, not a ΔH/ΔS/ΔG argument

cards.q: Explain why ΔS° for dissolving MgCl₂ in water is negative even though the ions of the solid become dispersed.
cards.a: Mg²⁺ is small and doubly charged, so its strong ion–dipole attractions hold many water molecules in tightly ordered hydration shells. The entropy lost by ordering that water outweighs the entropy gained by dispersing the ions, so ΔS° ≈ −115 J/(mol·K); dissolving is still favored because ΔH° is very negative.
cards.h: → small 2+ ion → strong ion–dipole pull → water ordered in shells → entropy lost > dispersal gained → ΔS° < 0
cards.n: Ignoring the solvent's entropy is the trap. The charge-and-size argument is Coulomb's law from Units 1 and 3.
o: The solvent-reorganization factor dominates the entropy change: a highly charged ion immobilizes more water than the dispersal of the ions frees.
The high charge density of Mg²⁺ means a stronger Coulombic pull on water dipoles, a more ordered hydration shell and a more negative entropy term.

w.a: ΔS° is negative because MgCl₂ does not dissolve.
w.why: MgCl₂ is very soluble; its ΔG° is very negative

w.a: ΔS° is negative because the Mg²⁺ ions form a new solid in the solution.
w.why: no solid forms; the ordering is of water molecules

w.a: ΔS° is negative because dissolving always decreases entropy.
w.why: NaCl dissolves with ΔS° > 0; the sign depends on the ions

cards.q: Explain why CaCO₃ is only sparingly soluble in water even though its dissolution is exothermic.
cards.a: Dissolving CaCO₃ has ΔH° ≈ −13 kJ/mol but ΔS° ≈ −203 J/(mol·K): the small, doubly charged Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ ions order many water molecules. At 298 K, −TΔS° ≈ +60 kJ/mol outweighs ΔH°, so ΔG° ≈ +47 kJ/mol and Ksp ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁹.
cards.h: → 2+ and 2− ions → strongly ordered hydration water → ΔS° very negative → −TΔS° > |ΔH°| → ΔG° > 0 → small Ksp
cards.n: Values are rounded from standard tables; the scoring idea is that the negative ΔS° term, not ΔH°, makes ΔG° positive. Ksp is Unit 7 content.
o: Dissolution is opposed by entropy more strongly than it is favored by enthalpy, so ΔH° − TΔS° is positive.
The same water-ordering that makes MgCl₂'s ΔS° negative acts here, but there is no large negative ΔH° to rescue it.

w.a: CaCO₃ is insoluble because its dissolution is endothermic.
w.why: the given ΔH° is negative

w.a: CaCO₃ is insoluble because carbonate is a covalent molecule.
w.why: CaCO₃ is ionic; the argument must use ΔH° and ΔS°

w.a: CaCO₃ is insoluble because the heat released stops it from dissolving.
w.why: not a free-energy argument

cards.q: Explain why the sign of ΔG° for dissolving a salt is hard to predict from the structure of the salt alone.
cards.a: ΔG° of dissolution sums three factors (breaking the solid's interactions, reorganizing the solvent, and ion–solvent attraction), each with sizable enthalpy and entropy parts of opposite sign. They largely cancel, so the net ΔG° is a small difference between large numbers and can fall on either side of zero.
cards.h: → three factors with opposing ΔH and ΔS → large terms cancel → net ΔG° small → sign not predictable by inspection
cards.n: CED 9.6.A.1 names this cancellation as the reason predictions are challenging; claiming a single factor decides earns nothing.
o: For NaCl, +787 kJ/mol to separate the ions and −783 kJ/mol of hydration leave only +4 kJ/mol, so a small error in either estimate would flip the conclusion.
The entropy contributions also oppose each other (ions disperse, water orders), so neither ΔH° nor ΔS° alone decides.

w.a: It is easy to predict, because ionic compounds always dissolve in water.
w.why: many, such as AgCl and CaCO₃, are sparingly soluble

w.a: You only need the lattice energy, since a large lattice energy means insoluble.
w.why: ignores the equally large hydration term

w.a: Salts with ΔS° > 0 always dissolve.
w.why: AgCl has ΔS° > 0 and is sparingly soluble

cards.q: Define a coupled reaction system and state the requirement for the two reactions to be linked.
cards.a: A coupled reaction system combines a thermodynamically unfavored reaction (ΔG° > 0) with a favored one (ΔG° < 0) so that their sum has ΔG° < 0. The reactions must share one or more common intermediates: a species produced by one reaction and consumed by the other, which cancels when the equations are added.
cards.h: → definition + the linking requirement
cards.n: Two reactions merely running in the same flask are not coupled; without a shared intermediate the favored one cannot drive the other.

cards.q: State the minimum condition on the sum of the individual ΔG° values for a coupled pair of reactions to be spontaneous overall.
cards.a: ΔG°₁ + ΔG°₂ < 0: the favored reaction's ΔG° must be more negative than the unfavored reaction's ΔG° is positive, with each value multiplied by the factor its equation is scaled by in the overall reaction.
cards.h: → one inequality + the scaling caveat
cards.n: Forgetting to scale: if the favored reaction is used twice, its ΔG° counts twice in the sum.

cards.q: Predict whether coupling a favorable reaction (ΔG°₁ = −80. kJ/mol) with an unfavorable one (ΔG°₂ = +20. kJ/mol) gives an overall favorable process.
cards.a: Yes. ΔG°overall = ΔG°₁ + ΔG°₂ = −80. + 20. = −60. kJ/mol < 0, so the coupled process is thermodynamically favored, provided the two reactions share a common intermediate so that their equations add to the overall reaction.
cards.h: → yes/no + the sum with sign
cards.n: ΔG° values add because the equations add (as in Hess's law); the K values would multiply instead.

cards.q: A cell couples reaction 1 $(ΔG°_1$ = -62 kJ/mol) with reaction 2 $(ΔG°_2$ = +38 kJ/mol). Compute the overall ΔG° and determine whether the coupled process is spontaneous.
cards.a: ΔG°overall = −24 kJ/mol; the coupled process is thermodynamically favored. ΔG°overall = ΔG°₁ + ΔG°₂ = (−62) + (+38) = −24 kJ/mol, which is negative.
cards.h: → value with sign, then the verdict
cards.n: The question says 'spontaneous'; answer 'thermodynamically favored', the CED's phrase, which does not imply the process is fast.

cards.q: Identify a common example of a coupled reaction and the source of the driving free energy.
cards.a: In cells, ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ, ΔG°' ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol) is coupled to unfavored syntheses such as making glutamine, linked by a phosphorylated intermediate. Industrially, reducing Fe₂O₃ to iron (ΔG° = +742 kJ/mol) is driven by coupling it to the oxidation of CO to CO₂ in a blast furnace, linked through oxygen.
cards.h: → one biological, one industrial, each with its partner
cards.n: ATP is the CED's named example; naming a reaction without its favored partner or the shared intermediate earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify what supplies the free energy that makes each thermodynamically unfavored process occur: electrolysis of water into H₂ and O₂ · recharging a lithium-ion phone battery · photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ · a cell building glutamine from glutamate and NH₃ · producing aluminum from Al₂O₃ · extracting iron from Fe₂O₃ in a blast furnace
cards.a:
electrolysis of water → electrical energy from the power supply (electrolytic cell)
recharging a battery → electrical energy from the charger (the battery runs as an electrolytic cell)
photosynthesis → light absorbed by chlorophyll
glutamine synthesis → coupling to ATP hydrolysis through a phosphorylated intermediate
aluminum production → electrical energy (electrolysis of molten Al₂O₃ dissolved in cryolite)
iron extraction → coupling to the oxidation of CO (from coke) to CO₂
cards.h: → external energy (which kind?) or a coupled reaction
cards.n: 'A catalyst' or 'heat speeds it up' earns nothing; only external energy (electrical, light) or coupling to a favored reaction makes an unfavored process occur.

cards.q: Write the overall reaction and calculate its ΔG°' for coupling (1) glutamate + NH₃ → glutamine + H₂O, ΔG°' = +14.2 kJ/mol, with (2) ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ, ΔG°' = −30.5 kJ/mol, and identify what must link the two steps.
cards.a: Glutamate + NH₃ + ATP → glutamine + ADP + Pᵢ; ΔG°' = +14.2 + (−30.5) = −16.3 kJ/mol, favored (the H₂O cancels when the equations are added). The steps are linked through a common intermediate, glutamyl phosphate: ATP phosphorylates glutamate (releasing ADP), and NH₃ then displaces the phosphate (releasing Pᵢ).
cards.h: → summed equation, summed ΔG°', the intermediate
cards.n: ΔG°' values are biochemical standard values at pH 7. Adding the two with no shared intermediate would describe two independent reactions, not a coupled system.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g) by coupling Fe₂O₃(s) → 2Fe(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) (ΔG° = +742.2 kJ/mol) with CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) (ΔG° = −257.2 kJ/mol), and identify the common intermediate.
cards.a: ΔG° = −29.4 kJ/mol, and the common intermediate is O₂. Tripling the CO reaction gives 3CO + 3/2 O₂ → 3CO₂ with ΔG° = 3(−257.2) = −771.6 kJ. Adding: +742.2 + (−771.6) = −29.4 kJ/mol, and the 3/2 O₂ released by the first reaction is consumed by the second, so it cancels.
cards.h: → scale the favored step, add, name what cancels
cards.n: Adding −257.2 only once (giving +485.0 kJ) forgets that the CO equation must be tripled to consume all of the O₂.

cards.q: Calculate the equilibrium constant at 298 K for the coupled glutamine reaction, glutamate + NH₃ + ATP → glutamine + ADP + Pᵢ, given K₁ = 3.2 × 10⁻³ for glutamate + NH₃ → glutamine + H₂O and K₂ = 2.2 × 10⁵ for ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ.
cards.a: K = 7.0 × 10². When equations are added, their equilibrium constants multiply: K = K₁ × K₂ = (3.2 × 10⁻³)(2.2 × 10⁵) = 7.0 × 10². This matches ΔG°' = −16.3 kJ/mol, since e^(16,300/2478) ≈ 7.2 × 10² (the difference is rounding).
cards.h: → multiply the two K values, then a ΔG° check
cards.n: K₁ + K₂ earns nothing: ΔG° values add, so the K values (exponentials of −ΔG°/RT) multiply. The rule for adding equations is Unit 7.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG° for photosynthesis, 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6O₂(g), given ΔG°f values in kJ/mol: CO₂(g) −394.4, H₂O(l) −237.1, C₆H₁₂O₆(s) −910.4, and identify how the process is made to occur.
cards.a: ΔG° = +2878.6 kJ/mol. Products: −910.4 + 6(0) = −910.4 kJ; reactants: 6(−394.4) + 6(−237.1) = −3789.0 kJ; ΔG° = −910.4 − (−3789.0) = +2878.6 kJ/mol. The process is strongly unfavored, so it occurs only because absorbed light supplies the free energy (CED 9.7.A.1).
cards.h: → ΔG°f sums, subtract, then name the energy source
cards.n: 'Photosynthesis is favored because plants do it' earns nothing; ΔG° > 0 and the free energy comes from absorbed light.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔG for the reaction occurring inside a rechargeable battery while it is being charged, and identify what makes that reaction proceed.
cards.a: ΔG > 0 for the charging reaction. Charging runs the battery's discharge reaction (which is thermodynamically favored, ΔG < 0) in reverse, so the charging reaction is unfavored; the charger supplies electrical energy, operating the battery as an electrolytic cell and forcing electrons through it in the opposite direction.
cards.h: → sign + what reverses + the energy source
cards.n: Saying the charger 'makes the reaction favorable' blurs the idea: ΔG of the charging reaction stays positive, and external electrical work pays for it.

cards.q: Explain how coupled reactions can drive a thermodynamically unfavorable process.
cards.a: An unfavored reaction (ΔG° > 0) is paired with a strongly favored one (ΔG° < 0) through a common intermediate that one produces and the other consumes. The equations add to one overall reaction whose ΔG° is the sum, and if that sum is negative the overall process, including the desired product, is favored.
cards.h: → unfavored + favored share an intermediate → equations add → ΔG° values add → sum < 0 → overall favored
cards.n: The answer needs both the shared intermediate and the negative sum; either one alone is incomplete.
o: The favored reaction's decrease in free energy more than pays for the unfavored reaction's increase, so the combined process has ΔG° < 0.
Because ΔG° is a state function, the ΔG° of the summed equation is the sum of the steps' ΔG° values, as in Hess's law.

w.a: The favored reaction gives off heat that the unfavored reaction absorbs.
w.why: heat transfer is not the free-energy argument, and no intermediate is named

w.a: Coupling lowers the activation energy of the unfavored reaction.
w.why: that describes a catalyst, which cannot change ΔG°

w.a: Coupling makes the unfavored reaction's own ΔG° negative.
w.why: each step keeps its ΔG°; only the sum is negative

cards.q: Explain why the two reactions in a coupled system must share a common intermediate species.
cards.a: The shared intermediate, made by one reaction and consumed by the other, turns the two into one overall reaction, so their ΔG° values add. Without it the reactions are independent: the favored one would run on its own and its free-energy decrease could not be used to form the unfavored product.
cards.h: → intermediate made by one, used by the other → equations combine into one → ΔG° values legitimately add
cards.n: Two reactions in one flask with no common species do not add; 'the energy is transferred' without naming the intermediate earns nothing.
o: The intermediate cancels when the equations are added, as in Hess's law, and that is what makes the overall equation and its summed ΔG° valid.
In cells, ATP transfers a phosphate group to the substrate (the intermediate), which is how its hydrolysis becomes part of the synthesis.

w.a: They must share an intermediate so that the reactions happen in the same container.
w.why: being in the same place does not link them

w.a: They must share an intermediate because it acts as a catalyst.
w.why: a catalyst is regenerated and changes no ΔG°

w.a: They must share an intermediate so that both run at the same temperature.
w.why: temperature is irrelevant to the linking

cards.q: Explain why an electrolytic cell can produce a substance whose formation from the cell's reactants has ΔG° > 0.
cards.a: An external power supply does electrical work on the cell, pushing electrons into the cathode and pulling them from the anode. That work supplies the free energy the reaction lacks, so the unfavored redox reaction proceeds, provided the applied voltage exceeds the magnitude of the negative E°cell.
cards.h: → ΔG° > 0 → will not run alone → external source does electrical work ≥ ΔG° → reaction is forced
cards.n: Say where the energy comes from (the external source) and that ΔG° of the reaction itself stays positive; ΔG° = −nFE° links the two (9.9).
o: Electrical energy is an external energy source, like light in photosynthesis, which CED 9.7.A.1 names as a way to make an unfavored process occur.
The applied voltage must be larger than |E°cell| so that the electrical work supplied is at least the ΔG° the reaction requires.

w.a: The electrolytic cell makes ΔG° negative by heating the solution.
w.why: electrical work, not heating, drives it, and the reaction's ΔG° is unchanged

w.a: Electrolysis works because the reaction is under kinetic control.
w.why: kinetic control describes favored reactions

w.a: The electrodes act as catalysts that make the reaction favored.
w.why: catalysts cannot change ΔG°

cards.q: Explain why ΔG° values add but equilibrium constants multiply when two reactions are coupled.
cards.a: Adding equations adds their ΔG° values because free energy is a state function. Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, adding ΔG° values adds ln K values, and ln K₁ + ln K₂ = ln(K₁K₂), so the overall K is the product K₁ × K₂.
cards.h: → equations add → ΔG° add (state function) → ΔG° = −RT ln K → logs add → K values multiply
cards.n: Writing K₁ + K₂ earns nothing. The 'add equations, multiply K' rule is borrowed from Unit 7.
o: K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), and e^(a+b) = e^a × e^b, so summing the exponents multiplies the constants.
For the glutamine example, (3.2 × 10⁻³)(2.2 × 10⁵) ≈ 7 × 10², which matches ΔG°' = −16.3 kJ/mol.

w.a: Both ΔG° and K add when reactions are added.
w.why: K is exponential in ΔG°, so it multiplies

w.a: K values add because K measures the amount of product.
w.why: K is a ratio, and the math of ln K gives a product

w.a: ΔG° values multiply because K values multiply.
w.why: reversed; ΔG° values add

cards.q: Contrast a galvanic (voltaic) cell with an electrolytic cell.
cards.a: A galvanic (voltaic) cell runs a thermodynamically favored redox reaction (ΔG° < 0, E°cell > 0) and converts chemical energy into electrical energy that can do work. An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to drive a thermodynamically unfavored reaction (ΔG° > 0, E°cell < 0), converting electrical energy into chemical energy. In both, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
cards.h: → favored vs unfavored, energy conversion, what is shared
cards.n: Contrasting them by which electrode is 'positive' or 'negative' earns nothing: the CED excludes labeling electrode signs.

cards.q: Identify which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode in any electrochemical cell.
cards.a: The anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs (a species loses electrons, which enter the external circuit); the cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs (a species gains electrons arriving from the circuit). This holds for galvanic and electrolytic cells alike.
cards.h: → two electrodes, one half-reaction type each
cards.n: 'AN OX, RED CAT' is safe; naming the anode by electrode sign is unreliable (signs flip between cell types) and excluded from the exam.

cards.q: State the direction of electron flow and of current in the external circuit of a galvanic cell.
cards.a: Electrons flow through the external wire from the anode to the cathode, because they are released by oxidation at the anode and consumed by reduction at the cathode. Conventional current is defined in the opposite direction, from cathode to anode through the wire.
cards.h: → electron direction + reason + current direction
cards.n: Electrons travel only through the wire and electrodes; drawing them through the salt bridge or the solution earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the direction that cations and anions migrate through a salt bridge.
cards.a: Cations in the salt bridge migrate toward the cathode compartment, replacing the positive charge removed as cations are reduced there; anions migrate toward the anode compartment, balancing the positive ions produced by oxidation. Each solution stays electrically neutral.
cards.h: → two ion directions, each with its reason
cards.n: Reversing the directions is the common loss; think 'the anode compartment gains cations, so anions move toward it'.
x: cations to cathode, anions to anode

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, a standard galvanic cell built from Zn(s) in 1.0 M Zn(NO₃)₂ and Cu(s) in 1.0 M Cu(NO₃)₂ joined by a KNO₃ salt bridge, labeling the anode, the cathode, the half-reactions and the directions of electron and ion flow.
cards.a: Left beaker: Zn strip in Zn(NO₃)₂(aq), labeled anode, Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Right beaker: Cu strip in Cu(NO₃)₂(aq), labeled cathode, Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). A wire through a voltmeter (reading 1.10 V) joins the strips, with an arrow for e⁻ from Zn to Cu along the wire. An inverted-U KNO₃ salt bridge dips into both: arrows for K⁺ toward the Cu beaker and NO₃⁻ toward the Zn beaker.
cards.h: → two beakers, wire + meter, bridge, four labels, arrows
cards.n: Electrons drawn through the salt bridge, or cations moving toward the anode, cost the point; '+' and '−' electrode labels are not required or assessed.

cards.q: Predict what happens to the mass of each electrode and to [Zn²⁺] and [Cu²⁺] as a Zn/Cu galvanic cell operates, and describe the change at the particulate level.
cards.a: The Zn electrode loses mass and [Zn²⁺] increases: Zn atoms at the surface each give up 2 electrons and enter the solution as Zn²⁺ ions. The Cu electrode gains mass and [Cu²⁺] decreases (the blue color fades): Cu²⁺ ions at the electrode surface each accept 2 electrons from the metal and are deposited as Cu atoms.
cards.h: → each electrode: mass, ion concentration, atom-level step
cards.n: 'The zinc electrode grows because zinc ions form' reverses the process; the anode metal is consumed as its atoms become ions.

cards.q: Identify the role of each component of a galvanic cell: anode · cathode · solution in the anode compartment · solution in the cathode compartment · salt bridge · external wire · voltmeter · inert Pt electrode (used for a couple such as Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ in which neither form is a metal)
cards.a:
anode → electrode where oxidation occurs; supplies electrons to the external circuit (often the metal being oxidized)
cathode → electrode where reduction occurs; surface where electrons from the circuit are delivered to the species being reduced
anode solution → receives the ions produced by oxidation (e.g. Zn²⁺) and conducts by ion motion
cathode solution → supplies the species being reduced (e.g. Cu²⁺)
salt bridge → lets ions migrate between compartments to keep each electrically neutral and complete the circuit, while keeping the solutions from mixing
external wire → carries electrons from anode to cathode
voltmeter → measures the cell potential (the driving force) while drawing negligible current
inert Pt electrode → conducts electrons to or from dissolved species without reacting itself
cards.h: → one job per component
cards.n: 'The salt bridge carries electrons' is the most common wrong role; charge crosses the bridge only as moving ions.

cards.q: State the cell notation convention for a galvanic cell.
cards.a: Anode | anode solution || cathode solution | cathode: oxidation on the left, reduction on the right; a single line marks a phase boundary and the double line the salt bridge. Example: Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq, 1 M) || Cu²⁺(aq, 1 M) | Cu(s). An inert electrode (Pt) is written at the outer end when no metal takes part in a half-reaction.
cards.h: → left-to-right order + what each line means
cards.n: Line notation is not named in the CED; AP stems usually describe a diagram instead, but reading anode-left, cathode-right is a safe skill.

cards.q: Decide whether a cell with $E_{cell} < 0$ under the given conditions is operating as a galvanic or an electrolytic cell.
cards.a: Electrolytic. A negative cell potential means the cell reaction is thermodynamically unfavored (ΔG = −nFE > 0), so it cannot run on its own; an external power source must be forcing it to proceed, which is what defines an electrolytic cell.
cards.h: → one cell type + the sign-to-ΔG reason
cards.n: 'Galvanic, because it has a voltage' ignores the sign; E < 0 means ΔG > 0 through ΔG = −nFE.

cards.q: Identify the product formed at each electrode, the two half-reactions and the direction of electron flow in the external circuit when molten NaCl is electrolyzed between inert electrodes connected to a battery.
cards.a: Cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(l); liquid sodium metal forms. Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻; chlorine gas bubbles off. The battery pulls electrons from the anode and pushes them into the cathode, so in the external circuit electrons still flow from anode to cathode. The overall reaction, 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl₂(g), is thermodynamically unfavored and occurs only because of the battery.
cards.h: → each electrode: product + half-reaction; then e⁻ path
cards.n: Putting Cl₂ at the cathode because 'chlorine is reduced' reverses it: chloride is oxidized, so chlorine gas forms at the anode.

cards.q: Identify the gas formed at each electrode when water containing a little Na₂SO₄ is electrolyzed between inert electrodes, and give the ratio of the gas volumes.
cards.a: H₂ forms at the cathode (4H₂O + 4e⁻ → 2H₂ + 4OH⁻, a reduction) and O₂ at the anode (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, an oxidation). For the same 4 mol of electrons, 2 mol of H₂ and 1 mol of O₂ form, so the volume ratio H₂ : O₂ is 2 : 1 at the same T and P. The Na₂SO₄ only makes the water conductive.
cards.h: → gas at each electrode + electron-based ratio
cards.n: Swapping the gases (O₂ at the cathode) is the trap: O₂ comes from oxidizing water, which happens at the anode. Volume ratios use Avogadro's law (Unit 3).
x: H2 at cathode, O2 at anode, 2:1

cards.q: Determine the anode, the cathode and the direction of electron flow in a galvanic cell made of metal X in 1.0 M X(NO₃)₂ and metal Y in 1.0 M Y(NO₃)₂ joined by a KNO₃ salt bridge, given that after one hour the X electrode has lost 0.52 g and the Y electrode has gained 0.61 g.
cards.a: X is the anode and Y is the cathode; electrons flow through the wire from X to Y. X lost mass, so X atoms were oxidized to X²⁺ and went into solution; Y gained mass, so Y²⁺ ions were reduced and deposited as Y atoms. In the salt bridge, NO₃⁻ moves toward the X compartment and K⁺ toward the Y compartment.
cards.h: → mass lost = oxidized = anode; then electron and ion flow
cards.n: The two mass changes need not be equal (the metals' molar masses differ); using their sizes to argue about E° earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify which half-reaction, iron oxidation or oxygen reduction, occurs at the anodic region of a corroding iron surface.
cards.a: Iron oxidation, Fe(s) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻, occurs at the anodic region. The electrons travel through the metal to a cathodic region, where dissolved O₂ is reduced (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻, or O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O in acid).
cards.h: → one half-reaction named, the other placed
cards.n: Corrosion is not named in the CED; the card applies 9.8.A.3 (oxidation at the anode) to a metal surface acting as a galvanic cell.

cards.q: Explain why iron corrodes (rusts) readily in the presence of both water and dissolved oxygen.
cards.a: Iron touching both water and O₂ forms tiny galvanic cells on its surface: Fe is oxidized to Fe²⁺ at anodic regions, electrons flow through the metal to cathodic regions where O₂ is reduced, and the water film is the electrolyte that carries ions between them. The overall reaction is thermodynamically favored; Fe²⁺ is then oxidized further to hydrated iron(III) oxide, rust.
cards.h: → anode, cathode, electrolyte: what each supplies
cards.n: Without water there is no electrolyte to carry ions, and without O₂ no good oxidizing agent. Corrosion lies outside the CED's named examples; redox is Unit 4.

cards.q: Explain the function of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell.
cards.a: Oxidation adds cations to the anode compartment and reduction removes cations from the cathode compartment. Ions from the salt bridge migrate to balance these changes (anions to the anode side, cations to the cathode side), keeping both solutions neutral and completing the circuit so electrons keep flowing.
cards.h: → oxidation adds + charge, reduction removes it → ions migrate from bridge → neutrality kept → circuit complete
cards.n: 'The cell stops without it' states the consequence; the point needs the reason, charge balance by migrating ions.
o: Without the salt bridge, charge would build up in each compartment within moments, opposing further electron flow, and the current would stop.
The bridge provides a path for ionic current that completes the circuit while keeping the two solutions from mixing.

w.a: The salt bridge lets electrons travel from one beaker to the other.
w.why: electrons move only through the wire; ions move in the bridge

w.a: The salt bridge supplies the ions that are reduced at the cathode.
w.why: the cathode's reactant comes from its own solution

w.a: The salt bridge keeps the two solutions at the same concentration.
w.why: its job is charge balance, not equal concentrations

cards.q: Explain why anions in the salt bridge migrate toward the anode compartment of a galvanic cell.
cards.a: At the anode, oxidation releases cations into the solution (e.g. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) while the electrons leave through the wire, so the anode solution gains positive charge. Anions from the salt bridge move into that compartment to balance the added positive charge and keep it neutral, which lets oxidation continue.
cards.h: → oxidation releases cations → excess + charge in anode solution → anions drawn in → neutral → current continues
cards.n: 'Anions go to the positive side' leans on electrode signs, which the CED excludes; argue from the ions made or used in each compartment.
o: For every electron that leaves the anode compartment through the wire, negative charge must arrive through the bridge, and anions carry it.
Equivalently, cations leave the bridge toward the cathode, where reduction removes cations from solution.

w.a: Anions move to the anode because the anode is positive.
w.why: electrode signs are excluded and are not the reason

w.a: Anions move toward the anode to carry electrons back to it.
w.why: no electrons pass through the solution; ions carry their own charge

w.a: Anions move toward the anode because oxidation uses up anions there.
w.why: oxidizing a metal produces cations; the anions balance them

cards.q: Explain why the blue color of the Cu²⁺ solution fades as a Zn/Cu galvanic cell operates.
cards.a: The blue color comes from Cu²⁺(aq). At the cathode each Cu²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons from the electrode and is deposited as a Cu atom, so the number of Cu²⁺ ions in solution, and [Cu²⁺], decreases; fewer light-absorbing ions give a paler blue.
cards.h: → Cu²⁺ causes the color → reduced at the cathode to Cu(s) → [Cu²⁺] falls → color fades
cards.n: Linking the macroscopic change to a particulate reduction step is what 9.8.A.1 asks for; the absorbance link is Beer's law from Unit 3.
o: The fading color and the cathode's gain in mass are two views of one particulate change: Cu²⁺ ions becoming Cu atoms.
Less Cu²⁺ in the light path means lower absorbance (Beer's law), so the blue is paler.

w.a: The color fades because the zinc ions bleach the copper solution.
w.why: Zn²⁺ is in the other compartment and does not react with Cu²⁺

w.a: The color fades because electrons flow into the solution and neutralize the color.
